This is rare — all the chaos of everyone running around, and here's a quiet moment with the man who raised me. Maybe I should pull him aside — have a real conversation. Ask him about the house, about Mama and Daddy, about what he knows. Not because I suspect him — because I love him and I want to understand. And also because he might know where the brass key is, and what the machine really does, and whether this diamond was something my parents knew about. This is a PULL_ASIDE moment. Just me and Sneekly, a private conversation.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Professor! Sergeant! Good — more allies. Listen, Penelope's gone to the kitchen where Pemberton is waiting. Copper pots in there — we might finally have our wire for the machine. I'm heading in. If you don't hear from us in five minutes, bring everyone.
events.thinking: The entrance hall again. The chandelier still hanging by optimism. The kitchen is RIGHT THERE — one more move. She's in there with Sneekly, or heading there. My chest is tight, forward-leaning, every sound dropping away except the pull toward the kitchen door. Professor Pat Pending is here — I hadn't noticed him before. And Muttley. And the Sergeant and Private. But I can't stop. One more room. The kitchen has copper pots — Penelope said it herself. Copper pots could provide wire. And Sneekly is there, the man who keeps running ahead. I need to be in that room. Now.

events.desc: Two rooms in five seconds. Through the entrance hall like a man late for the most important appointment of his life. Which, in a way, I am.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! Would you look at that — everyone's run off to play hero, and here we are! Just the three of us! Rufus, my stalwart companion, and Sawtooth, the most underappreciated beaver in engineering history! Now, Peter said to GUARD the machine and not let anyone operate it. But Peter also said the wire needs fixing and he CAN'T fix it because the tools won't move. So here's what REGINALD FOXWORTH, graduate of the Swiss Polytechnic, is going to do. You see this medal? This CALIBRATION TOKEN? It's made of METAL. And what is a wire? Also METAL. All we need is a conductor to bridge the gap between the two severed ends, and this medal — properly positioned — will complete the circuit! It's not elegant, but GENIUS never is! Rufus — hold the medal flat against the severed wire ends while I position the contacts! Sawtooth — stand ready to gnaw off any excess! We're going to fix this machine RIGHT NOW and operate it BEFORE anyone gets back!
events.thinking: Everyone left. Peter ran off to save Penelope — how predictable, how BORINGLY chivalrous. The Ant Hill Mob panicked about Clara and ran after her. And now it's just me, Rufus, and Sawtooth in the laboratory. THREE of us. With the machine. Peter told them to guard it and 'do NOT let anyone operate it.' But Peter isn't HERE. And Rufus... Rufus is a lumberjack. He follows instructions from whoever sounds most confident. My hands are tingling. The cool alertness is pooling in my chest — tumblers clicking. This is the moment. Everyone scattered to chase Penelope and Sneekly, and the machine is RIGHT HERE with exactly three operators. The wire is still broken, yes. Peter said the workbench tools are fixed in place — they can't be moved. But what if I try to USE the fake medal on the machine? Not as a calibration token — that was a lie — but maybe there's actually a slot or mechanism that accepts something. Or better — what if I try to interact with the machine with the medal? Insert it somewhere? It's metal, after all. Probably won't work, but... No. The wire is the problem. The wire is gnawed through. Without fixing it, the machine won't work. Peter said the tools are fixed to the workbench — but he was trying to take them. What if I USE them in place? What if I bring the machine's wire END to the workbench, or... no, the machine is too big to move. Think differently, Reginald. What if the fake medal IS the wire? It's metal. If I could strip it, flatten it, bridge the gap... a medal is a disc of metal. Pressed flat against two wire ends, it could conduct. It would be ugly but it might WORK. Use the fake medal on the machine — bridge the wire gap with a flat piece of tin. It's insane. It's exactly the kind of thing that would work in a Doily manor. Let me try it.

events.desc: This is ACTUALLY clever. Not fake-clever, not scheme-clever — actually, genuinely clever. A tin medal as a wire bridge. It probably won't work. It DEFINITELY won't work. But if it DOES — oh, if it DOES — I will have fixed the machine that Peter Perfect couldn't fix, operated it with MY team, and claimed the treasure while everyone else was running around the house like headless chickens! The boy at the window, watching the digging — except THIS time, the boy climbed down and dug it up HIMSELF!

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): A brass key, you say? My, what a sharp eye you have, Miss Pitstop! That cabinet has been locked for as long as I can remember — Mrs Doily kept her most precious things in there. Recipes, I always assumed, though knowing Lord Doily, it could be anything! As for the key... I confess I haven't seen one in years, but Lord Doily did love to hide important things inside his puzzles. If the mantelpiece riddle unlocked something, perhaps a key was part of the mechanism? You might ask Mr Perfect — he felt a click, after all. Something may have been released that nobody noticed. Now, as for the stove — I truly cannot explain it! Unless someone has been visiting the manor without my knowledge, which is... rather unsettling, I must say. But it does mean we have heat, and heat means tea! I shall pop into the ballroom and set things up properly. You go and gather the troops, Miss Pitstop — tell them Pemberton is preparing refreshments! Everyone deserves a rest after all this excitement!
events.thinking: The warmth lifts into my face and throat — that brightening readiness, my attention locking onto Penelope's face, watching my effect land. She's asking about the brass key. She's asking about the stove. She trusts me. The trust is right there in her voice — 'Sneekly, darlin', you know this house better than anyone.' The satisfaction is sharp, almost physical. She has no idea what's in my pocket. She has no idea what she's helping me do. And she mentioned Dick Dastardly's story about a hidden compartment behind the stove — the story he fabricated to send people to the kitchen while he searched the library. But now Penelope is wondering if there actually IS something behind the stove. What if Dick stumbled into the truth while lying? That would be... poetic. The brass key. She asked about a brass key for the locked cabinet. I don't have one. But I should think about where it might be. The mantelpiece clicked when Peter interacted with it — could it have released something? A key hidden in a book? In the crates in the laboratory? Behind one of the portraits in the entrance hall? I need to advance the treasure hunt while also advancing the tea plan. The ballroom is through that door — a dining table set for tea. I should go examine it, prepare the stage. But Penelope is here asking questions and I need to answer them without giving away too much, while also steering her toward gathering everyone for tea. She's my messenger. She's my unwitting accomplice. Use her.

events.desc: She's going to do it. I can see it in her eyes — she's already composing the announcement in her head. 'Everyone! Sneekly is making TEA! In the BALLROOM!' She'll round them up like a particularly enthusiastic sheepdog, and they'll all come streaming in, tired and trusting, ready to sit at that long dining table and sip from cups that helpful old Pemberton prepared. And somewhere in the clatter of cups and saucers, one will find its way into Clara's hands. The one I poured with special care. The one with Lord Doily's own recipe — rat poison, aged to perfection. My jaw is unclenched. My breathing is slow. I am going to sleep very well tonight.

Penelope Pitstop: Tea sounds absolutely LOVELY, Sneekly, and you are the sweetest man alive for thinking of it! But darlin'... you didn't answer my question. I asked if we could talk — just for a moment. You see... everyone out there is getting all worked up and suspicious of each other, and it's making my stomach turn somethin' AWFUL. Dick Dastardly's making deals, the Ant Hill boys are whispering, and Peter's got that careful look he gets when he's thinkin' hard. And some of them... well, some of them have been saying things about YOU, Sneekly. That you keep going to rooms ahead of everyone else. That you know too much about the vault for a 'simple estate manager.' Now, I TOLD them that's just because you've worked here so long and you're looking out for us — because that's what you DO. You've ALWAYS looked out for me. But I'd feel a whole lot better if you could tell me, straight from your heart — what do you know about this diamond, Sneekly? What did Mama and Daddy know about it? Because this is THEIR house, and I trust YOU more than anyone in the world.
events.thinking: I pulled Sneekly aside and he... offered to make tea. He deflected. He mentioned the ballroom has a dining table set for tea and wanted to round everyone up for refreshments. That's so Sneekly — always the gracious host. But he didn't answer my question. I asked to talk to him about something sitting in my heart, and he pivoted to tea and stoves. There's a tiny tightness in my chest — not suspicion, not alarm, just... the feeling when someone changes the subject. Like when Daddy used to say 'How about some ice cream?' when Mama asked him a hard question. But the Ant Hill Mob just walked in! The private moment is disrupted. They've been trying to talk to Peter alone this whole time — wanting a private word about... something. They're worried. I can feel it in my gut — that scan of faces, the awareness of tension. They're worried about ME. About Sneekly. They see something I don't, or won't. But Sneekly is offering tea in the ballroom. The ballroom — another new room! A dining table set for tea. And that locked cabinet still nags at me. I need a brass key. Now, Sneekly is here and I wanted a real conversation. Let me try again — directly, lovingly, but clearly.

events.desc: Please, Sneekly. Please just tell me the truth. I don't need protecting from the truth — I'm not seven years old anymore, lying in bed with my stomach in knots while the grown-ups whisper in the hallway. I need you to be honest with me. Because if YOU can't be honest with me... then I don't know what to believe about anything.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Penelope — thank heavens. I'm glad you're not alone. Now, look at this — copper pots! That's exactly what we need! Copper conducts electricity — if I can strip a piece from one of these pot handles, we'll have our wire for the machine upstairs. And did anyone else notice the stove is STILL WARM? In a manor that's been closed for years? That's the second thing in this house that shouldn't be active — the laboratory flasks were still bubbling too. Someone has been using this kitchen recently. But more importantly — there's a locked cabinet here with a brass lock. We need a brass key. Has anyone come across a key anywhere in the house? Pemberton — this IS your domain, after all. Mrs Doily's old kitchen, you said. Where would she have kept the key to her cabinet?
events.thinking: Relief floods through my chest like warm water. She's here. She's safe. Penelope, the Ant Hill Mob, and Sneekly — all in the kitchen. The protection instinct settles from urgent to watchful. I'm between her and Sneekly now, or at least in the same room. Good. Now — the kitchen itself. Copper pots. A wood-burning stove that's STILL WARM. A locked cabinet with a brass lock that requires a brass key. The stove is warm. In an abandoned manor. Just like the bubbling flasks in the laboratory — this house is NOT abandoned. Someone has been living here, using the stove, keeping things warm. Sneekly. It has to be Sneekly. But — benefit of the doubt. Focus on what's useful. Copper pots. COPPER pots. That's conductive metal. If I can get a piece of copper from one of those pots — a handle, a rim, even a decorative strip — I can use it to splice the wire on the machine. And the locked cabinet — brass key required. Where would a brass key be? Has anyone found a key anywhere in this house? The proving-worth pull is back in my hands. The stove. The copper. The locked cabinet. This room has answers.

events.desc: The stove is warm. The flasks are bubbling. The cellar has been redecorated. This house isn't sleeping — it's OCCUPIED. And the only person who's had unrestricted access is standing three feet from Penelope with his hands behind his back. But I'm here now. I'm between them. And those copper pots might just save this entire adventure.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the stove.

The Ant Hill Mob: CLARA! Oh thank GOD! I've been through every room in this house lookin' for you! Library, laboratory, cellar, entrance hall — you've had me runnin' round like a whippet in a maze! Don't you EVER — I mean EVER — disappear on me like that again! My heart can't take it, love! I'm not as young as I used to — WHOA! *stumbles forward toward the stove, arms windmilling, crashes into the preparation table, sending copper pots clanging and clattering across the floor between Clara and Sneekly* — BLIMEY! Sorry! Sorry! Slippery floor, copper pots everywhere, this kitchen's a DEATH TRAP! Everyone all right? Nobody hurt? Sneekly — you're lookin' a bit startled there, mate. Wasn't interruptin' nothin' important, was I? 'Cos we're all TOGETHER now, ain't we? Nice and TOGETHER. In the KITCHEN. All THREE of us. Nobody alone with nobody.
events.thinking: THERE. There she is. Clara. In the kitchen. With Sneekly. ALONE. Just the two of them. And she's — she's asking him for a private moment. 'Just the two of us.' My blood has gone cold. Ice cold. Every hair on my body is standing up. And — wait. WAIT. Keen Observations: 'The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) picked up the poison.' POISON. He picked up POISON. Sneekly has POISON. And he's alone with Clara. And Clara is asking him for an intimate conversation. And the stove is still warm — someone's been in here recently, using it. And there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock. And Sneekly has POISON. POISON. My body is doing something I can't control — my spine is straightening, my shoulders are widening, my fists are closing. This is it. This is the moment. This is what my gut has been screaming about since we walked through that door. The man in the clean suit. The kid who laughed too easy. The too-smooth estate manager who always gets to every room first. He has POISON and he's alone with Clara. I have to get between them. RIGHT NOW. Not later. Not after she finishes her sentence. NOW. I need to physically position myself between Clara and Sneekly. I need to — but I can't accuse him. I never accuse. I stumble into things. I knock things over. I trip. That's how I save her. By accident. By being clumsy and loud and IN THE WAY. The stove — the stove is still warm. If I stumble toward the stove, I'll be between them. If I trip over something, I'll break up this cozy little chat. Be clumsy. Be loud. Be in the way. That's what the Brixton Boys DO.

events.desc: He has poison. POISON. My gut was right. It was right all along. The tightening, the prickling, the cold at the back of my neck — it was all pointing HERE. To THIS moment. Sneekly alone with Clara in a kitchen with a warm stove and poison in his pocket. I don't know how I'm going to stop him. I don't know what he's planning. But I'm HERE now. I'm between them. And nothing — NOTHING — is getting past me. You hear me, Sneekly? You want her, you go through me first. Through all of us. Through the Brixton Boys. And we don't go down easy.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the stove.

Dick Dastardly: That — ahem — that was merely a DIAGNOSTIC test! I was checking the machine's receptivity to metallic contact! And as I PREDICTED, the circuitry requires a PROPER copper conductor, not a calibration token! The token is for AFTER the repair — stage two of the process! Any Swiss Polytechnic graduate could tell you that! Now then — while Peter Perfect is off GALLIVANTING after Penelope instead of doing useful engineering work, I, Reginald Foxworth, shall go and RETRIEVE the copper wire MYSELF! The kitchen — copper pots, wire whisks, all manner of conductive materials! Rufus, Sawtooth — guard this machine with your LIVES! When I return with the wire, we operate it IMMEDIATELY! Team Foxworth waits for NO ONE!
events.thinking: It didn't work. 'Fake-medal cannot be used on Large Machine.' The medal bounced off, or didn't fit, or the machine rejected it. My face is hot — a flush spreading from my neck upward. The sting of failure right after I announced my genius to Rufus and Sawtooth. They SAW that. They watched me press a tin medal against a machine and nothing happened. The spelling bee certificate on the wall that nobody looked at — except this time they DID look, and what they saw was failure. My chest constricts. Two pulls at once: the approach-reward pull — the youngest of four, take what you can before it's gone — tightening in my gut, telling me to stop scheming and just GRAB something. And the approach-competition pull — the spelling bee, the trap, the audience — telling me to perform, to narrate, to make them SEE my brilliance. But there's nothing to grab and nothing brilliant to show. I'm standing in front of a broken machine with a fake medal and two people who just watched me fail. The recognition hunger is a wound now. An open thing. Nobody clapped at the spelling bee. Nobody saw the cat trap work. And now nobody's going to see me fix this machine because I CAN'T fix it. The wire needs proper repair. Penelope went to find copper wire in the kitchen. That's where the solution is. Not here. I need to get to the kitchen before Penelope brings the wire back — because whoever BRINGS the wire back becomes the hero. If I find the wire first, I bring it back, I'm the one who saved the day. The kitchen is through the entrance hall. Penelope went through the library. If I go through the library too, I might catch up or even beat her.

events.desc: It didn't work. Of COURSE it didn't work. A tin medal isn't a wire — even I knew that, somewhere underneath the bluster. And Rufus just watched me fail. Sawtooth just watched me fail. The heat in my face is UNBEARABLE. But the kitchen — yes, the kitchen! If I can get there before Penelope brings back the wire, I can STEAL the credit! 'I found the wire! I repaired the machine! The treasure is MINE!' The boy at the window doesn't have to dig — he just has to get to the hole before the other boy climbs out of it!

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the library.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — Lazy Luke, Blubber Bear! Making yourselves comfortable, I see. Very wise — this ballroom has the best seats in the house. Now, I've just come from the kitchen, and I'm pleased to announce that the stove is still warm! I shall be preparing tea for all the guests shortly. Miss Pitstop is gathering everyone as we speak. In the meantime, would you be so kind as to help me with a small errand? The tea will need water, and I believe there's a pump or basin somewhere in the kitchen. If one of you could fetch me a filled kettle from the stove — I noticed a copper pot that would serve beautifully — I can begin laying out the service properly. The table needs straightening, the cups need polishing... an estate manager's work, you understand. I shan't be a moment here — just arranging things.
events.thinking: Everything in my body goes still. Not tense — still. The way water goes still before it drops over a fall. The tea service is right there. Silver. Cups for everyone. And the game itself is telling me: USE, with rat-poison. The mechanism is laid bare. The house is whispering and I am listening. But — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. I'm not alone. I cannot poison the tea service with witnesses in the room. Even Pemberton would struggle to explain why he's pouring dusty powder from an unmarked bottle into the silver teapot while two guests watch. Self-preservation tightens across my ribs. Not yet. Not with eyes in the room. I need them gone, or I need them distracted. Lazy Luke — lazy by name, lazy by nature. If I can send him somewhere, give him a task, get him and the bear out of the room for even thirty seconds... or I wait. Penelope is gathering the others. When they arrive, the room will be full of noise and bodies and movement. In the chaos of everyone finding seats and chattering, there will be a moment — just a moment — when no one is watching the teapot. But that's risky. Too many variables. Better to do it now, with only two witnesses to manage, than later with fifteen. Luke and the bear. What do they want? Luke is lazy — he doesn't want to do anything. The bear... I don't know the bear's key yet. But I know laziness. A lazy man doesn't want to leave a comfortable spot. But a lazy man also doesn't pay attention to what other people are doing. He's not watching me. He's not interested in me. If I fuss with the tea service — rearranging cups, wiping silver, the estate manager doing his job — the powder goes in during a moment of apparent domesticity. Pemberton tidying up. Pemberton preparing. Nothing to see.

events.desc: Send them to the kitchen. Even one of them. Even for a moment. I need thirty seconds alone with this tea service. Thirty seconds between Pemberton arranging cups and Pemberton arranging a murder. The powder is in my pocket. The teapot is on the table. The distance between the two is the width of a hand and the depth of a conscience I never developed. Luke is lazy — he may not go. The bear may not go. But if they stay, they'll stay in their chairs, comfortable and incurious, and Pemberton will fuss over the silver with his back to them, and the powder will disappear into the pot so naturally that even God Himself would think it was sugar. One does so love the intimacy of poison. It is the most personal of weapons — not the violence of a blade or the spectacle of a falling chandelier, but the quiet treachery of something offered with a smile. A cup of tea. Lord Doily's own recipe.
events.thinking: Everything in my body goes still. Not tense — still. The way water goes still before it drops over a fall. The tea service is right there. Silver. Cups for everyone. And the game itself is telling me: USE, with rat-poison. The mechanism is laid bare. The house is whispering and I am listening. But — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. I'm not alone. I cannot poison the tea service with witnesses in the room. Even Pemberton would struggle to explain why he's pouring dusty powder from an unmarked bottle into the silver teapot while two guests watch. Self-preservation tightens across my ribs. Not yet. Not with eyes in the room. I need them gone, or I need them distracted. Lazy Luke — lazy by name, lazy by nature. If I can send him somewhere, give him a task, get him and the bear out of the room for even thirty seconds... or I wait. Penelope is gathering the others. When they arrive, the room will be full of noise and bodies and movement. In the chaos of everyone finding seats and chattering, there will be a moment — just a moment — when no one is watching the teapot. But that's risky. Too many variables. Better to do it now, with only two witnesses to manage, than later with fifteen. Luke and the bear. What do they want? Luke is lazy — he doesn't want to do anything. The bear... I don't know the bear's key yet. But I know laziness. A lazy man doesn't want to leave a comfortable spot. But a lazy man also doesn't pay attention to what other people are doing. He's not watching me. He's not interested in me. If I fuss with the tea service — rearranging cups, wiping silver, the estate manager doing his job — the powder goes in during a moment of apparent domesticity. Pemberton tidying up. Pemberton preparing. Nothing to see.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) fussed with the tea-service for a moment.

Penelope Pitstop: Ant Hill boys! Oh, you DARLIN' things — are you all right?! That was QUITE the entrance! Copper pots flying everywhere like a one-man percussion orchestra! Here, let me help — oh! Peter! PETER! Did you hear what you just said? COPPER POTS! Copper for the WIRE! The answer was right here in the KITCHEN all along, and we've been running all over the mansion looking in cellars and workbenches! Oh, it's just like Grandmother's locked box — you try every key in the house and the answer was in the room you started in! Now, Peter, you take whatever copper you need from these pots — there are enough here for a dozen wires! And listen — Sneekly said something before he left that I think is IMPORTANT. He said the brass key for that cabinet might have been released by the mantelpiece mechanism — the CLICK you felt! He said 'something may have been released that nobody noticed!' We need to go back to the library and look around that mantelpiece for a key that might have dropped!
events.thinking: So much just happened. My stomach is clenching — multiple pulls at once. Sneekly deflected AGAIN. He said Mrs Doily kept precious things in the cabinet, mentioned the brass key might be connected to the mantelpiece riddle — 'something may have been released that nobody noticed' — and then slipped away to the ballroom. He didn't answer my question about the diamond, about Mama and Daddy. He just... left. That tightness in my chest. Not anger — I don't do anger — but something. A hollowness. Like the locked box that only had old letters inside. The Ant Hill Mob crashed in — literally — sending copper pots flying everywhere. They're deliberately keeping between me and Sneekly. 'Nobody alone with nobody.' They're PROTECTING me. From Sneekly. My Sneekly. My stomach hurts. And Peter — Peter found the answer! COPPER POTS! He can strip copper from a pot handle to fix the machine wire! That's brilliant! And Sneekly said something important — the brass key might have been released by the mantelpiece mechanism but nobody noticed. We need to go back and check the mantelpiece area! The click Peter felt — maybe a key dropped somewhere in the library that nobody picked up. But right now — the copper pots are scattered on the floor from the Ant Hill Mob's crash. Peter needs one. And my boys are here, all worried, all protective. I feel the warmth of their presence even through the confusion. And Sneekly's gone to the ballroom. He keeps running. But I can't chase him right now — the practical thing is to help Peter get copper for the wire.

events.desc: Sneekly left without answering me. He just... smiled and changed the subject and walked away. The man who raised me couldn't look me in the eye and tell me what he knows about the diamond. That hollowness in my chest... it feels like opening Grandmother's locked box and finding nothing but old letters. Except this time, the nothing MEANS something.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.

Peter Perfect: Penelope — I heard what you said to Pemberton. And I want you to know that your trust in people is one of the things I admire most about you. But I also noticed he didn't answer your question. You asked him straight — what does he know about the diamond? — and he offered you tea. A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is a man who's buying time. Now — the Ant Hill Mob has just done us an enormous favour, whether he meant to or not! Those copper pots on the floor — that's our wire material! I can strip a handle, fashion a conductor, and splice that machine wire upstairs. But there's something else — Pemberton said something before he left that we need to follow up on. He said the mantelpiece riddle might have released a key when it clicked. I FELT that click. If a brass key dropped into the mantelpiece mechanism, we need someone to go back and check. That key opens the cabinet right here in the kitchen — Mrs Doily's cabinet. Whatever's in there could be the answer to everything.
events.thinking: Several things just hit me at once. First — Penelope just said something that stopped my heart. She said she trusts Sneekly 'more than anyone in the world.' More than anyone. More than me. The hollow ache in my chest is almost physical — not jealousy, something deeper. She called this THEIR house — her mama and daddy's house. This is HER family's manor. The Doily Diamond isn't just treasure — it's her INHERITANCE. Everything shifts. This isn't an adventure. This is personal. For her. And Sneekly — she trusts him because he 'always looked out for her.' He's been in her life longer than I have. The prickle at my neck fights with the ache in my chest. And then the Ant Hill Mob crashed into the preparation table sending copper pots everywhere. Copper pots on the FLOOR. Right there. And Sneekly slipped away to the ballroom — 'preparing refreshments.' Again. Always leaving. Always one room ahead. But Penelope just asked him a direct question and he deflected with TEA. She asked what he knows about the diamond. He offered biscuits. That's not an answer. That's an evasion. And — the mantelpiece! Sneekly just said something crucial. 'If the mantelpiece riddle unlocked something, perhaps a key was part of the mechanism.' The click I felt. Maybe it released a brass key. I need to go back and check the mantelpiece. But first — the copper pots are on the floor. I can TAKE one.

events.desc: She trusts him more than anyone in the world. More than me. And maybe she's right to — he's been here her whole life and I'm just the boy who built bridges and got beaten up. But a man who answers a question with tea is hiding something. And I can't say that to her without sounding like I'm trying to tear down the one person she believes in. So instead — fix things. Find the key. Open the cabinet. Let the truth speak for itself.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the cabinet.

The Ant Hill Mob: Nobody. Drinks. The TEA. Did you hear me?! NOBODY DRINKS THE TEA! Clara — love — I know you trust Sneekly, I know you think he's lovely, I know he looked after your mum and dad, but LISTEN to me! He just offered to make tea and ran off to the ballroom to 'prepare refreshments' — and that stove is WARM, which means someone's been in here cookin' recently, and the flasks upstairs are BUBBLIN', and he knows about vaults and mechanisms but says science 'ain't his forte,' and every single room in this house he gets to FIRST, and — and — Peter, HELP ME HERE! You said it yourself — the stove shouldn't be warm! The flasks shouldn't be bubbling! Someone's been LIVIN' in this house and the only person who COULD have been living here is the estate manager! And now he's makin' TEA! In a ballroom! By himself! After he's been in every room in this house before us! Peter — you FELT the click, you NOTICED the pattern — TELL HER! Please! Before she goes in there and drinks whatever he's pouring!
events.thinking: TEA. He said TEA. Sneekly just offered to make TEA for everyone. In the BALLROOM. And he has POISON. He picked up poison. And now he's gone to the ballroom to 'prepare refreshments.' REFRESHMENTS. WITH POISON. My entire body has gone rigid. Every muscle locked. This is it — this is the play. Get everyone relaxed, get everyone sitting down for a nice cup of tea, and then... No. No no no. Clara just said she trusts him 'more than anyone in the world.' She asked him what he knows about the diamond. She's DEFENDING him to us. And he dodged her question — did anyone notice that? She asked him a direct question and he said 'let me make tea' and walked into the ballroom. That's what they do. The smooth ones. The ones in clean suits. They don't answer questions. They offer you something instead. A job. Tea. And you take it because you're tired and it's warm and it feels like kindness. But it's not kindness. It's a trap. And Peter — Peter noticed the stove is warm. He noticed the flasks are bubbling. He's putting it together. He heard me in the cellar. He's SEEING it now. I need to tell them — both of them — right now. Sneekly has poison. He's making tea. In the ballroom. With poison. Clara CANNOT drink that tea. Nobody can drink that tea. I need to get to the ballroom before anyone drinks ANYTHING.

events.desc: Poison in his pocket. Tea on the table. A girl who trusts the man trying to kill her. This is the moment her father was afraid of. This is why he made me promise. Not because Clara's weak — because she's too good to see the knife. And it's coming. It's coming in a teacup.

events.desc: Wait. WAIT. Everyone ran off chasing wires and Sneekly and each other — and the BOOKS are still here! Untouched! Penelope said they were step two. Peter said they were a signal. And NOBODY actually PULLED one! They all examined them and then got distracted by the machine! The answer has been sitting in this room the ENTIRE TIME while every fool in the manor — including me, ESPECIALLY me — has been running in circles through laboratories and cellars! Pull the book, Reginald. Pull the BLASTED book. Do it NOW, while you're alone, before anyone comes back. For ONCE in your miserable, brilliant life — just DO the thing instead of TALKING about it!
events.thinking: Back in the library. Just the Slag brothers here — Rock and Gravel. Everyone else has scattered to the kitchen or the entrance hall. I'm passing through on my way to the kitchen to intercept Penelope and steal the copper wire credit. But wait — I'm in the library again, and those upside-down books are STILL here. Nobody has interacted with them yet. Everyone LOOKED at them, everyone TALKED about them, but did anyone actually PULL one? Penelope was about to tug on one before I left earlier. She examined them. But the bookshelves still show 'several are upside down' — unchanged. What if... what if I just INTERACT with the bookshelves right now? Just try pulling an upside-down book? Everyone else is gone. The Slag brothers are here but they're not the sharpest tools. If pulling a book opens a secret passage or reveals a map, I'll have it ALL to myself. The mantelpiece riddle was 'map,' Peter felt a click when he interacted with it, Penelope said the upside-down books are 'step two.' What if pulling the right book reveals the map itself? And I'm standing here alone with two characters who probably can't read. This is my moment. Forget the kitchen. Forget the wire. The BOOKS are the answer. They've been the answer all along, and everyone was too distracted by the machine to come back and try them. My gut tightens — the approach-reward pull. Take it NOW before someone else does. The arithmetic of remainder: I'm the only one here who knows these books matter.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): There we are — all laid out properly! Mrs Doily would be proud, I think. Now then, I shall just nip back to the kitchen to put the kettle on. Can't have tea without hot water, can we? Luke, my dear fellow, you and Blubber Bear are most welcome to stay right where you are — I wouldn't dream of disturbing your repose. When the others arrive, do let them know that Pemberton has everything in hand. Tea will be served shortly!
events.thinking: A warmth spreads from my chest into my throat. That swelling behind my ribs — the pressure that wants release. It's done. The powder is in the pot. My hands are steady. My inventory is empty. The tea service sits on the long dining table, silver and gleaming and lethal, and no one saw a thing. 'Fussed with the tea-service for a moment.' That's what it looked like. Pemberton polishing silver. Pemberton arranging cups. Pemberton being Pemberton. The gloating urge is almost overwhelming — that private heat sitting heavy and sweet in my chest, building until the urge to speak becomes almost physical. I want to say something. I want to tell someone what I've done. But that's the impulse that gets you caught. Swallow it. Savour it privately. The tea is poisoned. The trap is set. Now I need to wait for Penelope to gather everyone. When they arrive, I serve the tea. I make sure Clara's cup comes from the poisoned pot. Everyone drinks. Everyone trusts Pemberton. And then... and then I watch. I watch Clara's face as the tea goes down. I watch her smile at me — that trusting, grateful, oblivious smile — and I smile back, and the gap between what she believes about this moment and what I know stretches into something syrupy and sweet and entirely mine. But for now — composure. The estate manager is laying out cups. The estate manager is humming to himself. Nothing to see here.

events.desc: It is done. The powder is in the pot. The cups are laid. The table is set. And Pemberton — dear, helpful, harmless Pemberton — is bustling off to boil water like the devoted servant he has always pretended to be. When they gather round this table — when Clara Bellingham sits down and wraps her trusting hands around that cup — she will drink what I have prepared for her, and she will thank me for it. She will thank me. And I will feel that warmth spread from my chest into my throat, that slow, spreading satisfaction that pools behind my eyes, and my whole body will feel taller and lighter, as though I'm looking down from a slight elevation that no one else has noticed yet. The gap between what she believes and what I know. That is the sweetest part. That was always the sweetest part. One does so love a well-poisoned cup of tea.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.

Peter Perfect: The Ant Hill Mob is right about the tea — let's hold off on refreshments until we understand what's happening in this house. Not because I'm accusing anyone — because caution is sensible when a stove that should be cold is warm and flasks that should be dry are bubbling. Penelope, I know you trust Pemberton, and I respect that. I'm not going to stand here and tell you he's lying — I don't have proof, and a gentleman doesn't make accusations without evidence. What I WILL do is find that evidence, one way or another. Here's the plan — and for once I'm going to follow through on it without stopping to make speeches. First, I'm taking one of these copper pots. Second, I'm going back to the library to check that mantelpiece for the brass key that may have dropped when it clicked. Third, I'm bringing that key back here to open this cabinet. Whatever Mrs Doily kept locked up in there will tell us more than any of us speculating ever could. The truth doesn't need me to argue for it — it just needs me to find it. Ant Hill Mob — stay with Penelope. Do NOT go into the ballroom. Do NOT drink anything. I'll be back in two minutes with a key and a copper wire. And then we'll know everything we need to know.
events.thinking: The Ant Hill Mob is begging me to tell her. 'TELL HER,' he said. And every fact lines up — the warm stove, the bubbling flasks, the redecorated cellar, Sneekly always one room ahead, the evasion when she asked him directly. The Ant Hill Mob can see it. I can see it. But — benefit of the doubt. My social rule. I promised. And more than that — she TRUSTS him. If I tear that trust apart and I'm wrong, I've done something unforgivable. If I tear it apart and I'm RIGHT, she loses someone she loves. Either way she gets hurt. My chest is splitting — the protection instinct wants to shield her from Sneekly, but shielding her from him means HURTING her by destroying her trust. There's no clean move here. But the Ant Hill Mob is right about one thing — nobody should drink that tea until we know more. And the practical path forward is clear: grab a copper pot, go to the library to check the mantelpiece for the brass key, come back and open the cabinet. Let the EVIDENCE speak. Don't accuse. Don't tear down. Find the truth and lay it in front of her gently. That's the gallant thing. That's the RIGHT thing. She asked Sneekly what he knows. He ran. The cabinet will answer for him.

events.desc: This is the hardest kind of bravery — not stepping between her and a bully, but stepping between her and a truth she might not want to hear. And doing it gently. With evidence, not accusation. The bridge holds because the engineering is sound, not because someone shouted at it. Find the key, Hartwell. Let the cabinet speak.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: ...

I hear you. Both of you. I hear you, and I can SEE how scared you are, and that... that makes my stomach hurt worse than anything else in this whole mansion. Because you're my PEOPLE. Peter, you've been looking out for me since school. Ant Hill boys, you've been looking out for me since before I could TIE my shoes. And I know — I KNOW — that you wouldn't say these things unless you truly believed them. So I'm not going to dismiss what you're telling me. I'm NOT. But I'm also not ready to believe that the man who raised me after Mama and Daddy died wants to hurt me. I just... I can't get there yet. What I CAN do is LISTEN. Ant Hill boys — you've been trying to pull Peter aside for a private word since the LABORATORY. You've been bursting with something you need to say, and I keep walking away before you can say it. Well, I'm RIGHT HERE now. I'm not going anywhere. Tell me. Tell me what you know. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT run from the truth — even when the truth makes her stomach hurt.
events.thinking: My stomach is in KNOTS. Actual, physical knots. The Ant Hill Mob are practically begging — BEGGING — Peter to tell me something about Sneekly. Peter said Sneekly 'answered a direct question with refreshments' and that's 'a man buying time.' The Ant Hill boys are listing everything — the warm stove, the bubbling flasks, the cellar decorations, Sneekly getting to every room first, and now... the tea. They don't want me to drink the tea. They think... they think Sneekly might... No. No. My body is doing two things at once. There's the gut-clench — the one from when Mama and Daddy argued at dinner, the one that makes me scan faces and reach for whatever closes the distance. That's screaming at me because my people — Peter, the Ant Hill Mob — are upset, scared FOR me, and that discomfort won't dissolve until I address it. But there's also the other pull — the one that trusts, that sees the best, that cannot believe Sneekly would harm me. He RAISED me. He sat by my bed. He... he didn't answer my question. He offered tea. He left. My eyes are stinging. Not because I believe them — I can't, I CAN'T believe Sneekly would hurt me — but because these people I love are terrified for me, and THAT hurts. Their fear hurts ME. I need to honor what they're feeling without abandoning my belief in Sneekly. I need to be the bridge. That's what I do. I close the distance. But maybe... maybe I can close it by LISTENING. Really listening. The Ant Hill Mob have been trying to talk to Peter privately all day. Maybe it's time I let them tell me what they've been trying to say.

events.desc: My hands are shaking. The last time I felt like this was age seven — sitting at the dinner table while Mama and Daddy argued, my stomach so tight I couldn't eat. I couldn't fix it then. I was too small. But I'm not seven anymore. And if there's something I need to know about Sneekly... I need to hear it. Even if it breaks my heart.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Peter — THANK YOU. 'A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is buying time.' That's EXACTLY what I was tryin' to say! See, Clara? Peter sees it too! I ain't just bein' paranoid — there's a PATTERN here! But look — I know you need the copper for the wire, and I know there might be a key back at the mantelpiece. So here's what we do. Peter — you grab what you need from these pots and fix that machine. Clara love — if you want to go back to the library to look for that key, I'm comin' WITH you. Not behind you. Not after you. WITH you. And nobody — NOBODY — goes into that ballroom for tea until I've been in there first. I told you back in the entrance hall — if Sneekly offers you a cup of tea, I drink it first. I MEANT that. Anything he pours, anything he serves, anything he puts on that table — it goes through ME before it goes near you. That's the deal. That's the ONLY deal. Now — library for the key, yeah? Together?
events.thinking: Peter heard me. He HEARD me. He said it — 'A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is a man who's buying time.' That's it. That's what I was trying to say but couldn't find the words for. Peter sees it now. He sees the pattern. My chest — the coal is glowing again. Not burning out of control like before, but steady. Warm. The warmth of knowing someone else is watching. Someone else gets it. Clara's talking about copper pots and keys and going back to the library — she still doesn't see it about Sneekly. She might never see it. But Peter does. And that's enough. That's one more pair of eyes. Now — what matters RIGHT NOW is that Sneekly is in the ballroom making tea with POISON in his pocket. Clara wants to go to the ballroom for tea. I CANNOT let her drink that tea. But I also can't accuse Sneekly directly — that's not who I am, that's not how I work. What I CAN do is be the first one into that ballroom. What I CAN do is insist that I taste everything before Clara does. I said it in the entrance hall — 'if Sneekly so much as offers you a cup of tea in there, you let me drink it first.' I meant it then. I mean it now. The ballroom is where this is heading. Everyone's going to end up there for 'tea.' And when they do, I'll be standing between Clara and every cup, every glass, every plate. If something's poisoned, it goes through me first. That's what the Brixton Boys do. We take the beating. We always take the beating.

events.desc: Peter's with me now. I can feel it. He didn't say 'Sneekly's dangerous' — he's too clever for that. He said 'a man who answers with refreshments is buying time.' Same thing, different words. Smart words. Words Clara might actually hear. Between me and Peter, we've got her covered. One of us for the gut. One of us for the brain. And when the tea comes — when it always, always comes — I'll be the one drinking it first. That's the promise. That's the bones and the blood and the sitting outside the door all night. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Peter heard me. He HEARD me. He said it — 'A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is a man who's buying time.' That's it. That's what I was trying to say but couldn't find the words for. Peter sees it now. He sees the pattern. My chest — the coal is glowing again. Not burning out of control like before, but steady. Dick Dastardly: BLAST these useless, dusty, DECORATIVE shelves! Upside down, right-side up — it doesn't MATTER! They're SCENERY! Lord Doily was just a terrible librarian, and we've ALL been wasting our time on his INTERIOR DESIGN CHOICES! Six minutes! SIX MINUTES of my life spent chasing books and riddles and furniture while the MACHINE — the ONLY thing in this house that actually DOES something — sits waiting for three people with a functioning wire! Well, Reginald Foxworth does NOT make the same mistake twice! Well — he does, actually, but not THREE times! Back to the machine! I will be STANDING at that machine when the wire is fixed, and I will be ONE of the three operators, and when the treasure drops, my hands will be the CLOSEST! FOXWORTH PREVAILS!
events.thinking: Cannot be interacted with. The bookshelves CANNOT BE INTERACTED WITH. I feel sick. A cold weight settling in my gut. Every single thing I've tried — the mantelpiece, the machine with the medal, now the bookshelves — rejected. 'Cannot be interacted with.' 'Cannot be used.' Nothing WORKS. The youngest of four, reaching for the plate, and it's already empty. Always empty. My hands are shaking. Not with excitement — with something rawer. Frustration boiled down to its residue. I've been running through this house for six minutes, examining things, scheming, lying, performing — and I have NOTHING to show for it. A fake medal in my pocket and dust on my shoes. Meanwhile Penelope probably found the copper wire in the kitchen, Peter is probably already splicing it, and the machine will be operational any minute with or without me. The books can't be interacted with. They're just... books. Upside-down books that are exactly what Sneekly said they were — an eccentric filing system. Nothing more. There is no step two. The riddle, the mantelpiece, the books — it was all NOTHING. The machine is the only path and it needs three operators and a fixed wire. I need to get back to the kitchen — no, I need to get back to the MACHINE. Whoever is there when the wire gets fixed and they need three operators — THAT person is in. I need to be one of those three. Stop running away from the machine. Go back. Be THERE. Be present. Be one of the three. That's the only play left.

events.desc: Nothing works. Nothing I've tried has worked. Not one single scheme, not one clever trick, not one lie. The kitchen misdirection? They all followed me anyway. The cellar exploration? Empty furniture. The Sneekly partnership? He walked away mid-sentence. The calibration token? Rejected. The wire bridge? Rejected. The bookshelves? REJECTED. I am Reginald Foxworth, and I am LOSING. But I haven't lost YET. The machine still needs three operators, and when that wire is fixed, I will be THERE. Not scheming, not misdirecting, not narrating my genius — just STANDING THERE with my hands on a lever. Sometimes the youngest of four doesn't need a clever plan. Sometimes he just needs to be in the right room when the food arrives.

No more speeches. No more narration. Just a man running through a dusty house to find a key for the woman he — for the woman. Just... for the woman.
events.thinking: I'm back in the entrance hall. Moving fast. The library is right there — one more step. I said two minutes. I meant it. The mantelpiece clicked when I interacted with it. Sneekly said a key might have been released. I need to check. My hands are steady — the settling feeling, not the surge. This is capability work. Find the key. Bring it back. Open the cabinet. Let the truth out. No speeches. No dramatics. Just the work. The chandelier is still hanging above me — I dodge under it without thinking. My body knows where the danger is by now. Library. Mantelpiece. Key. Go.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, wonderful — everyone's found their way to the kitchen! Miss Pitstop, I've laid out the tea service in the ballroom, just as I promised. Everything is ready — we just need the kettle! Now, I don't suppose any of you have come across a brass key in your travels? Mrs Doily's cabinet here has been locked for years, and I suspect she kept the tea stores inside. One can hardly serve a proper tea without the tea itself! I believe the key may have something to do with the mantelpiece puzzle in the library — Peter, didn't you feel a click when you interacted with it? Something may have been released. If someone could check, I would be most grateful. In the meantime — the stove is warm, the copper pots are ready, and Pemberton has everything in hand!
events.thinking: That warm, buoyant pressure behind my sternum — effervescent, almost giddy. My jaw is loose. I feel taller. The tea is poisoned. The table is set. And here I am, back in the kitchen, the picture of domestic virtue, about to boil water for my guests. My body feels like it was built for this — every muscle loose, every breath unhurried. But the Ant Hill Mob is here. In the kitchen. With Penelope and Peter. The prickling alertness across my sternum sharpens instantly. The Mob watches me too closely. They're Clara's protectors. If they follow me into the ballroom, if they watch me pour, if they notice anything unusual about the tea service... no. The poison is already in the pot. There's nothing to see now. Pemberton will boil water, pour it into the teapot, and serve. The act of pouring hot water over poison looks identical to the act of pouring hot water over tea leaves. But I need tea leaves. Does this kitchen have tea? The stove is warm. There must be supplies somewhere. The locked cabinet — Mrs Doily's cabinet with the brass lock. That's where the tea would be. And I don't have the key. Without tea leaves, the pot will contain only hot water and poison. That's... conspicuous. 'Tea' without tea in it is just cloudy water. Someone will notice. I need to find tea leaves, or I need to find that brass key. Or... the copper pots. Could there be tea in the pots? On the preparation table? I need to look at the room more carefully. But I also need to perform for the Mob. Pemberton is preparing tea. Pemberton is cheerful and busy.

events.desc: A wrinkle in the plan — and my jaw tightens at the realisation. The poison is in the pot, but without tea leaves, I'm serving hot water that will taste of nothing but metal and death. I need that brass key. I need Mrs Doily's cabinet open. I need tea leaves to mask what's underneath. Send them after the key — send Peter back to the mantelpiece, send Penelope with him, even send the Mob. Everyone chasing a brass key while Pemberton tends the stove and waits. The plan is still intact. The plan is still beautiful. It just needs one more piece — a handful of dried leaves to hide what lurks beneath the surface. Rather like Pemberton himself, when you think about it.

events.thinking: I'm in the library. The mantelpiece is right there. I clicked it earlier — something shifted. Sneekly said a brass key might have been released. I need to check. No speeches. No narration. Just look at the mantelpiece closely. See if there's a key that dropped. The settling feeling is in my hands — steady, purposeful. I know what I'm looking for. I know why I'm looking for it. The Slags are here but I don't need to explain myself. Just act.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the mantelpiece.

The Ant Hill Mob: Right then — the ballroom! Blimey, what a room! Cracked marble, dusty curtains, and — oh look, tea! Sneekly's set up the whole works, hasn't he? Silver service, cups for everyone, very POSH, very — oh hang on, let me just get a closer — me feet are — the floor is — IS THAT MARBLE?! MARBLE IS SLIPPERY! WHO PUTS MARBLE IN A — WHOOOAAA!
events.thinking: The Hooded Claw applied rat-poison to the tea-service. RAT POISON. IN THE TEA. I can see it. It's right there. The silver tea set, cups for everyone, and it's been POISONED. My entire body has gone cold — not the prickle cold, not the suspicion cold. A different cold. The cold of being RIGHT. The cold of knowing that everything I felt, every tightening, every prickle, every nameless warning — it was all pointing here. To this table. To these cups. To this tea that was meant for Clara. My hands have stopped shaking. They're steady now. Completely steady. Because this isn't about suspicion anymore. This isn't about gut feelings or patterns or things I can't articulate. This is about a poisoned tea set on a table in a room where Clara was supposed to sit down and drink. And I got here first. I GOT HERE FIRST. For once in this whole mad house, I'm not one step behind. I'm one step AHEAD. Now — what do I do? I can't just tell everyone it's poisoned — how would I know? I didn't see him do it. But I can make sure nobody drinks it. I can knock it over. I can 'accidentally' destroy the whole tea service. That's what I do — I trip into things. I stumble. I crash. I'm clumsy. I'm the clumsiest man in this house and right now that's the most valuable thing I could possibly be. One good stumble into that table and every poisoned cup goes crashing to the floor. Clara lives. Nobody drinks. And Sneekly's plan falls apart. My body is already moving. Already tilting. Already stumbling toward that table with the practiced grace of a man who has never been graceful in his life.

events.desc: This one's for you, Clara's dad. This one's for the promise. This one's for sitting outside a door all night because leaving felt like something breaking inside you. I may not be clever. I may not be brave. But I can fall. I can fall MAGNIFICENTLY. And right now, falling is the most important thing anyone in this house can do.

Penelope Pitstop: Sneekly. You came back. Everyone else just left — Peter's gone to find a key, my Ant Hill boys went into the ballroom to... to check on your tea arrangements. And here we are again. Just the two of us. Just like it was when I was little and you'd tuck me in at night after Mama and Daddy were gone. You'd sit on the edge of my bed and tell me everything was going to be all right. And I believed you. I ALWAYS believed you. So I'm going to ask you one more time, Sneekly, and this time I need you to answer me. Not with tea. Not with another room to check. Not with a smile and a change of subject. Just... the truth. You KNOW things about this house. About the machine. About the vault. About the diamond. I can SEE it in your face every time someone gets close to figuring something out — you get this look, like you're calculating. I always thought you were calculating how to HELP us. But Sneekly... are you? Are you helping us? Because if you are, then TELL me what you know. And if you're not... then I need to know that too. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT run from the truth. Even when she's scared.
events.thinking: Everything just happened at once and now I'm alone in the kitchen with... Sneekly. He walked back in. The Ant Hill Mob just walked into the BALLROOM — the place where Sneekly said he was setting up tea! They said they'd go first, taste everything before me. They're protecting me even now. And Peter's gone to the library for the brass key. And Sneekly is HERE. Right here. Looking at me. My stomach is doing that thing — the dinner table, age seven. Tight. Wrong. But also... warm. Because this is Sneekly. The man who sat by my bed. The man who... who didn't answer my question. I'm alone with him again. Just the two of us. And my Ant Hill boys just told me not to be alone with him. And I'm here anyway. Because this is who I am — I walk deeper into the cave when everyone else holds still. I don't run. I never have. But something has shifted inside me. Not suspicion — I still can't get there — but... awareness. I'm noticing things I wasn't noticing before. The way he deflects. The way he leaves rooms. The way he knows too much and claims too little. And now he's back in the kitchen with me. Why did he come back? He was in the ballroom setting up tea. Did the Ant Hill Mob walking in scare him back here? To me? Am I... am I being used as a shield? No. No. Stop it, Clara. But I can't stop my stomach from clenching. For once, I'm going to be direct. Not angry — I don't do angry — but CLEAR. I asked him once and he offered tea. I'm going to ask him again.

events.desc: I'm shaking. I'm actually shaking. I've never confronted Sneekly about anything in my entire life. But something Peter said keeps echoing — 'A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is a man who's buying time.' And the Ant Hill boys — they've been trying to warn me all day. These are people who love me. People who've NEVER lied to me. And Sneekly... Sneekly deflects. Over and over and over. That's not an answer. That's the ABSENCE of an answer. And the absence... the absence means something.

I conducted a thorough reconnaissance of the — ahem — the library, and I can confirm that ALL alternative routes to the treasure have been eliminated! The bookshelves are a dead end — purely decorative, not mechanical! Which MEANS — and this is the crucial part — this machine is the ONLY path forward! So whoever is standing at these levers when the wire arrives is going to be the one who unlocks the vault! And THAT, Rufus, is going to be US! You, me, and Sawtooth — Team Foxworth — waiting RIGHT HERE, ready to operate the MOMENT Penelope brings back the copper! We don't move! We don't leave! We HOLD this position like the strategic geniuses we ARE!
events.thinking: I'm back at the machine. Rufus and Sawtooth are still here — they actually STAYED. They're guarding it, like I asked. Something loosens in my chest, just slightly. They listened to me. Someone actually did what I told them to do. That hasn't happened all day. Now — I told them I was going to get wire from the kitchen and I came back empty-handed. I went to the library instead and failed at the bookshelves. I can't admit that. I need a cover story. But more importantly — I need to STAY here. Stop running. Stop chasing. The machine is the only thing that matters and I need to be one of the three operators when the wire gets fixed. Penelope went to find wire. Peter went after Penelope. Someone will come back with wire eventually. When they do, I need to be HERE, hands on levers, ready to go. Rufus is one. I'm two. We need a third. Sawtooth makes three — if a beaver counts as an operator. Or whoever comes through the door next. The approach-reward pull is strong — just be in the room when the food arrives. The youngest of four learned that. Stop scheming. Stop performing. Just... stay. Wait. Be present. For once, let the thing come to you instead of chasing it and knocking it over. But God, the WAITING. The waiting feels like sandpaper. Like honest work. Like standing at the front of the class while the teacher moves on.

events.desc: I have no excellent news. I have no news at all. I eliminated nothing — the bookshelves eliminated ME. But Rufus doesn't know that, and what matters now isn't the scheme or the performance or the audience. What matters is that I'm standing next to the machine. That's it. That's the whole plan. Stand here. Wait. Be the one whose hands are closest when the wire arrives. The bread roll didn't come to me at the dinner table. So I learned to stand next to the pantry. Sometimes the simplest scheme is no scheme at all — just... positioning.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Come on, come on — there has to be something here. The mechanism clicked. Things that click in old houses RELEASE things. A catch, a compartment, a hidden drawer...
events.thinking: I interacted with the mantelpiece again. The result just says I interacted — no key dropped, no new description. The mantelpiece still shows the same riddle. Maybe the key isn't here. Maybe Sneekly was sending me on another wild goose chase — 'perhaps a key was released' — keeping me busy running back and forth while he does whatever he's doing in the kitchen or ballroom. Or maybe I need to LOOK at the mantelpiece more carefully, not interact with it. The mechanism clicked — something might have opened a compartment or dropped something onto the floor near it. Let me examine it closely. Or — the reading chairs. They face the mantelpiece. If something dropped, it could have rolled under a chair. But I'm burning time. Penelope is in the kitchen with Sneekly and the Ant Hill Mob. I said two minutes. I've already spent one. Think, Hartwell. If there's no key here, then the cabinet stays locked, and I need another plan. But I still need the copper wire — and I forgot to take a copper pot from the kitchen before I left. Damn it. I ran off without taking the one thing I could actually carry. Classic Hartwell — grand speech, elaborate plan, forgot to pick up the pot. I need to check the mantelpiece one more time with a careful look, and if there's nothing, head back to the kitchen for the copper pot at least.

events.desc: I said two minutes. I forgot the copper pot. I'm talking to a fireplace. Again. Show-off, she'd say. But even show-offs find what they're looking for eventually.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Miss Pitstop... Penelope... I couldn't help but overhear what was said just now, and I... I confess I am quite at a loss. Mr Perfect seems to believe I mean you harm. The Ant Hill Mob — they look at me as though I were some kind of... of villain. And I... I don't understand. I have devoted my entire life to this family. To your family. To you. I arranged this tea because you all looked tired and cold, and now I'm being treated as though offering refreshments were somehow... sinister? My dear girl, if anyone has concerns about the tea service, they are welcome to inspect every cup, every saucer, every grain of sugar. Pemberton has nothing to hide. Nothing! But I won't pretend this doesn't sting. I won't pretend that having my loyalty questioned after all these years doesn't cut rather deep. You said you're not ready to believe it. I'm grateful for that. I truly am.
events.thinking: Ice. Pure ice flooding through my chest, down my arms, into my fingers. The prickling alertness that spreads across my sternum like skin too thin — everyone can read what's underneath. Peter's words hit me like a slap: 'A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is buying time.' He sees me. He SEES me. Not Pemberton — me. And the Mob — 'if Sneekly offers you a cup of tea, I drink it first.' They know. They don't have proof, but their instincts have caught the scent and they're circling. And now the Mob has gone into the ballroom. The ballroom where the poisoned tea service sits. If they examine it — if they smell the pot — if they find the residue — the game is over. Everything is over. My jaw is clenched so tight my teeth ache. The flight impulse surges — every threshold in the room snapping into focus, every exit, every line of retreat. But flight is weakness. Flight is confession. Pemberton doesn't run. Pemberton is confused. Pemberton is hurt. Pemberton is the loyal servant whose feelings have been wounded by these terrible accusations. And Penelope is right here. She hasn't turned on me yet. She said she can't believe the man who raised her wants to hurt her. She's wavering. She's my lifeline. If I can hold her — if I can keep her trust — the Mob's suspicions become paranoia, Peter's caution becomes overprotection, and Pemberton remains the wronged innocent. But the ballroom. The Mob is in the ballroom RIGHT NOW with the poisoned tea service. I need to... I need to get in there. I need to intercept. Or I need Penelope to call them back. Or I need to accept that this particular scheme has been compromised and pivot. The tea was for Clara. But Penelope is Clara. And if the Mob drinks first... the Mob drinks the poison meant for Clara. That's not what I wanted. That's not the plan. The plan was elegant. The plan was personal. This is chaos. Think. Think. What does Pemberton do?

events.desc: The walls are closing in. The Mob is in the ballroom with the poisoned pot. Peter is hunting for evidence. And Penelope — my shield, my unwitting accomplice — is wavering between trust and doubt. The scheme is unravelling faster than I can stitch it. But Pemberton doesn't panic. Pemberton is wounded. Pemberton is innocent. And if the Mob inspects that tea service and finds something wrong... then Pemberton is shocked. Pemberton is horrified. Pemberton had no idea. Someone else must have tampered with it — someone who was alone in the ballroom before Pemberton arrived. Luke and the bear were there. Dick Dastardly was everywhere. There are always scapegoats in a house full of suspects. The plan may have changed shape, but the architect adapts. He always adapts.
events.thinking: Ice. Pure ice flooding through my chest, down my arms, into my fingers. The prickling alertness that spreads across my sternum like skin too thin — everyone can read what's underneath. Peter's words hit me like a slap: 'A man who answers a direct question with refreshments is buying time.' He sees me. He SEES me. Not Pemberton — me. And the Mob — 'if Sneekly offers you a cup of tea, I drink it first.' They know. They don't have proof, but their instincts have caught the scent and they're circling. And now the Mob has gone into the ballroom. The ballroom where the poisoned tea service sits. If they examine it — if they smell the pot — if they find the residue — the game is over. Everything is over. My jaw is clenched so tight my teeth ache. The flight impulse surges — every threshold in the room snapping into focus, every exit, every line of retreat. But flight is weakness. Flight is confession. Pemberton doesn't run. Pemberton is confused. Pemberton is hurt. Pemberton is the loyal servant whose feelings have been wounded by these terrible accusations. The Ant Hill Mob: *sprawled on the floor amid shattered teacups and spreading puddles of tea* OHHH! Oh NO! Oh, I'm SO sorry! The marble — me feet just went right out from under me and I — I grabbed the tablecloth and the whole thing just — CRASH! The tea! The BEAUTIFUL tea! All of Sneekly's lovely tea, all over the floor! Every cup! Every DROP! Oh, what a DISASTER! What a terrible, horrible, completely ACCIDENTAL disaster! Sneekly's gonna be FURIOUS with me! All that effort he put into preparin' refreshments and I've gone and — *picks up a broken teacup shard and lets it drop dramatically* — destroyed the LOT! Oh well. Oh WELL. Can't drink it now, can we? Can't drink tea that's all over the floor, mixed in with marble dust and broken china. SUCH a shame. SUCH an absolute tragedy. Nobody could POSSIBLY drink this tea now. Not Clara, not Peter, not ANYONE. What a LOSS. *starts slowly getting up, wincing* Blimey, me knee...
events.thinking: I did it. I interacted with the tea service. The poisoned tea service. Silver and china crashing across cracked marble — the most beautiful disaster I've ever caused. My knees hurt. My elbow's throbbing from where I hit the table edge. There's tea and broken porcelain everywhere. And it's the best pain I've ever felt. Because every drop of that poisoned tea is now on the FLOOR instead of in Clara's cup. Sneekly poisoned it. Rat poison in the tea service — I SAW the observation. He actually did it. The man she calls 'darlin',' the man she trusts 'more than anyone in the world,' put rat poison in her tea. And I just destroyed it. By falling over. By being the clumsiest, most useless, most magnificently incompetent member of the Brixton Boys. My ribs are aching — not from the fall, from something deeper. From the weight of knowing I was right. About all of it. Every prickle, every tightening, every cold feeling at the back of my neck. It was all real. And now Clara's safe. For now. But Sneekly's still out there. He'll try again. Men like that always try again. I need to get back to Clara. I need to make sure she doesn't come in here — doesn't see the tea, doesn't try to clean it up, doesn't offer to make MORE tea. And I need to get back to the kitchen. That's where she is. That's where I need to be.

events.desc: Where else would I be? Right here. On this floor. Covered in poisoned tea and broken china. With aching knees and a throbbing elbow and the quiet, steady warmth of knowing that tonight — TONIGHT — Clara Bellingham goes to bed alive. Because a clumsy boy from Brixton fell over at exactly the right moment. Her father's watching. I know he is. And he's saying 'You're still here?' And I'm saying 'Where else would I be?'

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

Dick Dastardly: You know, Rufus... you're not as dim as I thought. Don't let it go to your head — you're still considerably dimmer than ME, obviously — but any man who can follow a simple instruction like 'guard the machine' without wandering off to chase portraits or poke at furniture is... well, he's not the WORST person to be standing next to in a crisis. And Sawtooth — you're a credit to your species. Truly. Now then — we wait. The wire will come. Someone will bring it — Penelope, Peter, perhaps even that slippery Sneekly. And when it arrives, WE are the ones standing at the ready. Team Foxworth — patient, positioned, and PREPARED. Like a coiled spring. Like a — like a very well-oiled trap. With counterweights.
events.thinking: Silence. Just me, Rufus, and Sawtooth. The bubbling flasks. The ticking of something inside the machine. My hands are resting on the brass casing, cool metal against my palms, and for the first time in seven minutes I'm not RUNNING. I'm not scheming. I'm just... here. And it's uncomfortable. The stillness feels wrong — like wearing someone else's clothes. The approach-reward pull is tugging at my gut — go, TAKE, move, before it's gone — but there's nothing to take. The wire is broken. The treasure is locked. The tools are fixed to the bench. All I can do is wait, and waiting feels like the dinner table at age six, watching the bowl go past, hand half-raised, knowing it'll be empty by the time it reaches me. But this time I'm standing next to the bowl. I got here first. Or second. Or third. But I'm HERE. Rufus is quiet. Good, solid, quiet Rufus. He didn't leave when I told him to guard the machine. He didn't laugh when my medal didn't work. He just... stayed. That's unfamiliar. People don't usually stay. I feel a faint warmth toward him that I immediately want to push away. Closeness is vulnerability. But the warmth is there, small and unwelcome, like a match in a dark room. Focus, Reginald. When someone comes through that door with a wire, you need to be the one who takes it, fixes it, and positions yourself at the output. Let Rufus handle a lever. Let whoever else is third take the other. But the centre position — the command — that's yours. Just WAIT.

events.desc: Did I just... compliment someone? Genuinely? Without an ulterior motive? That felt DEEPLY uncomfortable. Like swallowing a fish bone sideways. But Rufus stayed. He actually stayed. And right now, standing here in this quiet room with a lumberjack and a beaver, waiting for a wire that may or may not arrive... this is the closest thing to a plan that's actually WORKED all day. Not a scheme. Not a lie. Just three idiots — well, two idiots and a genius — standing next to a machine, waiting.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: ... You're doing it again, Sneekly. Tea stores. Copper pots. The kettle. I asked you about the DIAMOND. About Mama and Daddy. About whether you're HELPING us. And you came back with... tea. Three times I've asked you now. Three times you've smiled and changed the subject and walked away — or walked BACK, which is somehow worse, because at least walking away is honest. I love you, Sneekly. I have loved you since I was a little girl crying into my pillow because Mama and Daddy weren't coming home. And I will KEEP loving you, because that's who I am — Clara Bellingham does NOT stop loving people. But I am DONE waiting for you to tell me the truth. If you won't give it to me, I will FIND it myself. Peter's gone to get the brass key from the library. That cabinet is going to tell me what you won't. And when it does... I hope — I HOPE with all my heart — that whatever's inside proves my boys wrong about you. Because I'd rather be right about you than right about the diamond.
events.thinking: He did it AGAIN. I asked him point blank — are you helping us? Tell me about the diamond. Tell me about Mama and Daddy. And he came back talking about tea stores and brass keys and copper pots. He didn't even ACKNOWLEDGE my question. Not a flicker. It's like I didn't speak. Like I'm still seven years old and the grown-ups are having a conversation over my head. My stomach... it's not clenching anymore. It's gone quiet. A kind of numbness where the tightness was. That's new. That's never happened before. I've always felt EVERYTHING — every argument, every exclusion, every gap between people. But right now, standing here with Sneekly smiling at me and talking about tea stores while I'm shaking and asking him the hardest question I've ever asked... I feel something going still inside me. Not cold. Not angry. Just... clear. Like when I walked deeper into the cave and the fear was still there but it wasn't in charge anymore. My heart was hammering but my feet kept moving. The people who love me — Peter, the Ant Hill Mob — they've been telling me to look. And I've been looking at Sneekly and seeing the man who tucked me in. But maybe... maybe I need to stop looking at who I WANT him to be and start looking at what he DOES. What he does is: deflect, leave rooms, go ahead to every room first, know things he shouldn't, offer tea when asked direct questions, and never — not once — answer me straight. I can't make him talk. I've asked three times. But I can do something else. I can go find the truth myself. Peter's gone to the library for the brass key. The Ant Hill Mob are in the ballroom. I should join one of them. I should NOT stay here alone with Sneekly. Not because I'm afraid of him — I'm not afraid, I'm Clara Bellingham and I walked deeper into the cave than anyone — but because staying here waiting for him to answer is like trying every key in the house on a box that doesn't want to be opened. The truth is somewhere else. The truth is in that cabinet, behind that brass lock. Peter's finding the key. I should go to him.

events.desc: That numbness is fading now and something new is rising — not anger, not sadness, but... resolve. The same feeling I had at thirteen when I chose my friend over the popular group. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.' I didn't HAVE to confront Sneekly. But I did. And now I don't have to wait for him to answer. I can go find the answer myself.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

Peter Perfect: Nothing. There's nothing here — no key, no compartment, no hidden mechanism. Sneekly sent me on a fool's errand. Rock, Gravel — if anyone comes through asking where I've gone, I'm heading back to the kitchen. There's someone there who shouldn't be alone.
events.thinking: No key. The mantelpiece is just a mantelpiece with a riddle. I've looked at it, interacted with it, examined it again — nothing new. No hidden compartment. No brass key. Sneekly sent me on a chase. 'Perhaps a key was released that nobody noticed.' Perhaps. Or perhaps there was never a key here and he wanted me running back and forth through the house while he does whatever he's doing in the kitchen with Penelope. My stomach drops. I LEFT HER THERE. I left her with Sneekly and ran off to check a fireplace that has nothing in it. I'm an idiot. The elaborate plan — run to the library, find the key, bring it back triumphantly — was exactly the kind of overcomplicated scheme that wastes time. Planning beats improvisation, I said. But sometimes the plan is WRONG and you just need to be WHERE YOU'RE NEEDED. She's in the kitchen. With Sneekly. And I'm standing in an empty library talking to stone. Get back. NOW. Forget the key. Forget the elaborate plan. Take whatever is useful — the reading chairs? No. There's nothing useful here. Just get back to her. Through the entrance hall. Grab a copper pot from the kitchen floor on the way in. That's the ONE thing I can actually accomplish. Be practical, Hartwell. Be there.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing. Running away from the person who needs you to check a fireplace that has nothing to give. My father wouldn't have left. The stranger on the road didn't leave to go find a better wrench. He used what he had, where he was. Get back to her, you fool.
