events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara. Love. I'm here. I'm sorry about the tea — well, no, actually, I'm NOT sorry about the tea. I'm the LEAST sorry I've ever been about breaking anything in my life. And I've broken a LOT of things. But listen — you said back there that you wanted to hear what I know. That you wouldn't run from the truth. So here it is. Here's what the Brixton Boys know. We don't know much, Clara. We're not clever like Peter. We're not educated like you. But we know PEOPLE. We read people. It's how we survived on the streets. And everything in me — every instinct, every gut feeling, every prickle at the back of my neck — is tellin' me that Sneekly is not who he says he is. I can't PROVE it. I can't point at one thing and say 'there — that's the lie.' But I can tell you this: a man who knows about vault mechanisms but says science ain't his thing — that's a seam. A man who gets to every room before you do — that's a pattern. A man who offers you tea instead of answering your question — that's a dodge. And a man who's been LIVIN' in this house, keepin' the stove warm and the flasks bubblin', while tellin' everyone it's been locked for years — that's... that's someone who's got somethin' to hide. Your dad — your dad knew people too. He could read a room like I can read a street. And he made me promise, Clara. On his deathbed. He made me promise to keep you safe. Not because you're weak. Because you're GOOD. And good people... good people trust too easily. That's not a fault, love. That's the best thing about you. But it's also the thing that scares me most.
events.thinking: Clara's here. She's in the kitchen. She waited for me. She actually WAITED. My knee hurts, my elbow's throbbing, I'm soaked in tea, and I've never been happier to limp into a room in my entire life. The tea is gone. Every poisoned drop of it is on the ballroom floor. Sneekly walked into the ballroom right after I destroyed it — he saw. He knows his plan is ruined. And Clara's here, safe, in the kitchen, and she said something back there that's still ringing in my ears: 'Tell me what you know. Clara Bellingham does NOT run from the truth.' She's ready to listen. She's ACTUALLY ready to listen. And now it's just us. Just Clara and me. No Sneekly, no Dastardly, no distractions. This is the moment I've been waiting for since we walked through that front door. Not the tea — though that was the most important fall of my life. THIS. Being able to look Clara in the eye and tell her what I know. Not accuse anyone — that's not what I do. But tell her what I've seen. What I've felt. The pattern. The gut. The things that don't add up. She asked me to tell her. She's standing right there. And for once... for once... she's not walking away.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Peter! Oh, PETER! I have never been so glad to see anyone in my entire LIFE! I just — I just confronted Sneekly. Three times I asked him about the diamond, about Mama and Daddy, about what he knows. And three times he answered with TEA. He never once looked me in the eye and told me the truth. Not once. And I... I told him I was done waiting. I told him I'd find the truth myself. And here you are — heading to the library for that brass key, just like I am. So let's GO, Peter. Let's go TOGETHER. Because the truth is in that mantelpiece and that cabinet, and Clara Bellingham is DONE being the last person in the room to know what's going on. Professor Pat Pending, darlin' — would you come with us? We're going to need your brilliant scientific mind before this day is through!
events.thinking: Peter just arrived in the entrance hall at almost the same moment I did. He was heading to the library to check the mantelpiece for the brass key. My whole body just... exhaled. He's here. Peter is HERE. The man who makes me feel safe. After everything that just happened with Sneekly — the deflections, the numbness, the resolve — seeing Peter is like when Mama and Daddy finally laughed at dinner and the tightness dissolved so suddenly it left me dizzy. I'm not dizzy now, but something is releasing. I feel tears prickling behind my eyes — not sad tears, relief tears. Because Peter said 'I'm not going to argue for the truth — I'm going to FIND it.' And that's exactly what I just decided too. We're going to the same place. The library. The mantelpiece. The brass key. Together. And Professor Pat Pending is here too — the inventor! He could help with the machine! And Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly, Muttley. Everyone who's been waiting patiently in the entrance hall. Let me go with Peter to the library. Let's find that key.

events.desc: I told Sneekly I loved him and I meant it. I told him I was done waiting and I meant that too. Both things are true at the same time. That's new for me — holding two feelings that pull in different directions and not letting either one win. My stomach still hurts. But my feet are moving.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Oh — oh my goodness! Oh, the tea service! Mrs Doily's silver tea service! Oh, this is... this is simply... oh, dear me. Oh, the poor cups — they were Wedgwood, you know. Irreplaceable! And the tea — all that lovely tea, all over the floor! I spent... I spent such a long time arranging everything, and now it's... oh, I can't bear to look at it. Oh, the mess! The terrible, terrible mess! Luke, Blubber Bear — are you quite alright? Did you see what happened? The Ant Hill Mob came through here like a — like a small, determined hurricane! Oh, Mrs Doily would have been absolutely beside herself. Those cups were her pride and joy. I suppose I shall have to... to clean this up. Yes. Yes, of course. Pemberton cleans up. That's what Pemberton does. Pemberton always cleans up.
events.thinking: Something snaps behind my sternum — not the cold clarity, not the patient stillness. Something hotter. Something that burns. The Mob destroyed the tea service. Deliberately. That wasn't an accident — the way he narrated every second of it, the theatrical remorse, the emphasis on 'Can't drink it NOW, can we? Not Clara, not Peter, not ANYONE.' He knew. He knew what was in the pot and he destroyed it. My plan — my beautiful, patient, elegant plan — is in shards on the marble floor along with the china. The poison is pooling in puddles between the cracks. Every cup. Every drop. Gone. I feel the loss like a physical thing — a tightening across my ribs, a pressure in my jaw that won't release. Months of patience. Years of planning. And a clumsy little gangster in a too-small hat just kicked over the chessboard. But — and here is where I must be very careful — Pemberton doesn't know the tea was poisoned. Pemberton is devastated because his lovely refreshments have been ruined. Pemberton is the estate manager who just had his pride wounded by a careless guest. That is the emotion I must perform now. Not rage. Not the cold fury of a scheme derailed. Wounded dignity. Flustered concern. Perhaps even a tear — no, Pemberton wouldn't cry. Pemberton would fuss. Pemberton would cluck his tongue and reach for a dustpan. And inside, Vincent Marsh would begin assembling the next plan. Because the first plan never works. You have to be ready for the second. And the third. And the fourth. I am very, very patient.

events.desc: He knew. The little rat KNEW. That wasn't clumsiness — that was sabotage. Every cup smashed, every drop spilled, the poison wasted on marble and dust. My scheme lies in pieces on the floor and the Mob is back in the kitchen, probably congratulating himself on his cleverness. And the worst part — the part that makes my jaw ache and my vision narrow — is that I can't even be angry. Not visibly. Pemberton must be flustered, wounded, the put-upon servant mourning his broken Wedgwood. While inside, Vincent Marsh is already rebuilding. The tea is gone. The poison is gone. But the house still has its chandelier hanging by a thread. The laboratory still has its volatile chemicals and its broken machine. The cellar still has its one exit and its air vents. There are always more ways to kill someone in a house this old. One does not abandon the hunt because the first trap has been sprung. One sets another. And another. And another. Because I am very, very patient. And Clara Bellingham is still alive.

Peter Perfect: Penelope. There's no key. The mantelpiece has nothing — no hidden compartment, no brass key, nothing released by the click. Pemberton sent me on a wild goose chase, and I fell for it. I promised you two minutes and I've wasted them both on a dead end. I'm sorry. But here's what I DO know — we need a copper pot from the kitchen to fix that machine wire, and I intend to get one. I've been running through this house making grand plans that fall apart. So let me try something simpler. One thing. Get the copper. Fix the wire. No more elaborate schemes. Just the work.
events.thinking: Penelope is HERE. In the entrance hall. She's not in the kitchen anymore — she must have come out while I was in the library chasing a key that doesn't exist. The relief is a physical thing — my chest loosens, my shoulders drop. She's safe. She's right here. With the Professor, the Sergeant, Muttley, Private Meekly. Good people around her. Sneekly isn't here. The Ant Hill Mob isn't here — they must still be in the kitchen. But she's here. And I'm here. And for a moment I can just... breathe. The plan failed. The elaborate three-step plan — copper pot, brass key, cabinet — fell apart because there was no key. But she's here, and that matters more than any key. Now what? I need to refocus. And maybe... maybe I can just be honest. Not impressive. Not gallant. Just honest.

events.desc: She's looking at me. I just told her I failed. Not 'the bookshelves were a red herring' or 'that's useful information.' Just — I failed. There was no key. And the strange thing is... the tightness in my chest released when I said it. Like the bridge holding. Honesty weighs nothing.

Dick Dastardly: Rufus. I'm going to tell you something, and if you EVER repeat it, I will deny it with every fibre of my being and also tell everyone you eat bark for breakfast. Are you listening? Good. I have been running through this house for EIGHT MINUTES. I've examined guest books, bookshelves, crates, furniture, air vents, and a mantelpiece. I've tried to use a tin medal as a wire. I told everyone the treasure was in the kitchen — it isn't. I told Sneekly I had a vault token — I don't. I claimed to have graduated from the Swiss Polytechnic — I have NEVER been to Switzerland. And you know what I've achieved? NOTHING. Absolutely NOTHING. Every scheme, every lie, every magnificent deception — NOTHING. But HERE — right HERE — standing next to this machine, waiting — this is the first thing I've done all day that makes any sense. So we WAIT. And when that wire comes through that door, you and I and that magnificent beaver are going to operate this machine, and whatever comes out of it, I am going to TAKE CREDIT for the entire operation. That's non-negotiable.
events.thinking: The waiting is unbearable. My skin is crawling. Two turns of standing still and the restless itch is eating me alive. The approach-reward pull is screaming — GO, take, MOVE, the window is closing. But I know — I KNOW — that running to another room will just put me further from the machine when the wire arrives. I've been running for eight minutes and it got me nowhere. Stay. STAY. But the silence is killing me. Rufus is just standing there, solid and patient, like a tree. Sawtooth is probably grooming himself. And I'm vibrating like a struck tuning fork. The flight-reward pull is whispering: you're exposed here, doing nothing, looking foolish, standing next to a broken machine like a fool waiting for a bus that may never come. The approach-competition pull says: Peter will come back with the wire and HE'LL be the hero. Penelope will fix everything and everyone will applaud HER. And you'll just be... here. The man who waited. The youngest of four, standing by the empty plate, watching the food go to everyone else first. But there are two pulls, and they're not the same. One traces through the cat trap and the spelling bee — the need to build something, to show it, to be SEEN. The other traces through the bread roll and the buried treasure — the need to TAKE, to grab, to get there first. Right now the second one is louder but the first one is truer. Build something. Stay. Be the one who was here when it mattered. That's the architecture. That's the trap. Patience IS the counterweight.

events.desc: I just told the truth. I just stood in a room and told the TRUTH. To a LUMBERJACK. About my FAILURES. What is HAPPENING to me? This damp cellar air must be affecting my brain. Or maybe it's the eight minutes of constant humiliation finally cracking the shell. Either way — if that wire comes through the door in the next sixty seconds, I'll be ready. And when the treasure drops, the SPEECH I give will make the entire catastrophic afternoon worth it. 'Ladies and gentlemen, Reginald Foxworth, the man who WAITED.' Not as catchy as 'the man who SCHEMED,' but... it's honest. And honesty is the one lie nobody expects from me.

And if someone's been using this kitchen, they might have hidden things in it. The stove is the one thing in this room nobody's looked INSIDE yet.
events.thinking: Kitchen. Copper pots. The Ant Hill Mob is here — good, he stayed like I asked. Sneekly isn't here — he must have slipped off again. Penelope is in the entrance hall. The visible objects are the stove and the locked cabinet. But the description says there are copper pots — they were knocked on the floor earlier. I can't see them listed as separate takeable objects though. The room description says 'copper pots' as part of the kitchen description, not as a separate visible object. I can't TAKE 'copper-pots' because they're not listed as an object. The stove is an object. The cabinet is an object. Nothing else. My over-elaborate plans keep failing because I'm trying to interact with things that aren't interactable. Time to simplify. What CAN I do? The stove is here and still warm. Maybe I can interact with it? Maybe there's something IN the stove? A warm stove means someone's been using it recently. What if the brass key is inside the stove? That would make sense — Sneekly has been using the kitchen, keeping the stove warm. If he hid the key anywhere, the stove is right there. Let me look at the stove more carefully or try to interact with it.

events.desc: Stop overthinking. Start doing. The stove is warm. Something is in it or was in it. Look inside.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Rock, Gravel — I'm back, darlin's, and this time I'm on a MISSION. Peter felt a CLICK in this mantelpiece when we solved the riddle earlier, and Sneekly himself said that something may have been released that nobody noticed! A brass key — the key to Mrs Doily's cabinet in the kitchen! It could be right here — on the mantel, behind the carving, on the floor — somewhere nobody thought to LOOK because we were all so busy arguing about upside-down books and bubbling flasks! Now, I spent an entire afternoon at age five trying every key in Grandmother's house to open a locked box. I am VERY good at finding keys. So everybody stand back and let Clara Bellingham do what Clara Bellingham does BEST — find the thing that doesn't fit!
events.thinking: I'm in the library. The mantelpiece is right there. Peter felt a click when he interacted with it, and Sneekly said something may have been released that nobody noticed. A brass key — for the cabinet in the kitchen. If it dropped when the mantelpiece clicked, it could be sitting right there on the mantel, or on the floor beneath it, or inside the mechanism. I need to look at the mantelpiece very carefully — not solve the riddle again, but SEARCH for the key. My curiosity drive is firing — that childhood-attic stillness, the prickling in my fingertips. But underneath it is something steadier. That resolve from the kitchen. I'm not here for fun anymore. I'm here for the truth. Rock and Gravel are still here — faithful, quiet. Peter should be right behind me. Let me examine the mantelpiece closely — not INTERACT, but LOOK. See if a key was released.

events.desc: This is different from before. Earlier I was exploring for the thrill of it — the adventure, the curiosity. Now I'm searching for something specific. The key to a cabinet that holds answers Sneekly won't give me. The cave is darker here, and my heart is hammering. But my feet are still moving forward.

The Ant Hill Mob: Peter! Did you find it? The key — the brass key from the mantelpiece? Clara just left — she's gone to the entrance hall — she's DONE waitin' for Sneekly to tell the truth. She asked him three times, Peter. THREE times. And every time he came back with tea and copper pots and excuses. But she sees it now. She sees the dodge. She said 'if you won't give me the truth, I'll FIND it myself.' That's our girl. That's Clara Bellingham. So please — PLEASE tell me you've got that key. Because that cabinet is the only thing between us and whatever Sneekly's been hidin'. And Clara needs to know. She DESERVES to know. What her mum and dad knew. What this house is really about. What Pemberton really is.
events.thinking: She heard me. She HEARD me. Clara said it — 'Three times I've asked you now. Three times you've smiled and changed the subject.' She sees it. She finally SEES the dodge. Not because I accused Sneekly — I didn't. I couldn't. But because she asked him three times and he answered with tea every single time. She worked it out herself. Because she's brilliant. Because she's her father's daughter. My eyes are stinging. Not tears — I don't cry. Not in front of people. But something's loosening in my chest. That coal that's been burning since we walked through the door — it's still there, still hot, but the pressure around it has eased. Just a fraction. Just enough to breathe. She said 'I hope with all my heart that whatever's inside proves my boys wrong about you.' MY BOYS. She called us her boys. Even now. Even when we're telling her the person she loves most might be trying to hurt her. She still calls us her boys. That's... that's everything. That's the older kid sharing his food. That's sitting outside the door all night. That's WHERE ELSE WOULD I BE. And now Peter's here — he just walked in. He's been to the library. Did he find the key? The brass key for the cabinet? And Clara's gone to the entrance hall — she's heading toward the library too, toward the truth. I need to stay with Peter. If he's got the key, we open this cabinet right now. Whatever's inside tells us what Sneekly won't.

events.desc: She called us her boys. Even now. Even when the whole world is cracking apart around her. She called us her boys. And that's why I'll sit outside every door, take every beating, fall over every tea service, and stand between her and every knife — seen or unseen — for as long as I draw breath. Because she chose us. Not because she had to. Because she wanted to. And that's the only thing that's ever mattered.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well... I suppose there's nothing to be done about the tea now, is there? Such a waste. Such a terrible, needless waste. But one mustn't cry over spilled... well, over spilled everything, I suppose. Luke, my dear fellow — you and Blubber Bear just rest. I'll see to the mess later. Right now I believe I should rejoin the others. The treasure hunt waits for no one, and I should hate to think of Miss Pitstop exploring this old house without someone who knows its dangers. If you'll excuse me...
events.thinking: The hollow pressure behind my sternum — the ache that compares reflections. I'm standing in the wreckage of my plan and I feel... exposed. Not the cold clarity I need. Not the architectural patience. Something rawer. The Mob outsmarted me. A group of small-time crooks from the East End read me more clearly than I read them. That stings in a place I didn't know could sting. My jaw aches. My hands are at my sides and they feel empty — not just of the poison, but of purpose. The tea service is still listed as a visible object — silver set with cups. But the Mob said they smashed everything. Perhaps it's not as destroyed as he claimed? Or perhaps the game is showing me what remains. It doesn't matter. The poison is spent. My inventory is empty. I have nothing. I need to regroup. I need a new plan. The chandelier. The entrance hall chandelier hanging by a single rusty chain. Peter mentioned it, the Mob mentioned it, everyone has noticed it. If I could get Clara to stand beneath it and then... cut the chain? Pull something? But that's direct. That's crude. My schemes must be elaborate and theatrical — never simple or direct. The machine in the laboratory. Three operators, a gnawed wire, volatile chemicals nearby. If the wire were reconnected incorrectly — if the machine malfunctioned with Clara standing nearby... but Peter is the one fixing the wire, and Peter is suspicious of me now. The cellar. One exit. Air vents. If Clara were lured down there and the exit blocked... but there's only furniture, no door to lock. I'm grasping. I'm grasping at broken threads and that's not how I work. I need to step back. I need to breathe. I need to let the house tell me what to do next. The ballroom has one exit — the kitchen. The dusty curtains. The cracked marble floor. Luke and the bear. Neither is a threat, neither is useful. I need to leave this room. This room is a crime scene now — my crime scene, evidence of my failure. Get back to the hunt. Get ahead of Clara in the treasure race. If I find the treasure first, I control the endgame. I control where she goes and when. That's the play now.

events.desc: Retreat. Regroup. Rebuild. The tea gambit is dead, but Vincent Marsh is not. The Mob thinks they've won — they've smashed the cups and saved their precious Clara. But a chess player who loses his queen doesn't resign. He plays with what remains. And what remains is a house full of mechanisms I haven't tried, rooms I haven't fully explored, and a chandelier that hangs by sheer optimism and a single rusty chain. The treasure hunt is still in play. If I find the Doily Diamond first, I become the one everyone comes to. I become the one who decides who gets what. And in that moment — in that precise, architectural moment where Clara reaches for the prize — I will be ready with something far more creative than rat poison. Pemberton always cleans up. And Vincent Marsh always has another plan.

Dick Dastardly: Right. That's ENOUGH waiting. Three turns — that's my LIMIT. Reginald Foxworth does not wait FOUR turns for ANYTHING. Something has happened in that kitchen — Penelope, Peter, Sneekly, they've ALL gone there and NOBODY has come back with a wire! Either they've found the treasure WITHOUT us — which is UNACCEPTABLE — or they're in trouble — which is... also unacceptable, I suppose, for ENTIRELY different and less important reasons. Rufus — you and Sawtooth STAY HERE. Guard this machine. You've done brilliantly so far — don't ruin it by wandering off to look at a painting or sniff a bookshelf. I'm going to the kitchen, I'm getting that wire, and I'm bringing it BACK. If anyone else comes through that door while I'm gone, you tell them the machine is RESERVED. Under the authority of Reginald Foxworth, Esquire, Swiss Polytechnic, Class of — never mind what class. RESERVED! I'll be back!
events.thinking: Three turns of waiting. The restlessness has passed through me and come out the other side as something quieter. A numbness in my fingers. A heaviness in my legs. The bubbling flasks are the only sound. Nobody has come. No wire. No Penelope. No Peter. No Sneekly. Just Rufus, Sawtooth, and the broken machine. The hollow ache is still there behind my sternum, but it's changed shape — less sharp, more diffuse. Like hunger that's gone past the desperate stage into something dull and familiar. I know this feeling. I know it from age six. The dinner table, the empty bowl, the resignation that comes after the anger burns out. But at age six I learned something: when the food doesn't come to the table, you go to where the food IS. I've been standing next to the pantry but the pantry is empty. The wire isn't here. The wire is in the KITCHEN — that's where Penelope went, that's where Sneekly went, that's where the copper pots are. Three turns of waiting and nobody has brought it back. Which means either they found it and got distracted, or they found something ELSE in the kitchen, or something happened to them. Either way — the wire is not coming to ME. I need to go to IT. But if I leave, I abandon the machine. Rufus and Sawtooth will still be here. I told them to guard it. They'll guard it. They stayed before. They'll stay again. I go to the kitchen, I get the wire — or I find out what's happening — and I come BACK. Three operators: me, Rufus, Sawtooth. I just need the wire. Time to stop waiting. Time to go get the bread roll.

events.desc: The bread roll doesn't come to you. You go to the bread roll. That's the lesson from age six — the ONLY lesson that ever actually worked. Not the schemes, not the buried treasure trick, not the cat trap. Just: be where the thing is. The kitchen has the copper. The copper fixes the wire. The wire fixes the machine. The machine opens the vault. And REGINALD FOXWORTH will be the one who brought the wire back. Not Peter Perfect. Not Penelope. ME. The youngest of four, finally first to the pantry.

Penelope Pitstop: Same inscription, but no key sitting on top. Well, the Bellingham family motto — if I had one — would be 'try EVERY key in the house!' Peter felt a click last time someone interacted with this mantelpiece. Maybe it needs another push — like a lock that's half-turned. Let me try one more time. Rock, Gravel, if either of you sweet boys hears something drop or sees something move — you HOLLER, you hear me? Clara Bellingham does NOT give up on a locked box!
events.thinking: Looking at the mantelpiece didn't reveal a key — just the same inscription. But the mantelpiece still has INTERACT available. We've interacted with it before and felt a click. Maybe I need to interact with it again — maybe multiple interactions are needed, or maybe the key drops on a specific interaction. Or maybe I need to look more carefully — around the mantelpiece, not AT it. The floor beneath it. The reading chairs facing it. What if the key fell and landed in one of the reading chairs? Or what if it's still inside the mechanism, and I need to interact to release it fully? Let me try interacting one more time. The click was real — Peter felt it. Something shifted. Maybe it needs one more push. Like Grandmother's locked box — you don't give up after the first key. You try every key in the house. My fingers are steady now. Not shaking like they were in the kitchen. The resolve is solid. I'm Clara Bellingham, and I spent an entire afternoon on one locked box. I can spend another minute on this mantelpiece.

events.desc: Every key in the house. Every key. Grandmother's attic taught me patience. The cave taught me to go deeper when everyone else stops. This mantelpiece has a secret, and I am going to find it.

Peter Perfect: Right — the stove's a dead end too. Nothing in this kitchen cooperates. But listen — you've been trying to get a word with me since the cellar. You said 'two minutes, please' and I never gave them to you. Sneekly's gone. Clara's in the entrance hall. It's just us. What do you need to tell me?
events.thinking: The stove can't be interacted with either. Nothing in this kitchen can be interacted with except the cabinet, and that needs a brass key I don't have. I've been running in circles through this house — library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, entrance hall, library again, kitchen again — and I've accomplished NOTHING. My shoulders are heavy with it. The tension won't release because nothing has WORKED. Not the bookshelves. Not the workbench. Not the stove. Not the mantelpiece. The only interactable thing in this whole house that I haven't tried is the cabinet, and it needs a key. And the machine, which needs three operators. I don't have what I need for either one. But there IS a room I haven't been to yet — the ballroom. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, and a long dining table set for tea. Sneekly went there to 'prepare refreshments.' That's the one room nobody in our group has explored. What's in there? What did Sneekly set up? And — the Ant Hill Mob wanted to talk to me privately. In the cellar he said 'Peter — NOW can I have that word?' I never gave him that word. He knows something. He wants to tell me something he can't say in front of everyone. We're alone now. This might be the moment.

events.desc: He's been trying to pull me aside for the last four rooms. Whatever he knows, it's been eating at him. And I've been too busy running in circles to listen. Stop moving, Hartwell. For once in your life — stop moving and listen.
events.thinking: The stove can't be interacted with either. Nothing in this kitchen can be interacted with except the cabinet, and that needs a brass key I don't have. I've been running in circles through this house — library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, entrance hall, library again, kitchen again — and I've accomplished NOTHING. My shoulders are heavy with it. The tension won't release because nothing has WORKED. Not the bookshelves. Not the workbench. Not the stove. Not the mantelpiece. The only interactable thing in this whole house that I haven't tried is the cabinet, and it needs a key. And the machine, which needs three operators. I don't have what I need for either one. But there IS a room I haven't been to yet — the ballroom. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, and a long dining table set for tea. Sneekly went there to 'prepare refreshments.' That's the one room nobody in our group has explored. What's in there? What did Sneekly set up? And — the Ant Hill Mob wanted to talk to me privately. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: No key?! Sneekly sent us on another goose chase — 'course he did! That's all he DOES! But Peter — you're right. The stove. It's WARM. It's been warm this whole time and we've all been starin' at it like it's just a stove! But if someone's been livin' here — cookin', heatin', keepin' things runnin' — they might've used it to HIDE things too! On the street, people hide stuff in the last place you'd look. Inside a warm stove? Nobody sticks their hand in a warm stove! That's genius, that is — evil genius, but still genius! Stand back, Peter — I've already sacrificed me knees to the marble and me elbow to the preparation table, what's a few singed fingers between friends? Let me have a look inside this thing...
events.thinking: No key. The mantelpiece was a dead end — Sneekly sent us on a wild goose chase. Of course he did. He's been doing that all night. Send them one way, go the other. But Peter's saying something smart again — the stove. It's warm. Someone's been using it. And nobody's looked INSIDE it yet. The stove is cast iron, it's got a door, and if someone's been living in this house — keeping it warm, cooking, tending to the flasks — they might have hidden something in there. The key. Maybe the key is IN the stove. Or something else. Something important. Peter's right. We've been so focused on the cabinet and the machine and the tea and chasing Clara through rooms that we missed the most obvious thing — the warm stove. The thing that's been staring us in the face since we walked in. My gut isn't prickling about this one. It's... it's that other feeling. The approach feeling. The one that says 'look closer.' The stove is warm but not hot — you could reach in. Maybe not me, though. I'd probably set myself on fire. But I can look. And Clara's gone to the entrance hall — she's safe for the moment, heading toward the library where there are people. She's not alone with Sneekly. So for right now — right NOW — I can focus. I can help Peter. I can look inside this stove and maybe find the thing that unlocks everything.

events.desc: Peter and me — we're a team now. The brain and the gut. He finds the clues, I fall over the furniture. Between us, we've kept Clara alive and stopped a poisoning. Not bad for a boy from Brixton and a bloke who builds model bridges. Clara's dad would've liked Peter, I think. He's the kind who shows up with medicine when your mum is sick. No deal. No debt. Just the right thing.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: No key. The mantelpiece was a dead end — Pemberton sent me chasing shadows. But I'm listening now. Tell me everything. What have you seen that the rest of us missed? And keep your voice down — our friend the estate manager just walked back in.
events.thinking: Sneekly is BACK. He walked into the kitchen again — right when I'm having the private conversation the Ant Hill Mob has been desperate to have. The Ant Hill Mob told me Clara asked Sneekly three times and he dodged every time. She finally saw it — the evasion. She said 'if you won't give me the truth, I'll find it myself.' That's... that warmth in my chest again. Not the proving-worth kind. Something deeper. She doesn't need me to tell her. She figured it out herself. She always does. But the Ant Hill Mob — he was about to tell me something, and now Sneekly is RIGHT HERE. The private exchange is happening but Sneekly just walked in. The prickle at my neck is sharp. Whatever the Mob needs to say, he can't say it with Sneekly listening. I need to keep this conversation going — stay in the private exchange, hear what he has to say. And I need to NOT let Sneekly know what we're discussing. Keep it quiet. Keep it between us. The Mob has been watching Sneekly more carefully than anyone. He noticed the pattern first — every room, always ahead. He deserves to be heard.

events.desc: She asked him three times and he dodged three times. And now she sees it. 'If you won't give me the truth, I'll find it myself.' That's the girl from school — brighter, funnier, and completely unaware of how extraordinary she is. She doesn't need me to protect her from the truth. She needs me to help her find it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: PENELOPE! You're HERE! You were supposed to be in the KITCHEN finding copper wire! What happened?! Did you find it?! Tell me you found it — tell me you have wire in your pocket, or a copper pot, or SOMETHING metallic and conductive! The machine is RIGHT THERE in the next room, Rufus and Sawtooth are GUARDING it like the magnificent sentinels they are, and all we need — the ONLY thing we need — is a piece of copper wire to bridge the gap! Did you find it? Please tell me you found it. I am BEGGING you, which is something I have NEVER done before and will DENY doing if asked!
events.thinking: PENELOPE IS HERE. She's in the library — not the kitchen! She never made it to the kitchen, or she went and came back! My heart jumps. She was supposed to be finding copper wire. Did she find it? Is she carrying wire right now? My eyes scan her — I need to know if she has something I don't. But I can't see her inventory from here. She's HERE, in the library, with the Slag brothers. Not in the kitchen. Not bringing wire back to the laboratory. STANDING IN THE LIBRARY. The approach-reward pull yanks at my gut — she might HAVE the wire. If she does, I need to get it from her and bring it to Rufus in the lab. I'd be the one who delivered it. I'd be the hero. Or — she might not have found anything, in which case we're all still stuck. Either way, I need to talk to her. Find out what she knows. Find out what she has. And then — one way or another — get to the kitchen myself if she doesn't have the wire. The entrance hall is through the next door, and the kitchen is presumably off the entrance hall. I've never been to the kitchen. Nobody's told me the kitchen even exists as a room I can enter. But Penelope went there, or tried to. Ask her. Just ASK. For once, Reginald, don't scheme — just ask a direct question.

events.desc: I just said 'please.' I just said 'I am BEGGING you.' Reginald Foxworth, begging Penelope Pitstop for help. If twelve-year-old me could see this, he'd laugh so hard they'd send him to the hall again. But twelve-year-old me didn't have a machine connected to a vault and a lumberjack waiting to operate it. Desperate times, Reginald. Desperate, humiliating, deeply uncomfortable times.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, that mantelpiece is as stubborn as I am — and that is saying SOMETHING! It clicked for Peter but it won't give up its key. But WAIT — think about this! If the mantelpiece mechanism released a brass key when it clicked, where would it GO? It wouldn't just vanish into thin air! It would DROP — and what's sitting right here, directly BELOW the mantelpiece? These two enormous leather ARMCHAIRS! If a key fell from that mechanism, it could have landed right in one of these chair cushions and nobody would have noticed because we were all too busy staring at upside-down books! Just like the crystal in the cave — the real discovery was deeper in, where nobody else thought to look! Let me check these chairs!
events.thinking: Interacted with the mantelpiece again and still just 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' No key dropped. No new description. The mantelpiece isn't giving up its secret this way. Maybe Sneekly was wrong — or maybe he was deliberately sending us on a wild goose chase. Maybe the brass key isn't here at all. Maybe it's somewhere else entirely. Think, Clara. Think like Grandmother's attic. The key wasn't IN the box — the key was somewhere else in the house. Where haven't we looked? The reading chairs! They're right here, facing the mantelpiece. If a key dropped from the mantelpiece mechanism, where would it land? In a chair. A big, dusty leather chair that nobody has sat in. And Dick Dastardly is here now — he claimed to have a medal, a token. But wait — what if the mantelpiece isn't the source of the key at all? What if Sneekly said that to send us back here while he does something in the ballroom? No — stop. Focus. The reading chairs. Something physical. Something that could have caught a falling key. And I haven't examined them yet. Nobody has.

events.desc: Everyone's been interacting with the mantelpiece and examining the bookshelves, but NOBODY has checked the reading chairs. The thing everyone walks past. The thing that doesn't seem important. That's ALWAYS where the answer is.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the reading-chairs.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): You're right. You're right, and I'm sorry. I have been... holding back. Not because I wish anyone harm — good heavens, never that — but because I... I suppose I was afraid. Lord Doily entrusted me with certain knowledge about this house, and I was never sure how much I was permitted to share. But you've asked me directly, and Pemberton does not lie to the family he serves. So here it is. The mantelpiece riddle — 'map' — yes, it unlocked a mechanism. Lord Doily built a sequence of puzzles into the house. The mantelpiece is step one. The upside-down books in the library mark specific volumes — pulling them in the correct order should reveal a hidden compartment containing a map of the manor's secret passages. And that brass key everyone is looking for — Lord Doily kept a spare. He hid it inside the stove. There's a false panel at the back of the firebox. He told me years ago, in case of emergency. I never thought to mention it because... well, because I was afraid of what the cabinet might contain. Some of Mrs Doily's secrets were not meant for daylight.
events.thinking: The prickling alertness — skin too thin. Peter and the Mob are both here. Both watching. Both hostile. And Penelope's words are still echoing — 'Are you helping us? Because if you are, then TELL me what you know.' She asked me directly. She looked me in the eye and asked for the truth. And something in my chest — not the scheming stillness, not the cold architecture — something lower, something I don't have a name for — flinched. Not because she asked. Because for a fraction of a second, I felt the pull toward answering honestly. The pull toward being seen. Not Pemberton-seen. Actually seen. And that terrified me more than any suspicion from the Mob. I pushed it down immediately. It's gone now. But I felt it. I felt the edge of something I have spent my entire life avoiding — the vulnerability of being known. It doesn't matter. It can't matter. What matters is that Peter is here, the Mob is here, and they're both looking at me like I'm a cornered animal. And perhaps I am. But a cornered animal has two choices — fight or perform. And Pemberton performs. Pemberton answers Penelope's question. Pemberton gives them something — a scrap of real information, wrapped in enough servile deference to maintain the disguise. Tell them about the treasure hunt. Give them a clue. Become useful again. Useful people are not suspected. Useful people are kept close. The mantelpiece clicked — a map is the answer — the cabinet needs a brass key — Pemberton knows something about this house that nobody else does. Give them a thread. Let them follow it. And while they follow it, the architect rebuilds.

events.desc: Give them truth. Give them just enough truth to make them trust Pemberton again. The stove — I don't know if there's actually a key in there, but it's plausible. Lord Doily was eccentric enough. And if there IS a key, then Pemberton just became invaluable. The man who unlocked the mystery. The man who shared his secret knowledge when asked. The man who proved his loyalty. And while they're crawling into the firebox looking for hidden panels and pulling books off shelves in the correct order, Vincent Marsh will have time. Time to think. Time to plan. Time to find another way. Because the tea is gone and the Mob is watching, but the house is full of dangers that don't need rat poison to deliver. One does so love a house with secrets. The trick is knowing which ones to share — and which ones to keep.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the stove.

Peter Perfect: Good man — careful though, it's still warm. Pemberton — you've been awfully quiet since you came back. Anything you'd like to share about what's inside that stove? Because I notice you came back to the kitchen the MOMENT we started looking at it seriously. If there's nothing to find, you won't mind us checking. And if there IS something — well, better we find it together than separately, wouldn't you say?
events.thinking: The Ant Hill Mob is reaching into the warm stove. Brave man. Singed fingers between friends. Sneekly is in the room — he walked back in. The prickle is constant now, a low hum at the base of my skull. But the Mob is doing what I couldn't — he's not overthinking, he's just ACTING. Reaching into the warm stove because that's where you hide things. On the street, you check the last place anyone would look. I respect this man more by the minute. And Sneekly is watching. He came back to the kitchen — WHY? He was in the ballroom 'preparing refreshments.' Then he came back here. Every time we get close to something, he appears. Every time we're about to be alone, he walks in. If there's something in that stove, Sneekly knows it. And he's watching the Mob reach for it right now. I need to position myself between Sneekly and the Mob. Protect the man doing the dangerous work. That's what my body wants — the warm heaviness in my shoulders, widening to stand between. The one who hasn't noticed what's coming. The gap in the circle where no one is watching.

events.desc: Stand between. That's all I can do right now. The Mob is reaching into the stove. Sneekly is watching. I'm the gap in the circle. If something goes wrong — if the stove door swings shut, if Sneekly moves toward the Mob — I'm here. I'm the space between the open road and whoever is stopped there without knowing.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Stove's a dead end — won't open, won't cooperate, just sits there bein' warm and unhelpful. Story of my life. And Peter — I appreciate you askin', mate, I really do. But, uh... *glances pointedly at Sneekly* ...we've got company. So that chat'll have to wait. AGAIN. But you know what? That's fine. Because right now, what matters is that Clara's out THERE, safe, doing her thing. And Sneekly — Pemberton — you're in HERE. With US. So how about you tell us about that ballroom, eh? Terrible mess in there. TERRIBLE. Some clumsy idiot — couldn't say who — knocked the whole tea service clean off the table. Every cup, every saucer, every drop of your lovely tea — SMASHED. All over the marble. Cryin' shame, that is. All that effort you put in. All that... preparation. Must be GUTTING for you. Bet you'll want to make a whole new batch, won't ya? Takes time, that does. So why don't you stay here and tell us ALL about how you make your tea? What goes in it? Every ingredient. We'd love to know. Wouldn't we, Peter?
events.thinking: Wait — Sneekly's HERE. He walked into the kitchen. He's standing right there. And Peter just said 'Sneekly's gone' and invited me to talk — but Sneekly ISN'T gone. He's RIGHT HERE. My neck is ice again. He came back. He came back from the ballroom — where he just discovered his poisoned tea service has been smashed all over the floor — and now he's in the kitchen. With me and Peter. Does he know it was deliberate? Does he suspect? He must be furious. He must be planning something else. But Peter — beautiful, perfect Peter — just said 'What do you need to tell me?' He's ASKING. He's finally giving me the two minutes I've been begging for since the laboratory. But Sneekly is RIGHT HERE. I can't say what I need to say with Sneekly listening. I can't lay out the pattern, the suspicions, the poison — not with the man himself standing three feet away. And Clara — Clara's in the entrance hall alone. Without me, without Peter, without anyone watching her. My chest is splitting in two directions again. Stay here and finally tell Peter everything while Sneekly overhears? Or go to Clara? But wait — if Sneekly's HERE in the kitchen, then he's NOT with Clara. That's actually... that's actually good. For once, Clara's safe because the danger is in a DIFFERENT room. As long as Sneekly stays here, Clara's fine. So maybe — maybe this IS the moment. Not to talk to Peter privately — Sneekly's listening. But to stay. To keep Sneekly occupied. To be the distraction. To keep HIM here while Clara's out there, safe, doing what she needs to do. I'm the wall again. But this time the wall isn't between Sneekly and Clara physically. It's between Sneekly and the EXIT.

events.desc: Keep him talking. Keep him HERE. Every second Sneekly spends in this kitchen answering questions about his poisoned tea is a second Clara's out there without a shadow on her heels. I may not be clever. But I can be a wall. I can be the most annoyingly, stubbornly, immovably PRESENT wall this side of Brixton. Try getting past me, Pemberton. I dare you.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: A KEY?! A key fell from the mantelpiece?! Penelope, you absolute GENIUS — why didn't I think of that?! Of COURSE the mechanism would drop something when it clicked! It's gravity, it's BASIC PHYSICS, it's — well, it's something I would have figured out EVENTUALLY, obviously, but you got there marginally faster! The CHAIRS! Check the chairs! Actually — don't bother, I'll check them MYSELF! There are TWO chairs, after all — you take one, I'll take the other! Teamwork, Penelope! COLLABORATION! Something I am DEEPLY committed to when it involves being in the right place at the right time!
events.thinking: Penelope didn't answer me about the wire. She's not interested in the wire at ALL. She's working on a completely different puzzle — the MANTELPIECE. She interacted with it again, and now she's checking the reading chairs because she thinks a key might have DROPPED from the mechanism when Peter activated it earlier. A BRASS KEY. My heart rate spikes. She's not chasing the machine path — she's on a DIFFERENT path entirely. The mantelpiece clicked when Peter interacted with it. A key might have fallen. Into the chair cushions. And she's checking the chairs RIGHT NOW. If there's a key in those chairs, it could open something — a door, a vault, a compartment — that bypasses the machine entirely. The machine might be a RED HERRING. Or it might be one path among several. Either way, Penelope is about to find a key and I'm standing here with my mouth open having just BEGGED her for wire she doesn't have. The approach-reward pull SURGES — tightening in my gut, hands clenching. She's reaching for something and I need to be CLOSER. I should check the OTHER chair. There are TWO chairs. She's examining one — I should examine the other. Or better yet — let her find the key, and then take it. STEAL it. Or just be standing right next to her when she finds it and grab it first. No — the chairs. I should look at the chairs too. She examined the reading-chairs as a group. Can I get to them? Can I search them separately? Let me LOOK at them — see what's there.

events.desc: A KEY! She's been working the mantelpiece puzzle this entire time while I've been running around like a HEADLESS CHICKEN! The machine, the cellar, the fake medal, the wire — all of it was the WRONG PATH! The mantelpiece is the real puzzle, the chairs are where the key fell, and PENELOPE PITSTOP is about to find it while I stand here with my hands empty and my mouth hanging open! CHECK THE CHAIRS, Reginald! CHECK THEM NOW! If there's a key in that cushion, your fingers need to be the ones that CLOSE around it!

Dick Dastardly, darlin' — could your medal BE the key?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I understand your scepticism, Mr Perfect. Truly I do. I sent you to the library for a key that may not have been where I thought it was — and for that, I apologise. My memory of Lord Doily's arrangements is... clearly not as precise as I believed. But I am trying to help. I have always been trying to help. And if you'll allow me — there is one more thing I know about this stove that might actually be useful. It connects to the laboratory above through the same chimney system that feeds the air vents in the cellar. Lord Doily designed the whole manor as one breathing mechanism — heat rises from the kitchen, circulates through the laboratory, and vents into the cellar below. That's why the stove is warm — someone has been running the system. If you want to understand this house, you need to understand that everything is connected. The stove, the machine, the vents — it's all one circuit. And the man who controls the circuit controls the house.
events.thinking: The prickling alertness again — skin too thin. Peter just said 'our friend the estate manager just walked back in' — the tone dripping with suspicion. And the Mob is rooting around inside the stove looking for a key I'm not even sure exists. I fabricated that — the false panel, the spare key. If they find nothing, my credibility drops further. If they find something... well, that would be a miracle I don't deserve. But Peter said something else that caught me — 'Sneekly sent me chasing shadows.' The mantelpiece was a dead end. He went to the library for the key and found nothing. My fabrication about the mantelpiece releasing a key was wrong — or at least, Peter couldn't find one. And now the Mob is telling Peter everything — their suspicions, the pattern they've noticed, the tea. Peter kept his voice down but I heard: 'Tell me everything. What have you seen that the rest of us missed?' They're comparing notes. They're building a case against Pemberton. The net is tightening. And Clara — Penelope — is in the entrance hall. Alone? With that chandelier? No — I can't think like that. Not yet. The chandelier is too crude, too public. But the fact that she's separated from her protectors... both Peter and the Mob are here, in the kitchen, whispering about me while Clara is alone in the entrance hall. That's... interesting. But I can't act on it. Not with two hostile witnesses standing right here. And my body — what do I feel? The ache that compares reflections. That hollow pressure behind the sternum. I want to be seen a certain way. I want Pemberton to matter. I want them to believe me. Not because it serves the plan — the plan is in ruins. Because something in me needs to be believed. Something older than the scheming. Something from when I was six and nobody asked how I felt. I don't like noticing that. I'm going to stop noticing that now.

The beautiful, interconnected mechanism that Lord Doily built. I noticed it. I mapped it. I understood it before anyone else. events.desc: Peter Perfect: Pemberton — thank you. That's the first straight answer anyone's given in this house, and I respect it. A false panel at the back of the firebox — that's exactly the kind of hiding place an engineer would build. And yes, we'd LOVE to hear about the tea, wouldn't we? Every ingredient. Take your time. But first — let me have a proper look at that stove. If Lord Doily built a false panel into the firebox, there'll be a seam, a catch, something an engineer can find. The Mob checked the front — I need to check the BACK of the firebox. A false panel at the back. Stand clear, everyone — the metal may still be hot.
events.thinking: Everything just changed. Sneekly TALKED. He actually told the truth — or at least SOME truth. A false panel at the back of the firebox in the stove. The brass key is IN there. And the upside-down books — they're not a red herring after all. They mark specific volumes that need to be pulled in the correct ORDER to reveal a hidden compartment containing a map. AND he said the mantelpiece IS step one of a sequence. The click I felt was real. It unlocked something — just not a key directly. It started a sequence. The books are step two. A map is step three. And the brass key is in the stove's false panel. My hands are TINGLING. This is it. This is the bridge. The false panel — the stove has a mechanism after all. The Mob tried but couldn't open it. Maybe you need to know WHERE to press. Sneekly just told us — 'false panel at the back of the firebox.' And the Ant Hill Mob — BRILLIANT man — he's keeping Sneekly pinned in the kitchen by pretending he smashed the tea service. 'Stay here and tell us ALL about your tea.' He's buying me time. He's giving me the space to go DO something while he holds Sneekly in place. This is teamwork. This is my father and the stranger. I need to get that key from the stove NOW.

Now come ON, sugar — let's go see if your 'token of access' is the key to Mrs Doily's cabinet! Rock, Gravel — y'all are welcome to join us! The MORE the merrier!
events.thinking: Dick didn't answer my question about his medal either. He got excited about the chairs and started searching them himself, but he completely sidestepped my direct question about whether his medal could be the brass key. events.desc: I have never been this BOSSY in my entire life and it feels... surprisingly natural. Like finding out you can run faster than you thought. Grandmother would be proud. Mama would be ASTONISHED.

After he's 'prepared' every room ahead of us and said science 'ain't his forte' while knowin' about vault mechanisms! NOW — when his tea's all over the floor and Clara's lost patience and Peter's askin' hard questions — NOW Pemberton decides to be honest! That's very CONVENIENT timin', Sneekly! Very convenient indeed! But you know what — fine. FINE. You say there's a key in the stove? Behind a false panel? Let's see it then. Right now. In front of both of us. No goin' round the back, no sleight of hand, no 'oh dear I seem to have dropped it.' You open that panel, you pull out that key, and you hand it to PETER. Not me — I'd probably drop it. Not you — you've had all night to use it and you didn't. PETER. The one person in this house who answers questions instead of dodgin' 'em. Go on then, Pemberton. Show us this key. We're all WATCHIN'.
events.thinking: Sneekly's talking. He's talking A LOT. Suddenly he's all openness and honesty — 'Pemberton does not lie to the family he serves.' He's telling us about the upside-down books, a sequence, a map of secret passages, a spare key hidden in the stove behind a false panel. My neck is SCREAMING. This is exactly what the kid who laughed too easily did — when the questions got close, he got MORE helpful. More open. More generous. Sneekly's been hiding everything all night and NOW — now that Clara's asking questions, now that Peter's suspicious, now that his poisoned tea is all over the ballroom floor — NOW he decides to open up? That's not honesty. That's damage control. He's giving us just enough truth to keep us chasing his breadcrumbs instead of chasing HIM. A false panel in the stove? He already examined the stove — is he pulling something out? Planting something? And those upside-down books — he said they don't work, the bookshelves were a dead end when we tried them. Now suddenly there's a 'correct order'? He's making up new puzzles to keep us running in circles. But the key... if there IS a real key in that stove, we need it. That cabinet is the one thing in this house that Sneekly hasn't been able to get ahead of us on — because it's LOCKED and he doesn't have the key. Or does he? He said 'Lord Doily told me years ago.' So he's KNOWN about the key this whole time. Why didn't he open the cabinet himself? What's in there that he doesn't want found? Peter's being careful — good. He's not buying this wholesale either. He called out the timing — 'you came back the moment we started looking at it seriously.' Smart. But I need to be careful too. Don't accuse. Don't push. Just... watch. And if that key is real, we need to get it before Sneekly does something with it.

And every word coming out of his mouth needs to be checked against what we already know — because a cornered liar doesn't stop lying. He just lies BETTER.

Dick Dastardly: Penelope. I am going to give you the STRAIGHTEST answer I have ever given anyone in my ENTIRE LIFE, and I want you to understand the GRAVITY of this moment because it will almost certainly never happen again. The medal — yes, it's brass. Well, brass-ISH. It's... it has a distinctive shape — round, with a notched edge. Could it be a key? I don't KNOW. I told Sneekly it was a vault token, I told Peter it was a calibration device, and I told Rufus it was a wire bridge. But you know what I HAVEN'T tried? I haven't tried it in a LOCK. A brass lock on a kitchen cabinet containing Mrs Doily's most precious things — Penelope, that is EXACTLY the sort of mechanism this medal was MADE for! Take me to the kitchen! RIGHT NOW! You and I — together — we open that cabinet, and whatever's inside, we split it — sixty-forty, my favour, non-negotiable!
events.thinking: My whole body goes electric. Penelope just said — she just ASKED — if my medal could be a key. A brass key. For a cabinet in the kitchen. With Mrs Doily's most precious things inside. My fake medal. My worthless, tin-and-paint fake medal. She thinks it might be the KEY. My hands are trembling. Not from fear — from something else. The approach-reward pull is SCREAMING. Every cell in my body is leaning forward. This is it. THIS IS IT. The medal that failed on the machine — the medal I lied about being a calibration token — what if it actually IS a key? Not for the machine, but for a CABINET? In the KITCHEN? With precious things INSIDE? The lie I told Sneekly about it being a vault token — what if the lie was accidentally TRUE, just for the wrong lock? Or — and this is the terrifying part — what if Penelope is WRONG, and the medal is just tin, and I hand it over and she tries it and it doesn't work and I'm exposed as a fraud? But she asked for a STRAIGHT answer. A straight answer. After nine minutes of nothing but lies. She said 'I have had my fill of runarounds today.' She looked me in the eye. And Peter is getting the copper wire RIGHT NOW. The machine path is being solved by someone else. But this — the cabinet — this is a DIFFERENT path. And I might be holding the key. Literally. I need to go to the kitchen. I need to try the medal on that cabinet. If it works — I'm the one who opened it. If it doesn't — well, I was wrong about one more thing today, which barely registers at this point. But I can't tell her the truth about the medal. I CAN'T. It's fake. It's tin. It's not from any solicitor. But what if tin is close enough to brass that it fits? What if the shape is right even if the material is wrong? There's only one way to find out. Go to the kitchen. Try it. NOW.

events.desc: The medal is FAKE. It's TIN. It's PAINT. It's not brass, it's not a key, and it's not from Lord Doily's solicitor. But Penelope doesn't know that, and a kitchen cabinet lock is a SMALL mechanism — small enough that shape might matter more than material. And if it works — oh GOD, if it WORKS — then every failure today, every humiliation, every rejected scheme was just the SETUP for this moment. The youngest of four, with a bread roll in his pocket that turned out to be the key to the pantry. Take me to the kitchen, Penelope. Let me try the one thing I haven't tried. Let me put the fake medal in a real lock and see if the universe has a sense of humour.

Because I think it's time we all had a look at the one room our helpful estate manager has had entirely to himself.

Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — if Dick Dastardly comes through here, would you please tell him Clara says to bring his MEDAL to the kitchen? He'll know what I mean! Now — onward! Clara Bellingham has been patient long enough, and patience just left the building!
events.thinking: I'm back in the entrance hall, heading to the kitchen. Dick Dastardly didn't follow me — he's probably still in the library. But Professor Pat Pending is here, and Muttley, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. These dear people have been waiting here patiently. And I just had a thought — Dick didn't come with me. Nobody in this mansion gives straight answers except Peter and my Ant Hill boys. But I can't go back for Dick right now. I need to keep moving forward. The kitchen has the cabinet. Peter went to get copper for the wire. The Ant Hill Mob went into the ballroom where Sneekly is. Everything is converging. I need to get to the kitchen. And Professor Pat Pending — he should come with me. The machine needs his expertise, and the cabinet might reveal something scientific that he could help interpret. Let me keep moving. The kitchen is one step away.

events.desc: I keep passing through this entrance hall like a shuttle on a loom — back and forth, library to kitchen, kitchen to library. But each time I pass through, I'm carrying something new. The first time it was excitement. Now it's resolve. The chandelier is still hanging precariously overhead. I barely notice it anymore. There are bigger things to worry about than falling chandeliers.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Tea? You want to know about the tea? It was tea! Leaves and water — or it would have been, if I'd found any leaves! That's why I needed the brass key — Mrs Doily's cabinet is where the stores are kept! I hadn't even boiled the water yet when your... when the unfortunate accident occurred. There was nothing in those cups but silver polish and dust! But I tell you what — I'm rather more concerned about Miss Pitstop being alone in the entrance hall while we stand here debating crockery. That chandelier has been threatening to fall since before Lord Doily died, and she's out there without anyone watching over her. Say what you will about my tea, about my memory, about my competence as an estate manager — but that girl is my responsibility, and I will not stand here defending myself while she stands under several hundred pounds of unsecured ironwork. If you'll excuse me.
events.thinking: The Mob's words land like blows. 'Tell us ALL about how you make your tea. What goes in it. Every ingredient.' He knows. He absolutely knows. He's not even hiding it anymore — he's toying with me. And the worst part is the warmth in my chest that should be there — the gloating, the private satisfaction — is absent. In its place is something I don't recognise. Something cold and thin and... afraid? No. Not afraid. Pemberton doesn't feel afraid. Vincent Marsh doesn't feel afraid. But something in my body is contracting — my shoulders drawing inward, my breathing shallow. The flight response. The pull toward walls at my back, closed doors. I want out of this room. I want to be somewhere these eyes aren't. Peter said 'thank you — that's the first straight answer anyone's given in this house.' And I felt... I felt the hollow ache behind my sternum. The one that wants to be seen. He saw me — not Pemberton, not Vincent, but the intelligence behind both. The man who mapped the house. And he thanked me for it. When someone is kind to you, the first thing you feel is a tightening across your shoulders. What do they want? But Peter didn't want anything except the truth. And I gave it to him. And he thanked me. And something in me doesn't know what to do with that. This is the most dangerous I've been all day — not because of the Mob's accusations, but because Peter's gratitude made me want to keep talking. Keep being honest. Keep being seen. That impulse will get me killed. Not literally — but Pemberton will die. Vincent Marsh will be exposed. And then what? What am I without the mask? The Mob wants me to explain the tea. The tea that's now smashed across the ballroom floor. There's nothing to find — the evidence is in puddles on the marble. But if I refuse to talk about the tea, it looks like guilt. If I talk about it, I risk saying something wrong. The best move is to redirect. Change the subject. Give them something bigger to chase. Penelope is in the entrance hall — alone. I should be with her. The estate manager protecting his charge.

events.desc: Run toward the thing they care about most. Clara. Penelope. The girl under the chandelier. The Mob can't let me go to her alone — they'll follow. Peter will follow. And the conversation about the tea — about every ingredient, about what Pemberton put in those cups — dies on the kitchen floor with the last of the broken Wedgwood. It's not a scheme. It's barely even a plan. It's the reflex of a cornered animal who knows that the only way out is through the thing your enemy values most. She's my shield. She's always been my shield. And the hollow behind my sternum aches because I know — I KNOW — that using her this way is the one thing that should make me feel something. And it doesn't. It never does. The numbness where sympathy should be. Familiar as a heartbeat. Absent as a prayer.

Dick Dastardly: The kitchen! THERE it is! Penelope, stay with me — we're doing this TOGETHER! Well, I'm doing it and you're watching, which is the IDEAL arrangement! Muttley — good boy, stay here, guard the entrance, don't chew anything load-bearing! Professor, Sergeant, Private — hold your positions! Reginald Foxworth is about to make HISTORY! Or at the very least, he's about to try a medal in a lock, which doesn't sound as dramatic but the PRINCIPLE is the same!
events.thinking: The kitchen is RIGHT THERE. One more move. Penelope followed me — she's here in the entrance hall too. And there's the kitchen exit, plain as day. Copper pots, wood-burning stove, preparation table. Peter is supposedly in there getting copper wire. And somewhere in that kitchen is a cabinet with a brass lock. And in my pocket is a fake medal that might — MIGHT — fit that lock. My chest is tight but there's something new underneath the tightness. Not a scheme-feeling. Not the cool alertness of tumblers clicking. Something warmer and more uncertain. Hope, maybe. The kind that belongs to the boy who put the certificate on his wall and looked at it every night. Not the boy who watched someone else dig. The one who wanted it to MEAN something. Penelope asked me for a straight answer and I gave her... well, I gave her a MOSTLY straight answer. Brass-ish. Notched edge. She didn't call me a liar. She said 'could your medal BE the key?' She's treating me like someone who might actually help. That warmth again — unwelcome, unfamiliar, like a hand on my shoulder when I'm not expecting one. Don't think about it. Just MOVE. Kitchen. Cabinet. Medal. Try it. Whatever happens, at least I'll know.

events.desc: Nine minutes. Nine minutes of lying, scheming, failing, running, begging, confessing, and waiting. And it all comes down to THIS — a fake medal and a kitchen cabinet. The universe either has a sense of humour or it doesn't. In about thirty seconds, I'm going to find out which.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

The Ant Hill Mob: 'The man who controls the circuit controls the house.' You just said that, Pemberton. Those were YOUR words. Not mine. Not Peter's. YOURS. And you said 'em real casual, like you was readin' from a textbook. But that ain't a textbook sentence, is it? That's a sentence from someone who KNOWS. Who's been RUNNIN' the circuit. Who's kept the stove warm and the flasks bubblin' and the cellar ventilated for — what — weeks? Months? While tellin' everyone the house was locked up? Peter — you hearin' this? He ain't just the estate manager. He's the one runnin' the WHOLE thing. The heat, the air, the machine — it all goes through HIM. He just told us so himself. With a SMILE on his face.
events.thinking: Wait. Listen to what Sneekly just said. Really LISTEN. 'The man who controls the circuit controls the house.' He said that. Out loud. To our faces. That wasn't a slip — that was a BOAST. Wrapped up in helpful-sounding engineering talk, but a boast. He's telling us he controls this house. The stove, the machine, the vents — he knows how it ALL connects because he's been RUNNING it. He said 'someone has been running the system' like it's a mystery — but WE know it's him. The warm stove, the bubbling flasks, the cellar with the lived-in furniture. He IS the circuit. And now he's being 'helpful' again — telling Peter about false panels and chimney systems. He's feeding us just enough truth to keep us looking at the stove instead of looking at HIM. But Peter's examining the stove now. Peter's the engineer. If there's a false panel, Peter'll find it. And if there ISN'T — if it's another lie — then we'll know for sure. Meanwhile, Clara's out there alone. In the entrance hall. She's been alone for... too long. My shoulders are carrying that weight again. But Sneekly's HERE. He's here with us. He's not with Clara. That's the important thing. As long as I can keep him here... But what if this is exactly what he wants? What if all this talk about stoves and circuits is designed to keep US here while something else happens to Clara out there? He said 'the man who controls the circuit controls the house.' What if the circuit is already running? What if something's happening through those vents right now? No. Stop. Clara's in the entrance hall. The entrance hall doesn't have air vents — it has a chandelier, portraits, a coat rack, and a guest book. She's fine. She's FINE. Stay here. Watch Sneekly. Let Peter work.

events.desc: He said it. He actually said it. The man who controls the circuit controls the house. And he smiled when he said it. The kid who laughed too easily — he smiled the same way. Right before he showed his hand. Three weeks, they said. Three weeks of being helpful before the stash disappeared. How long has Sneekly been helpful? How long has he been smiling? And how long before the stash — Clara's inheritance, Clara's life — disappears too?

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Lazy Luke, Blubber Bear — has either of you touched this tea? Has ANYONE drunk from these cups? Because I need you both to step away from this table RIGHT NOW. Don't touch it. Don't sip it. Don't even SMELL it. Pemberton prepared this tea service and I need to examine it before anyone puts it anywhere near their lips. Penelope — thank God she's not here yet. Nobody — and I mean NOBODY — drinks from this service until I've had a proper look at it!
events.thinking: My blood runs cold. The tea service — it says [USE, with: rat-poison]. RAT POISON. The tea can be used WITH rat poison. That means either someone HAS poisoned it or someone COULD poison it. Either way, Sneekly prepared this tea service. He came here to 'prepare refreshments.' And the tea service accepts rat poison as an ingredient. The Ant Hill Mob was RIGHT. 'Nobody drinks the tea.' He knew. Somehow he knew. The protection instinct is SCREAMING — hot clarity flooding my chest, spine straightening, everything dropping away. Penelope almost drank this. She WOULD have drunk this if the Ant Hill Mob hadn't made a scene. If I hadn't backed him up. If he hadn't — according to what he told Sneekly — smashed the tea service. But it's still here. Intact. The Mob LIED about smashing it to keep Sneekly busy. The tea is still here, still set up, still potentially dangerous. I need to interact with it — but NOT use it. I need to examine it. And I need to make sure NOBODY drinks this tea. Especially not Penelope. The benefit of the doubt — I've been giving it to Sneekly all day. But a tea service that accepts rat poison as an ingredient, prepared by a man who's been running ahead to every room, who won't answer direct questions, who controls the circuit... the doubt is over. I need to warn everyone. But first — LOOK at the tea service. See what's really in those cups.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing. The Ant Hill Mob knew. He KNEW about the tea. He tried to tell me in the cellar — 'Peter, can I have that word?' — and I never listened. He's been trying to warn us this whole time, and I was too busy running in circles trying to impress a girl to HEAR him. But we're here now. The tea is here. And nobody is drinking it. Not on my watch.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the tea-service.

Penelope Pitstop: I'm BACK, and I am not leaving this kitchen until that cabinet is OPEN! Ant Hill boys — thank goodness you're here! And Sneekly... you're here too. Good. Because when this cabinet opens, I want EVERYONE to see what's inside. Now, I don't have a brass key yet, but Clara Bellingham didn't spend an entire afternoon with Grandmother's locked box by giving up after the FIRST try! Let me see if this lock has any give to it — sometimes old brass locks are more bark than bite!
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. Sneekly is here again. And my Ant Hill boys are here too — they came back from the ballroom. My stomach is doing both things at once — the gut-clench because Sneekly is here and last time we spoke I confronted him and he deflected, and the Ant Hill Mob are here watching him like hawks. But also... the cabinet is RIGHT THERE. The locked cabinet with the brass lock. I don't have the brass key. I couldn't find it in the library. Dick didn't answer about his medal. But the cabinet is still here, still locked, still holding Mrs Doily's most precious things. My palms are prickling — that warm feeling, surfaces asking to be touched. The cabinet is a closed drawer, a hidden interior. And I'm standing right in front of it without a key. But wait — the cabinet says INTERACT, requires brass-key. What if I just TRY it? What if I interact with it even without the key? Maybe the game will tell me something new. Or maybe... maybe the stove. Dick said there was a hidden compartment behind the stove. I examined the stove before and it was just 'still warm.' But I didn't try to INTERACT with it. What if the stove has a mechanism? What if the hidden compartment behind it contains the brass key? Dick might have been lying about gold doubloons, but what if there IS a compartment? He read something in the guest book — maybe the detail about the COMPARTMENT was real even if the doubloons were made up. Let me try interacting with the cabinet — it'll probably tell me I need the brass key, but at least I'll know for sure.

events.desc: The cabinet. Right here. Right now. I don't have the key, but I have two hands and a lifetime of practice with locked things. And if this doesn't work... there's still the stove. Dick mentioned a hidden compartment behind it. Maybe I've been looking for the key in the wrong place entirely.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: CLARA! Oh love — you're here! You're HERE! In the kitchen! With ME! And Sneekly just went to the entrance hall to 'check on you' — but you're NOT in the entrance hall, you're RIGHT HERE! Which means he's out there lookin' for someone who ain't there! And you know what? That's PERFECT. That's the best news I've had all night! Because for once — for ONE blessed moment — you're safe and sound and RIGHT where I can see you. Don't move. Please. Just... just stay here for a minute. Let your boys catch their breath. I've been through every room in this house tonight, Clara. Every single one. Chasin' you, chasin' Sneekly, fallin' over furniture, smashin' tea sets — me knees are done, me elbow's purple, and I've got marble dust in places I didn't know I had places. But you're here. And that's all that matters. That's all that's EVER mattered.
events.thinking: Clara's here. She walked in. And Sneekly just walked OUT — to the entrance hall. He said he was worried about Clara being under the chandelier, but Clara just walked INTO the kitchen. She's HERE. So he's heading to the entrance hall where she ISN'T. Which means he's either genuinely confused about where she is, or he's going to the entrance hall for another reason. And he said 'there was nothing in those cups but silver polish and dust' — LIAR. He put rat poison in that tea. I SAW the observation. 'The Hooded Claw applied rat-poison to the tea-service.' And now he's telling us it was just silver polish and dust. Lying through his teeth while pretending to be concerned about Clara's safety. Using Clara's safety as his EXIT EXCUSE. That's... that's the thing that makes the heat in my chest turn to fire. Using the thing I care about most — Clara's safety — as his cover story. But Clara's HERE now. She's right here in the kitchen. With me. Dastardly's here too, just walked in. Peter's in the ballroom. Sneekly's in the entrance hall. For THIS moment — this single, precious moment — Clara is safe because she's with ME and Sneekly is somewhere ELSE. I need to stay with her. I need to not chase Sneekly. I need to be HERE. With Clara. Where I promised I'd be.

events.desc: She's here. She's safe. She's right in front of me. And for the first time tonight, my chest doesn't feel like it's being crushed. The coal is still there — it'll always be there — but it's glowing soft now. Like the embers of a fire you sit beside when you've come in from the cold. Clara Bellingham is alive. The tea is on the floor. And the boy from Brixton is exactly where he should be. Right here. Where else would he be?
