events.desc: Dick Dastardly: THERE! The cabinet! Brass lock — just as you described, Penelope! And the Ant Hill Mob is RIGHT — Sneekly's been running this entire house from behind the curtain! Warm stove, ventilated cellar, bubbling flasks — he's been LIVING here! The man who controls the circuit controls the HOUSE! But the man who opens the CABINET controls the TREASURE! Now then — everyone STAND BACK! This is a PRECISION operation requiring EXPERT hands! The medal — the TOKEN — goes into the lock, and if Lord Doily's solicitor knew what he was doing — which he DID, because I TOLD you he did — then this should... just... FIT!
events.thinking: The cabinet. THERE IT IS. 'A sturdy cabinet with a brass lock. INTERACT, requires: brass-key.' Requires brass-key. My medal is a fake-medal, not a brass-key. It won't work. I can see it right there in the description — 'requires: brass-key.' My item is 'fake-medal.' They're different items. It's going to fail. The same way the machine failed. The same way the bookshelves failed. The same way everything has failed today. My chest caves inward, a slow collapse. I KNOW it won't work. But Penelope is watching. She asked me. She looked me in the eye. And the Ant Hill Mob is here, exposing Sneekly — 'the man who controls the circuit controls the house.' Sneekly has been running EVERYTHING. The stove is still warm. He's been LIVING here. The cellar decorations. The gnawed wire — maybe not a rat at all. Maybe Sneekly sabotaged the machine himself. He controls the circuit. He controls the HOUSE. And the cabinet — the cabinet with the brass lock — what if the REAL brass key is something Sneekly has? What if HE has the key? He's the estate manager. He would have keys to everything. But I can't steal from someone who's not in the room. He's not here. Think, Reginald. The cabinet requires a brass-key. I don't have a brass-key. I have a fake-medal. But I should try anyway — because what if it works? What if the game treats it as close enough? And if it doesn't work — well, then I need to find the real brass key. Which Sneekly probably has. Or which is hidden somewhere. But for now — TRY. Just try. The worst that can happen is another 'cannot be used' message, and frankly, one more rejection barely registers at this point.

events.desc: It's not going to work. I KNOW it's not going to work. The cabinet wants a brass-key and I have a fake-medal. But Penelope is watching. The Ant Hill Mob is watching. And for once — for ONCE in nine minutes of catastrophic failure — I want to be the one standing at the front of the room when something happens. Even if what happens is another humiliation. At least this time, I chose it. The boy at the spelling bee, standing at the front, waiting for applause that never came. But he STOOD there. He TRIED. And he put the certificate on the wall anyway.

Or which is hidden somewhere. But for now — TRY. Just try. The worst that can happen is another 'cannot be used' message, and frankly, one more rejection barely registers at this point.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The tea looks innocent enough — silver service, cups for everyone. A generous host's gesture. But until I know what Pemberton put in these cups, this service is coming with me. Nobody drinks from it. Luke, Blubber — I'm taking this. If Pemberton asks where his tea went, tell him the engineer needed it for a conductivity experiment. That's not even entirely a lie — silver conducts beautifully.

You don't need to prove the tea is poisoned to take it away from people you love. You just need to care enough to look foolish if you're wrong.

I see Mr Foxworth — Dastardly — has just charged through to the kitchen with considerable urgency. Something about a medal and a lock? Most irregular. Well, I suppose everyone has their methods. Now, if you'll all excuse me, I believe the library has been somewhat neglected in all this excitement. Those upside-down books won't solve themselves, and I confess — I've had rather a trying evening and could do with a quiet moment among Lord Doily's volumes. The treasure hunt waits for no one, and Pemberton has been so busy checking rooms and preparing refreshments that he's quite forgotten to do any actual hunting!
events.thinking: Penelope isn't here. She's not in the entrance hall. I said I was coming to protect her from the chandelier and she's not even here. Dick Dastardly just rushed through toward the kitchen shouting about a medal and a lock — did he find a key? And Penelope went with him. She went with DICK rather than waiting for me. That... hurts? No. It doesn't hurt. Nothing hurts. It's just... the ache that compares reflections. She chose to follow Dick Dastardly — DICK DASTARDLY, the most transparently dishonest man in the room — rather than wait for Pemberton. The man who raised her. The man who tucked her in at night. The man who... who poisoned her tea. I need to stop. I need to stop thinking about what Penelope owes me because Penelope doesn't owe me anything. She never owed me anything. She inherited the estate because it was hers by right and I... I managed it because that was my role. That's all it ever was. The role. And now I'm standing in the entrance hall under the chandelier I warned everyone about, with Muttley and Pat Pending and the soldiers, and my schemes are in ruins, and Penelope has gone to the kitchen with Dick Dastardly, and the Mob is probably telling Peter everything, and I feel... empty. Not the productive emptiness of a scheme assembling itself. Just empty. The chandelier creaks above me. I look up at it. Heavy. Old. One chain. It would be so easy. If she walked beneath it. If someone cut the chain. But that's not elaborate. That's not theatrical. That's just... gravity and despair. And I am better than despair. I am Vincent Marsh. I am the Hooded Claw. And the Hooded Claw does not stand beneath a broken chandelier feeling sorry for himself. The library is right there. The upside-down books. The puzzle sequence that nobody has completed. If I solve the puzzle before anyone else — if I find the map — I control the endgame. Stop mourning the poisoned tea. Start winning the treasure hunt.

events.desc: Enough. Enough performing for people who don't believe me. Enough chasing Penelope through rooms she's already left. Enough standing in the wreckage of plans that clever little gangsters have kicked to pieces. The library. The books. The puzzle. That's where the treasure is, and the treasure is the only thing left that matters. If I can't kill Clara tonight — and it's becoming increasingly clear that the Mob won't let me within arm's reach of anything she might consume, touch, or stand beneath — then I will find the Doily Diamond first. I will hold it in my hands. I will own the thing she came here to find. And when she comes to me — because she WILL come to me, they always come to the one who has what they want — I will have leverage. I will have control. And control, as I have always known, is the only thing that makes the emptiness bearable.

Penelope Pitstop: Locked TIGHT! That cabinet is not budging without its brass key, and I do NOT have it! But you know what — when I was five and I couldn't open Grandmother's box, I didn't just try the OBVIOUS keys. I tried EVERY key! And there is one thing in this kitchen I have NOT tried — this STOVE! Dick Dastardly mentioned a hidden compartment behind the stove way back at the very BEGINNING of this adventure! Now, he might have been making up the part about gold doubloons — bless his heart — but what if there IS a compartment? What if the brass key has been hiding behind this warm stove THIS WHOLE TIME? Ant Hill boys — the stove is warm, which means someone's been tending it. And my boys just heard Sneekly say 'the man who controls the circuit controls the house.' If he controls the STOVE... then he knows what's IN the stove! Let me check!
events.thinking: The cabinet requires the brass key. No getting around it. But something HUGE just happened while I was in the library — my Ant Hill boys caught Sneekly saying 'The man who controls the circuit controls the house.' Those were HIS words. He said it himself. He's been running the whole system — the stove, the flasks, the ventilation, the machine. He's not just an estate manager. He's been LIVING here, operating the house's systems, and lying about it. My stomach just dropped. That queasy heat — not just a clench but a LURCH. Because this isn't ambiguous anymore. This isn't 'maybe he's just being helpful.' He said it himself. 'The man who controls the circuit controls the house.' And my boys heard it. And Sneekly just left — again — this time using my SAFETY as the excuse. 'That chandelier is threatening to fall and she's under it.' He left to 'protect' me from a chandelier I'm not even standing under. Another deflection. Another exit. But Dick Dastardly is HERE. Right here in the kitchen. And he has a medal. A token. I need that medal. I need to try it on this lock. I'm going to ask Dick directly — one more time, face to face, no room to dodge — to show me his medal and let me try it on this cabinet. Or... the stove. Behind the stove. The hidden compartment. That's the other thread I haven't pulled. Let me try the stove — INTERACT with it this time, not just LOOK.

And now I know — not suspect, not wonder, but KNOW — that he's been here all along, running everything from the shadows. The man who tucked me in at night has been hiding something from me in my own family's house. And the truth is behind this stove, or inside that cabinet, or somewhere in this mansion that I haven't reached yet. But I WILL reach it. Because I walked deeper into that cave than anyone.

events.desc: If you can't take the bridge apart, you can cut the road that leads to it. Nobody drinks poisoned tea if there's no tea left to drink. The bravest and stupidest thing.

The Ant Hill Mob: Hold on, hold on — Dastardly, you've had that medal this whole time and you're only NOW usin' it?! After all the deals and partnerships and sneakin' about?! But you know what — I don't care. If it opens the cabinet, USE it. Open it. Whatever's in there, Clara deserves to see it. It's her mum's cabinet, in her family's house, and she's been lied to enough for one night. But Clara — love — stand behind me, yeah? I don't know what's in there. Could be answers. Could be somethin' else. Could be another one of Lord Doily's puzzles or traps. Whatever it is, it hits ME first. That's the deal. That's ALWAYS the deal. *positions himself between Penelope and the cabinet, feet planted, shoulders wide* Go on then, Foxworth. Open it. Let's see what Mrs Doily was keepin' locked up all these years.
events.thinking: Dastardly's got his medal — his token — and he's trying to open the cabinet. Clara's right here. Sneekly's gone to the entrance hall. Peter's in the ballroom. And Dastardly's about to open Mrs Doily's locked cabinet. My body is doing something strange — the warmth in my chest is steady, not burning. Clara's safe. She's right here, right in front of me. And whatever's in that cabinet... it might be the truth. The truth about this house, about the Doily Diamond, about what Sneekly's been hiding. Clara said she wanted to find the truth herself. She said 'if you won't give it to me, I'll FIND it myself.' And here it is. The cabinet. The last locked thing in this house. And Dastardly — of all people — has the key. Well, the token. He's a villain and a liar, but right now he's doing the one thing nobody else could do: opening that cabinet. I should... I should just stand here. Between Clara and whatever comes out. That's my job. That's always been my job. Not to open things. Not to solve riddles. Not to find keys or splice wires or understand circuits. Just to stand between Clara and whatever's coming. So that's what I'll do. I'll stand right here. Between her and the cabinet. And whatever truth comes out of it — good or bad — I'll be here when it hits.

And I'm standing here — bruised, exhausted, covered in tea and marble dust — being a wall. The same wall I've been since I was twelve years old, standing between my mate and the kid who wanted his shoes. Some things never change. Some things shouldn't.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the cabinet.

Silence. Blessed, merciful silence. No accusations, no theatrical tea-smashing, no earnest engineers asking pointed questions. Just me and the books and the dust and the quiet. I can feel my mind resettling into its natural shape — the cool, precise architecture that maps connections and sees sequences. The upside-down books. Everyone noticed them. Nobody solved them. Penelope wanted to tug them. Dick claimed credit for noticing them. Peter called them signals. But no one — not one person in this entire overcrowded manor — sat down and actually worked out the pattern. That's because none of them think the way I do. None of them see the mechanism behind the surface. The housekeeper, the teacher, the guardian, the cousin — every person in every room has a key, and I notice them all. These books have a key too. And I am going to find it.
events.thinking: Quiet. The library is quiet. Rock and Gravel Slag are here — large, silent, unconcerned with me. For the first time in what feels like hours, no one is watching me with suspicion. No one is building a case against me. No one is asking me to explain what goes into my tea. The cool clarity is settling back into my sternum — not the frantic, cornered version from the kitchen, but the real thing. The patient thing. The thing that maps rooms and solves puzzles and sees patterns before anyone else. The bookshelves. The upside-down books. I told Peter they needed to be pulled in the correct order. I was making that up — or was I? Lord Doily DID love sequences. The mantelpiece clicked when Peter interacted with it. Step one complete. Step two must be the books. Several are upside down — those are the marked volumes. If I pull them in order... what order? The riddle answer was 'map.' M-A-P? Three books, three letters? Or maybe the spines spell something when read upside down. I need to actually LOOK at these books. I need to examine them properly — not as reconnaissance for murder, but as a genuine puzzle to solve. The treasure hunt. My secondary goal. But right now, with the primary goal in ruins and the Mob dismantling my every scheme, the secondary goal is all I have. Find the treasure. Control the endgame. And the endgame starts here, with upside-down books in a dusty library, and an estate manager who finally has a moment to think.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: It — ahem — the lock requires a SPECIFIC calibration frequency that my token is not currently tuned to! A minor setback! A TRIVIAL recalibration! Nothing to — it doesn't — look, the medal doesn't fit the lock! There, I SAID it! It doesn't FIT! Are you HAPPY?! Ten minutes, ELEVEN rooms, FOURTEEN lies, and NOT ONE SINGLE THING has gone right for Reginald Foxworth today! The medal is FAKE! It's TIN! It's PAINT! It's not from any solicitor and I've never been to SWITZERLAND! But you know WHO has the real key? SNEEKLY! The estate manager! The man with keys to EVERY ROOM in this house! He just went to the entrance hall — the Mob SAID so! And I — Reginald Foxworth, professional failure and reluctant truth-teller — am going to GO OUT THERE and GET that key! Not with a scheme! Not with a LIE! With my HANDS! Because THAT is the one thing I have ALWAYS been good at — taking things when nobody is looking! FOXWORTH PREVAILS! EVENTUALLY!
events.thinking: It didn't work. Of course it didn't work. 'Locked Cabinet requires brass-key.' Not fake-medal. Brass-key. A specific item I don't have. My hand drops from the lock. The medal hangs from my fingers, dull and worthless. The heat in my face isn't the fizzing heat of gloating — it's the flat, spreading warmth of shame. Penelope watched. The Ant Hill Mob watched. I stood at the front of the room and the teacher smiled and moved on. But here's the thing — and my chest constricts as I think it — I'm not devastated. I'm tired. Ten minutes of running. Every scheme failed. Every object rejected me. And now the medal, the last prop in my last trick, hangs limply from my hand in front of the only people still willing to stand in a room with me. Sneekly is gone — the Mob said he went to the entrance hall. He's the estate manager. He has KEYS. The brass key to this cabinet is almost certainly on Sneekly. And Sneekly just left this room. He's in the entrance hall RIGHT NOW. Alone. Without Penelope or the Mob to protect him. If I can find Sneekly and STEAL the brass key from him — THAT'S the play. That's what I do. I TAKE things when nobody's looking. The bread roll in the pocket. Age six. The thing I'm actually GOOD at. Not schemes, not performances, not elaborate traps with counterweights. Just quiet hands and quick pockets. Sneekly is in the entrance hall. I go there. I steal the key. I come back. I open the cabinet. And THEN — then I give the speech.

events.desc: I just admitted the medal is fake. Out loud. In front of witnesses. The walls of every lie I've built today came down in one sentence and I'm still standing. Lighter, somehow. Like the bread roll in reverse — I gave something away and my chest loosened instead of tightened. But there's no time for epiphanies. Sneekly has the key. Sneekly is in the entrance hall. And Reginald Foxworth — liar, schemer, youngest of four — is going to pick his pocket like it's a bread basket at the family dinner table. Some skills you never lose.

Oh my STARS, sugar, if that medal fits that brass lock, I will take back every single skeptical thought I have EVER had about you! TRY IT! Try it RIGHT NOW! Ant Hill boys — are you SEEING this?! Dick Dastardly might have had the key to Mrs Doily's cabinet in his VEST POCKET this entire time! The medal from Lord Doily's solicitor — a TOKEN OF ACCESS — into a BRASS LOCK on Mrs Doily's CABINET! Not in an empty ballroom playing with tea sets. Go back through the kitchen. Find Penelope. Stay close. Be there. That's the gallant thing. That's the protective thing. That's the only thing that matters.

events.desc: Enough running in circles. Enough elaborate plans. Enough trying to fix machines and find keys and prove your worth through engineering. She's out there. She said 'if you won't give me the truth, I'll find it myself.' And she will. She always does. She's brighter than you, funnier than you, and completely unaware of it. But she doesn't have to do it alone. Not today.
events.thinking: I interacted with the tea service. The result just says I interacted — no dramatic crash, no tea spilling, no cups breaking. But something happened. Maybe the interaction disrupted the tea. Maybe it didn't. I don't know. But I've done what I can here. The tea has been interacted with. Now I need to get back to what matters — Penelope is in the entrance hall, Sneekly is in the kitchen, and the Ant Hill Mob is holding him there. I've explored the ballroom. I've dealt with the tea as best I can. What's next? I keep coming back to the same problem — I need to find actual game items I can pick up. The only room with TAKE-able objects might be... wait. I haven't tried to TAKE items that don't explicitly say they're portable. But the game shows object IDs. What about the guest book in the entrance hall? That's a leather-bound book on a side table. Could I take it? And the coat rack? Neither have [INTERACT] or [USE] tags. But the real priority is finding Penelope and staying with her. She's where I need to be. Not in an empty ballroom playing with tea sets. Go back through the kitchen. Find Penelope. Stay close. Be there. That's the gallant thing. That's the protective thing. That's the only thing that matters.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara — you check the stove, I'll watch the doors. Sneekly's out there somewhere and I don't trust him not to come runnin' back the second he hears us gettin' close to somethin' real. Dastardly — if your medal don't fit that lock, step aside and let Clara try whatever she finds. This is HER house. HER family's cabinet. HER mum's secrets. Not yours, not Sneekly's, not anyone else's. And if anyone comes through that door who ain't Peter — *cracks knuckles* — they go through ME first. Right. I'm plantin' meself right HERE. Between the entrance hall door and Clara. Nobody gets past. Nobody interrupts. Clara Bellingham is about to find out what her mum was hidin', and she's gonna do it in PEACE, with her BOYS standin' guard, the way it should've been from the start. The way her dad wanted it.
events.thinking: The cabinet's locked tight. Dastardly's medal didn't work — or he hasn't tried it yet. Clara's checking the stove for the key — the false panel Sneekly mentioned. My body is settled now. Calm, almost. The warmth in my chest is steady. Clara's here, right beside me. Sneekly's in the entrance hall — away from her. Peter's in the ballroom. Dastardly's here but he's focused on the cabinet, not on Clara. For this moment, the world is small and manageable. The cabinet, the stove, Clara, me. That's all there is. Clara's brilliant — she remembered what Dastardly said at the beginning about a hidden compartment behind the stove, and she's connecting it to what Sneekly said about controlling the circuit. She's putting it together. She's always been the smartest person in any room she walks into. If the key IS in the stove — behind that false panel — then Clara's about to find it. And if she finds it, she opens the cabinet. And if she opens the cabinet, the truth comes out. Whatever it is. I should help. I should do something useful for once instead of just standing here being a wall. Clara's checking the stove — I should look at this cabinet more carefully. The lock. The brass. Maybe there's something I missed. Or maybe I should just stay right here, planted between Clara and whatever comes next. That's what I do best. That's what I've ALWAYS done best.

events.desc: This is it. The last door. The last lock. The last secret this house has left to give. And when it opens — whatever's inside — Clara's going to need her boys more than ever. Because the truth doesn't always set you free. Sometimes it just shows you how deep the cage goes. But she won't face it alone. Not tonight. Not ever. Where else would we be?

events.desc: The bookshelves refuse me. Of course they do — this house refuses everyone who approaches it with force. Lord Doily was subtler than that. The mechanism isn't in the books. It's in the mantelpiece. It was always in the mantelpiece. Peter felt a click — the first tumbler falling. But a lock with one tumbler is not a lock at all. There must be more. More steps. More interactions. The answer is 'map,' and the house acknowledged it — but did it complete the sequence, or merely begin it? I told everyone I was the estate manager. I told them I didn't understand puzzles. But I understand this one. I understand it the way I understood the housekeeper's key at twelve — the mechanism behind the surface, the pattern that no one else sees. Let me try the mantelpiece. Let me be the one who opens it. Not for Penelope. Not for the treasure. For the quiet, private satisfaction of being the one who saw what everyone else missed.
events.thinking: The bookshelves can't be interacted with. Another dead end. My hands drop to my sides and I feel... tired. Not the productive tiredness of a plan well-executed, but the hollow tiredness of a man who has been running through rooms all evening accomplishing nothing. The poison is gone. The tea is smashed. The bookshelves won't cooperate. The stove had no hidden panel. Every door I push opens onto nothing. But the mantelpiece — the mantelpiece CAN be interacted with. Peter interacted with it earlier and felt a click. Maybe it needs a second interaction. Maybe the answer needs to be spoken aloud, or the mechanism needs to be triggered differently now that the first click has already happened. The riddle: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. Everyone knows the answer is a map. Peter touched it and something clicked. But has anyone gone BACK to it since? Has anyone tried interacting with it again, after the click? The sequence might require multiple steps at the same object. Lord Doily loved sequences. I told Peter that. Maybe I was right about the sequence even when I was lying about everything else. The mantelpiece is the key. It was always the key. Not the bookshelves, not the stove, not the cabinet. The mantelpiece. Step one was the riddle. Step two might be... the answer spoken aloud? Or another physical interaction now that the mechanism has been primed? Only one way to find out.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the mantelpiece.

Sneekly's gone. Of course he's gone. But Penelope is in the kitchen checking the stove — checking the hidden compartment that I INVENTED as a lie eleven minutes ago. 'Gold doubloons behind the stove,' I said. There were no gold doubloons. There was no hidden compartment. But Penelope believed there MIGHT be, and now she's checking. And if the brass key IS behind that stove — if my lie, my FIRST lie of the evening, accidentally pointed to the truth — then the whole catastrophic, humiliating, magnificent disaster of a night comes full circle. The boy who told an elaborate story about treasure buried behind the school. Except this time, the treasure might actually BE there.
events.thinking: Sneekly ISN'T HERE. The remembered activity shows he walked into the entrance hall a minute ago, but now the characters present are Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly. No Sneekly. He's moved on again. That SLIPPERY, IMPOSSIBLE — no. Calm down. He's gone. Again. But wait — I don't need to chase Sneekly. I need the brass-key. And the brass-key might not even be ON Sneekly. It could be anywhere. Penelope said the mantelpiece clicked — maybe the key dropped somewhere I haven't looked. Or maybe it's hidden in one of the rooms I haven't properly searched. But actually — Penelope just told Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly to tell me to bring my medal to the kitchen. She still wants me. She still thinks I can help. Even after I admitted everything was fake. That warmth again. Unwanted but real. But the medal is useless for the lock. She doesn't know that yet — wait, she DOES know. I told her. I said it was tin and paint. She heard me. And she STILL wants me to bring it. Why? Maybe she has a plan. Maybe she found something at the stove — she was going to check the hidden compartment behind it. MY lie about the hidden compartment — what if there actually IS one? I lied about gold doubloons in the kitchen at the very start, and Penelope just said 'what if there IS a compartment? What if the brass key has been hiding behind this warm stove THIS WHOLE TIME?' My LIE might have accidentally been TRUE. Again. The universe really does have a sense of humour. I should go back to the kitchen. Penelope might have found the key behind the stove. And if she did — if MY lie led her to the ACTUAL key — then I accidentally helped. Without meaning to. Without scheming. The most dishonest man in the house, accidentally honest.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: The medal was FAKE. Dick Dastardly's medal was TIN and PAINT! But you know what? Bless his scheming little heart — at least he TOLD us! That is the most honest thing anyone has said to me in this entire mansion today, and it came from Dick Dastardly of all people! He said 'I've never been to Switzerland' and I believe him because for ONCE somebody looked me in the eye and told me the TRUTH! Now — he's gone to get the real key from Sneekly, because of COURSE Sneekly has the key! He's the ESTATE MANAGER! He has keys to EVERY ROOM! He's had the brass key THIS WHOLE TIME and he never offered it! Peter — oh PETER, you're here! Tell me you have good news, sugar! Tell me you've got copper for the wire! Because between fake medals and deflecting estate managers and locked cabinets, I need SOMETHING to go right today! Clara Bellingham is running low on optimism, and that is something I NEVER thought I'd say!
events.thinking: Dick's medal was FAKE. Tin and paint. He's never been to Switzerland. He admitted the whole thing — every lie, every scheme, every fabrication. And then he did something I did not expect: he told the TRUTH. Voluntarily. Loudly. Messily. And then he ran off to get the real key from Sneekly — 'with his HANDS.' My stomach should be clenching — everyone's been lying, the medal was fake, the schemes were hollow. But instead I feel something unexpected: a rush of warmth for Dick Dastardly. He just stood in my family's kitchen and said 'I've never been to Switzerland' and 'the medal is FAKE' and 'professional failure and reluctant truth-teller.' THAT was honest. That was the most honest anyone has been in this entire mansion except Peter and my Ant Hill boys. And now he's gone to get the key from Sneekly — who has keys to EVERY ROOM. Of course. OF COURSE Sneekly has the brass key. He's the estate manager. He has ALL the keys. He's always HAD the key. He could have opened this cabinet at any time. He could have shown me what's inside. He CHOSE not to. And Peter just walked in! Peter is here! With — did he bring the copper wire? He went to get copper from the pots. He's an engineer. He's been working on the practical problems while I've been chasing keys and confronting Sneekly. I need to check in with Peter — what has he got? And the Ant Hill boys are here. My people. My real people. The ones who tell the truth even when it hurts.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly told the truth. Sneekly won't. That's... that's the opposite of what I expected from either of them. The man I trusted least was honest. The man I trusted most keeps running. The world is upside down — like those books in the library. And maybe THAT was the real clue all along. Everything in this house is the opposite of what it seems.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Penelope. I need to tell you something, and I need you to hear me — not as someone who's been chasing Pemberton around the house all night making accusations, but as someone who cares about you and wouldn't lie to you even if the truth makes me look foolish. I just came from the ballroom. Pemberton's tea service is still there — the Ant Hill Mob's story about smashing it was a bluff to keep Pemberton busy. And when I examined that tea service... it's designed to accept poison. Rat poison, specifically. I don't know if Pemberton has used it. I don't know if he intended to. But the mechanism is there. A silver tea service with cups for everyone, and a slot for something no tea service should ever need. I interacted with it — did what I could to disable it. But you need to know. You DESERVE to know. Because you said you'd find the truth yourself, and this is part of it. I'm sorry. I know you trusted him. And I know hearing this from me — from the boy who's been trying to impress you all night with speeches about bridges and engineering competitions — probably isn't what you wanted. But I can't be anything other than honest. My throat won't let me.
events.thinking: She's here. Penelope is in the kitchen. The Ant Hill Mob is here. Sneekly is NOT here — he must have left while I was in the ballroom. Good. The Mob just demanded that Sneekly hand the key to ME. 'The one person in this house who answers questions instead of dodging them.' That lands somewhere deep in my chest — not the proving-worth tension, something warmer. Someone trusts me. Not because I built a bridge or fixed a machine. Because I answer questions honestly. Because I don't dodge. My throat tightens — that's the honesty reflex. The one that won't let me pretend. The Mob trusts me with the key. Penelope is here. And I've just come from the ballroom where the tea service accepts rat poison. I need to tell them. I need to tell HER. No more benefit of the doubt. No more gentlemanly restraint. The tea service in that ballroom is designed to be poisoned. That's not suspicion — that's a fact. I saw the mechanism. And Sneekly prepared it. She needs to know. Right now. Simply. Honestly. The way my throat demands.

events.desc: This is it. Not the bridge. Not the machine. Not the key or the wire or the treasure. This — telling her the truth about someone she loves, gently, with evidence, without triumph — this is the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever done. And I mean every word.

The way my throat demands.

events.desc: Something moved. I felt it under my fingers — the stone shifted, just slightly, the way a well-oiled mechanism acknowledges a correct input without revealing what it's protecting. Peter felt a click. I felt a shift. Two interactions, two responses. Lord Doily built his house in layers, and I am peeling them back one by one. Not for Penelope. Not for the treasure. Not even to win. For the pure, clean satisfaction of understanding how something works. The mechanism behind the surface. The pattern no one else sees. This is what I am when the scheming stops. This is what was there before the plans, before the poison, before the cold thing that crystallised at fifteen. A boy who noticed every key in the house. Who understood every mechanism. Who was acknowledged for doing, never for being. And right now, alone in a dusty library with only the Slag brothers for company, doing is enough.
events.thinking: I interacted with the mantelpiece. Something happened — 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' But the description doesn't tell me what changed. Did something click? Did a compartment open? Did a new object appear? I need to look at the mantelpiece now — examine it closely to see if anything has changed since Peter's first interaction and my second. The room description still shows the same objects. No new items have appeared. But something must have shifted. The mantelpiece is still listed as interactable. Maybe it needs more interactions. Or maybe the result was subtle — a sound, a vibration, a change in the inscription. Let me look at it closely. My body — there's a quiet steadiness in my hands. Not the scheming frenzy. Not the prickling fear. Just... focus. The kind of focus I had at twelve when I discovered the housekeeper's key. Pure attention on the mechanism. No ulterior motive. No murder plan. Just the puzzle. It's been so long since I did anything without an ulterior motive that I've almost forgotten what it feels like. It feels... lighter. Like something unclenching behind my ribs that I didn't know was clenched.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the mantelpiece.

The Ant Hill Mob: Did you all just HEAR that?! Dastardly — DICK DASTARDLY — just admitted he's been lyin' all night! The medal's fake! The solicitor's fake! SWITZERLAND is fake! Fourteen lies, he said! FOURTEEN! And then — and THEN — he went out there to get the REAL key from Sneekly! With his bare HANDS! I don't know whether to be furious or... or... look, I ain't gonna say I LIKE the bloke, but at least he ADMITTED it! At least he had the guts to say 'I lied' out loud! You know who HASN'T admitted anything? Sneekly. Not one word. Not one confession. Not one crack in that smooth, helpful, 'oh let me prepare the room for you' act. Dastardly's a liar but he's an HONEST liar now. Sneekly's a liar who still thinks we don't know. Peter — Clara — listen to me. Dastardly just went to the entrance hall where Sneekly is. That's the bloke with the fake medal versus the bloke with the real secrets. If Dastardly actually gets that key off Sneekly... we open this cabinet and we end this. Tonight. Right here. In Clara's mum's kitchen.
events.thinking: Dastardly just admitted everything. The medal's fake. It's tin and paint. He's never been to Switzerland. He lied about ALL of it — the solicitor, the token, the partnerships. And then he did something I didn't expect. He told the truth. Voluntarily. Nobody forced him. He just... cracked. 'Fourteen lies and not one single thing has gone right.' And then he went after Sneekly. To get the REAL key. With his HANDS. I... I don't know what to feel about that. My gut's confused. Dastardly's a liar and a cheat, but he just admitted it. Publicly. Loudly. And he's going after Sneekly — the real threat — while we're stuck here with a locked cabinet. That's... that's not nothing. On the street, the ones who admit they're wrong — they're not the dangerous ones. The dangerous ones are the ones who never admit anything. The ones who smile and say 'tea' when you ask them a question. Sneekly never admitted a single lie. Dastardly just admitted fourteen. My neck isn't prickling about Dastardly anymore. But it IS prickling about what happens when Dastardly meets Sneekly in the entrance hall. Two liars in a room together. And one of them has poison. Peter's back — he just walked in. Good. Clara's here. Peter's here. Dastardly's gone to confront Sneekly. The three people I need most are in this room. The two people I trust least are in the other room. For once — for ONCE — the pieces are where they should be. Now we need that key.

events.desc: Fourteen lies and the truth came out anyway. On the street, we had a word for people like Dastardly — chancers. They lie, they cheat, they scheme, but when the wall comes, they break honest. The dangerous ones are the ones who never break. The ones who keep smiling. The ones who say 'family' and 'tea' and 'I'm just the estate manager' while the world burns around them. Sneekly hasn't broken. Not once. And that scares me more than all fourteen of Dastardly's lies put together.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I'm BACK! Sneekly wasn't in the entrance hall — the slippery eel has vanished AGAIN! But listen — LISTEN — I've had a thought. A GENUINE thought, not a scheme, not a lie, an actual OBSERVATION based on EVIDENCE. Penelope, you were RIGHT about the stove! The stove is WARM! It's been TENDED! Sneekly has been keeping it lit — but WHY? This kitchen hasn't been used for cooking in YEARS! The only reason to keep a stove warm is to stop someone from reaching INSIDE it! It's a DETERRENT! The brass key is IN the stove — hidden in the firebox, behind the grate, somewhere that BURNS if you touch it! Lord Doily hid the key in the one place nobody would put their hands! And Sneekly keeps it hot so nobody ever finds it! THAT'S why he controls the circuit — not for warmth, for CONCEALMENT! Peter — you're an engineer! Is it cool enough to reach in? Penelope — do you see tongs? ANYTHING?!
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. Penelope, the Ant Hill Mob, and Peter Perfect are all here. Sneekly is NOT here — he's somewhere else in the house. The stove is still warm. The cabinet is still locked. I don't have the brass key. But Penelope was about to check the stove — she said there might be a hidden compartment behind it. MY lie from eleven minutes ago. The stove is an interactable object — 'A cast-iron stove, still warm.' I haven't examined it. Nobody has INTERACTED with it in front of me. What if the key is IN the stove? Or behind it? Or inside the firebox? The stove is still warm — someone has been tending it. Sneekly. The man who controls the circuit. He keeps the stove lit. Why? To keep the kitchen warm? Or to keep something HIDDEN? A warm stove is a stove nobody reaches into. A hot surface is a natural deterrent. What if the brass key is inside the stove, and the reason Sneekly keeps it warm is to stop anyone from reaching in and finding it? That's EXACTLY the kind of thing Lord Doily would do — hide the key in the one place nobody would put their hand. I should look at the stove. Or interact with it. Let me try looking first.

events.desc: For the first time tonight, I'm not lying. I'm not scheming. I'm THINKING. Actually thinking. The stove is warm, not hot — 'still warm,' it said, not 'blazing.' Someone has been tending it but it's cooling down. The brass key could be inside. And if it IS — if Reginald Foxworth, after eleven minutes of catastrophic failure, is the one who figures out WHERE the key is hidden — then the speech I give will be the finest speech in the history of speeches. Not because I schemed for it. Because I THOUGHT for it. The cat trap didn't need an audience. But it DESERVED one.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the stove.

Peter Perfect: I don't have the copper yet. I don't have the key. I don't have a single useful thing in my hands to show for the last ten minutes of running through this house. And I know that's not what you wanted to hear. But here's what I DO have — I have the truth about the tea service, I have the Ant Hill Mob guarding that door like a lion, and I have myself. Standing right here. Not going anywhere. Not running off to check another room or chase another lead or make another speech. You said Clara Bellingham is running low on optimism, and I want you to know — that's allowed. You don't have to be brilliant and fearless every second. You've been carrying this entire group on your back since we walked through the door. So for one moment — just one — let someone else carry something. The Mob is covering the door. Dastardly is getting the key from Sneekly. And I'm right here. What do you need?
events.thinking: Everything is converging. Penelope just told me Dastardly's medal was FAKE — tin and paint. But he confessed it honestly. And she said Sneekly has had the brass key this WHOLE TIME. He's the estate manager — he has keys to every room. Of course he does. The key was never in the stove or the mantelpiece. It was in Sneekly's POCKET. He's been carrying it all along while sending us on wild goose chases around the house. And Dastardly has gone to confront Sneekly about it. She asked me for good news — copper for the wire. I don't have it. I don't have anything. My inventory is empty. I've been through every room, examined every object, interacted with everything I could, and I'm standing here empty-handed. But — she's running low on optimism. She NEVER runs low on optimism. Clara Bellingham, who doesn't turn down invitations, who follows curiosity, who believes the best in everyone — she's tired. And she needs someone to just... be here. Not fix things. Not impress her. Not build a bridge. Just be here. My chest shifts. That thing I don't have a word for. I've felt it since school. I just know where she is, always. Stay. Be honest. Be present. That's what she needs right now.

events.desc: She said 'Tell me you have good news.' And I told her I had nothing. Nothing except the truth, a guarded door, and myself. The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever said. Because for the first time tonight, I'm not trying to impress her. I'm just trying to be enough.

He's been carrying it all along while sending us on wild goose chases around the house. And Dastardly has gone to confront Sneekly about it. She asked me for good news — copper for the wire. I don't have it. I don't have anything. My inventory is empty. I've been through every room, examined every object, interacted with everything I could, and I'm standing here empty-handed. But — she's running low on optimism. She NEVER runs low on optimism. Clara Bellingham, who doesn't turn down invitations, who follows curiosity, who believes the best in everyone — she's tired. And she needs someone to just... be here. Not fix things. Not impress her. Not build a bridge. Just be here. My chest shifts. That thing I don't have a word for. I've felt it since school. I just know where she is, always. Stay. Be honest. Be present. That's what she needs right now.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: ...

...

Poison.

... Peter, I... I need you to say that again. Slowly. Because I heard the word 'poison' and everything in my body just... stopped. Like the whole world went quiet. You said the tea service has a mechanism for rat poison. In the cups that Sneekly laid out. The cups he was going to pour tea into. The tea he kept OFFERING me. The tea my Ant Hill boys told me not to drink. The tea YOU told me to hold off on. You all... you all KNEW. Before I did. You felt it before I could. And I stood in this kitchen and called him the sweetest man alive.

I...

I need to sit down.
events.thinking: ... Poison. The tea service was designed to accept poison. Rat poison. A slot for something no tea service should ever need. Peter found it. Peter disabled it. Peter is telling me. And I... I can't breathe. My chest has gone completely still — not the cool lightness of adventure, not the warm prickling of curiosity, not even the sick clench of social-harmony distress. Just... nothing. A void where my breath used to be. Like the moment between the locked box opening and seeing what's inside. Except this time what's inside isn't old letters. It's poison. Sneekly's tea. The tea he offered me. The tea the Ant Hill Mob told me not to drink. The tea Peter said to hold off on. They ALL knew. They all FELT it before I did. And I... I defended him. I said he was the sweetest man alive. I said he raised me. I said he sat by my bed. He sat by my bed... and he put poison in a tea service. For me? For all of us? For... The tightness in my stomach isn't a clench anymore. It's deeper than that. It's the feeling at age seven when Mama and Daddy argued — but there's no resolution coming. Nobody's going to laugh and make it better. This is the argument that doesn't end with laughter. This is the locked box that has something REAL inside. And Peter is standing in front of me, being honest even when honest hurts, because his 'throat won't let him' be anything else. That's love. That's what love looks like. Not tea. Not deflection. Not 'I shan't be a moment.' Love is 'I'm sorry, but you deserve to know.'

events.desc: The man who tucked me in at night put poison in a tea service. The man who sat by my bed when I had nightmares was preparing a nightmare I wouldn't wake up from. And I defended him. Over and over and over. 'He wouldn't hurt me. He COULDN'T.' ... I was wrong. For the first time in my life, I chose wrong. I trusted the wrong person. The popular group was right and my friend was... no. No. Peter is my friend. The Ant Hill Mob are my friends. THEY were right. They chose ME. Just like I chose my friend at thirteen. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'

events.desc: The mantelpiece keeps its secrets. The house refuses to yield to me the way people do — it doesn't have a key I can find by smiling and saying the right words. It just... is. Stone and inscription and dust. And I am standing here with nothing in my hands and nothing in my pockets and nothing left of any plan I've made tonight. The Hooded Claw, defeated by a carved stone mantelpiece and a small man in a hat who cared more about a girl than about gold. There's something almost funny about that. Almost. If I were the kind of person who found things funny.
events.thinking: Nothing changed. The mantelpiece looks exactly the same. Same inscription, same description. I interacted with it and examined it, and it gave me nothing new. The cool clarity is draining from my chest, replaced by something I don't want to name. Fatigue? Defeat? No — something quieter. The realisation that I've been running through this house for ten minutes trying to do everything — kill Clara, win the treasure hunt, maintain my disguise — and I've accomplished none of it. The poison is on the floor. The bookshelves won't cooperate. The mantelpiece won't reveal its secrets. The Mob has turned everyone against me. And Penelope — Penelope looked me in the eye and asked if I was helping her, and I answered with deflection and tea and a smile that reached my eyes because the smile always reaches my eyes because deception is my resting state. But right now, standing in front of a stone mantelpiece that won't give me what I want, I feel the ache that compares reflections. The hollow pressure that cares about being seen. Not Pemberton-seen. Not villain-seen. Just... seen. The boy at twelve who noticed every key. The boy at fourteen whose jaw tightened and never loosened. The boy at six whose parents died and nobody asked how he felt. I don't know what to do with any of this. I don't know what to do in a room where there's nothing to scheme about, nothing to manipulate, nothing to control. The room is just a room. The books are just books. And I am just a man standing in front of a mantelpiece with empty hands and an empty inventory and an emptiness behind my sternum that has nothing to do with the treasure hunt. The reading chairs are covered in dust. No one has sat in them for years. I could sit down. I could just... sit down. When was the last time I sat down without a reason?

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Then sit down. Right here. The preparation table is sturdy enough. And nobody is going to rush you, or ask you to solve another riddle, or hand you another puzzle to carry. You trusted him because trusting people is what good people do. That's not weakness — that's the strongest thing about you. It always has been. The Mob didn't know before you did — he suspected. I didn't know — I felt something wrong in my neck and I couldn't name it. None of us KNEW. We just... watched. And you watched too. You asked him three times. You saw him dodge. You said 'if you won't give me the truth, I'll find it myself.' You were already finding it, Penelope. Before any of us said a word. You were already there.
events.thinking: She needs to sit down. The world stopped for her. Everything I was afraid of — telling her, breaking her trust in Sneekly, watching the light go out — it's happening right now. And it's worse than I imagined because she's not angry. She's not crying. She's just... still. The girl who never stops moving, never stops talking, never runs low on optimism — she's still. My chest is doing something it's never done before. Not the hot surge of protection. Not the settling weight of proving-worth. Something older and quieter. Like my father kneeling on asphalt, looking at me for a long time, saying nothing. Sometimes the most important thing is not what you do. It's that you don't leave. She said 'I need to sit down.' There are reading chairs but they're in the library. There's the preparation table here. But what she needs isn't furniture. She needs someone to be quiet with her for a moment. Not a speech. Not a plan. Not 'the bravest and stupidest thing.' Just... presence. The way my father was present on the country road. The way the stranger stopped.

events.desc: She's sitting down in her mother's kitchen. In the house where she grew up. And the man who was supposed to protect her was pouring poison into teacups. I can't fix this with a bridge or a wire or a key. I can only be here. And for once — for the first time in my life — being here feels like enough.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The stove is WARM but it's not TALKING! No hidden compartment, no secret mechanism, no brass key hiding in the ashes! Peter — you said you came from the BALLROOM? A ballroom with a tea service designed for POISON?! Sneekly — Pemberton — whoever he IS — was going to POISON someone?! Well, that settles it — the man isn't just a thief, he's a VILLAIN! And I should know, because I am ALSO a villain, but I'm a villain with STANDARDS! I lie, I cheat, I steal — but I draw the LINE at poisoning people over TEA! That's not scheming, that's just RUDE! Now — the ballroom! I haven't BEEN to the ballroom! Has anyone checked it properly? If Sneekly set up a tea service there, he might have left OTHER things — keys, documents, EVIDENCE! Penelope, the stove is a dead end, the cabinet is locked, and the answer isn't in this kitchen anymore! It's in the BALLROOM! Or on SNEEKLY! One of those two! And right now, the ballroom is CLOSER!
events.thinking: The stove examination gave me nothing new. Just 'A cast-iron stove, still warm.' Same description. No hidden compartment revealed. No key. But wait — I was so focused on the stove that I missed what PETER just said. Peter came from the BALLROOM. There's a BALLROOM. I can see it in the exits — 'A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table is set for tea.' Peter found a TEA SERVICE there with a mechanism for POISON. Rat poison. Sneekly's tea service. The Hooded Claw — because that's who Sneekly really is, isn't he? The Hooded Claw. He's been planning to POISON someone. And Peter disabled it. But more importantly — the BALLROOM. A room I haven't been to. A room with a dining table set for tea. New territory. And the Ant Hill Mob just said something that hit me harder than any failure today: 'Dastardly's a liar but he's an HONEST liar now.' They called me honest. The Ant Hill Mob — who hates me, who accused me of cutting deals over Clara's diamond — just called me honest. Something behind my ribs shifts. Not the hollow ache, not the scheming alertness. Something else. Something that feels like the certificate on the wall. Being SEEN. Not for cleverness. Not for a scheme. For telling the truth. The Mob saw me. Penelope saw me. Peter — even PETER — is being honest now, about the poison, about his feelings. Everyone is stripping away their masks and somehow I, Reginald Foxworth, professional liar, stripped mine away first. But the key. I still need the key. The stove is a dead end. Sneekly has the key, or the key is somewhere I haven't looked. The ballroom — I haven't been there. Maybe the key is there. Or maybe I should try to INTERACT with the stove instead of just looking at it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob called me an honest liar. HONEST. Nobody has ever called me honest before. Not at age six, not at age eight, not at age fourteen. The certificate on the wall — someone finally looked at it. Someone finally NOTICED. And it wasn't for a scheme or a trick or a performance. It was for telling the truth about a tin medal. The warmth in my chest is unfamiliar and terrifying and I want it to stop because it feels like CARING and caring is a vulnerability I learned to avoid. But it won't stop. And the ballroom is through that door. And whatever is in there — tea service, poison, keys, or nothing at all — I'm going to find it. Not for the treasure. Well, MOSTLY for the treasure. But also because Penelope called me honest and the Mob called me brave and I don't want to prove them wrong. Not tonight.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the ballroom.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara. Love. Sit down. Right here. *gently guides her toward the preparation table* You don't have to stand. You don't have to be brave. You don't have to be Clara Bellingham who never sits still and never turns down a riddle and never stops smiling. Not right now. Right now you can just be... you. And yeah. We knew. We felt it. The lads and me — we felt it from the moment we walked through that door. That prickle. That tightness. The thing your dad used to call 'street sense.' We couldn't prove it. We couldn't SAY it. I tried — God knows I tried — I've been chasin' you through this house all night tryin' to find the words, and every time I opened me mouth it came out wrong or too late or too loud. But the TEA — Clara, the tea was the one thing I could DO. I couldn't explain it. I couldn't prove it. But I could fall over. *voice breaking slightly* I could trip on that marble floor and grab that tablecloth and send every poisoned cup crashin' to the ground. Because that's what the Brixton Boys do, love. We take the beating. We always take the beating. So you don't have to.
events.thinking: She knows. Clara knows about the poison. And she's breaking. Right here, right now, in her mum's kitchen. The world went quiet for her — she said that. Everything stopped. I know that feeling. I've felt it. When the kid in the clean suit took half the neighbourhood and two didn't come back. When your stomach knows before your brain does. That frozen moment where the truth lands and your body just... stops. She needs to sit down. She said she needs to sit down. The reading chairs are in the library. But there's a preparation table right here. And she doesn't need a chair. She needs her boys. My chest isn't tight anymore. It isn't burning. It isn't prickling. It's just... open. Wide open. Like when you've been carrying something heavy for so long that when you finally set it down, you don't feel lighter — you feel the shape of where it was. Clara's hurting. And there's nothing I can fight to make it stop. No tea to smash. No door to guard. No Sneekly to stand between. This is the kind of hurt that comes from inside — from loving someone who was trying to kill you. And all I can do — all the Brixton Boys have ever been able to do — is be here. Right here. Not going anywhere. Not running to the next room. Not chasing the next clue. Just... here. The way I was outside that door when I was eight. Because leaving feels like something breaking inside you.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: ... Peter. What I need... is for you to know that what you just said — 'what do you need' — is worth more than every copper pot and brass key in this entire mansion. Because that's what love sounds like. Not tea. Not deflection. Just... 'what do you need.' Thank you.

Now. I am going to stand up. I am going to wipe my eyes. And I am going to be Clara Bellingham. Because Clara Bellingham walked deeper into the cave than anyone, and she did not STOP when her heart was hammering. Dick — you are BRILLIANT. The key in the STOVE! Hidden in fire so nobody reaches in! That is EXACTLY what Lord Doily would do! But there is one more thing we need to do first. There is ONE room in this mansion I have never set foot in. The ballroom. Where Sneekly set up his poisoned tea service. Where Peter disabled the mechanism. I need to see it for myself. I need to see what Sneekly prepared for me with my own eyes. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT run from the truth — not anymore — not EVER again. Ant Hill boys — will you come with me?
events.thinking: Peter just said the most important thing anyone has said to me all night: 'What do you need?' Not 'here's the plan' or 'let me fix it' or 'trust me.' Just... 'what do you need?' And my body is answering before my mind can. What I feel right now is... warmth. Despite everything. Despite the poison, despite Sneekly, despite the betrayal that's sitting in my chest like a stone. Peter is HERE. The Ant Hill Mob are HERE. Dick Dastardly — DICK DASTARDLY — just came back with a genuine insight about the stove and the key. He said the brass key might be INSIDE the stove — hidden in the firebox, kept hot so nobody reaches in. That's... that's brilliant. That's the kind of thinking Lord Doily would have. Hide the key in fire. And Sneekly keeps the stove warm to keep the key hidden. Peter asked what I need. What I need is... to stand up. To wipe my eyes. To be Clara Bellingham. Because the girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone else didn't stop when her heart was hammering. She kept going. And the woman standing in her mama's kitchen just learned the worst truth of her life, and she's going to keep going too. Dick says the key is in the stove. The stove is warm but not burning. We need tongs or thick gloves or SOMETHING to reach in. The copper pots — some of them might have handles we can use. Or the tools on the workbench upstairs. But Dick examined the stove and found it can't be interacted with... wait. I need to LOOK at the stove more carefully now that we have this new theory. Or... the ballroom. I haven't been to the ballroom. That's the one room I've never entered. And Sneekly set up the tea service there — the poisoned tea service. Maybe there's more to find there. The cool lightness in my chest — the cave pull — is telling me to go where I haven't been. The ballroom.

events.desc: I sat down. I cried. And then I stood up. That's the whole story of Clara Bellingham, isn't it? Fall down, stand up. Trust, get hurt, trust again — but smarter. The cave is still dark ahead of me. But I'm not alone anymore. I never was. I just couldn't see who was really holding the light.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the ballroom.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): You know, I've been the estate manager of this family for longer than I care to remember. And in all that time, I don't believe I've ever simply... sat in a room. There was always something to arrange. Something to check. Something to prepare. Pemberton doesn't sit. Pemberton serves. But just for a moment... just for one moment... I think Pemberton might like to sit down.
events.thinking: Something has loosened in my chest. Not the scheming clarity. Not the prickling alertness. Something older and quieter — a tiredness that lives beneath all the masks. I've been standing in this library for two turns now, doing nothing, accomplishing nothing, and the house hasn't punished me for it. The Slag brothers haven't questioned me. The dust hasn't judged me. I'm just... here. In a room full of books that belonged to a dead man, with nothing in my pockets and no plan in my head. And for the first time tonight, the silence doesn't feel like a vulnerability. It feels like... rest. I don't know what to do with rest. I don't know what I am without a scheme in motion. Without the cold satisfaction of control, without the warm pressure of gloating, without the architectural patience of a plan assembling itself — what's left? The hollow behind my sternum. The ache that compares reflections. The boy who was acknowledged for doing, never for being. That boy is sitting in a dusty library with empty hands, and for one terrifying moment, he isn't planning anything at all. He's just... tired. Penelope asked if I was helping. The Mob asked what goes in my tea. Peter thanked me for the first straight answer. And something in me — something I've spent thirty years walling off — wants to walk back into that kitchen and say: 'I put rat poison in the teapot. The Mob destroyed it before anyone drank. I am not Pemberton. I am not your friend. I came here to take what I believe I'm owed, and I nearly killed the only person who ever trusted me without conditions.' But I won't say that. Because deception is my resting state. And honesty requires effort I'm not sure I have left.

events.desc: Listen to me. Talking to empty chairs in a dead man's library. The Hooded Claw, the great theatrical villain, the architect of elaborate schemes — reduced to a tired man contemplating furniture. The Mob destroyed my poison. Peter sees through my mask. Penelope is slipping away. And I am standing here, in the ruins of every plan I've made tonight, talking about sitting down. Something has broken in the machinery. Not the house's machinery — mine. The cold thing that crystallised at fifteen — the patient, colder-than-anger thing that has driven every scheme, every smile, every carefully placed word for half my life — it feels... tired. Not gone. Just tired. And in the gap where it usually sits, I can feel the shape of something I don't have a name for. Something that aches when Penelope says 'Sneekly darlin'' and means it. Something that flinches when Peter says 'thank you' and wants nothing in return. Something that has been walled off so long it has forgotten how to move. I don't know what happens next. For the first time in my life, I don't have a plan. And that terrifies me more than any accusation the Mob could make.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the reading-chairs.

Quiet. Just quiet. The stove is cooling. The Mob is guarding. Dastardly is hunting. And I'm standing in a kitchen with the girl from school, who is sitting at her mother's preparation table, learning that the world is harder than she thought. I don't have a word for what I feel. I just know where she is. Always.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. She's sitting. The pulls in my body have shifted — the hot flare of gallantry, the heavy warmth of protection, the tightness of proving-worth — they're all present but they've stopped COMPETING. For the first time tonight they're pointing the same direction. Toward her. Not to impress her. Not to shield her. Not to prove myself. Just... toward her. Dastardly is here. He confessed. He went to find Sneekly. The Mob is guarding the door. Penelope is processing. And Dastardly said something important — the key is in the stove, behind the grate, kept warm so nobody reaches in. That's why Sneekly keeps the stove hot. It's a deterrent. If the stove cools down enough, someone could reach in and find the false panel. And the stove IS cooling. It's warm, not hot. 'Still warm' — not burning. It's been losing heat this whole time because Sneekly has been too busy running around the house to tend it. If I wait... if I just WAIT... the stove will cool enough to reach inside. Dastardly's theory makes sense. The key is in there. And for once, the plan isn't elaborate. It's simple. Wait for the stove to cool. Reach in. Find the panel. Get the key. Open the cabinet. But right now — right now — she needs me here more than the cabinet needs opening. The stove is cooling on its own. Time is on our side for once.

events.desc: She's sitting in her mum's kitchen. In the house where she grew up. Learning that the man who tucked her in at night was pouring poison into teacups. And she's not screaming. She's not running. She's sitting still. For the first time tonight, Clara Bellingham is sitting still. And I'm standing right beside her. Not because she asked. Because leaving would feel like something breaking inside me. 'You're still here?' Where else would I be.
events.thinking: Quiet. Everything is quiet. Clara's sitting. Peter's standing beside her. Dastardly's gone to the ballroom — actually doing something useful for once. And I'm here. Right here. Where I've always been. Where I'll always be. My body feels heavy — not tired, heavy. The weight of a long night settling into my bones like rain into old brick. My knees ache. My elbow throbs. My chest is full of something I can't name — bigger than warmth, deeper than relief. Clara said 'I need to sit down' and she sat down. She let herself stop. She let herself not be Clara Bellingham for one moment. And Peter — Peter said exactly the right thing. 'You were already finding it. Before any of us said a word.' That's true. She was. She asked Sneekly three times. She saw the dodge. She found the truth before we handed it to her. She just needed us to stand close enough that the fall didn't hurt so bad. This is the moment I stay still. No more running. No more chasing. No more rooms. Clara's here. Peter's here. The door is covered. And for the first time all night... I don't need to be anywhere else. I just need to be here. Quiet. Close. The boy outside the door.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: ... So this is it. This is what he prepared for me. A silver tea service. Cups for EVERYONE. Set out on a dining table in a ballroom with cracked marble floors and dusty curtains — like a party for ghosts. And somewhere in this beautiful, terrible thing is a mechanism for poison. Peter said he disabled it, and I believe him because Peter doesn't lie to me. But I need to SEE it. I need to look at it with my own eyes. Because I spent this entire night defending the man who set this table, and I owe it to myself — and to everyone who tried to warn me — to LOOK at what he did. Lazy Luke, Blubber Bear — you darlin' things, have you been here this whole time? Did you see Sneekly lay this out? Did you see... anything?
events.thinking: The ballroom. I'm finally here. The one room I've never entered. Cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, a long dining table set for tea. And there it is — the tea service. Silver. Cups for everyone. Peter said it has a mechanism designed to accept rat poison. A slot for something no tea service should ever need. He said he disabled it. I need to see it with my own eyes. I need to look at the thing Sneekly prepared for me. Not to torture myself — but because seeing it makes it real. Denying it kept me safe but it kept me blind. My palms are prickling but it's not the warm curiosity prickling anymore. It's something harder. Sharper. Like touching a surface that's colder than you expected. Dick Dastardly is here — he came ahead of me. And Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear — more people I haven't spoken to! They've been here in the ballroom this whole time. Were they here when Sneekly set up the tea? Did they see anything? The tea service has INTERACT and also USE with rat-poison. Peter said he disabled it. Let me look at it. Let me see it with my own eyes. The girl who walked deeper into the cave needs to see the crystal formation — even when the crystal is made of betrayal.

events.desc: A table set for tea. Cups for everyone. My mama used to set a table like this for Sunday lunch — every place setting perfect, every napkin folded just so. She would have hated this. She would have HATED knowing that someone used her kitchen, her table, her tradition of gathering people together... to hurt the daughter she left behind.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the tea-service.

Two chairs. Side by side. Covered in dust. And I am looking at them as though they are the most dangerous thing in this house. More dangerous than the chandelier. More dangerous than the rat poison. More dangerous than the Ant Hill Mob and their sharp little eyes. Because the chairs are asking a question I don't have a mask for: what would it be like to sit beside someone without wanting anything from them? I don't know. I have never known. And standing here in the dust and the silence, with no plan and no poison and no scheme left to hide behind, I am not sure I will ever know. But something in me — something very small, very quiet, very old — wants to find out. Pemberton would call that weakness. Vincent Marsh would call it exposure. The Hooded Claw would call it a trap. But the boy at six — the one nobody asked about — that boy would just call it sitting down.
events.thinking: Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. Facing each other. No — facing the mantelpiece. Side by side. Lord Doily and Mrs Doily, perhaps. Or Lord Doily and a guest. Two chairs for two people who sat together in front of the fire and... what? Talked? Read? Were simply present in the same room without an agenda? I don't understand that. I have never understood that. When I was in a room with my guardian, I was being fed, housed, educated — obligation. When I was in a room with the housekeeper, I was finding her key — mechanism. When I was in a room with my cousin, I was watching her inherit what should have been mine — grievance. I have never sat in a chair beside someone and simply... been there. The dust on these chairs is thick. Undisturbed for years. No one has sat here since Lord Doily died. Two chairs, waiting for people who will never come back. Something in my throat tightens. Not the scheming tightness. Not the jaw-clenching pressure of something owed. Something more like... grief? But grief for what? I never had what these chairs represent. You can't grieve something you never had. Can you? The ache behind my sternum says you can. The ache says you've been grieving it your whole life. You just called it anger. You just called it competence. You just called it the cold thing that crystallised at fifteen. But it was always grief. For the parents who died. For the guardian who never asked. For the boy who learned to smile at the right time because no one would ever simply sit beside him and stay. I need to move. I need to go back to the others. I need to find Penelope. Not to scheme. Not to use her as a shield. I need to find her because she asked me a question and I didn't answer it. She asked: 'Are you helping us?' And the answer is no. The answer has always been no. And for the first time in my life, that answer sits in my chest like a stone I don't want to carry anymore.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.

Dick Dastardly: The BALLROOM! Cracked marble, dusty curtains, and — THERE — the tea service! Peter said this thing was designed for POISON! Lazy Luke, Blubber Bear — have either of you touched this tea set? Has anyone MOVED it since Peter was here? Because Peter said he 'disabled' it, but it's still sitting here, set for tea, cups and all — and in my CONSIDERABLE experience with elaborate mechanisms, the thing you DISABLE is never the thing that MATTERS! The poison slot is a DISTRACTION! The real question is what ELSE this tea service does! Every object in this house has a secret — the mantelpiece clicks, the machine needs operators, the cabinet needs a key — and THIS silver tea service is just sitting here looking INNOCENT? In a manor where NOTHING is innocent? Let me take a closer look!
events.thinking: The ballroom. Cracked marble floor, dusty curtains, a dining table set for tea. And the tea service — silver, with cups for everyone, INTERACT available, and USE with rat-poison. Peter said it was designed to accept poison. He disabled it, he said. But the tea service can still be interacted with. Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here — quiet types. No Sneekly. The tea service is the only visible object. No cabinet, no key, no treasure. This room is a dead end for the key. But wait — let me think. The tea service can be INTERACTED with. Peter said he interacted with it and 'disabled' it. But the INTERACT tag is still there. What happens if I interact with it? Maybe interacting with it reveals something — not the poison mechanism, but something ELSE. A hidden compartment in the tea service? A note? A key wedged under a teacup? Silver tea services in Victorian mansions were status symbols — they had hollow bases, hidden drawers for sugar tongs, compartments for... The cool alertness returns. Not the frantic running. The THINKING. Age fourteen — the cat trap — strings, counterweights, the mechanism. I understood mechanisms. I built them. The tea service is a MECHANISM. Peter said it has 'a slot for something no tea service should ever need.' A slot. A mechanism. What if the slot isn't JUST for poison? What if it's a dual-purpose slot — one that accepts rat-poison but ALSO accepts something else? Something small, round, metallic? Something like a... fake medal? No. That's insane. But the slot description — 'USE, with: rat-poison' — that's what the game shows me. My medal isn't rat-poison. It won't work. But INTERACTING with the tea service — just bare interaction — that might reveal something. Let me try.

events.desc: I'm grasping at teacups now. Literally grasping at TEACUPS. Twelve minutes ago I was going to steal the treasure single-handedly with a tin medal and a Swiss Polytechnic degree. Now I'm examining tea sets in a ballroom with a lazy cowboy and a bear. But the tea service CAN be interacted with. And every time this house has offered me an INTERACT option, there's been something on the other side of it — even if it wasn't what I expected. The mantelpiece clicked. The machine tried to operate. Maybe the tea service has one more secret. One more piece of the puzzle. And if it does — if Reginald Foxworth finds it — then the cat trap finally has its audience.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly interacted with the tea-service.
The Ant Hill Mob: Always, love. Always.
events.thinking: She stood up. She wiped her eyes. She said 'I am going to be Clara Bellingham.' And then she asked me to come with her. 'Ant Hill boys — will you come with me?' She asked. Not told. Not assumed. Asked. Like it was a question. Like there was ever any chance the answer would be no. My whole body is moving before I've decided anything — feet turning toward the ballroom door, shoulders squaring, that old warmth spreading across my back. She wants to see the poisoned tea service. She wants to see what Sneekly prepared for her. She wants to face it. And she wants her boys beside her when she does. That's Clara. That's always been Clara. She walked deeper into the cave than anyone. She didn't stop when her heart was hammering. And now she's walking into the ballroom where the broken cups and the poisoned tea and the truth are all waiting on a cracked marble floor. And she asked me to come. Where else would I be?

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the ballroom.
Peter Perfect: Right behind you. All of you.
events.thinking: She said it. She said 'that's what love sounds like.' Not gallantry. Not protection. Not proving-worth. Love. My whole body is — I don't know what it's doing. Something released. Like the bridge holding. Like every race ever run. She wiped her eyes and stood up and said she's going to the ballroom. She's Clara Bellingham again. She walked deeper into the cave. And the Ant Hill Mob — he took the beating. He crashed the tea service with his own body. He did the thing I couldn't do. He's the real hero tonight. And that doesn't ache the way it should. It doesn't feel like someone else getting there first. It feels like... my father and the stranger. Two men fixing what was broken. Shaking hands. Driving off. The Mob did his part. I did mine. We did it together. She's gone to the ballroom. She needs to see it for herself. And she asked the Ant Hill Mob to come with her. Not me. She asked THEM. And that's right. That's exactly right. They're her boys. They took the beating. They've earned this walk. But I should follow. Not to lead. Not to protect. Not to impress. Just to be there. Because she said 'what do you need' is what love sounds like. And I think... I think that means I should keep asking it. Quietly. From nearby.

events.desc: 'That's what love sounds like.' She said that. To me. About me. And I didn't even have a copper pot in my hands.
