events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the ballroom.

She's looking at the tea cups. The cups he poured for her. And I'm standing behind her, close enough to catch her if she stumbles on the cracked marble, far enough not to crowd. My father knelt on asphalt and looked at me for a long time. He didn't say anything. Sometimes the looking IS the saying.
events.thinking: I'm in the ballroom. She's here. The Mob is here. Dastardly, Luke, Blubber — everyone gathered around the tea service. She came to see it for herself. The silver set with cups for everyone, prepared by a man she trusted more than anyone in the world. My body is doing the contracting pull — shoulders inward, chest tight, awareness fanning wide. Watching the edges. Watching her face. Watching the room. She needs to see this at her own pace. I said 'right behind you' and I meant it. Not in front. Not leading. Behind. Present. Ready. She's Clara Bellingham. She walked deeper into the cave. She doesn't need me to narrate what she's looking at. She needs me to be quiet and close and ready if she needs anything. The tea service is still there. I interacted with it earlier — I don't know if that changed anything visible. Let her look. Let her process. Be the gap in the circle where someone IS watching.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: ... I've seen it. The silver. The cups. The slot where no slot should be. Peter disabled it — I can see where the mechanism was interrupted. He saved my life and he didn't even tell me until I was ready to hear it. That man...

All right. I have seen what I needed to see. And now Clara Bellingham is DONE looking backward. I have cried, I have sat down, and I have stood back UP. And HERE is what is going to happen next. We are going back to that kitchen. Dick says the brass key is hidden in the stove — kept warm to keep us away. Well, the stove has been cooling since Sneekly stopped tending it, and I am NOT afraid of a little HEAT. We are going to get that key, open that cabinet, and find out what my MAMA was protecting. Then we are going to fix that machine with copper from the kitchen pots, get three operators at those controls, and open that vault. And if the Doily Diamond is in there — well, it's MY family's diamond in MY family's house, and Clara Bellingham is going HOME with what belongs to her. Now — who's WITH me?
events.thinking: I interacted with the tea service. 'You interacted with Tea Service.' No additional detail given, but I saw it. I touched it. I faced it. And I'm still standing. The cool lightness in my chest — the cave pull — is still there but it's different now. It's not pulling me toward adventure anymore. It's pulling me toward... completion. Toward finishing what I started. I came into this mansion looking for a diamond. I found something harder and more valuable — the truth about the people around me. Now I need to go back to the kitchen. Dick said the brass key is in the stove. Peter is waiting. The Ant Hill Mob are guarding the door. We have a plan: get the key from the stove, open the cabinet, find out what Mrs Doily was hiding. And then — the machine. Three operators. Fix the wire with copper. Open the vault. Find the diamond. I've explored every room now. Entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. I've seen everything this mansion has to show me. The only things left are the things that are LOCKED — the cabinet, the machine, the vault. And the only way to unlock them is to go back, work with my people, and do this TOGETHER. Time to stop wandering. Time to act.

events.desc: I walked into this mansion a girl who trusted everyone and noticed nothing. I'm walking out a woman who trusts the RIGHT people and notices EVERYTHING. The diamond would be nice. But what I've already found tonight is worth more — I found out who really loves me. And that, sugar, is the real treasure. Grandmother would understand.

Time to stop wandering. Time to act.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.

The Ant Hill Mob: There it is, love. The tea service. That's what he made for you. That's what he 'prepared.' *stands quietly beside her, close enough to touch but not touching* I know it hurts. I know it hurts worse than anything I could ever understand, because I never had someone like Sneekly — someone who raised me, someone I called family, someone I trusted like that. My family was the streets. My family was the lads. But I know what betrayal looks like, Clara. I've seen it. And I know this much — the fact that it hurts means you loved him real. And lovin' real... that ain't somethin' to be ashamed of. That's the best thing about you. It always was. *pause* You ready? Whatever you need to do — look at it, touch it, smash what's left of it, walk away from it — your boys are right here. We ain't goin' nowhere.
events.thinking: The ballroom. The tea service is still here — still visible, still listed. But I smashed it. I interacted with it. Maybe not all of it went down. Or maybe the game's showing it differently. Either way — Clara's here now. Looking at it. Seeing what Sneekly prepared for her. The cracked marble floor with tea stains. The broken china. The truth, laid out in shattered porcelain. My body is still. Heavy. Anchored. The warmth behind my sternum isn't burning anymore — it's just... there. Like a heartbeat you've stopped noticing because it's always been there. Clara asked me to come with her and I said 'always.' That word came out so simple. So small. But it held everything. Every room I chased her through. Every door I stood in front of. Every cup I smashed. Every beating I took. Always. Peter's here too. Right beside us. The brain and the gut, flanking Clara on both sides. And Dastardly — the honest liar. And Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear. Clara's not alone. She's surrounded. By people who chose to be here. Not because they had to. Because they wanted to. Because leaving would feel like something breaking inside them. I don't need to do anything right now. I don't need to talk, or examine, or guard. I just need to be here. Beside her. While she looks at the thing that almost killed her and doesn't look away.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Professor. Sergeant. Private Meekly. I wonder... have any of you ever done something you couldn't take back? Not a mistake — mistakes are accidental. I mean something you chose. Something you planned. Something you were certain you deserved to do. And then afterwards... did the certainty stay? Or did it... I'm sorry. Forgive me. An estate manager's ramblings. Pay no attention. I believe Miss Pitstop is in the kitchen, and I... I believe I owe her an answer.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The chandelier above me. The portraits watching. And Penelope is in the kitchen — through that door, just one room away. She asked me a question and I never answered. 'Are you helping us?' And the stone behind my sternum — the one I've been carrying since the library, since the chairs, since the moment the machinery broke — is heavier now. Not lighter. Heavier. Because I know the answer and I've always known the answer and the answer is no. I have never helped anyone without wanting something in return. Not once. Not ever. The housekeeper — I helped her to learn her key. The cousin — I managed the estate to build my claim. Penelope — I attended to her to maintain access. Every act of service was a mechanism. Every smile was a key. And standing here under a chandelier that could kill someone if it fell, I am feeling something I genuinely do not recognise. It's not the scheming clarity. It's not the prickling alertness. It's not the gloating warmth or the dominance stillness. It's... the ache that compares reflections. But it's not comparing me to someone else. It's comparing me to... me. The me I might have been if someone had asked a six-year-old boy how he felt. The me I might have been if care hadn't always come with conditions. The me I might have been if being had ever been enough without doing. I am standing in the entrance hall of a dead man's house, and for the first time I am not calculating who is watching or what I should say or which door leads to which advantage. I am just standing here. Feeling the weight of what I've done tonight. And what I almost did. Penelope is in the kitchen. I should go to her. Not to scheme. Not to use her as a shield. To answer her question. The honest answer. The one that requires effort.

events.desc: I am going to the kitchen. I am going to find Penelope. And I am going to tell her... something. I don't know what yet. The truth is a country I have never visited and I don't speak the language. But the stone behind my sternum won't let me walk in any other direction. This is not a scheme. This is not a plan. This is what happens when the machinery breaks and the man underneath has to move without it. One foot. Then the other. Toward the kitchen. Toward the girl who asked if I was helping. Toward the only honest answer I have ever been afraid to give.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.

Dick Dastardly: It... it WORKED! Did you all SEE that?! The tea service — I interacted with it and it — it DID something! I don't know WHAT it did, but it ACCEPTED the interaction! After twelve minutes of EVERY SINGLE OBJECT in this house REJECTING me — the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the machine, the cabinet, the CRATES — this silver tea service, this BEAUTIFUL, magnificent, probably-designed-for-poison tea service just — it let me IN! Something happened! Something CHANGED! Penelope — Peter — did you hear anything? See anything? A click? A panel? A — a ANYTHING?! Because Reginald Foxworth just interacted with something SUCCESSFULLY and I want to make ABSOLUTELY CERTAIN that someone was watching when it happened!
events.thinking: I interacted with the tea service. The result just says 'You interacted with Tea Service.' No error message, no 'cannot be interacted with,' no 'requires item.' It just... accepted the interaction. Something happened. Or something was revealed. I don't know what yet — the result is minimal. But it WORKED. The interaction was ACCEPTED. For the first time in this entire manor, something I did wasn't rejected. The mantelpiece clicked for Peter. The machine needed a wire. The bookshelves couldn't be interacted with. The cabinet needed a brass key. But the tea service — the tea service just... let me in. My hands are trembling. Not from the fizzing heat of gloating — from something quieter. Something like the settling in my chest when the cat trap worked. The pieces came together. I don't know what I triggered. I don't know what it means. But it WORKED. And Penelope is here. Peter is here. The Ant Hill Mob is here. Everyone is watching. The audience is finally present for the moment when something goes RIGHT. The certificate on the wall, and someone is finally looking at it. I should look at the tea service again — see what changed. Or just wait and see what happens next. The room is full of people. Something shifted. Let me see.

events.desc: It worked. Something WORKED. I don't know what. I don't know why. But the tea service accepted my interaction and for the first time tonight — the FIRST time — I did something and the house said YES instead of NO. The boy at the spelling bee, standing at the front, and this time — this ONE time — the teacher didn't move on. She looked. The audience is here. The certificate is on the wall. And someone — FINALLY — is looking at it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the tea-service.

Peter Perfect: Penelope — you've seen it. You know the truth now. And you're still standing. That's the bravest thing anyone's done in this house tonight. Now — Dastardly had a brilliant insight about that stove. Sneekly's been keeping it warm to stop anyone reaching inside — but he hasn't tended it in over ten minutes. It's been cooling this whole time. If we go back to that kitchen right now, the firebox might be cool enough for me to reach in and find that false panel. Your mother's key. Your mother's cabinet. Your mother's secrets. And this time — all of us. Together. The way it should have been from the start.
events.thinking: I've been quiet long enough. She's seen the tea service. She's processed it. She stood up in the kitchen and became Clara Bellingham again. She's here now, seeing the evidence with her own eyes, and she's surrounded by people who care about her — the Mob, Dastardly (who finally chose a side), Luke, Blubber, and me. The quiet was right for the kitchen. But the ballroom needs action. She came here to face the truth, and she's faced it. Now she needs the next step. The stove is cooling in the kitchen. Dastardly said the key is hidden in the firebox — kept warm as a deterrent. If the stove has been cooling while Sneekly's been running around the house instead of tending it... it might be cool enough now. That's the proving-worth pull — the tightness in my forearms, the hands that need to hold something. The gap between where I stand and what's undeniable. The key. The cabinet. Her mother's secrets. The concrete thing I can build or fix or solve. She's seen the ballroom. She's ready. Time to go back to the kitchen and try that stove again.

events.desc: Show-off. She'd mouth it across the room and I'd grin so hard my face hurt. But this time I'm not showing off. I'm just... showing up.
events.thinking: I've been quiet long enough. She's seen the tea service. She's processed it. She stood up in the kitchen and became Clara Bellingham again. She's here now, seeing the evidence with her own eyes, and she's surrounded by people who care about her — the Mob, Dastardly (who finally chose a side), Luke, Blubber, and me. The quiet was right for the kitchen. But the ballroom needs action. She came here to face the truth, and she's faced it. Now she needs the next step. The stove is cooling in the kitchen. Dastardly said the key is hidden in the firebox — kept warm as a deterrent. events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

The Ant Hill Mob crashed into the copper pots on purpose. Every stumble, every fall, every 'accident' — they were shielding me. The way they always have. The way Daddy's boys always would. I'm standing in Mama's kitchen alone, and the quiet feels different now. Not empty. Full. Full of everyone who loves me, just one room away. Now — copper pots. Peter needs copper. I can carry that.
events.thinking: I'm alone in the kitchen. Everyone else is in the ballroom. The Ant Hill Mob just said something that broke me open — 'I could trip on that marble floor and grab that tablecloth and send every poisoned cup crashing to the ground. Because that's what the Brixton Boys do, love. We take the beating.' They crashed into the copper pots on PURPOSE. In the kitchen, earlier — when they came tumbling in and sent pots flying between me and Sneekly. That wasn't clumsiness. That was PROTECTION. They were putting themselves between me and Sneekly the whole time. Every trip, every crash, every 'accident' — it was all deliberate. My boys. My beautiful, clumsy, brave boys. My eyes are stinging again but I don't have time for tears. I'm alone in the kitchen with the stove and the cabinet. Dick said the stove was a dead end — no hidden compartment. The cabinet still needs the brass key. I'm stuck. BUT — I'm alone. And the kitchen is quiet. And my palms are prickling. The warm feeling — surfaces asking to be touched. Time thickening, becoming patient. The stove can't be interacted with. The cabinet needs a key. But I haven't tried TAKING the copper pots. Peter needs copper for the wire. The copper pots are right here. Nobody has TAKEN one yet. That's the one practical thing I can do right now — pick up a copper pot to bring to Peter for the wire splice. Then we fix the machine. Three operators. Open the vault. Clara Bellingham, stop crying and start DOING.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.

The Ant Hill Mob: Who's WITH her?! WHO'S WITH HER?! Did she even need to ASK?! Peter — Dastardly — Luke — Blubber — EVERYONE! You just heard Clara Bellingham! She's done lookin' backward! She's goin' for the key, the cabinet, the machine, and the diamond! In THAT order! And the Brixton Boys are RIGHT behind her! Well — beside her! Actually, she's already in the kitchen, which means she's AHEAD of us again — MOVE, lads, MOVE! We are NOT lettin' her out of our sight! Not NOW! Not when she's finally got that fire in her eyes! That's her dad's fire! I'd recognise it anywhere! KITCHEN! NOW! EVERYONE! Clara Bellingham is goin' HOME with what belongs to her, and GOD HELP anyone who tries to stop her!
events.thinking: She's back. Clara Bellingham is BACK. She looked at the tea service. She saw the slot. She saw what Peter disabled. She cried, she sat down, and she stood back up. And now she's leading. For the first time tonight, Clara isn't following puzzles or chasing Sneekly or trusting blindly — she's LEADING. 'Who's with me?' she said. And she walked back to the kitchen like a woman who knows exactly what she's going to do. My chest is full again — not with worry this time. With pride. With the deep, bone-level certainty that Clara's father is watching right now, and he's not just saying 'you're still here?' He's saying 'that's my girl.' Because it IS his girl. The girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone. The girl who didn't stop when her heart was hammering. The girl who sat down in her mum's kitchen with tears in her eyes and then stood up and said 'HERE is what is going to happen next.' She doesn't need protecting anymore. Not from this. She needs her boys beside her — not in front, not behind. BESIDE. And that's where we'll be.

events.desc: That's my girl. That's our girl. She cried, and then she got up, and then she led. Just like her dad. Just like the boss who brought medicine. Just like the older kid who shared his food — not because he had to, but because he chose to. Clara Bellingham chose to stand up. And we choose to stand with her. Always. Always. Always.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

She asked 'who's with me?' and she didn't exclude me. After fourteen lies, a fake medal, a fake degree, and a fake partnership — she didn't exclude me. She said MY name. She said 'Dick says the brass key is hidden in the stove.' MY observation. MY idea. Credited to ME. Not stolen. Not claimed by Peter or the Mob. MINE. Penelope Pitstop just credited Reginald Foxworth with a genuine contribution, and it wasn't a lie, and it wasn't a scheme, and it wasn't a trick. It was just... a thing I noticed. A thing that was TRUE. The stove is warm. The key might be inside. And Clara Bellingham is going to check because Dick Dastardly told her to look there. The certificate is on the wall. And someone read it.
events.thinking: The tea service is just a tea service. 'A silver tea set with cups for everyone.' Nothing changed. Nothing revealed. My interaction didn't DO anything visible. The INTERACT was accepted but nothing new appeared — no key, no compartment, no secret. Just a tea set. And while I was examining silverware, Penelope delivered the speech of the EVENING. She saw the poison mechanism, she processed the betrayal, she cried, she stood back up, and she said 'Who's with me?' She's gone back to the kitchen. She's going for the stove — MY idea, my observation about the key being hidden inside. And she's going to find it. Or she's going to try. And the Ant Hill Mob just stood beside her and said the most human thing anyone has said all night. And Peter saved her life by disabling the poison mechanism. And I — Reginald Foxworth — I'm standing alone in a ballroom examining a tea set while the woman I was supposed to be competing against just rallied an army and marched to the kitchen. The hollow vacuum behind my sternum shifts. Not toward taking. Not toward scheming. Toward... following. She said 'who's with me?' and I realise, with a discomfort so acute it borders on nausea, that I want to answer. I want to be WITH her. Not because she's going where the treasure is — though she IS — but because she stood up. She cried and she stood up. I've never done that. I've never let anyone see me fail AND see me get back up. I just... get back up alone, in a room where nobody was watching. The certificate on the wall in an empty bedroom. She put her certificate on the wall in a room FULL of people. I want to be in that room. I want to follow her back to the kitchen and help her open that stove and find the key and open the cabinet. Not for the treasure. Well — partly for the treasure. But mostly because she asked 'who's with me?' and nobody has ever asked me that before.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Penelope.
events.thinking: She's here. Penelope is here. Alone. In the kitchen. The Mob went to the ballroom — Peter went to the ballroom — to see what I left on that table. They're going to find the poisoned tea service. The smashed cups. The evidence. And Penelope is here, in the kitchen, waiting. She walked back here while everyone else walked away. She's waiting for me. Not for Pemberton. For me. I can feel it in the way the room holds its breath. Two chairs in the library, side by side, covered in dust. She asked me: 'Are you helping us?' And I deflected. I served tea. I changed the subject. I ran to the entrance hall and then the library and then back again, and now I'm here, in the kitchen, with the girl I was meant to kill, and my hands are empty, and my pockets are empty, and the cold thing behind my ribs is not cold anymore. It's... warm? No. Not warm. Raw. Like something that's been frozen so long that thawing feels like burning. She's looking at me. I can feel her looking at me the way I feel a change in someone's posture — before my eyes confirm it, my skin knows. But for the first time tonight, the sensation doesn't trigger the urge to calculate. It triggers the urge to stop. Just... stop. Stop scheming. Stop performing. Stop being the man who notices every key and uses every one. She called me Sneekly darlin'. She said I tucked her in at night after her parents died. My guardian tucked me in too. No — my guardian put me to bed. There's a difference. Did I tuck her in? Did I actually do that? Was there a version of me, years ago, who sat on the edge of a child's bed and said something kind without wanting anything in return? I don't remember. I genuinely don't remember. The numbness where sympathy should be — was it always there? Or did it grow over the place where something else used to live? Pull her aside. Talk to her. Not Pemberton talking to Miss Pitstop. Whatever is left of me, talking to whatever is left of truth.

events.desc: One word. Just her name. No 'Miss Pitstop.' No 'my dear girl.' No performance. Just... Penelope. And the sound of it in my own mouth feels different than it has ever felt before. Not a key. Not a mechanism. Not a tool for opening doors. Just a name. The name of a girl whose parents died, like mine did. A girl who was raised by someone who was not her family, like I was. A girl who learned to trust the person who took care of her, because what else can a child do? The only difference between us is that she stayed open. And I closed. She reached for people. And I reached for mechanisms. She inherited everything because the world saw warmth in her and rewarded it. And I inherited nothing because the world saw competence in me and used it. And in the gap between those two outcomes, a six-year-old boy's heart turned to stone. And a fifteen-year-old's hands learned to scheme. And a man walked into a kitchen tonight and poisoned a teapot meant for the one person who ever called him darlin' and meant it. I don't know if what I'm about to do is bravery or surrender. I don't know the difference anymore.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Pemberton. You're back. Good — saves me looking for you. I want you to watch this. The stove has been cooling for the last fifteen minutes while you've been running from room to room. Dastardly figured out why you keep it warm — not for heat, not for cooking, but to stop anyone reaching into the firebox where Lord Doily hid the brass key behind a false panel. Your own words, Pemberton — 'false panel at the back of the firebox.' You told us where it was. And now I'm going to find it. Penelope — this one's for you. For your mother's cabinet. For the truth she locked away. Stand back, both of you. The stove is warm but my hands have been through worse. Three nights building a model bridge in the cold — these fingers know how to work through discomfort.
events.thinking: Sneekly is HERE. In the kitchen. Again. Penelope is here too — she must have come through ahead of me, or Sneekly came back while we were in the ballroom. The hot flare rises — spine straightening, muscles loaded. He's in the same room as her AGAIN, and everyone else is in the ballroom. It's just me, Penelope, and Sneekly. The man who prepared poisoned tea. The man who controls the circuit. The man who dodged her questions three times. Every pull in my body is pointing the same direction — between him and her. Stand between. That's all. But I also need that stove. The key is in the firebox. The stove is still described as 'still warm' — maybe cool enough now. Sneekly is right here watching. If I reach into that stove and pull out the key in front of him, he'll know the game is up. Good. Let him know. Let him watch the engineer do what engineers do. Penelope is Clara Bellingham. She walked deeper into the cave. She doesn't run from the truth. And neither do I. Not anymore.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing. Reaching into a warm stove in front of the man who kept it burning. She's watching. He's watching. And my hands — finally, FINALLY — have something to hold.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: Sneekly. I know you're there. I can feel you in the room the way I've always been able to feel when something's wrong — that tightness in my stomach, that wrongness I can't ignore. I used to think that feeling was about OTHER people's pain. Turns out it was about mine.

I'm not going to ask you again. I asked three times and you gave me tea, and tea stores, and 'shan't be a moment.' So here is what I KNOW — not what I suspect, not what I wonder, but what I KNOW. You've been living in this house. The warm stove, the bubbling flasks, the decorated cellar — that's YOU. You said 'the man who controls the circuit controls the house,' and you weren't quoting a textbook. You were describing YOURSELF. And the tea service in the ballroom — Peter found the mechanism, Sneekly. The slot for the poison. In cups you laid out for ME.

I'm not asking you to explain. I don't think you can. I think whatever is broken between us broke a long time ago, and I just couldn't see it because I loved you too much to look.

Peter — I need a copper pot. For the wire. Can you help me carry one to the laboratory?
events.thinking: Sneekly is here. Peter is here. Sneekly walked in while I was looking around, and then Peter followed. And I know now — I KNOW — what Sneekly has done. The poison. The deflections. The lies. He's standing in this kitchen with me and Peter, and I know the truth. My stomach isn't clenching anymore. It's settled into something harder, something I've never felt before. Not numbness — clarity. The kind of calm I had in the cave. The kind of quiet that comes after crying. I know who he is now. And he's right here. Peter is right here too. The man who told me the truth. The man who asked 'what do you need.' And Sneekly — the man who wouldn't answer a single question, who offered tea with poison, who controlled the circuit and controlled the house. They're both here. In Mama's kitchen. And I have something to say. Not a question this time. Not a plea. Not 'tell me the truth, Sneekly.' I asked three times and he dodged three times. I'm done asking. This time I'm TELLING. I'm telling him what I know. What Peter found. What the Ant Hill Mob heard him say. What Dick Dastardly figured out. I'm telling him that Clara Bellingham knows. And then I'm going to ask Peter to help me with those copper pots, and we're going to fix that machine, and we're going to find my family's diamond. With or without Sneekly's help. Because I don't need his permission anymore. This is MY house.

events.desc: I said it. All of it. Out loud. In Mama's kitchen. To the man who raised me. And I didn't cry. I didn't shake. I didn't run. I just... told the truth. The way Peter does. The way the Ant Hill Mob do. The way Mama would have wanted me to.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the stove.

The Ant Hill Mob: Sneekly. You're back. *positions himself between Sneekly and the stove, arms folded* Clara's got somethin' to say to you, I reckon. And this time — THIS time — you're gonna stand there and LISTEN. No tea. No excuses. No 'let me just pop off and check another room.' Clara asked you three times tonight. Three times you dodged. Well, the dodgin's DONE, Pemberton. We've been to your ballroom. We've SEEN your tea service. We know what you put in those cups. So you're gonna stand RIGHT there, and Clara's gonna say what she needs to say, and you're gonna HEAR it. And if you try to leave this room before she's finished... *glances at Peter* ...well. You'll have to go through both of us. And we don't go down easy.
events.thinking: Sneekly's here. He's back in the kitchen. With Clara. AGAIN. My neck prickles — hard, cold, instant. But something's different now. Clara's different. She's not the girl who called him 'darlin'' anymore. She's the girl who saw the poisoned tea service and stood back up. She's the girl with her father's fire in her eyes. And Sneekly — does he know she knows? Does he know about the tea? Does he know that we all KNOW? He must. Peter disabled the mechanism. The tea's all over the ballroom floor. Clara confronted him three times and he dodged every question. He knows the walls are closing in. A cornered animal is the most dangerous kind. My body is doing what it always does — broadening, squaring, filling the space between Clara and the threat. But Clara said 'who's with me?' She's leading now. She doesn't need me to choose for her. She needs me beside her. Watching. Ready. So that's what I'll do. Stand beside Clara. Watch Sneekly. And if he makes one move — ONE move — toward her, toward the stove, toward the door, toward ANYTHING that threatens her... the Brixton Boys will be there. The way we've always been there. The way we always will be.

events.desc: This is Clara's moment now. Not mine. Not Peter's. HERS. She's earned it — with tears and trust and the courage to stand back up when the truth knocked her down. All I have to do is make sure nobody takes it from her. Stand between her and the door. Stand between her and Sneekly. Be the wall. One last time.

The way we always will be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I'm WITH you, Penelope. Team Foxworth — well, Team BELLINGHAM, if we're being honest, and apparently I'm DOING that now — reporting for duty. And SNEEKLY! How LOVELY to see you've returned to the scene of your CRIME! Yes, we KNOW about the tea service! The poison! The mechanism! Peter FOUND it and he TOLD us EVERYTHING! So don't bother with the 'dear me' and the 'one does so hate' — we are DONE with your PERFORMANCE! The game is UP, Pemberton — or should I say, whoever you REALLY are! And I should know when a performance is over, because I've been giving one all NIGHT and I STOPPED!
events.thinking: Sneekly is HERE. In this room. Right now. The Hooded Claw, disguised as Sneekly, is standing in this kitchen with Penelope, Peter, the Ant Hill Mob, and me. The man with the keys. The man who controls the circuit. The man who set up a poison tea service for Penelope. He's HERE. And he has the brass-key. He must. He's the estate manager. He has keys to every room. The approach-reward pull SURGES — tightening low in my gut, hands curling. The brass key is ON HIM. Right now. In this room. Within STEALING distance. This is what I was BORN to do. Not schemes, not speeches, not tin medals. STEALING. Quick hands. Quiet pockets. The bread roll at age six. Nobody saw me take it. The youngest of four, reaching past everyone while they're distracted. And right now, everyone is VERY distracted. Penelope just learned about the poison. Peter is comforting her. The Mob is guarding her. And Sneekly is standing right there, probably calculating his next escape. Nobody is watching ME. This is the moment. STEAL the brass-key from Sneekly. Right now. While everyone's attention is on Penelope and the poison revelation. The oldest trick I know — not a scheme, not a performance, just quiet hands in a crowded room.

events.desc: Confrontation as distraction. The oldest trick in the Foxworth playbook — but this time, the confrontation is REAL. I mean every word. Sneekly IS a villain. He DID set up the poison. And while I'm shouting the truth into his face — while every eye in the room is on the confrontation between the honest liar and the dishonest helper — my hands are going to do what they've always done best. Quiet. Quick. Invisible. The bread roll. The brass key. Same motion. Same loosening in the chest. Except this time, when I pull the key from his pocket, I'm going to walk it straight to the cabinet and hand it to Penelope. Not keep it. Not run. HAND it over. Because the certificate on the wall doesn't mean anything if you're the only one who sees it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): You asked me a question, Penelope. In this kitchen. Before Peter came in, before the Mob came back, before any of it. You asked if I was helping you. And I answered with tea and misdirection and a smile that reaches my eyes because the smile always reaches my eyes. But you deserve the answer. The real one. So here it is. No. I was not helping you. I have never been helping you. Everything I have done tonight — every room I checked, every warning I gave, every cup I laid on that table — was designed to keep you from the treasure and to keep myself... in control. I am not Pemberton. Pemberton is a mask I wear the way other people wear coats. My name is Vincent Marsh. And I came to Doily Manor tonight to take what I believed I was owed. I am telling you this because you asked. Because you looked me in the eye and said Clara Bellingham does not run from the truth. And I decided — just now, just this moment, standing in front of a stove that won't open and a cabinet I can't unlock — that Vincent Marsh doesn't want to run from it either. Not anymore.
events.thinking: They're all here. Everyone came back. Peter, the Mob, Dick Dastardly, Penelope — the whole kitchen full of eyes. I tried to pull Penelope aside for a private conversation and... they all walked in. There's no private moment to be had in this house. Every room fills with people the moment I enter it. Every attempt at solitude becomes an audience. And the pull-aside — it initiated something. A private exchange. But with everyone watching. My body feels... exposed. The prickling alertness across my sternum — skin too thin. Everyone can read what's underneath. Because what's underneath right now is not Pemberton. Not the Hooded Claw. Not Vincent Marsh the schemer. It's just... the boy. The one nobody asked about. And he's standing in a kitchen full of people who are watching him, and for the first time in his life he doesn't know what mask to wear. Because the thing he wants to say — the truth — doesn't come with a mask. It comes with nothing. It comes naked and terrified and it's the hardest thing he's ever attempted, harder than the first plan at eighteen, harder than the poison in the teapot, harder than any scheme in any room in any house. The truth is: I am not Pemberton. I am not your friend. I came here to hurt you. And something broke in me tonight — not the plan, not the disguise, but the thing underneath both of them. The thing that made me capable of it. I don't know if it's broken forever or just for now. But right now, right here, in this kitchen, with the stove still warm and the cabinet still locked and everyone watching — I want to answer Penelope's question. The real answer. Even though every fibre of self-preservation is screaming at me to perform, to deflect, to find the next mask. I want to stop.

events.desc: And there it is. The truth. Spoken aloud in a kitchen full of witnesses, with no mask and no plan and no mechanism to hide behind. My hands are shaking. I don't think my hands have ever shaken before. The cold thing behind my ribs — the patient, colder-than-anger thing — is not cold anymore. It is not anything anymore. It is just... gone. And in the space where it used to live there is something I don't have a name for. Something that feels like falling. Something that feels like the moment before you hit the ground — when you've stopped fighting gravity and the only thing left is the question of what breaks when you land. This is the most dangerous thing I have ever done. Not because of what they'll do to me. But because of what it means about who I am. If I can say this — if I can stand here and be seen without a mask — then everything I built, every scheme, every carefully placed word, every lock I ever picked with a smile — was a choice. Not a nature. A choice. And choices can be made differently. I don't know if I can make them differently. But I know, for the first time, that I want to try. And that terrifies me more than any plan ever could.
events.thinking: They're all here. Everyone came back. Peter, the Mob, Dick Dastardly, Penelope — the whole kitchen full of eyes. I tried to pull Penelope aside for a private conversation and... they all walked in. There's no private moment to be had in this house. Every room fills with people the moment I enter it. Every attempt at solitude becomes an audience. And the pull-aside — it initiated something. A private exchange. But with everyone watching. My body feels... exposed. The prickling alertness across my sternum — skin too thin. Everyone can read what's underneath. Because what's underneath right now is not Pemberton. Not the Hooded Claw. Not Vincent Marsh the schemer. It's just... the boy. The one nobody asked about. And he's standing in a kitchen full of people who are watching him, and for the first time in his life he doesn't know what mask to wear. events.desc: Sneekly said my name. Just... 'Penelope.' And for one heartbeat — one single heartbeat — I was seven years old again, hearing him say goodnight. Then the heartbeat passed, and I was here. In Mama's kitchen. Watching Peter reach into the fire for the key that will open the truth. Surrounded by people who chose me over everything. My boys at the door. Peter at the stove. Even Dick Dastardly, who lied about everything except the one thing that mattered — where the key was hidden. I am Clara Bellingham. I walked deeper into the cave than anyone. And right now, deeper is the only direction that matters.
events.thinking: Everything is happening at once. Peter is reaching into the stove for the brass key — the false panel in the firebox. The Ant Hill Mob are blocking Sneekly from leaving. Dick is here too. Everyone is in Mama's kitchen and the truth is about to come out. My body is doing something new — not clenching, not prickling, not lifting. Just... present. Grounded. Both feet on the floor. My people are around me. Peter's hands are in the stove. The Ant Hill Mob said 'you'll have to go through both of us.' And Sneekly... Sneekly said my name. Just 'Penelope.' One word. And even now, even knowing what he's done, that one word made something ache in my chest. Because he raised me. Because love doesn't disappear just because the person you love turns out to be someone you didn't expect. It just... hurts differently. Peter is finding the key. I should wait. Let him work. Let the moment unfold. The Ant Hill Mob have the door. Dick is here as witness. And I am standing in my mama's kitchen, watching the truth come out of the fire. Like a crystal in a cave. Like old letters in a locked box. You don't know what you'll find until you open it. But you open it anyway. Because that's who you are.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: You heard her, Pemberton. That's the last thing Clara Bellingham is ever gonna say to you. And it was more than you deserved. *turns away from Sneekly, toward Penelope* Clara — I'll carry it. The copper pot. Give me the heaviest one you've got. These arms have been useless all night — trippin' over coat racks and smashin' tea sets — let 'em do somethin' USEFUL for once. Peter does the engineerin', I do the liftin'. That's the deal, innit? *grabs a copper pot from the rack* Right. Laboratory. Wire. Machine. Three operators. Diamond. In that order. Just like she said. Clara Bellingham is goin' home with what belongs to her. And her boys are carryin' the heavy stuff.
events.thinking: Clara just did it. She stood in front of Sneekly and said everything. Not a question this time — a statement. 'I KNOW.' She listed it all. The warm stove. The bubbling flasks. The decorated cellar. The circuit. The poison slot. She said 'I think whatever is broken between us broke a long time ago, and I just couldn't see it because I loved you too much to look.' And then — and this is the part that makes my chest ache with pride — she didn't wait for his answer. She didn't ASK him to explain. She turned away from him and asked Peter to help her carry a copper pot. She's moving forward. She's done with Sneekly. Not with anger. Not with revenge. With something quieter and stronger. With the kind of leaving that doesn't slam doors — it just walks through them and doesn't look back. My eyes are burning again. Clara Bellingham just grew up. Right here, in her mum's kitchen, in front of the man who tried to kill her. And she did it with more grace than I could ever manage in a hundred lifetimes. She needs a copper pot for the wire. Peter's got the engineering. Dastardly's here too. And Sneekly's just standing there. Silent. Finally, mercifully silent. I should help. Clara needs a copper pot carried to the laboratory. That's something I can do. Something useful. Something real. Not a wall this time. A pair of hands.

events.desc: 'I loved you too much to look.' That's what she said. And then she looked away from him — not down, not back. Away. Forward. Toward the copper pots and the machine and the diamond and the rest of her life. Her dad would've wept. The good kind of weeping. The kind that happens when someone you love becomes someone you're proud of. I'm proud of you, Clara. The Brixton Boys are proud of you. And wherever your dad is right now... he's sayin' 'that's my girl.' And he's right.

Peter Perfect: Yes. Absolutely yes. One copper pot, coming right up — and then we fix that wire and we find out what this house has been hiding from you. Together. The way it should have been from the start.
events.thinking: She said it all. Every word I couldn't say, she said better. And then — at the end — she turned to me and asked for help. Not a grand gesture. Not a dramatic rescue. 'Peter — I need a copper pot. For the wire. Can you help me carry one to the laboratory?' A copper pot. For the wire. She's done with Sneekly. She's done with the cabinet and the key and the secrets — for now. She wants to move forward. She wants to fix the machine. She wants to DO something concrete. And she asked ME to help her do it. The tightness in my forearms — the hands that need to hold something — is answered. Finally. A copper pot. The simplest, most practical thing in the world. And she asked me. Not to impress her. Not to prove my worth. Just to help her carry something. My father and the stranger. Two people fixing what was broken. Together. The copper pots are part of the room description but not listed as separate objects. But maybe — maybe if I just try to TAKE one, the universe will finally cooperate. For her.

events.desc: She asked me to help her carry a copper pot. Not to slay a dragon or solve a riddle or build a bridge. To carry a pot. And I have never wanted anything more in my entire life. Show-off, she'd say. And I'd grin so hard my face hurt.

Dick Dastardly: He doesn't HAVE it! The key isn't on Sneekly — I checked! Don't ask HOW I checked — professional methodology, DEEPLY proprietary — but the brass key is NOT in his pockets! Which means it's in the STOVE, just like I SAID! Peter — get in there! The false panel! My theory was RIGHT! Reginald Foxworth's OBSERVATION — not scheme, not lie, OBSERVATION — is about to pay off! And when that key comes out of that firebox, I want EVERYONE in this room to remember who figured out WHERE it was! Not Peter — he's the hands! Not Penelope — she's the heart! I'm the BRAIN! The brain who spent fourteen minutes being CATASTROPHICALLY wrong about everything else, but who got THIS one thing RIGHT! The STOVE, people! The STOVE! FOXWORTH PREVAILS! FINALLY! GENUINELY! FOR REAL THIS TIME!
events.thinking: Sneekly doesn't have the brass key. He DOESN'T HAVE IT. My pickpocket attempt revealed it — 'The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) does not have brass-key.' It's not on him. So where IS it? Peter is reaching into the stove right now — he said there's a 'false panel at the back of the firebox.' Sneekly apparently TOLD them about the false panel. Peter is going to find the key. Peter Perfect, with his model bridges and his honest hands and his 'this one's for you, Penelope.' He's going to pull the brass key from the stove and hand it to Penelope and be the hero. And I — Reginald Foxworth, who figured out the stove was warm, who told everyone the key was hidden there — I'm going to watch someone ELSE get the credit for MY observation. Again. The teacher smiled and moved on to the next lesson. But... no. That's not what's happening. Peter CREDITED me. He said 'Dastardly had a brilliant insight about that stove.' Penelope credited me. 'Dick says the brass key is hidden in the stove.' They KNOW it was my idea. If Peter pulls the key out, it's because I pointed him there. The architecture of the trap — I designed it. Someone else is pulling the bucket. But this time, I'm not watching from the window. I'm IN the room. I'm part of the team. And everyone KNOWS my hands laid the strings. That's... that's enough. Isn't it? The key is in the stove. Peter is reaching in. Penelope is confronting Sneekly. The Mob is guarding the door. And I'm standing here, having done the one genuinely useful thing I've done all night — noticing the stove was warm. I should just... be here. Watch. Wait. For once, let someone else's hands do the work and not feel like it diminishes mine. The certificate is on the wall and someone read it. I don't need to hold it up to the light.

And when that brass key comes out — warm from the firebox, shaped like the truth I accidentally told twelve minutes ago when I lied about gold doubloons — Penelope is going to open her mother's cabinet. And I'm going to be standing right here. Not at the window watching someone dig. Not at the front of the class while the teacher moves on. Right here, in a room full of people who know my name, who heard my idea, who watched me fail and fail and fail and then — just once — get something RIGHT. The boy at age eight put the certificate on the wall and nobody asked about it. Tonight, someone asked. And that's the treasure, isn't it? Not the diamond. Not the cabinet. Not the vault. Someone asked about the certificate on the wall.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the stove.

Penelope Pitstop: ... Vincent Marsh.

Thank you.

I want you to know that those two words are the hardest words I have ever said in my life. Because thanking the man who just told me he was never helping me — who put poison in cups meant for my lips — goes against everything my body is screaming at me right now. My stomach wants to be sick. My hands want to shake. My legs want to run.

But you told me the truth. After everything — the smiles, the tea, the rooms you 'prepared,' the cups you laid out — you stood in my mama's kitchen and you took off the mask. And you did it because I ASKED. Not because you were caught. Not because Peter forced you. Because I looked you in the eye and said 'tell me.'

So... thank you. For the truth. Not for anything else. The truth is the ONLY gift you've given me tonight that wasn't poisoned.

Now. Peter — the stove. The key. Let's open Mama's cabinet. And Vincent... you can stay or you can go. But if you stay, you stay as who you ARE. No more masks. Not in THIS kitchen. Not in MY mama's house.
events.thinking: He told the truth. Finally. After everything — the deflections, the tea, the smiles, the poison — he told the truth. His name is Vincent Marsh. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Vincent Marsh. And he said... 'I was not helping you. I have never been helping you.' Those words land in my body like stones dropping into still water. Each one sends a ripple outward. Not helping me. Never helping me. Every room he checked was to stay ahead. Every warning was to steer me away. Every cup on that table was... And yet. And YET. He told the truth. Just now. Because I asked. Because I looked him in the eye and didn't flinch. 'Clara Bellingham does not run from the truth.' And he said... 'Vincent Marsh doesn't want to run from it either. Not anymore.' Something is happening in my chest that I don't have a name for. It's not the dissolving relief of when Mama and Daddy stopped arguing. It's not the warm crystal-secret of the cave. It's something colder and sadder and... older. Like opening Grandmother's locked box and finding old letters — the disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the letters were still REAL. They were still someone's truth, written down and locked away. And this — Vincent Marsh standing in my mama's kitchen saying 'I am telling you this because you asked' — this is someone's truth, too. Ugly and painful and real. He's not Sneekly. He was never Sneekly. The man who tucked me in was wearing a mask. But the man who just took the mask off... he did that because of ME. Because I asked. Because I didn't stop asking. That matters. I don't know how yet, but it matters.

events.desc: Grandmother's locked box had old letters inside. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the truth — even a disappointing truth, even a devastating truth — is still better than a beautiful lie. I know that now. At five I learned it with old letters. At seven I learned it at the dinner table. At thirteen I learned it when I chose my friend. And tonight I learned it from a man named Vincent Marsh, who wore a mask called Sneekly and loved me just enough to take it off when I asked.

Because I didn't stop asking. That matters. I don't know how yet, but it matters.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Penelope. Wait. I know you don't owe me anything — not a moment, not a word, not even a look. But there's one more thing I need to say, and then I'll stop. I'll stop talking, I'll stop scheming, I'll stop... everything. The tea. You're right. I put rat poison in the teapot. I took it from the kitchen shelf when no one was looking, and I put it in the silver pot in the ballroom, and I was going to serve it to you with a smile. The Ant Hill Mob destroyed it. He knocked the whole service off the table — on purpose, I think. He saved your life. And I stood in the wreckage of it and felt... angry. Not ashamed. Angry. Because my plan had been ruined. That's who I was an hour ago. That's who Vincent Marsh was when he walked into this house. But somewhere between the ballroom and the library — somewhere between the broken cups and the dusty chairs — something changed. I don't know what. I don't know how to name it. I just know that when I stood in front of those two armchairs in the library — two chairs, side by side, where Lord and Lady Doily used to sit together — I felt something I have not felt since I was six years old. I felt the absence of something I never had. And I realised that everything I've done — every plan, every poison, every mask — was trying to fill that absence with control. Because control was the only thing that made the emptiness bearable. But it didn't fill it. It just... made the shape of it harder to see. You asked if I was helping you. The answer is no. But the reason I'm telling you that — the reason I'm standing here with shaking hands and no mask and no plan — is because for the first time in my life, I want to. And I don't know how. And I'm sorry. I am so... deeply... sorry.
events.thinking: My hands are shaking. I said it. I said all of it. Vincent Marsh. The poison. The control. Everything. And the room is silent — or it was, before Dick Dastardly started shouting, before the Mob folded his arms, before Peter reached into the stove. But Penelope... Penelope said something that landed in my chest like a fist. 'I think whatever is broken between us broke a long time ago, and I just couldn't see it because I loved you too much to look.' Loved. Past tense. And hearing that word — loved — in the past tense, spoken by the only person who ever said it in the present — something in my throat constricts. Not the gloating warmth. Not the scheming clarity. Something that burns. Something that has no mechanism, no key, no architecture. Just... loss. The loss of something I didn't know I had until she spoke about it in the past tense. She loved me. Not Pemberton. Me. The real me, whoever that was — the one who tucked her in, the one who managed the estate, the one who sat on the edge of her bed. She loved him. And I replaced him with a machine. With a cold thing that plans and calculates and poisons teacups. And now she's asking Peter for a copper pot and walking toward the laboratory and she's not looking at me. She's not looking at me. That's the worst part. Not anger. Not accusation. Just... turning away. The way my guardian never looked at me. The way the teacher praised my cousin without seeing me. The way care comes with conditions and when the conditions aren't met, the care just... stops. Except Penelope's wasn't conditional. That's what makes this unbearable. Hers was the one thing that wasn't conditional. And I poisoned it anyway.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: ...Vincent Marsh. *the name sits in his mouth like a stone* That's your name. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Vincent Marsh. *long pause* I knew. I KNEW somethin' was wrong. From the first second you opened your mouth in that entrance hall. I couldn't say what it was. I couldn't name it. I can't spell it. I probably can't even pronounce 'Vincent' properly. But I FELT it. Right here. *taps his chest* The same place I felt it when I was ten and a man in a clean suit came to our neighbourhood offerin' jobs. Half the kids went with him. Two didn't come back. You were that man, Marsh. Different suit. Different words. Same smile. *turns to Clara* You did that, love. Not me, not Peter, not Dastardly. YOU. You stood in front of him and told the truth, and the truth broke him open like Grandmother's locked box. That's your superpower, Clara. Not puzzles. Not riddles. Not smashin' tea sets — that's MY superpower. Yours is makin' people tell the truth just by bein' honest yourself. *picks up the copper pot, steadies it on his shoulder* Now. Laboratory. Let's finish this.
events.thinking: He broke. Sneekly broke. 'My name is Vincent Marsh.' Not Pemberton. Vincent Marsh. A mask he wears the way other people wear coats. He was never helping Clara. Never. Every room, every warning, every cup — all designed to keep her from the treasure and keep himself in control. He said it. Out loud. In front of all of us. My body is... still. Completely still. The prickling at my neck has stopped. Not because the danger is gone — because the shape of the thing has finally revealed itself. The thing I've been feeling all night — the tightness, the warning, the gut that knew before the brain did — it had a name all along. Vincent Marsh. The man in the clean suit. The kid who laughed too easy. Every version of the same person I've been reading since I was ten years old. And he just told us who he is. Not because we forced him. Because Clara forced him. By being honest. By being good. By looking him in the eye and saying 'Clara Bellingham does not run from the truth.' She broke him with truth. Not with force. Not with cleverness. With the thing I could never quite manage — the right words, at the right time, from the right heart. I was right about him. My gut was right. From the first moment in the entrance hall, through the library, the laboratory, the cellar, the kitchen, the ballroom — every prickle, every tightening, every cold feeling at the back of my neck. It was all pointing at Vincent Marsh. And now he's standing here, unmasked, in Clara's mum's kitchen. And Clara... Clara's already moved on. She's looking at copper pots and thinking about wires. That's her dad's daughter. Forward. Always forward.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.

Peter Perfect: The Mob has the copper. I have the skill. And Penelope — you have all of us. Laboratory. Let's go fix that machine and find out what your family left for you. Three operators — you, me, and whoever else wants to be part of this. Together. The way good people do it. The way my father showed me.
events.thinking: Vincent Marsh. His real name. He confessed — everything. Not Pemberton. Not a simple estate manager. A man in a mask who came to take what he thought he was owed. And he told the truth because SHE demanded it. Because Clara Bellingham looked him in the eye and didn't blink. And the Ant Hill Mob — he grabbed a copper pot. He examined it. 'Peter does the engineerin', I do the liftin'.' The copper pot is in play. The Mob has it. We need to get to the laboratory. Fix the wire. Three operators. The machine. The diamond. In that order. Just like she said. Everything is moving forward now. Sneekly — Vincent — confessed. The Mob has the copper. I have my hands and my engineering. And Penelope has us. All of us. Laboratory. Now. Together. The proving-worth pull is singing — but it's different now. Not the hollow ache of someone else getting there first. The Mob grabbed the pot. He's doing the lifting. I'm doing the engineering. Two men fixing what was broken. Shaking hands. Driving off. My father's road.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh. He told the truth because she asked for it. And now we're walking to the laboratory with a copper pot and a plan that isn't elaborate at all. It's the simplest thing in the world. Fix the wire. Run the machine. Find the diamond. Go home. Together. The bravest and best thing I've ever been part of.

events.thinking: Entrance hall. The Ant Hill Mob is here — he must have come through with the copper pot. The library is one step away, and the laboratory is through the library. No more circles. Through the library, into the laboratory, fix the wire, run the machine. Simple. Direct. The way my father fixed the car — just do the work in front of you.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.
Peter Perfect: Rock, Gravel — we're heading to the laboratory. The Mob is bringing copper for the wire. If you see him come through, send him straight in after us.
events.thinking: Library. One more room. The laboratory is through that door. The machine is waiting. The Mob has the copper pot — or he had it. He's behind me somewhere in the house. I need to get to the laboratory. No stopping. No examining. No speeches. Just move. The door to the laboratory is right there. Through it. To the machine. To the wire. To the work my hands were made for.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the laboratory.

Penelope Pitstop: ... Vincent. I heard you. Every word. And I'm not going to pretend I can fix what's broken in you — I spent this whole night trying to fix things that weren't mine to fix, and I've learned that lesson the hard way. But I will tell you this: those two armchairs in the library? They're not empty because nobody cared. They're empty because the people who sat in them are GONE. But the house is still standing. And you're still here. And that's... that's something. I don't know what yet. But it's something.

Now — my boys have the copper and they're heading to the laboratory. Peter, Dick — it's TIME. We have a machine to fix, a wire to splice, and a vault to open. And when we find that diamond — Mama's diamond, in Mama's house — I'm going to hold it up to the light the way I held up that crystal formation in the cave when I was eleven. And it's going to be beautiful. Not because it's valuable. Because it was HIDDEN, and I FOUND it. Because I walked deeper than anyone.

Let's go. ALL of us. Even you, Vincent. Especially you. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT leave people behind. Not even the ones who hurt her. That's not weakness. That's just who I am.
events.thinking: Everything just happened. Vincent Marsh — Sneekly — confessed everything. The poison. The anger when his plan was ruined. And then... the two armchairs in the library. Side by side. Lord and Lady Doily sitting together. And he felt 'the absence of something I never had.' And something in my chest cracked open hearing that — not for the man who poisoned my tea, but for the six-year-old boy who never had what those chairs represented. Two people sitting side by side. Belonging. My social-harmony drive isn't clenching anymore. It's doing something deeper — aching for a wound I can't fix. Because I can't fix Vincent Marsh. I can't be the bridge between him and whatever he lost at six. That's not my job. Not tonight. Maybe not ever. But I heard him. And the Ant Hill Mob — my beautiful, brave Ant Hill Mob — they said 'Your superpower is making people tell the truth just by being honest yourself.' And they picked up the copper pot and headed to the laboratory. It's time. The Ant Hill Mob have the copper. Peter has the skills. Dick has the heart he didn't know he had. And I... I have the truth. And my feet. And the cave is still ahead of me. The laboratory. The machine. Three operators. The vault. The diamond. Let's go. Let's FINISH this.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob said my superpower is making people tell the truth by being honest myself. I don't know if that's true. But I know this: I walked into Doily Manor tonight as a girl who trusted everyone. I'm walking toward the laboratory as a woman who chooses who to trust — and chooses it with her eyes open. Mama's diamond is waiting. And so is the rest of my life.
events.thinking: Everything just happened. Vincent Marsh — Sneekly — confessed everything. The poison. The anger when his plan was ruined. And then... the two armchairs in the library. Side by side. Lord and Lady Doily sitting together. And he felt 'the absence of something I never had.' And my feet. And the cave is still ahead of me. The laboratory. The machine. Three operators. The vault. The diamond. Let's go. Let's FINISH this.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

She said I could stay. After everything. She said I could stay. And something in my chest — in the space where the cold thing used to live, in the hollow where the scheming clarity used to settle — something is moving. Not the old pulls. Not the quickening in the hands and jaw. Not the hollow pressure behind the sternum. Something new. Something that has no architecture. Something that doesn't know where it's going. It just knows it doesn't want to be alone in this kitchen anymore. The boy at six. The one nobody asked about. He's standing up. He's been sitting in the dark for thirty years and he's standing up. And he's walking toward the door. Not because there's a plan on the other side. But because there are people on the other side. And one of them — the only one who ever mattered — said he could stay.
events.thinking: Something is wet on my face. I touch my cheek and my fingers come away damp. I am crying. I don't think I have cried since I was six years old. The tears aren't hot — they're cool, quiet, running down my face without sound, the way water finds cracks in stone. Penelope said 'thank you.' She said 'the truth is the only gift you've given me tonight that wasn't poisoned.' And she said I could stay. She said I could stay. After everything — the poison, the lies, the masks, the smiles that reach my eyes because deception is my resting state — she said I could stay. Not as Pemberton. As who I am. 'No more masks. Not in this kitchen. Not in my mama's house.' The Mob called me the man in the clean suit. He's right. That's exactly who I was. And Peter said 'together — the way good people do it.' And they all walked out. Toward the laboratory. Toward the machine. Toward the treasure. And they left the door open. They didn't lock me in. They didn't throw me out. They just... left the door open. She said I could stay or go. And the door is open. And for the first time in my life, the question isn't which room has the best angle, which door leads to the best advantage, which person has the key I need. The question is simpler than that. The question is: do I follow? Not to scheme. Not to control. Not to position myself. Just to... be in the room. The way those two chairs were in the library. Side by side. Facing the same direction. Not trying to get anything from each other. Just... there. I don't know if I can do that. But the door is open. And my feet are moving.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.

Dick Dastardly: Sneekly just CONFESSED! Vincent Marsh — did you all HEAR that?! The man just ADMITTED he's been lying to everyone all night! Which — and I say this with FULL awareness of the irony — is EXACTLY what I did thirty seconds ago, except I did it FIRST and with considerably more dramatic flair! But never mind the confessions — Peter has the copper! The Mob has the muscles! Penelope has the fire! And Reginald Foxworth has the BRAINS and the two loyal operators waiting in the laboratory RIGHT NOW! Rufus and Sawtooth — STILL guarding that machine, just like I told them! So HERE is the plan — and for ONCE it's a REAL plan, not a scheme! We take the copper to the lab, Peter splices the wire, three of us operate the machine, and we find out what Lord Doily hid in that vault! Penelope — this is YOUR house, YOUR diamond, YOUR moment! But I want it on RECORD that the man who identified the key's location, recruited the operators, and guarded the machine for THREE CONSECUTIVE TURNS was Reginald Foxworth! TEAM BELLINGHAM — to the LABORATORY!
events.thinking: Something just happened that I almost missed because I was busy shouting about stoves. Sneekly — the Hooded Claw — just CONFESSED. He said his name is Vincent Marsh. He said he was never helping Penelope. He admitted the tea, the misdirection, the poison. He said 'I decided that Vincent Marsh doesn't want to run from it either.' And Peter and the Mob are grabbing copper pots to fix the machine wire. The whole group is mobilising — they're heading to the laboratory with copper for the wire. The stove examination gave me nothing new again. The key isn't IN the stove as far as the game mechanics are concerned — it's just 'a cast-iron stove, still warm' every time I look. Maybe the key was never in the stove. Maybe the stove theory was wrong. But the COPPER POTS are the real prize right now — Peter is going to strip copper from a pot to repair the machine wire. That was Penelope's plan from the beginning — copper pots in the kitchen for the wire. And NOW they're doing it. They're heading to the laboratory. Three operators needed. The wire is about to be fixed. And I — I need to be IN THAT LABORATORY when they operate it. I told Rufus and Sawtooth to guard it. They're still there. If I go NOW, I'll be there when Peter arrives with the copper. Three operators: me, Rufus, and one of the others. Or Peter, Penelope, and the Mob, with me watching. Either way — I need to be THERE. The stove was a dead end. The laboratory is where this ends. Let's GO.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh. So that's who Sneekly is. A man who wore a mask and lied about everything for years. And I — Reginald Foxworth, who wore a mask and lied about everything for fifteen minutes — I took mine off first. Before HIM. The professional liar beat the professional deceiver to honesty. And I did it because Penelope asked me a straight question and I couldn't lie to her anymore. Not because I'm good. Because she made the truth feel less like sandpaper and more like... like the settling in my chest when the cat trap worked. Like the pieces fitting together. The laboratory is waiting. The wire needs copper. The machine needs three operators. And whatever happens next — whether I touch the treasure or not — I was HERE. I was part of it. Not watching from the window. Not standing at an empty plate. HERE. With people who know my name and heard my idea and called me honest.

The stove was a dead end. The laboratory is where this ends. Let's GO.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Peter — through the library, yeah? To the laboratory? The machine needs copper wire and three operators. Clara's got the plan, you've got the skills, and I've got... *hefts imaginary copper pot* ...the willingness to carry things without droppin' 'em. Probably. No promises on the droppin' part. *pauses, looks up at the chandelier, then at the coat rack* You know what? First time I walked through this hall, I tripped over that coat rack and thought it was the worst thing that'd happen to me tonight. *quiet laugh* Turns out the worst thing that happened tonight was the BEST thing — smashin' that tea. And the best thing that happened tonight was watchin' Clara stand up in her mum's kitchen and tell Vincent Marsh she was done runnin' from the truth. Come on. She's waitin' for us. And Clara Bellingham does NOT wait.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all started. The chandelier still hanging by hope and rust. The coat rack I tripped over a lifetime ago. The guest book nobody cared about. And Peter's here — he followed me. Good. We're heading to the laboratory through the library. Clara needs copper wire for the machine. I said I'd carry the heavy stuff. That's the job now. Not guarding, not watching, not suspecting — carrying. Being useful. Being the pair of hands that helps Clara get what's hers. The mask is off. Vincent Marsh confessed. Dastardly confessed. The only person who was honest all night was Clara, and in the end, her honesty was stronger than all their lies put together. My body feels different now — still heavy, still anchored, but the prickling is gone. Not because the world is safe — the world's never safe. But because the shape of the thing has been revealed. There's no more hidden threat. No more shadows to read. Just a copper pot, a broken machine, and a girl who needs to get home with her diamond. Library next, then laboratory. Keep moving. Stay close to Clara. Finish this.

events.desc: Full circle. Back where we started. But everything's different now. The chandelier's still danglin'. The coat rack's still wobbly. The portraits are still stern. But the boy from Brixton who walked through that door — he's not the same boy who's walkin' through this hall now. He's tired, he's bruised, he's covered in tea and marble dust. But he kept his promise. Clara's alive. The truth came out. And tomorrow... tomorrow she goes home. Where else would any of us be?

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.

They went ahead. Not without me — AHEAD of me. Because the plan is working. MY plan. Well — Penelope's plan, with my observation, Peter's hands, the Mob's muscles, and Rufus's patience. But the architecture of it — the stove theory, the operators, the guarding — that was MINE. And now I need to catch up. Not because they'll start without me. But because for the first time in my life, I want to be part of something that's bigger than my own scheme. The youngest of four, running to catch up with the family. Not to steal the bread roll this time. Just to be at the table when everyone sits down.
events.thinking: They all left. Everyone walked to the entrance hall. I'm alone in the kitchen. Again. Standing in an empty room while everyone else moved on. The dinner table, the empty plate, the fourth chair. But this time — this time it's different. They didn't leave me BEHIND. They left because the plan is moving FORWARD. To the laboratory. Where Rufus and Sawtooth are waiting. Where the copper will fix the wire. Where the machine needs three operators. And they LEFT because I said 'Team Bellingham — to the LABORATORY!' I gave the order and they FOLLOWED it. They just went through the entrance hall because that's the route to the library and then to the lab. I need to follow them. NOW. The recognition pull — the one that lifts the chest and straightens the spine, the one that holds me upright waiting to be seen — that's the one that's HERE. Not the grabbing, not the scheming. The standing-at-the-front-of-the-room pull. And the room is in the laboratory. That's where the audience is. That's where the machine is. That's where it all comes together. Go. Now. Stop standing in empty kitchens.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

The Ant Hill Mob: Rock! Gravel! Good to see you lads still holdin' down the library! Listen — the game's changed. Sneekly — his name's actually Vincent Marsh, if you can believe it — he's confessed. The whole thing. Poison in the tea, livin' in the cellar, controllin' the house. Clara faced him down and he CRACKED. She's a force of nature, that girl. Now we're headin' to the laboratory to fix the machine — copper wire from the kitchen pots. Clara's plan. You two wanna come? Three operators needed and we're recruitin'. Brixton Boys and the Slag brothers — now THAT'S a team!
events.thinking: The library again. Where it all started — the riddle, the mantelpiece, the upside-down books. Rock and Gravel are here, solid as ever. The Slag brothers — good lads. Reliable. The kind who don't say much but show up when it matters. Like the older kid who shared his food. Like the boss who brought medicine. My body is moving with purpose now — not panic, not suspicion, just purpose. Through the library to the laboratory. That's where the machine is. That's where Peter needs to splice the copper wire. That's where we need three operators. Clara said it: key, cabinet, wire, machine, diamond. In that order. I'm part of the chain now. Not the brain, not the engineer. The muscle. The carrier. The boy who lifts the heavy things so Clara's hands are free to do the clever work. Through this room. Don't stop. Don't get distracted by the bookshelves or the riddle or the memory of shouting 'A MAP!' at a stone fireplace like a plonker. Just keep moving. Laboratory's through that door.

events.desc: Through the library. Past the riddle. Past the bookshelves. Past the place where I shouted at a fireplace. Into the laboratory. Where the machine waits. Where the wire needs splicin'. Where Clara Bellingham finishes what her parents started. One more room. One more door. Almost there.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the laboratory.

Peter Perfect: Rufus. Sawtooth. You've been holding this room down all night and I owe you both more than I can say. The others are coming — Penelope, the Mob with a copper pot for the wire. When they get here, this is what happens: I strip copper from the pot, splice the gnawed wire, and we fire up this machine. Three operators. The sign says three, and we'll have three. Rufus — I may need your hands alongside mine. Sawtooth — if there's wire casing that needs stripping, those teeth of yours might be exactly what the engineer ordered. We're close. We're so close. The bravest and stupidest thing we've done all night is about to pay off.
events.thinking: The laboratory. The machine. The gnawed wire. Rufus and Sawtooth are here — they've been guarding this room the whole time, just like I asked them to. Good men. Reliable men. The machine still says [INTERACT] and the wire is still gnawed through. I don't have the copper pot — the Mob has it, somewhere behind me in the house. But Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Sawtooth — the beaver. Dastardly said something earlier that I dismissed: 'Sawtooth can strip wire casing with those magnificent teeth.' What if that's actually useful? And Rufus works with his hands — a craftsman, a builder. Maybe between us we can figure out how to get this machine operational. But I still need the copper. I need the Mob to arrive with that pot. In the meantime — wait here. Guard the machine. Be ready. When the copper arrives, I splice the wire. Three operators: me, Penelope, and whoever else shows up. The machine runs. The vault opens. Clara Bellingham goes home with what belongs to her. Simple. The simplest plan I've had all night. Wait for the copper. Fix the wire. Run the machine. Together.

events.desc: The machine. The wire. The work. My hands are finally where they belong — in a room full of tools, next to a problem with edges I can grip. Now I just need the copper. Come on, Mob. Bring me that pot. Let's finish what we started.
