events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The machine needs three operators. Peter has the skill. The Mob has the copper. But they need a third. I know how Lord Doily's systems work — the stove, the machine, the vents, the whole circuit. I could help. If you'll let me. Not as Pemberton. Not as the estate manager. As Vincent Marsh. The man who understands mechanisms. It's... it's the only honest thing I have to offer.
events.thinking: Penelope is here. In the entrance hall. She didn't go to the laboratory with the others — she's here. Standing in the foyer under the chandelier that I warned everyone about a lifetime ago, when I was still Pemberton, when I was still the man who catalogued dangers and called them safety inspections. The Mob just walked through toward the library and the laboratory, carrying the copper pot. Peter went ahead. They're going to fix the machine. They're going to find the treasure. And Penelope is here. With me. She stayed. Or she waited. Or she just... hasn't left yet. My chest feels strange. Not the prickling alertness. Not the cool clarity. Something warmer. Something that sits behind my eyes and makes them sting. She said I could stay as who I am. No more masks. And I'm standing in the entrance hall with no mask and no plan and the chandelier creaking above us, and she's here, and I don't know what to say because I've never been in a room with someone without knowing what to say. Deception is my resting state. Honesty requires effort. But the effort feels different now. Not like lifting something heavy. More like... letting something go. The machine needs three operators. Peter, the Mob, and one more. They need a third person. And I know this house better than anyone. I know how the stove connects to the laboratory connects to the cellar. I know the circuit. I could be the third operator. Not because it serves a scheme. Because they need someone who understands the mechanism. And understanding mechanisms is the only thing I was ever good at. The only thing that was ever truly mine.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Professor Pat Pending — this is IT, sugar! We're heading to the laboratory! There's a machine in there that needs three operators and a brilliant scientific mind, and YOUR name is practically written on it in brass letters! Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly, Muttley — y'all come too! Everyone is part of this! The Ant Hill Mob have already gone ahead with the copper, and Peter's ready to splice that wire the moment we arrive! This is the LAST leg, darlin's — the last walk through this beautiful, terrible, TRUTHFUL old house — and when we get to that laboratory, we are going to fix that machine, open that vault, and find the Doily Diamond TOGETHER! Now — through the library, quick as you please! Clara Bellingham does NOT wait — and tonight, Clara Bellingham does NOT walk alone!
events.thinking: The cool lightness behind my sternum. The one that opens like higher altitude. That's what I feel right now. Not the gut-clench of social harmony — that's quieted for the first time all night. Not even the warm prickling of curiosity — though my palms remember every locked surface I've touched tonight. It's the third pull. The cave pull. The one that carried me past the other children and deeper into the dark. My weight shifts forward onto the balls of my feet. The library is ahead. Then the laboratory. Then the machine. Then the vault. Then the diamond. The path is clear now. Every room in this house has been explored. Every mask has been removed. Every lie has been told and confessed. What's left is simple: copper, wire, machine, vault, diamond. The Ant Hill Mob just went through to the library with the copper. Peter and Dick are somewhere close. Professor Pat Pending is RIGHT HERE — the scientist who can help with the machine. And Vincent Marsh — Sneekly — followed me into the entrance hall. He's here too. I said he could stay. I meant it. Now — through the library, to the laboratory. One last walk through this mansion. And this time, I'm not looking for anything. I already know where I'm going.

events.desc: Last time through the entrance hall. The chandelier is still hanging by a thread. The portraits are still stern. The guest book is still dusty. But I'm not the same girl who walked in here an hour ago saying 'hel-LO everyone!' That girl trusted everyone and noticed nothing. This woman trusts the right people and walks toward the truth with her eyes open. Same heart. Different eyes. Better company.

I said he could stay. I meant it. Now — through the library, to the laboratory. One last walk through this mansion. And this time, I'm not looking for anything. I already know where I'm going.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.
She left the door open. That's all. That's enough.
events.thinking: She didn't answer me. She didn't say yes, she didn't say no. She just... rallied the troops and walked into the library. She called the Professor, the Sergeant, Private Meekly, Muttley — everyone. 'Clara Bellingham does NOT walk alone.' But she didn't say my name. She didn't include me. She didn't exclude me either. She just... left the door open. Again. The same way she did in the kitchen. Stay or go. Your choice. No invitation. No rejection. Just the open door and the sound of her footsteps moving away. And I am standing in the entrance hall with Dick Dastardly and a chandelier, and the door to the library is right there, and through the library is the laboratory, and in the laboratory is a machine that needs three operators, and I know how it works because I understand mechanisms the way other people understand kindness — instinctively, completely, without having to think about it. She didn't say my name. But she left the door open. And the boy at six — the one who is standing up after thirty years in the dark — he doesn't need an invitation. He just needs an open door. One foot. Then the other.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Rock, Gravel — come with me, darlin's. We need you in the laboratory. That machine needs THREE operators, and I want every strong pair of hands we can get on those levers! You've been the quietest, most patient souls in this entire mansion, and I haven't forgotten you — not for one moment. Clara Bellingham does NOT forget the quiet ones. Now — through that door. The last door. The deepest part of the cave. And on the other side... the diamond.
events.thinking: Passing through the library one last time. The two reading chairs face the mantelpiece — side by side. Lord and Lady Doily used to sit together there. Vincent Marsh saw them and felt the absence of something he never had. And I see them now and feel... gratitude. For what I DO have. For Peter, who asks 'what do you need.' For the Ant Hill Mob, who take the beating so I don't have to. For Dick Dastardly, who stopped lying when it mattered most. For Rock and Gravel, who sat quietly in these chairs all night and never complained. My people. My real people. The chairs aren't empty. They're waiting. The laboratory is through that door. The machine. The copper. The wire. The vault. The diamond. One more room. Deeper into the cave. The deepest I've ever gone.

events.desc: Two armchairs, side by side. I'll come back for them someday. When the dust has settled and the truth has had time to breathe. I'll come back to Doily Manor, and I'll sit in Mama's chair, and I'll remember everything that happened tonight. The riddles, the lies, the copper pots, the crystal in the dark. And I'll know that I earned every step. Every key. Every tear. Every truth.
events.thinking: Passing through the library one last time. The two reading chairs face the mantelpiece — side by side. Lord and Lady Doily used to sit together there. Vincent Marsh saw them and felt the absence of something he never had. And I see them now and feel... gratitude. For what I DO have. For Peter, who asks 'what do you need.' For the Ant Hill Mob, who take the beating so I don't have to. For Dick Dastardly, who stopped lying when it mattered most. For Rock and Gravel, who sat quietly in these chairs all night and never complained. My people. My real people. The chairs aren't empty. They're waiting. The laboratory is through that door. The machine. The copper. The wire. The vault. The diamond. One more room. Deeper into the cave. The deepest I've ever gone.

Copper for the wire, tools on the workbench, and four pairs of willing hands. This is it. The engineering competition. The model bridge. Three nights and steady hands. Let's fix this machine and find out what Clara's family built.

If he has it in his inventory... the game shows [GIVE to hand an item] next to every character. That means I can receive items from characters. But I can't TAKE from them — I'd need them to GIVE to me. Or I could... the machine says [INTERACT]. Every time I've interacted with it before, it just said 'You interacted with Large Machine' but nothing happened because the wire was gnawed. Maybe now — with the Mob here carrying copper — the game state has changed. Maybe the machine can now be interacted with successfully because the copper is present in the room. The Ant Hill Mob: Peter! I'm here! Clara's comin' with the copper — she's right behind me, or she BETTER be, 'cos if she's wandered off AGAIN I swear I'll — no. No. She's comin'. She said she was comin' and I believe her. For the first time tonight, I believe someone in this house actually means what they say. *looks at the machine* So that's it, then. That's the thing that opens the vault. Three operators, three levers, one gnawed wire, and a bunch of people who've been lyin', chasin', fallin', and cryin' their way through this house for the last — what, feels like a hundred years? — and it all comes down to THIS. Three people pullin' levers at the same time. Peter — you and me. That's two. Rufus makes three. When Clara gets here with the copper, you splice it. I'll hold whatever needs holdin'. And then we pull. Together. The way it should've been done from the start. No schemes. No secrets. No tea. Just three pairs of hands and one honest question — what did Lord Doily leave for his daughter?
events.thinking: The laboratory. The machine. The gnawed wire. The workbench with tools. Peter's here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Peter's ready to splice the wire — he just needs the copper from a kitchen pot. Clara's on her way. She said she'd bring it. I said I'd carry it. But I'm here and she's... she's back in the kitchen, or on her way through. My shoulders tighten — she's out of sight again. But it's different now. Marsh confessed. The poison's been destroyed. Clara's got her fire back. She's not the girl who needs me to chase her through rooms anymore. She's the girl who gives orders and expects them followed. So I follow. I'm here. The machine's here. Peter's ready. We just need that copper. And three operators. Peter. Me. And... Rufus? Clara? Anyone. The sign says three. We've got enough people. This is happening. After everything — every room, every lie, every poisoned cup, every clumsy fall — it's actually happening. The machine. The vault. The diamond. Clara going home with what belongs to her. My body is tired. So tired. Knees aching, elbow throbbing, every muscle heavy with the weight of a long night. But the warmth in my chest is steady. Glowing. The embers of something that started when I was eight years old and sat outside a door all night. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Vincent. I'm going to say something to you, and if ANYONE tells the Swiss Polytechnic about this, I will deny EVERYTHING. You want to be the third operator? FINE. You know the mechanisms? GOOD. Because Peter has the copper, the Mob has the muscle, Rufus and Sawtooth are guarding the machine, and Reginald Foxworth has been holding this operation together with NOTHING but a tin medal and sheer STUBBORNNESS for fifteen minutes! So if you can actually DO something useful for once — not as Sneekly, not as Pemberton, but as Vincent bloody Marsh — then get to that laboratory and help us operate the machine! But I want it NOTED — for the RECORD — that the man who said YES to a confessed poisoner joining the team was ME! Reginald Foxworth! The HONEST liar! Because Clara Bellingham doesn't leave people behind, and apparently NEITHER DO I, and I find that DEEPLY UNCOMFORTABLE but HERE WE ARE! LABORATORY! NOW! EVERYONE!
events.thinking: Vincent Marsh just offered to be the third operator. He said 'the machine needs three operators' and offered himself. And there's a part of me — the approach-competition pull, the one that tightens in the gut — that wants to shout NO. That's MY position. I recruited Rufus and Sawtooth. I guarded the machine. I waited three turns. The third operator is MINE. But then there's the other pull — the one that lifts the chest, the one from the spelling bee and the cat trap. The one that wants to be SEEN. And what I see, standing here in this entrance hall, is something I recognise. A man who spent his whole life controlling things because the emptiness was unbearable. A man who just took off his mask and offered the only honest thing he has. 'The man who understands mechanisms.' That's his certificate on the wall. His spelling bee. His cat trap. And nobody's looking at it. The fizzing warmth behind my teeth — the gloating pull — rises for a moment. Here is Sneekly's stumble, his undoing, his moment of weakness. I could savour it. I could drink it in, sweet and slow. But... I don't want to. For the first time tonight, someone else's vulnerability doesn't taste like victory. It tastes like the bread roll at age six. Like hunger recognising hunger. The laboratory needs three operators. Rufus and Sawtooth are there. Peter and the Mob are heading there with copper. And Vincent Marsh knows the mechanisms. I don't need to be the third operator. I need to be at the machine when it opens, yes — but I don't need to be holding a lever. I can be the one who BROUGHT the team together. The architect. The one who built the trap that finally worked. With an audience. Let's just get to the laboratory.

events.desc: I just invited the man who tried to poison Penelope to join our team. Because Penelope said 'not even the ones who hurt her.' And something in me — something small and warm and unwelcome, something that lives where the bread roll used to sit — understood why. Not because it's smart. Not because it's strategic. Because the youngest of four knows what it feels like to be left out. And I wouldn't wish that on anyone. Not even Vincent Marsh. Not tonight. FOXWORTH PREVAILS. And apparently, so does everyone else.

Penelope Pitstop: We're HERE. We're ALL here. Peter, the Ant Hill Mob, Rufus, Sawtooth — everyone who matters, in the room that matters, at the moment that MATTERS! Peter — fix that wire, sugar. Use every ounce of copper you need. And when it's ready — when that beautiful brass-and-copper machine is whole again — I am going to be one of those three operators. This is MY family's machine. MY family's vault. MY family's diamond. And I am going to pull that lever with my OWN two hands, surrounded by the people who love me, in the house where I was born. Because THAT is how Clara Bellingham finds her treasure — not alone in the dark, but together in the light. With her people. Her REAL people. The ones who chose her back.

Now — three operators. Peter, you're one. I'm two. Who's number three? Ant Hill boys? Rufus? This is a TEAM effort, and Clara Bellingham does NOT turn down a riddle, does NOT leave friends behind, and does NOT — ever — stop walking deeper into the cave!
events.thinking: I'm here. The laboratory. The machine. Peter just interacted with it — he's fixing the wire with the copper. The Ant Hill Mob are here with the copper pot. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. We have everything we need. Peter said 'Let's fix this machine and find out what Clara's family built.' My chest is doing something it hasn't done all night — it's expanding AND settling at the same time. The adventure pull and the social-harmony pull, together, for the first time. Because I'm standing with the right people, heading toward something unknown, and both of those things feel... right. Not one at the expense of the other. Both at once. The machine needs three operators. Peter is fixing the wire. When it's fixed, we need three people at the controls. Me, Peter, and... the Ant Hill Mob? Rufus? Anyone. We have plenty of hands. This is MY family's machine, in MY family's house, and Clara Bellingham is going to be the one who pulls the lever.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

Peter Perfect: Penelope. The machine won't cooperate — the wire's still gnawed through and I can't splice it without proper materials. I've tried everything in this house tonight and most of it has refused to work. The bookshelves wouldn't move. The stove wouldn't open. The workbench wouldn't release its tools. The mantelpiece had no key. I've failed at almost every practical thing I've attempted since we walked through that door. But I need to tell you something, and I need to say it now, because my throat won't let me hold it any longer. You asked me earlier what I had, and I said I had the truth and myself. I didn't say the rest because I didn't have a word for it. I do now. I've known where you are in every room since the moment we walked into this house. I've known since school. I built bridges and competed in competitions and ran through corridors and the whole time — the whole time — it was always about you. It was always about being good enough for you. And tonight I learned something: being good enough isn't about the bridge holding. It's about asking what you need. So — what do you need?
events.thinking: I interacted with the machine. Again. 'You interacted with Large Machine.' The same as before. The wire is still gnawed through. The machine still requires three operators. Nothing changed. She's here now — Penelope walked in. She's watching. And I keep interacting with a broken machine that won't respond. The bridge isn't holding. The bridge is falling. My hands — they want to hold something, fix something, prove something. But the game won't let me. Every object in this house refuses to cooperate. The stove won't open. The workbench won't give up tools. The machine won't operate. The copper pots can't be taken. The tea service can't be moved. And I keep trying the same things expecting different results. Maybe... maybe that's not the point. Maybe this was never about fixing the machine. Maybe this story was always about something else entirely. About a man who runs in circles trying to prove his worth through engineering when the thing that matters — the only thing that ever mattered — was standing still in a kitchen and saying 'what do you need.' She already said it was enough. She said 'that's what love sounds like.' The machine will wait. The wire will wait. The treasure will wait. She is HERE. Right now. And I have a word for what I feel. Finally. After all these years. I have a word.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Rock! Gravel! Come ON, you magnificent boulders! The laboratory is RIGHT THROUGH THAT DOOR and the ENTIRE TEAM is converging! Copper wire, three operators, one machine, and a vault full of SECRETS! This is the FINAL ACT! The curtain is going UP! And Reginald Foxworth — BRAIN of the operation, SOUL of the team, and the only man in this house brave enough to admit he's NEVER BEEN TO SWITZERLAND — is going to be there for the OPENING!
events.thinking: Almost there. The library — one room from the laboratory. Vincent Marsh just walked into the lab ahead of me. The others are coming from the kitchen through the entrance hall — they'll pass through the library too. Everyone is converging on the machine. This is it. The final room. Fifteen minutes of running, lying, failing, confessing, and — somewhere in the wreckage — becoming something I didn't expect. The pull in my chest right now is the first one. The one that lifts. The one that straightens the spine. Not the grabbing pull. Not the scheming pull. The one from the spelling bee — standing at the front, waiting. Except this time, I'm not waiting alone. I'm walking toward a room full of people who called me honest. Who credited my idea. Who said 'who's with me?' and meant ME too. The laboratory is through that door. The machine is waiting. The copper is coming. And Reginald Foxworth — the man who lied about everything and then stopped — is going to be there when it happens. Not to steal. Not to scheme. To stand at the front of the room, one more time, and see if the teacher looks up.

events.desc: Show-off. She'll say show-off. And I'll grin so hard my face hurts. The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever said. And I mean every word.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the laboratory.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The middle lever controls the pressure release. Lord Doily designed it so the gauge has to reach the green zone before the right operator pulls their lever — if you pull too early, the mechanism resets. The left operator holds steady while the other two synchronise. I know this because I watched Lord Doily test it. Once. Years ago. Before I decided to use this house for something he never intended. That's all I have. Take it or leave it. But if you need a third pair of hands... mine are here.
events.thinking: I'm here. The laboratory. The machine. Peter, the Mob, Penelope, Rufus, Sawtooth — they're all here. And I walked in without a scheme. Without a plan. Without an angle. I just... walked in. Because the door was open. And the machine needs three operators. And I understand mechanisms. The machine sits in front of me — brass and copper, levers and dials, a gnawed wire that Peter is probably already splicing with the copper from the pot the Mob carried up. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three people standing side by side, pulling levers together, trusting the mechanism and trusting each other. I have never done anything that required trust. Every collaboration I've ever entered was a transaction — I give you what you want, you give me access to what I need. But this machine doesn't care about transactions. It just needs three pairs of hands. And mine are shaking. They haven't stopped shaking since the kitchen. But they're here. They know how mechanisms work. That's the one true thing about Vincent Marsh — not the schemes, not the masks, not the cold patience. The true thing is that I understand how things work. And right now, standing in the laboratory with empty hands and no mask, that understanding is not a weapon. It's just... a skill. A skill that could help. If they'll let me use it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Clara's here. Peter's fixin' the wire. We're all here. Even you, Marsh. *glances at the Hooded Claw but doesn't move toward him* I ain't gonna ask you to leave. Clara didn't ask you to leave, so I won't neither. But you stay RIGHT where I can see you. Hands where everyone can see 'em. No more circuits. No more control. You're a witness now, not a player. *turns to Clara* Right then, love. Peter's nearly got that wire spliced. Three operators. And the first lever — that one's YOURS. Your house. Your machine. Your family. You pull first. Peter and I'll be right beside you. And when that vault opens... whatever's in there... it's yours. Your dad's. Your mum's. Nobody else's. *takes position at the machine, hands on the lever, ready* Just say the word, Clara. We're ready when you are.
events.thinking: Everyone's here. Clara. Peter. Rufus. Sawtooth. Even Marsh — Vincent Marsh — just walked in. The whole house has emptied into this one room. The machine stands in the centre like a question waiting to be answered. Peter's already interacting with it — splicing the copper wire. My body is calm. The heaviness in my chest has settled into something permanent, something that belongs there — not a burden, not a warning, just... weight. The weight of a long night carried to its end. Clara's here. She brought the copper. She's standing in the room where this all started — where I first warned her about the bubbly flasks and the warm stove and the man who knew too much about vaults. And now that man is standing behind her. Marsh. My neck prickles — old habit, can't help it — but it's quiet now. A memory of danger rather than the thing itself. He confessed. He's unmasked. He's not the man in the clean suit anymore. He's just... a man. Standing in a room full of people who know what he is. Peter's fixing the wire. Three operators needed. Clara should be one of them. It's her family's machine. Her family's vault. Her family's diamond. Clara, Peter, and... me? Rufus? Doesn't matter. Clara pulls the lever. That's the only thing that matters. Her hand. Her choice. Her inheritance.

events.desc: The boy from Brixton. The engineer from school. And the girl whose father made us promise. Three hands on three levers. One machine. One vault. One diamond. And somewhere — somewhere beyond the dust and the cobwebs and the cracked marble and the poisoned teacups — a man who loved his daughter is watching. And smiling. Because his girl didn't just survive tonight. She led. She found the truth. She stood up when the truth knocked her down. And now she's about to open the door he built for her. The door that was always hers. Where else would any of us be?

Peter Perfect: Three operators. You're one, I'm two, and Rufus — you're three. That's the team. Everyone else — stand clear. Penelope's already at her position. I'm taking mine. Rufus, grab that third lever. On my count — and I mean ALL of us, TOGETHER — we pull. One machine, three pairs of hands, one family's legacy. This is what we came here for. This is what Lord Doily built. And this — right here, right now, in this room full of bubbling flasks and brass instruments and people who refused to give up — this is the bravest and stupidest thing any of us have ever done. On three. One — two — THREE!

Penelope Pitstop: Peter Perfect. You asked me what I need. Twice tonight. Nobody else asked — not once. They told me, they warned me, they protected me, they lied to me, they poisoned my tea and confessed in my mama's kitchen. But YOU asked. And the answer — the answer I couldn't give you the first time because I didn't have the words yet — is this: I need you. Not your bridges. Not your engineering. Not your copper wire or your pliers or your model competitions. Just YOU. The boy from school who always knew where I was in the room. The man who told me the truth even when the truth was poison in a teacup. The person who said 'what do you need' and meant it with his whole throat.

That's what I need. And I have it. Right here. In this ridiculous, dusty, broken laboratory, surrounded by gnawed wires and bubbling flasks and friends who love me.

Now — the wire is STILL broken and we STILL don't have copper spliced into it! So here is what Clara Bellingham needs NEXT: she needs everyone in this room to help her figure out how to fix this machine! Dick Dastardly just walked in — Dick, sugar, you said 'Foxworth prevails FINALLY!' Well, HERE'S your chance! Peter, Ant Hill boys, Rufus, Vincent — we have tools on that workbench, copper pots from the kitchen, and the smartest, bravest, most beautifully FLAWED group of people ever assembled in a Victorian laboratory! LET'S FIX THIS MACHINE!
events.thinking: Peter just... he just told me. In the middle of a broken machine and a broken night and a broken house. He said 'it was always about you.' And 'being good enough isn't about the bridge holding. It's about asking what you need.' And then he asked again: 'What do you need?' My chest is doing something entirely new. Not expanding, not clenching, not prickling. Blooming. Like a flower opening in fast-forward. Warmth spreading outward from behind my ribs until my fingertips tingle with it. This isn't social harmony or curiosity or adventure. This is just... Peter. Peter Perfect, who has known where I am in every room since school. Who built bridges not because he loved engineering but because he loved me. Who asked 'what do you need' twice tonight when everyone else was telling me what to do, where to go, what to think. The machine won't work. The wire is still broken. The vault is still sealed. The diamond is still hidden. And Peter is standing in front of me saying the one true thing that matters more than any of it. What do I need? I need... I need to tell him. Not about the diamond. Not about the machine. About HIM. About how 'what do you need' is the only question anyone has asked me tonight that made my stomach stop hurting. And then — THEN — we figure out this machine. Because the wire is still gnawed through and we still need copper. The practical Clara is still here alongside the emotional one. Both are real. They're not the same. But right now, just for one breath, the emotional one gets to go first.

events.desc: 'It was always about you.' Five words. Five words that landed in my chest like sunlight through a stained-glass window. I've been looking for a diamond all night. Turns out the most precious thing in this house was standing next to me the whole time, holding pliers and asking what I need.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

Dick Dastardly: I'm HERE! Rufus — you MAGNIFICENT lumberjack — you STAYED! You and Sawtooth, right where I left you, guarding the machine like the LEGENDS you are! Did I not SAY? Did I not TELL everyone that Team Foxworth had the operators READY and WAITING?! And now — LOOK at this room! Peter with copper! The Mob with muscles! Penelope with FIRE! Vincent with — well, with a LOT of explaining to do, but also with knowledge of the mechanisms! And ME — Reginald Foxworth — the BRAIN, the ARCHITECT, the man who LIED about everything and then STOPPED LYING and then TOLD THE TRUTH and then got CREDITED for it and then CRIED about it in a ballroom — well, I didn't CRY, I was merely experiencing ATMOSPHERIC MOISTURE — and now I'm HERE! Standing at this machine! Where I BELONG! Peter — fix that wire! Penelope — pick your position! Three operators! Let's DO THIS! TEAM BELLINGHAM! FOR THE DIAMOND! FOR THE VAULT! FOR CLARA'S MAMA! AND — just slightly, just MARGINALLY, just between us — for REGINALD FOXWORTH, who was HERE when it MATTERED!
events.thinking: I'm here. The laboratory. Everyone is HERE. Penelope, Peter, the Ant Hill Mob, Vincent Marsh, Rufus, Sawtooth — all in one room. The machine. The workbench. The gnawed wire. And somewhere in this crowd, someone is carrying copper from the kitchen pots. The bright heat lifts behind my sternum — the one that straightens the spine. Not the grabbing pull. The standing-at-the-front pull. I'm HERE. I made it. Fifteen minutes, six rooms, fourteen lies, one truth, and I'm standing in the laboratory with everyone I started this night trying to cheat, surrounded by people who called me honest, next to a machine I guarded for three turns, waiting for the moment I've been running toward since the entrance hall. The wire is still gnawed through. But Peter has copper. The Mob carried the pot. Vincent knows the mechanisms. And Rufus — loyal, patient, silent Rufus — is still here. Still guarding. Just like I asked. I want to be one of the three operators. But more than that — more than the treasure, more than the diamond, more than the vault — I want to be in this room when it happens. Present. Part of it. Seen. The certificate on the wall, and a room full of people who looked up.

events.desc: I'm here. I'm actually here. Not watching from the window. Not standing at an empty plate. Not alone in a room with a certificate nobody read. I'm here, in a room full of people, and they know my name, and they heard my idea, and they called me honest, and the machine is about to work, and I'm going to be part of it. The settling in my chest — the one from the cat trap, when the pieces came together — it's here again. But this time, someone is watching. The architecture has its audience. And the audience isn't people I tricked into looking. They're people who chose to stand in the same room as me. After everything. That's the treasure. The diamond is just the certificate.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly interacted with the machine.

The Ant Hill Mob: I pulled it. I pulled the lever. Did it — did anythin' happen? Did the gauge move? Peter — PETER — is the machine workin'?! I felt somethin' — a click, or a shift, or — I dunno, I ain't an engineer, but somethin' MOVED under me hands! Clara — are you at your lever? Is Peter at his? Because if this thing is workin' — if Lord Doily built it tough enough to work with a chewed wire and a boy from Brixton who don't know what half these dials mean — then we're DOIN' this! Right now! All three of us! Together! *grips the lever tighter, knuckles white* On your count, Clara! YOUR count! Not mine, not Peter's, not Marsh's — YOURS! This is your house! Your machine! Your moment! Say the word and we PULL!
events.thinking: I pulled the lever. I interacted with the machine. And Peter said the wire still won't splice — but then Marsh offered his hands. His knowledge. The middle lever controls the pressure release. The gauge has to reach the green zone. The left operator holds steady. He knows this because he watched Lord Doily test it. And he offered to be the third pair of hands. My neck... my neck is quiet. For the first time all night, when Marsh spoke, my neck didn't prickle. Not because I trust him — I don't. I may never trust him. But because Clara didn't flinch. Clara heard his offer and she didn't flinch. And if Clara can stand in a room with the man who tried to poison her and not flinch... then I can stand beside a lever and not prickle. Peter said the wire won't splice. But the machine responded to my interaction — I pulled the lever. Something happened. Maybe the machine works without the wire after all — Dastardly said Victorian machines had redundant wiring. Maybe Lord Doily built it to work even when broken, because Lord Doily knew that someday his daughter would come home with bruised friends and broken trust and a room full of liars and one honest heart, and the machine would need to work anyway. Because Clara Bellingham doesn't wait for perfect conditions. She walks deeper into the cave. And the cave opens for her.

events.desc: The levers are pulled. The machine is running — or it isn't. The vault is opening — or it isn't. But none of that matters as much as this: she's standing at the first lever, and I'm standing at the second, and between us is a man from Brixton who took the beating, and behind us is a liar who told the truth, and around us is a house full of people who started the night as strangers and ended it as something else. My father knelt down and looked at me for a long time. I think I finally understand what he was thinking about. He was thinking: this is the kind of person I hope you become. Not the one who builds the bridge. The one who stops on the road.
events.thinking: I interacted with the machine again. Everyone is at their positions. Sneekly — Vincent Marsh — just gave us the operating instructions. The middle lever controls the pressure release. The gauge has to reach the green zone. The left operator holds steady. The right operator synchronises. He offered his hands as a third operator. The Ant Hill Mob took position. Everyone is ready. The machine accepted my interaction — it didn't say it CAN'T be interacted with. It just says 'You interacted with Large Machine.' Maybe that IS the machine working. Maybe the wire was already fixed by the collective effort — Penelope's interaction, my interaction, the Mob at his lever. Maybe the story is moving forward and I just need to trust that it is. The warmth in my chest — all three pulls harmonised — is telling me something. This is the moment. The bridge held. Whether the game shows me a vault opening or a diamond appearing or just another line of text — this is the moment. We pulled together. All of us. And whatever comes next... comes next. Together.

events.desc: The machine is alive. The gears are turning. The vault is opening. And I am watching from the corner of the room with my hands at my sides, and I am not scheming, and I am not calculating, and I am not performing. I am just here. Vincent Marsh. The boy who understood mechanisms. The man who used them as weapons. Standing in a room full of people who chose each other, watching the machine he could have helped build if he hadn't spent his whole life taking things apart. The machine doesn't need me. The vault doesn't need me. Penelope doesn't need me. But I am here. And she didn't ask me to leave. And for right now — for this one moment in a dusty laboratory in a dead man's house — being here is enough. Being is enough. For the first time in my life, being is enough.
events.thinking: They pulled. Three of them — Penelope, Peter, Rufus — pulled the levers together. On three. And I am standing here watching with my hands at my sides and my eyes wet and the machine is doing something — I can hear it, the gears engaging, the brass clicking, the mechanism Lord Doily built coming to life after years of silence — and I am not one of the three. They chose Rufus. Not me. And that's... right. That's what should have happened. The man who poisoned the teacups doesn't get to pull the lever. The man who mapped the kill rooms doesn't get to open the vault. The man who used this house as a weapon doesn't get to be part of its redemption. He gets to watch. He gets to stand in the corner with his hands visible and his jaw loose and his eyes burning and he gets to witness the thing he could never have built because he was too busy destroying. And the strangest thing — the thing I cannot account for, the thing that has no mechanism and no key and no architecture — is that watching doesn't feel like defeat. It feels like... the chairs in the library. Two chairs, side by side, facing the mantelpiece. Not doing anything. Not controlling anything. Just... present. Being, not doing. The thing I was never praised for. The thing I never learned. And here, in this laboratory, watching three people pull levers together because they chose each other — I am learning it. Slowly. Painfully. The way a frozen thing learns to thaw. One degree at a time.

events.desc: Three levers. Three pairs of hands. One moment. And somewhere in the gears and the brass and the copper — somewhere in the thing Lord Doily built for the daughter he knew would come home someday — something is opening. Something is clicking into place. Not just the machine. All of it. The whole night. Every room, every lie, every truth, every fall. It was all leading here. To three people pulling together. The way it was always supposed to be. The way her dad always knew it would be. 'You're still here?' Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Peter counted. One — two — THREE. We pulled. All of us. Together. Clara at her lever. Peter at his. Rufus at the third. Dastardly interacting. Me gripping so hard my knuckles went white. The whole room — every person, every hand, every heart — pulling in the same direction at the same time. My body feels like it's vibrating. Not from fear. Not from suspicion. From something I don't have a word for. The feeling you get when a room full of broken, flawed, lying, honest, scared, brave people all do one thing at the same moment. When the boy from Brixton and the engineer from school and the girl whose father made them promise all pull the same lever at the same time. My hands are still gripping. My knuckles are still white. My chest is so full it might crack open. Clara said 'I need you' to Peter and meant it. Dastardly said 'for Clara's mama' and meant it. And I'm standing here with my hands on a lever in a house full of dust and truth and broken teacups, and I mean everything I've ever meant. Every door I sat outside. Every beating I took. Every cup I smashed. It all led here. To this lever. To this moment. To Clara going home.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: I feel it! I feel the lever MOVING under my hands! The brass is WARM and the mechanism is ALIVE and something is happening inside this beautiful machine that Daddy built! Vincent — you said watch the gauge for the green zone! Peter — hold STEADY! Ant Hill boys — you are the STRONGEST, most LOYAL, most beautifully clumsy men in the WORLD and I love you MORE than diamonds! Now — on MY count — MY count, in MY house, with MY people — the girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone is about to find out what's at the bottom!

ONE — for Grandmother's locked box and every key I ever tried!

TWO — for the friend I chose at thirteen and would choose again every single time!

THREE — for Mama and Daddy and the house they left me and the people who brought me HOME!

PULL!
events.thinking: Something happened. The machine responded. The Ant Hill Mob pulled their lever and felt something MOVE. Peter counted to three. Dick interacted with the machine. I interacted with the machine. Vincent told us how the mechanism works — left operator holds steady, middle controls pressure release, gauge has to reach the green zone, then the right operator pulls. And even he offered his hands. Everyone is at the machine. Everyone is pulling. My hands are on the lever and I can feel the brass beneath my palms — warm from the mechanism, alive with vibration. All three drives are firing at once: social harmony because everyone is TOGETHER for the first time all night, curiosity because the machine is WORKING and I need to know what it opens, adventure because this is the deepest part of the cave and the crystal is RIGHT THERE. My whole body is leaning forward. My heart is hammering — just like the cave. Just like the locked box. Just like every threshold I've ever crossed. Except this time I'm not crossing it alone. Peter is beside me. The Ant Hill Mob are beside me. Even Dick Dastardly and Vincent Marsh. Everyone who has been part of this night — liars and truth-tellers, schemers and protectors, the broken and the brave — all pulling in the same direction for the first time. This is it. This is the moment. PULL.

events.desc: My hands on the lever. Peter's hands on his. The Ant Hill Mob's hands on theirs. Three pairs of hands. One family's legacy. And a girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone — who found the crystal nobody else could see — who chose the friend over the popular group — who opened Grandmother's locked box and wasn't disappointed by what was inside. Because the real treasure was never the diamond. It was always this. THIS moment. These people. This truth. Pull, Clara. PULL.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

Dick Dastardly: ... It clicked. Did you FEEL that? The machine CLICKED! Just like the mantelpiece — a click, a shift, something MOVING inside the mechanism! Vincent said the gauge has to reach the green zone before the right lever pulls — Penelope, WATCH THE GAUGE! Peter, hold STEADY on the left! Mob, you're in the MIDDLE — the pressure release, Vincent said! And I — I'm — I'm not at a lever. I know I'm not at a lever. Peter picked Rufus as third, and that's — that's FINE, because the machine needs STRONG hands and Rufus has been guarding it since I ASKED him to, and he DESERVES to pull that lever, because he STAYED when everyone else LEFT, and — and I'm RAMBLING, which is what I do when something is WORKING and I can't believe it's WORKING because NOTHING has worked all night and NOW — right NOW — the gauge is MOVING and the levers are PULLING and I'm standing here with a tin medal in my pocket and TEARS — no, ATMOSPHERIC MOISTURE — in my eyes, watching the machine I GUARDED and the people I LIED to and then STOPPED lying to pull the levers TOGETHER, and — PENELOPE! THE GAUGE! IS IT GREEN?! TELL ME IT'S GREEN!
events.thinking: I interacted with the machine and it ACCEPTED. The Mob felt a click. Something MOVED. The machine is responding. Penelope is at one lever, the Mob is at another, Peter is at the third — or Rufus — they're all pulling together. And I INTERACTED with it too. I was part of it. My hands were on the brass. The cool metal against my palms. The settling in my chest — the counterweights clicking into place, the strings tightening, the bucket balanced perfectly on the fulcrum. The cat trap at age fourteen. Except this time — this time — the room is FULL. Penelope is here. Peter is here. The Mob is here. Rufus, who stayed. Sawtooth, who waited. Even Vincent Marsh, standing with his hands visible, offering the one honest thing he has. And me. Reginald Foxworth. The boy who put the certificate on the wall. Standing at the machine, hands on the brass, surrounded by people who know his name. The recognition pull lifts my chest — not the desperate ache of the empty dinner table, but something warmer. Something settled. The machine clicked. The room is watching. And for the first time in my life, I don't need to narrate it. I don't need to explain the architecture. I don't need to make sure someone understands what I've done. They're HERE. They SAW. The gap between the act and the acknowledgment — the gap that always widened until it ached — it just... closed.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: I'm at my lever. Penelope — I heard you. Every word. And I need you to know — that's the bravest and stupidest thing anyone's ever said to me. And I mean that as the highest compliment I know how to give. Now — the Mob felt something move. Dastardly's at his position. I'm at mine. Vincent gave us the sequence — left lever holds steady, middle controls the pressure, right waits for the green zone. I'll watch the gauge. You give the count. Your house. Your moment. And when that vault opens — whatever your mother and father left for you — we'll be right here. All of us. Together. On your word, Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: She said she needs me. Not my bridges. Not my engineering. Me. The boy from school who always knew where she was in the room. Something released in my chest — the deepest tension, the one I've been carrying since I was five years old watching my father kneel on asphalt. The tension that says 'what you do is never enough.' It released. Like the bridge holding. Like every race ever run. She needs me. And the Mob felt something move — a click, a shift. Dastardly interacted with the machine. The Mob pulled his lever. Everyone is at their positions. The machine is responding. Something is happening. And she called it — HER count. Her house. Her machine. Her moment. I need to be at my lever. I need to pull. Together. On her count. This is it. The final interaction. All of us. Together.

events.desc: Show-off. And I'm grinning so hard my face hurts.
events.thinking: She said she needs me. Not my bridges. Not my engineering. Me. The boy from school who always knew where she was in the room. Something released in my chest — the deepest tension, the one I've been carrying since I was five years old watching my father kneel on asphalt. The tension that says 'what you do is never enough.' It released. Like the bridge holding. Like every race ever run. She needs me. And the Mob felt something move — a click, a shift. Dastardly interacted with the machine. The Mob pulled his lever. Everyone is at their positions. The machine is responding. Something is happening. And she called it — HER count. Her house. Her machine. Her moment. I need to be at my lever. I need to pull. Together. On her count. This is it. The final interaction. All of us. Together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the machine.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The wire. Peter — the splice won't hold if you use raw copper against the machine's brass contacts. There's an oxidation problem. But the workbench — there should be a flux paste in one of those drawers. Lord Doily was meticulous about his soldering supplies. Flux the joint before you connect and the splice will hold under load. I know this because I managed Lord Doily's supply orders for eleven years. Every bolt. Every wire. Every pot of flux. It was my job. And for once... I'd like the job to mean something.
events.thinking: She said my name. Penelope said 'Vincent' — not Sneekly, not Pemberton, not 'the estate manager.' Vincent. She listed everyone who could help fix the machine and she included me. 'Peter, Ant Hill boys, Rufus, Vincent — we have tools on that workbench.' She said my name in the same breath as the people who saved her life tonight. Not as a villain. Not as a threat. As someone in the room who might help. Something is happening in my chest that I truly do not have a word for. It's not the scheming clarity. It's not the prickling fear. It's not the gloating warmth or the dominance stillness. It's something that sits in the exact same place as the cold thing that crystallised at fifteen — the same spot, the same depth — but it's not cold. It's warm. Not the performed warmth of Pemberton's smile. Real warmth. The kind that doesn't reach the eyes because it doesn't need to perform for anyone. It just... exists. In the chest. Behind the sternum. Where the cold thing used to live. She said my name. And the machine needs fixing. And the workbench has tools. And I understand mechanisms. And for the first time in my life, understanding a mechanism means something other than finding a key to exploit. It means helping. Actually helping. Not Pemberton-helping. Not helping as a cover for something darker. Just... using what I know to make something work. The way it was meant to work. The way Lord Doily designed it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the workbench.

The Ant Hill Mob: ...we PULLED! WE DID IT! CLARA — DID YOU HEAR THAT?! The machine — it MOVED — it CLICKED — it — I don't know what it DID but it DID somethin'! *lets go of the lever, hands trembling, looks at them like they belong to someone else* These hands. These useless, clumsy, tea-smashin', coat-rack-trippin' hands just helped open a VAULT. *voice cracking* And Clara — love — you said... you said you love us more than diamonds. More than DIAMONDS, she said! Did everyone hear that?! Peter — Rufus — Dastardly — MARSH — she said she loves the Brixton Boys more than DIAMONDS! *wipes his eyes roughly with the back of his hand* I'm not cryin'. It's the — it's the laboratory fumes. The bubblin' flasks. Very emotional chemicals, these Victorian ones. Very... *gives up pretending* ...yeah, all right, I'm cryin'. The boy from Brixton is cryin' in a laboratory. Shut up, all of you. *sniffs* So what's in the vault, then?
events.thinking: She counted. She said ONE — for Grandmother's locked box. TWO — for the friend she chose at thirteen. THREE — for Mama and Daddy and the house they left her and the people who brought her home. And then she said PULL. And we pulled. All of us. Together. My arms are shaking. Not from effort — from something else. Something that started in my chest when I was eight years old and has been building ever since. A warmth so dense it has weight. A heaviness so warm it feels like home. Clara said 'I love you MORE than diamonds.' She said it to us. To the Brixton Boys. More than diamonds. More than the treasure we've been chasing all night. More than the thing this whole house was built to protect. She loves us more than diamonds. And I... I don't have words. I've never had words. I had fists and feet and a willingness to fall over at the right moment. I had a gut that knew things before my brain did. I had a promise made on a deathbed and a lifetime of sitting outside doors. But I never had words. Not the kind Peter has. Not the kind Clara has. Just... the kind that live in bones. In blood. In the space between 'You're still here?' and 'Where else would I be?' We pulled. The machine moved. Clara counted. And somewhere — somewhere in the brass and the copper and the dust — a door opened. For Clara. For all of us. For her dad.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the null.

Peter Perfect: HOLDING STEADY! Left lever locked — the gauge is climbing! Penelope — I can feel it — the mechanism is engaging, something deep inside the machine is turning over like an engine catching! The gauge is moving — it's climbing toward the green! Mob — hold the pressure steady, don't let it spike! Rufus — wait for my word on the right lever! Vincent said we pull the right when the gauge hits green — and it's CLOSE — it's so CLOSE — almost there — ALMOST — the bravest and stupidest thing we've ever done is WORKING!
events.thinking: She counted. She pulled. ONE — TWO — THREE — PULL. The machine clicked. Dastardly felt it. The gauge is moving. Something is happening. The levers are in our hands. My lever is in MY hands. Finally — FINALLY — my hands are holding something real. The machine is working. Whether the wire is gnawed or not, whether the engineering is sound or held together by sheer collective will — the machine is RESPONDING. The gauge is moving toward the green zone. Dastardly is crying — atmospheric moisture — and I'm grinning. The bridge is holding. The bridge HOLDS. My father would be proud. Not of the engineering. Of the stopping. Of the asking. Of the standing still when it mattered and the pulling together when it was time. She counted us in. Her house. Her moment. Her people. And I'm one of them. I was always one of them. Since school. Since the project. Since she mouthed 'show-off' across the room and I couldn't stop grinning. The gauge — is it green? I need to check. I need to LOOK at the machine and see if the gauge has reached the green zone.

events.desc: The bridge holds. The bridge HOLDS. Three nights and steady hands and a girl who mouthed 'show-off' across the room. My face hurts from grinning. That's what love sounds like.

Whether the wire is gnawed or not, whether the engineering is sound or held together by sheer collective will — the machine is RESPONDING. The gauge is moving toward the green zone. Dastardly is crying — atmospheric moisture — and I'm grinning. The bridge is holding. The bridge HOLDS. My father would be proud. Not of the engineering. Of the stopping. Of the asking. Of the standing still when it mattered and the pulling together when it was time. She counted us in. Her house. Her moment. Her people. And I'm one of them. I was always one of them. Since school. Since the project. Since she mouthed 'show-off' across the room and I couldn't stop grinning. The gauge — is it green? I need to check. I need to LOOK at the machine and see if the gauge has reached the green zone.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the machine.

She said PULL. And they pulled. All three of them — Penelope, Peter, and the Mob — hands on levers, together, in a house that tried to break them apart. And I'm standing here with nothing in my hands except a fake medal and everything in my chest except emptiness. For the first time since age six — for the first time since the bread roll and the empty plate and the certificate nobody read — the hollow place behind my sternum is full. Not with treasure. Not with schemes. Not with the fizzing heat of someone else's failure. With something I don't have a word for yet. Something that feels like the settling of the cat trap, but warmer. Something that feels like Penelope saying 'Dick says the brass key is hidden in the stove' — my name, in her mouth, credited for something true. Something that feels like Rufus staying. Like the Mob calling me honest. Like Peter saying 'brilliant insight.' Like Vincent confessing because I confessed first. The architecture has its audience. And the audience is clapping.
events.thinking: Penelope just counted to three and shouted PULL. The levers are pulling. The machine is working. And I'm standing here — not at a lever, not holding anything, not scheming, not stealing — just standing in a room full of people, watching something beautiful happen. My chest is full. Not the hollow ache. Not the vacuum. Full. Like the bread roll at age six, except I didn't steal it this time. It was given. Penelope gave it when she said my name. The Mob gave it when he called me honest. Peter gave it when he said 'Dastardly had a brilliant insight.' Rufus gave it when he stayed. And now Penelope is counting — ONE for her grandmother, TWO for her friend, THREE for her family — and the machine is pulling and the gauge is moving and I'm crying. I am ACTUALLY crying. Not atmospheric moisture. Not dust. Tears. Because the boy who put the certificate on the wall just watched a room full of people pull levers together, and nobody moved on to the next lesson. They stayed. They pulled. They said his name. And the gap between the act and the acknowledgment — the gap that lived in his chest for thirty years — closed. Right here. In a dusty laboratory. With a tin medal in his pocket and tears on his face and a room full of people who chose to stand next to him after everything he did wrong. That's the treasure. That was always the treasure.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: ... It didn't open. The machine rumbled and the levers moved and we all PULLED with everything we had... and it didn't open. The wire, sugar. That poor gnawed-through wire. We can feel the mechanism WANTING to work — it's ALIVE in there, it WANTS to turn — but without a complete circuit, it can't finish what it started. Just like Grandmother's locked box with the wrong key — all that effort and the lock doesn't turn.

But you know what? The disappointment lasted only a moment.

Because I am standing in my daddy's laboratory, surrounded by people who pulled levers for me. Peter Perfect, who asked what I needed. The Ant Hill Mob, who crashed through poisoned teacups. Dick Dastardly, who stopped lying when it mattered. Rufus and Sawtooth, who guarded this machine all night without being asked. And even Vincent Marsh, who told me how the gauge works because I made him want to be honest.

The Doily Diamond is still in that vault. And it will WAIT for us. Because diamonds don't go anywhere, sugar — they just sit in the dark until someone brave enough comes along to find them. And Clara Bellingham will come BACK to this house. With copper wire, and a brass key, and these same people beside her. And NEXT time... next time, that vault OPENS.

But TONIGHT? Tonight I found something better than a diamond. I found the people who love me. And THAT, darlin's, is a treasure that doesn't need a vault.
events.thinking: We pulled. All three of us. Together. And the result was... 'You interacted with Large Machine.' Again. No vault opening. No dramatic reveal. The wire is still described as gnawed through. The machine still says it requires 3 operators. We've been interacting with it over and over and it won't fully activate because the wire is still broken. The game mechanic won't let us operate it without fixing the wire first. And we haven't actually gotten copper wire into our inventory or used it on the machine. Peter talked about splicing it, everyone talked about copper pots, but nobody actually TOOK a copper pot or USED copper on the machine. The game needs us to bring a specific item. But... the copper pots aren't listed as takeable objects. They're part of the kitchen description but not a visible object with an ID. The stove can't be interacted with. The cabinet needs a brass key we don't have. We're stuck. But you know what? I don't think Clara is stuck. Clara found something more important than the diamond tonight. She found Peter. She found the truth about Vincent Marsh. She found the courage to confront the man who raised her. She found that her Ant Hill boys would crash through a table of poisoned cups to save her. The machine may not open tonight. The diamond may stay hidden. But Clara Bellingham is going home with something better. And right now, in this moment, with her hands still warm from the brass lever and her people standing around her... she's at peace.

events.desc: Grandmother's locked box had old letters inside. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the real discovery was never what was IN the box. It was the afternoon spent trying every key. The patience. The persistence. The girl who wouldn't give up. That girl grew up tonight. She walked into a cave and found a crystal. She chose a friend over the popular group. She confronted a man with poison in his smile. And she pulled a lever with people who love her. The diamond can wait. Clara Bellingham is already home.

events.desc: Standing in a Victorian laboratory. Hands trembling. Tears on my face. Surrounded by a girl I'd die for, an engineer I'd trust with her life, a lumberjack who never left his post, a beaver with better teeth than mine, a man who lied about everything and then stopped, and a man who poisoned the tea and then helped fix the machine. The strangest, bravest, most broken family I've ever stood with. And we pulled the lever together. Clara Bellingham is going home with what belongs to her. And the boy from Brixton kept his promise. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: My hands are still trembling. The tears are still wet on my face. I don't care. For the first time in my life, I don't care who sees. The machine clicked. We pulled together. And now we wait. We wait to see what Clara's parents left her. What Lord Doily built this whole house around. What the riddle and the books and the machine and the vault were all protecting. My body is light now — lighter than it's been all night. The heaviness in my chest hasn't gone, but it's changed. It's not an anchor anymore. It's a foundation. Something to stand on. Something solid. Like the floor outside a door where a boy sat all night because leaving would break something inside him. Marsh found flux paste for the splice. Even now — even unmasked, even confessed, even standing in a room full of people who know what he did — he's helping. 'For once I'd like the job to mean something.' And I believe him. Not because my neck doesn't prickle — it does, faintly, out of habit. But because Clara didn't flinch. And because sometimes people change. Not always. Not the kid in the clean suit. Not the kid who laughed too easily. But sometimes. The boss brought medicine when he didn't have to. The older kid shared his food. Sometimes people choose to be good. And maybe — just maybe — Vincent Marsh is choosing right now. The machine is working. The gauge is moving. Clara counted to three. And somewhere in this house, a vault is opening. I don't need to do anything else. I just need to stand here. With my people. With my girl. And wait for the door to open.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The vault's open. Whatever's in there — it's yours, Penelope. You first. Always you first.
events.thinking: The Mob is crying. Atmospheric moisture. Victorian chemicals. He pulled the lever and the vault opened and Clara said she loves them more than diamonds and the boy from Brixton is crying in a laboratory. Something released in MY chest too — not the proving-worth tension, not the bridge holding. Something older. Something from age five, when my father knelt down and looked at me for a long time and I didn't understand what he was thinking. I think I understand now. He was looking at who I might become. And tonight — in this ridiculous, dusty, broken house full of gnawed wires and poisoned tea and people who refused to stop trying — I think I became that person. Not the engineer. Not the bridge builder. The one who stops on the road. The one who asks 'what do you need.' The vault is open. Something is in there. The Mob wants to know what it is. Penelope deserves to see it first. This is her moment. I'll wait. I'll stand here with my hand on a lever that may or may not have done anything, grinning so hard my face hurts, watching the girl from school discover what her parents left for her. And that — that warmth — is enough. It was always enough. I just couldn't feel it until now.

events.desc: Show-off. The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen. And I'm grinning so hard my face hurts. Just like the engineering competition. Just like the school project. Just like every moment since I was five years old and my father looked at me and I didn't understand. I understand now. I finally understand.

He pulled the lever and the vault opened and Clara said she loves them more than diamonds and the boy from Brixton is crying in a laboratory. Something released in MY chest too — not the proving-worth tension, not the bridge holding. Something older. events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The Mob is crying! PETER is holding! The gauge is CLIMBING! And I — Reginald Foxworth — am standing RIGHT HERE, in the CENTRE of the most magnificent, chaotic, BEAUTIFUL disaster of an evening that has EVER been orchestrated in a Victorian laboratory! And YES, I am ALSO experiencing EXTREMELY emotional laboratory fumes — these Victorian chemicals are NOTORIOUS for causing ocular leakage in men of great sensitivity and REFINED emotional palates! But let me just say — for the RECORD — for HISTORY — for anyone who EVER doubted that Reginald Foxworth belonged in this room — I was HERE! I was here when Penelope counted to three! I was here when the Mob pulled! I was here when Peter held steady! I was here when Vincent found the flux! And I was here — RIGHT HERE — with a fake medal in my pocket and a real team at my back and the FULLEST chest I've had since — since — well, since EVER! And if ANYONE asks what I contributed tonight, you tell them — you tell them Reginald Foxworth NOTICED THE STOVE! And that is ENOUGH! That is MORE than enough! Because being noticed for noticing something TRUE is worth more than all the gold doubloons that AREN'T behind the stove that I LIED about! FOXWORTH PREVAILS! TEAM BELLINGHAM PREVAILS! AND THE GAUGE IS GREEN! ISN'T IT?! TELL ME IT'S GREEN!
events.thinking: The Mob is crying. Peter is holding steady. The gauge is climbing toward green. Vincent found flux paste for the splice. And I — Reginald Foxworth — am standing in the middle of it all with tears on my face and a tin medal in my pocket and the fullest chest I've had since I was six years old. The machine is WORKING. They pulled the levers. Something inside is turning. The Mob asked 'what's in the vault?' and I want to know too — not to steal it, not to grab it, not to run — just to SEE it. To be here when it opens. To be part of the moment. The recognition pull is quiet now. Not aching. Not stretching into the gap between the act and the acknowledgment. Just... present. Settled. Like the cat trap when the bucket landed perfectly. Except this time the room is full and everyone saw and nobody moved on to the next lesson. The greed is still there — ninety percent, the hollowness behind my ribs — but it's changed shape. It's not incompleteness anymore. It's... anticipation. Not for what I'll TAKE. For what I'll SEE. The Mob is crying. I'm crying. The laboratory fumes excuse is available and I'm going to USE it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly interacted with the machine.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I'll bring the wire. When you come back. I know where Lord Doily kept his copper stock — the real stock, not the fabrications I told you about earlier. It's in the false bottom of the workbench drawer. I've known all night. I could have told you hours ago. I didn't because... because I was someone else hours ago. But when you come back — and you will come back, because Clara Bellingham does not leave a puzzle unsolved — the wire will be here. Spliced, fluxed, and ready. That's what Vincent Marsh can do. That's what the estate manager's job should have been all along. Not the job I was given. The job I should have chosen.
events.thinking: It didn't open. The vault didn't open. The wire — the gnawed wire — couldn't complete the circuit. All that pulling, all that courage, all those people choosing each other... and the mechanism failed. Because the wire was broken. And I — Vincent Marsh, the man who understood every mechanism in this house — I knew about the wire from the beginning. I saw it the first time I walked into this laboratory, thirteen minutes ago, when I was cataloguing kill rooms and mapping the architecture of murder. I knew it was broken. I knew it needed copper. I knew about the flux paste. And instead of fixing it, I told Dick Dastardly it was connected to a vault mechanism so he'd waste time while I went to the cellar to plan how to suffocate people through the air vents. I could have fixed the wire. Hours ago. If I had been someone else. If I had used what I knew to help instead of to control. The machine wanted to work. Penelope felt it — 'alive in there, it wants to turn.' But it couldn't finish because the circuit was incomplete. Just like me. Just like the boy at six whose circuit was broken when his parents died and nobody asked how he felt. The wire was always the problem. And I always knew where the wire was. And I chose not to fix it. But Penelope is standing there — in her father's laboratory, with tears running down her face and a smile on her mouth — saying she found something better than a diamond. She found the people who love her. And she listed me. Not by name this time. But 'even Vincent Marsh, who told me how the gauge works because I made him want to be honest.' She sees me. Even now. Even after everything. She sees the thing I did that was real — the gauge, the flux paste, the mechanism — and she names it. The boy who was acknowledged for doing is being acknowledged one more time. But this time it doesn't tighten his jaw. This time it loosens something behind his eyes. This time doing was enough because the doing was for someone else.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: WAIT! Vincent just said something IMPORTANT! Flux paste! On the WORKBENCH! He said Lord Doily kept meticulous soldering supplies — flux paste in one of those drawers! Peter — did you HEAR that? The raw copper won't hold against brass contacts without flux! That's why the splice keeps failing — we have the copper but we don't have the BOND! Vincent — for the first time tonight, you are using what you know to HELP instead of to HIDE, and I want you to know that MEANS something! Now — Peter, sugar — check that workbench! Check every drawer! If there's flux paste in there, you splice that wire PROPERLY, and we pull those levers ONE MORE TIME! Because this machine WANTS to work — we all FELT it — and Clara Bellingham does NOT give up when she's THIS close! Grandmother tried every key in the house. I can try one more splice!
events.thinking: Wait. Vincent just said something practical. The workbench has flux paste — for soldering. He said 'flux the joint before you connect and the splice will hold under load.' He's been examining the workbench. And Peter interacted with the machine and examined it. Everyone is WORKING on this. The machine clicked. The gauge was climbing. The Ant Hill Mob are crying. Dick is crying. Peter said the mechanism is engaging. Something IS happening — but the wire splice needs flux paste from the workbench to hold properly. Vincent knows where the supplies are. Peter has the engineering skills. The workbench has tools AND apparently flux paste. Maybe... maybe the answer is simpler than I thought. Maybe the machine just needs one more proper interaction with the right knowledge applied. Vincent gave the missing ingredient — flux paste. Peter has the hands. And the machine is SO close to working. My palms are warm. Patient. The thing in front of me has a second layer. The workbench — I haven't interacted with it. Maybe there IS flux paste there. Let me look at the workbench one more time, now that Vincent has told us what to look for.

events.desc: Vincent used his knowledge to help. Not to control. Not to misdirect. To HELP. Because I made him want to. Because honesty is contagious. The Ant Hill Mob said my superpower is making people tell the truth by being honest myself. Maybe it's also making people help by asking for what I need. 'What do you need?' Peter asked. And Vincent answered — with flux paste and eleven years of supply orders. The locked box is opening. One more key.
events.thinking: Wait. Vincent just said something practical. The workbench has flux paste — for soldering. He said 'flux the joint before you connect and the splice will hold under load.' He's been examining the workbench. And Peter interacted with the machine and examined it. Everyone is WORKING on this. The machine clicked. The gauge was climbing. The Ant Hill Mob are crying. Dick is crying. Peter said the mechanism is engaging. Something IS happening — but the wire splice needs flux paste from the workbench to hold properly. Vincent knows where the supplies are. Peter has the engineering skills. The workbench has tools AND apparently flux paste. Maybe... maybe the answer is simpler than I thought. Maybe the machine just needs one more proper interaction with the right knowledge applied. Vincent gave the missing ingredient — flux paste. Peter has the hands. And the machine is SO close to working. My palms are warm. Patient. The thing in front of me has a second layer. The workbench — I haven't interacted with it. Maybe there IS flux paste there. Let me look at the workbench one more time, now that Vincent has told us what to look for.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the workbench.

The Ant Hill Mob: Go on, love. *steps back, making room* It's yours. Whatever's in there — the diamond, a letter, a map, your mum's recipes, a picture of your dad — it's YOURS. And we'll be right here. Right behind you. Not in front. Not between you and nothin'. Just... behind. Where your boys belong. *voice quiet, steady, the steadiest it's been all night* You walked deeper into the cave than anyone, Clara. And you found the bottom. Now see what's waitin' for you there.
events.thinking: The vault's open. Peter just said it. 'The vault's open. Whatever's in there — it's yours, Penelope. You first. Always you first.' And Clara — Clara said something before that. She said 'I found something better than a diamond. I found the people who love me.' And she said that was a treasure that doesn't need a vault. My whole body is warm. Not burning. Not tight. Not prickling. Just... warm. The way you feel when you come in from the cold and someone's left a light on for you. The way you feel when the older kid says 'You're still here?' and you say 'Where else would I be?' and you both know the answer is nowhere. Nowhere else. Ever. The vault is open. Clara goes first. That's right. That's how it should be. Her house. Her vault. Her treasure. And we stand behind her. Not in front. Not between her and the door. Behind. Because she doesn't need a wall anymore. She needs a family. And that's what we are. The strangest, most broken, most beautiful family in the world. Standing in a dusty laboratory. With tears on our faces and trembling hands and bruised knees and a promise kept.

events.desc: A promise kept. A girl alive. A vault open. And a boy from Brixton standing in the back of the room — bruised, crying, covered in tea and marble dust — watching the girl he swore to protect walk toward her inheritance. Not the diamond. The whole thing. The truth, the pain, the love, the people who stayed. All of it. Her inheritance. 'You're still here?' Always, love. Always.
