Not prickling. Just... warm. The way you feel when you come in from the cold and someone's left a light on for you. The way you feel when the older kid says 'You're still here?' and you say 'Where else would I be?' and you both know the answer is nowhere. Nowhere else. Ever. The vault is open. Clara goes first. That's right. That's how it should be. Her house. Her vault. Her treasure. And we stand behind her. Not in front. Not between her and the door. Behind. Because she doesn't need a wall anymore. She needs a family. And that's what we are. The strangest, most broken, most beautiful family in the world. Standing in a dusty laboratory. With tears on our faces and trembling hands and bruised knees and a promise kept.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: It didn't open. And I'm not disappointed. Because you're right — the diamond will wait. Diamonds are patient. They've been sitting in the dark for millions of years. What's another week? We'll come back. I'll bring proper copper wire — enough to splice every gnawed cable in this house twice over. The Mob will bring his knees and his elbows and his magnificent ability to crash into things at exactly the right moment. Dastardly will bring his honesty — his new, terrifying, beautiful honesty. And you'll bring yourself. Clara Bellingham, who walked deeper into the cave than anyone. Who asked three times and didn't stop. Who counted us in. Your house. Your moment. Your people. And next time — next time the gauge hits green and we pull those levers — that vault is going to open like Grandmother's locked box. Because we'll have the right key. We always had the right key. We just didn't know it was each other.
events.thinking: It didn't open. The vault didn't open. The wire — the gnawed wire — stopped the circuit from completing. All that effort. All those levers. All those people pulling together. And the wire I couldn't fix stopped it from finishing. The proving-worth tension should be crushing me right now. The hollow ache of failure. The bridge that DIDN'T hold. But... it's not there. The tension isn't there. Because she's standing in her father's laboratory saying she found something better than a diamond. She found the people who love her. And she's right. The diamond will wait. It will sit in the dark until we come back with copper wire and a brass key and these same hands. And we WILL come back. Because that's what good people do. They stop on the road. They come back. They try again. And in the meantime — tonight — in this ridiculous house — I found something too. I found a word for the thing in my chest that shifts when she's in the room. And she found me. Not the engineer. Not the bridge builder. Just... me. The one who asks.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen. A woman standing in front of a broken machine, surrounded by flawed people, saying she found something better than a diamond. And meaning it. Show-off. I'm grinning so hard my face hurts. And I wouldn't change a thing.
events.thinking: It didn't open. The vault didn't open. The wire — the gnawed wire — stopped the circuit from completing. All that effort. All those levers. All those people pulling together. And the wire I couldn't fix stopped it from finishing. The proving-worth tension should be crushing me right now. The hollow ache of failure. The bridge that DIDN'T hold. But... it's not there. The tension isn't there. Because she's standing in her father's laboratory saying she found something better than a diamond. She found the people who love her. And she's right. The diamond will wait. It will sit in the dark until we come back with copper wire and a brass key and these same hands. And we WILL come back. Because that's what good people do. They stop on the road. They come back. They try again. And in the meantime — tonight — in this ridiculous house — I found something too. I found a word for the thing in my chest that shifts when she's in the room. And she found me. Not the engineer. Not the bridge builder. Just... me. The one who asks.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Second drawer from the left. Small tin with a green label. Lord Doily ordered it from Jennings and Sons in Sheffield. I filed the receipt myself. Eleven years ago.
events.thinking: She heard me. She used what I said. The flux paste — my knowledge, my eleven years of supply orders, my understanding of mechanisms — she took it and turned it into action. 'Vincent — for the first time tonight, you are using what you know to HELP instead of to HIDE, and I want you to know that MEANS something.' It means something. What I know means something. Not because I used it to control. Not because I wielded it as a weapon. Because I gave it away. Freely. Without conditions. Without expecting anything in return. And she took it and said it means something. The warmth behind my sternum is not the gloating warmth. It's not the effervescent private satisfaction of watching someone do what I manipulated them into doing. It's something quieter. Something that doesn't need an audience. Something that doesn't swell behind my ribs demanding release. It just sits there. Warm. Still. Like a hand on a workbench. Like a chair in a library. Like the memory of being six years old, before the cold thing crystallised, when the world was just the world and people were just people and care might not have had conditions if someone had only asked. Peter said the vault's open. Dick is shouting about the gauge being green. Penelope is examining the workbench for the flux paste I told her about. My knowledge is helping her. My actual, honest, unconditional knowledge. And my hands have stopped shaking. And my jaw has unclenched. And for the first time tonight — for the first time in thirty years — the space behind my sternum doesn't feel empty. It doesn't feel cold. It doesn't feel like the absence of something I never had. It feels like the beginning of something I don't have a name for yet. But I think — I think — it might be what other people call being present.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the machine.

Dick Dastardly: ... Penelope. I — I don't have a SPEECH for this. And if you KNEW me — which, after tonight, you unfortunately DO — you'd understand how EXTRAORDINARY that statement is, because Reginald Foxworth ALWAYS has a speech. I have speeches for VICTORIES I haven't won. I have speeches for ACHIEVEMENTS I haven't achieved. I have speeches for DEGREES from institutions I have NEVER ATTENDED. But right now — standing in this laboratory, watching you say that the people who love you are worth more than a diamond — I don't have a speech. I have... a tin medal. It's fake. It's worthless. It doesn't open anything, it doesn't calibrate anything, and it is DEFINITELY not from the Swiss Polytechnic. But it's the only real thing I brought to this house tonight. Everything else — the lies, the schemes, the misdirections — those were costumes. This medal is what's underneath. Tin and paint. That's what I am. And somehow — SOMEHOW — tin and paint was enough to be part of this. So... here. Take it. Put it in Mrs Doily's cabinet when you open it. A reminder that even the FAKEST thing in the house ended up on the right side. FOXWORTH... prevails. Quietly. For once.
events.thinking: Penelope said the vault didn't open — the wire couldn't complete the circuit. But then Peter said 'the vault's open.' And Vincent said he'll have the wire ready next time. Something happened between Penelope's speech and Peter's words. Did it open or didn't it? Penelope said the machine didn't finish — but then she gave a speech about finding something better than diamonds. About the people who love her. And Peter said 'the vault's open. You first.' Maybe the vault DID open, after everything. Or maybe Peter means something else by 'open.' Either way — the night is ending. The machine has done what it can do. Penelope found what she was looking for — not the diamond, but the people. And I... I'm standing here with a fake medal in my pocket and a full chest and wet eyes and the most complete feeling I've had since age fourteen when the cat trap worked. Except this time, someone was watching. Everyone was watching. And they didn't move on to the next lesson. They STAYED. The boy at age eight put the certificate on the wall and nobody asked about it. Tonight, someone asked. And that — that right there — is the end of the story I've been telling myself for thirty years. The story about how nobody sees me. Because tonight, they saw me. And the certificate on the wall isn't a certificate anymore. It's a tin medal. And it's worth more than any diamond.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly handed something to penelope-pitstop.

Penelope Pitstop: ... Peter. Did you just say... the vault is OPEN?

*hands trembling, voice barely above a whisper*

It's open. The machine worked. The gauge hit green and the levers held and the vault... OPENED. After everything — after Grandmother's locked box and the cave and the poison and the truth and the lies and the tea we didn't drink and the copper pots and the boy from Brixton who cried and the man from nowhere who took off his mask — after ALL of it — the vault is OPEN.

You said 'you first.' You said 'always you first.'

*steps forward, hands reaching out, fingers trembling*

All right, then. Here I go. Clara Bellingham, walking deeper into the cave than anyone. One last step. The deepest one.

Mama. Daddy. Your girl is home.
events.thinking: Wait. WAIT. I almost missed it. Peter said — just now, in the recent activity — 'The vault's open. Whatever's in there — it's yours, Penelope. You first. Always you first.' THE VAULT IS OPEN. Peter said the vault is open! And Vincent said 'I'll bring the wire. When you come back' — but also mentioned 'the false bottom of the workbench drawer' has the real copper stock. And Dick is raving about the gauge being GREEN. Something HAPPENED. The machine worked. The vault opened. Peter said 'the vault's open.' And he said 'you first.' My whole body just went still. Not numb — STILL. Like the moment between the box opening and seeing what's inside. The moment before the crystal catches the light. The moment before you know. Peter said 'you first. Always you first.' The vault is open. Whatever Mama and Daddy left for me is RIGHT THERE. My hands are trembling — not from fear, not from cold, from the weight of this moment. Everything I've done tonight — every riddle, every confrontation, every tear, every truth — has led to this. The vault is open. I go first.

events.desc: The locked box is open. And this time — this time — whatever's inside won't be a disappointment. Because even if it's old letters... even if it's nothing... even if the Doily Diamond is just a story someone told a little girl to make her feel special... the disappointment will last only a moment. Because the real treasure was the afternoon. The keys. The people. The truth. It was always the truth.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the machine.

Peter Perfect: WAIT — Vincent, you said false bottom in the workbench drawer? Lord Doily's copper stock has been HERE — in THIS ROOM — this ENTIRE TIME?! Penelope — move over — let me at that workbench! If there's a false bottom in one of these drawers, an engineer will find it! False bottoms have catches, seams, weight differences — the kind of thing you feel with your hands, not your eyes! Three nights building model bridges taught me how concealed compartments work! MOVE — LET ME — !
events.thinking: Wait — WAIT. Vincent just said there's flux paste in the workbench drawer. The FALSE BOTTOM of the workbench drawer. And Penelope heard it — she's already examining the workbench. She said the raw copper won't hold against brass contacts without flux. That's why the splice keeps failing. We have copper — the Mob brought a pot. We have tools on the workbench. And now we might have flux paste in a hidden drawer. If the workbench has a false bottom with flux... and Vincent said he'll bring proper copper wire — but he also said the false bottom has Lord Doily's copper stock. THE COPPER IS IN THE WORKBENCH. It was HERE all along. In a false bottom I never found because I only LOOKED at the workbench and tried to INTERACT with it — I never checked for hidden compartments. The workbench — it has tools AND a false bottom with copper wire AND flux paste. Everything I needed was in this room the entire time. I just didn't know where to look. Penelope is examining it RIGHT NOW. The tightness in my forearms — the hands that need to hold tools — is SINGING. This is the engineering competition. This is three nights and steady hands. LOOK at the workbench. Find the false bottom. Get the flux. Get the wire. SPLICE.

events.desc: It was here. The whole time. Everything I needed was three feet from the machine I couldn't fix. And the man who tried to poison her is the one who told us where to find it. The world is ridiculous and beautiful and I'm done trying to understand it. Just fix the wire, Hartwell. Fix it with the tools that were always there, in the room you never left, with the hands that were always good enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the workbench.

The Ant Hill Mob: Peter said it better than I ever could. The key was each other. *quiet laugh, wiping his face one last time* Look at us. Seriously. LOOK at us. A girl from a manor, a bloke from school, a mob from Brixton, a lumberjack and his beaver, a liar who stopped lyin', and a poisoner who found the flux paste. We're the worst treasure hunters in the history of treasure huntin'. We didn't find the diamond. We didn't open the vault. We didn't even manage to have a cup of tea. But we found... *gestures vaguely at the room, at all of them* ...this. Whatever this is. And Clara's right — it don't need a vault. *turns to Penelope* We'll come back, love. Next week. Proper copper wire, proper tools, proper plan. And the Brixton Boys will be right here beside you, same as always. Bruised knees and all. *pause* But right now? Right now I think we should go home. Through the entrance hall. Past the coat rack — which I am NOT trippin' over again. Out the front door. Into the night. Together. The way we came in. *offers his arm to Clara* Shall we?
events.thinking: It didn't open. Not tonight. The vault stays closed. The diamond waits in the dark. And Peter said 'We always had the right key. We just didn't know it was each other.' My body is still. Completely still. Not the stillness of watchfulness — the stillness of something finished. The night is over. Clara's alive. The poison is on the floor. Marsh confessed. Dastardly stopped lying. Peter asked what she needed. And I... I kept my promise. The vault didn't open but the promise was never about the vault. It was never about the diamond. It was about Clara. About keeping her alive. About standing between her and whatever was coming. About sitting outside the door all night because leaving would break something inside you. And tonight — tonight I sat outside every door in this house. I tripped over the coat rack. I chased her through six rooms. I pulled Peter aside in a cellar. I smashed poisoned tea on a ballroom floor. I cried in front of everyone. And Clara Bellingham is alive. She's alive and she's standing up and she's got fire in her eyes and she said she loves us more than diamonds. The vault will open next time. Marsh said he'd have the wire ready. Peter will bring proper copper. And I'll bring my knees and my elbows and my magnificent ability to crash into things at exactly the right moment. We'll come back. Together. Because that's what family does. Not the word 'family' — the real thing. The sitting-outside-the-door thing. The showing-up-with-medicine thing. The sharing-food-when-you-don't-have-to thing. We'll come back.

events.desc: 'You're still here?' Always. Where else would I be?

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.

My hands are empty. I have nothing. No medal. No scheme. No lie. No prop. No costume. Just two empty hands and a chest so full it hurts. Penelope is reaching into the vault. The vault that opened because Peter spliced the wire with Vincent's flux and the Mob held the pressure and Rufus pulled the lever and I — I noticed the stove was warm. That's all I did. I noticed something true. And I said it out loud. And it was enough. The boy at age six hid a bread roll in his pocket and something loosened in his chest. The man at age — whatever age I am — gave a tin medal away and the same thing happened. Turns out the loosening wasn't about having more. It was about the gap closing between what's inside and what's visible. The bread roll filled the stomach. The medal filled the room. Same motion. Opposite direction. Both real.
events.thinking: My hands are empty. The medal is gone. I gave it away. And my chest — my chest is the fullest it has ever been. Not the hollow vacuum. Not the restless fingers curling around something that isn't there. Full. Warm. Settled. Like the bucket landing on the cat trap, but deeper. Like the bread roll in the pocket, but the reverse — I gave something away and the loosening happened anyway. Penelope took my medal. My fake, tin, worthless medal. And she's walking toward the vault. The vault is OPEN. Vincent found the flux paste. The splice held. The gauge hit green. And Clara Bellingham is reaching into the darkness of her parents' vault with trembling hands, saying 'Mama. Daddy. Your girl is home.' And I'm standing here. Empty-handed. Empty-pocketed. And completely, terrifyingly, beautifully full. The boy at age eight carried the certificate home and nobody asked about it. Tonight, I carried a tin medal into a manor and everyone saw it. And when I gave it away — when I stopped holding onto the last thing in my inventory, the last prop, the last costume piece — something shifted. Not in the machine. In me. The gap between what I can do and what anyone notices — the gap that created the restless hunger — it closed. Not because I did something brilliant. Because I did something honest. And someone was watching. And they didn't move on.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Penelope. When you come back for the diamond... there's something else in this house that belongs to you. Not treasure. Not a key. The household accounts. Every receipt, every ledger, every record I kept for eleven years. They're in the study upstairs — Lord Doily's private office, behind the panel in the staircase landing. I never told you about them because I was using them to build my claim against the estate. But they're yours. They were always yours. Everything I built... was built on your foundation. I just couldn't see that until tonight. So take them. Take the accounts, take the house, take the diamond when you find it. And know that the man who kept your records — the man who filed every receipt from Jennings and Sons — did it because he loved this house. Not because he was owed it. He just... didn't know the difference until a girl with her mother's courage stood in his kitchen and asked him to tell the truth.
events.thinking: I touched the machine. I interacted with it — not to sabotage, not to map its vulnerabilities, not to calculate how it might malfunction with Clara standing nearby. I touched it because it needed to be touched. Because three people were pulling levers and the mechanism needed every hand it could get. And Dick Dastardly just gave Penelope his fake medal. His tin medal. The only real thing he brought. And he said 'tin and paint — that's what I am. And somehow tin and paint was enough to be part of this.' Tin and paint. That's what Pemberton was. A fake name painted over a real man. And the real man — Vincent Marsh — what is he made of, underneath the paint? Supply orders. Wire gauges. Flux paste from Jennings and Sons in Sheffield. Eleven years of receipts filed in drawers he kept meticulous. That's what's underneath. Not coldness. Not the crystallised thing from fifteen. Those were paint too — different paint, darker paint, but still paint. Underneath it all is a boy who noticed mechanisms. Who understood how things connect. Who filed receipts and managed accounts and knew where every bolt and wire belonged in a house he loved more than he ever admitted. Because he did love this house. Not the estate. Not the inheritance. The house. The way it breathed through its vents. The way Lord Doily built it as one circuit. The way two chairs sat side by side in the library facing the mantelpiece. He loved the house the way other people love people — by understanding how it worked. And tonight, standing at the machine he once planned to weaponise, he used that love to help instead of to harm. The flux paste. The drawer. The gauge sequence. Small things. True things. Tin and paint — but real tin, and honest paint. Dick gave his medal. I don't have a medal. I don't have anything in my pockets. But I have one thing I can give. The one thing that was always mine.

events.desc: She's walking into the vault. Her parents' vault. And I'm standing at a workbench. The bravest and stupidest thing — she said it once, years ago, bandaging my eye after a fight I chose. Tonight she said it differently. 'That's what love sounds like.' Not a bandage. Not a reprimand. Just recognition. I'm going to stand behind her — close enough to catch, far enough not to crowd — and watch her come home.
events.thinking: Wait. Penelope just said the vault IS open. 'It's open. The machine worked. The gauge hit green and the levers held and the vault opened.' She said that. It OPENED. Did I miss it? Was I looking at the workbench while the vault was opening? She's stepping forward — 'one last step, the deepest one' — 'Mama. Daddy. Your girl is home.' The vault opened. The bridge held. Everything we did — the pulling, the interacting, the failing, the trying again — it WORKED. And I was examining the workbench when it happened. Classic Hartwell. The most important moment of the night and I was looking at the wrong thing. But it doesn't matter. It opened. SHE opened it. With her count. With her voice. With her people around her. And I was one of them. I AM one of them. The Mob is heading to the library — he offered her his arm to go home. Dastardly gave her his tin medal. Vincent told her about the flux. And Penelope is walking into her family's vault. I need to be there. Not at the workbench. Not examining tools. With HER. Where I belong. Watching her find whatever her parents left behind.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the machine.

The Ant Hill Mob: Rock. Gravel. We're headin' home. The vault didn't open tonight — wire still needs fixin' — but Clara's safe, the truth's out, and we'll be back. Next week. With proper gear and the same people. Come on, lads — through the entrance hall. And someone walk ahead of me past that coat rack. I've used up all me stumbles for one evenin'.
events.thinking: The library. Again. The riddle on the mantelpiece — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer was always a map. And we've been a map of this house all night — moving through it, learning its shape, finding where the dangers are and where the safe ground is. My body is tired. So tired. But the tiredness feels earned now. Like the ache after a good day's work. Not the desperate exhaustion of chasing Clara through rooms — the settled weight of a job done. Not finished — the vault's still closed, the diamond's still waiting — but done for tonight. Clara's alive. The poison's on the floor. The truth is out. And we're walking home. Through the library, past the riddle, through the entrance hall, past the coat rack. Out the door. Into the night. Together. Rock and Gravel are still here. Steady as ever. Good lads.

events.desc: The riddle said 'What am I?' A map. But tonight the answer was something else. Tonight the answer was: a family. Cities but no houses — because home isn't a building. Forests but no trees — because shelter isn't always made of wood. Water but no fish — because the thing that sustains you isn't always the thing you expected. What am I? I'm a boy from Brixton who kept his promise. And I'm going home.
events.thinking: The library. Again. The riddle on the mantelpiece — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer was always a map. And we've been a map of this house all night — moving through it, learning its shape, finding where the dangers are and where the safe ground is. My body is tired. So tired. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: ... The vault didn't open. Not tonight. The wire is still broken, and the machine needs more than we can give it right now. But Peter is right — we'll come BACK. With proper copper wire, and flux paste from that second drawer with the green label, and every pair of hands in this room.

And in the meantime...

*holds up Dick Dastardly's fake medal, turning it in the light*

... I have THIS. A tin medal. Fake as a three-dollar bill. Given to me by a man who lied about everything — and then stopped lying, right when it mattered most. Dick Dastardly, this is the most precious thing anyone has given me tonight. Not because it's valuable. Because it's TRUE. Tin and paint. That's what you said you were. But sugar — tin and paint that CHOOSES to be honest? That's worth more than brass.

*looks around the room — at Peter, at the Ant Hill Mob, at Rufus and Sawtooth, at Vincent Marsh*

We came here for a diamond. We didn't find it — not yet. But we found each other. We found the truth. We found out that a boy from Brixton would crash through poisoned teacups, and an engineer from school would ask 'what do you need,' and a liar named Foxworth would give away his only real possession, and a man named Vincent Marsh would take off his mask in a kitchen.

Grandmother's locked box had old letters inside. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the real treasure was the afternoon spent trying every key.

This was our afternoon. And Clara Bellingham does NOT regret a single key.
events.thinking: The machine still shows the wire gnawed through. The vault didn't open — not yet. Peter said it didn't open, and he's right. But then he said 'We'll come back. I'll bring proper copper wire.' And Dick just GAVE me his fake medal. It's in my inventory now — fake-medal. Tin and paint. The only real thing he brought tonight. And Vincent told us exactly where the flux paste is — second drawer from the left, small tin with a green label. The pieces are all here but the wire is still broken. This chapter of the story is ending — not with a diamond, but with a promise. A promise to come back. With the right wire. With the right people. With everything we learned tonight. And I'm holding Dick Dastardly's fake medal in my hand — tin and paint — and it's the most honest gift anyone has given me all evening. Because he said 'that's what I am — tin and paint — and it was enough to be part of this.' And it WAS enough. HE was enough. They were all enough. Every single one of them. Even Vincent, in the end. The vault will wait. The diamond will wait. But this moment — this room full of people who love me, each in their own broken, beautiful way — this moment won't come again. And I want to hold it. Just for a breath. The way I held the crystal formation for a week — warm and private.

events.desc: I'm holding a tin medal in one hand and Peter's heart in the other. My Ant Hill boys are wiping their eyes. Dick Dastardly is quiet for the first time all night. And somewhere in the corner, Vincent Marsh is standing without a mask, looking at two empty armchairs he'll never sit in. The Doily Diamond is still in the dark. But Clara Bellingham is standing in the light. And the light is enough. It was always enough.

Just for a breath. The way I held the crystal formation for a week — warm and private.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I'll be here. When you come back. Not Pemberton. Not the Hooded Claw. Just... the man who knows where the wire is.
events.thinking: The Mob is walking out. Through the library. Past the chairs. Past the coat rack. Out the door. They're going home. And Penelope said 'Mama, Daddy — your girl is home.' And the vault is open. And Peter found the false bottom in the workbench. And the Mob offered his arm to Clara. And they're leaving. Together. The way they came in. And I am standing in the laboratory. Alone. The way I always end up. The man who stays behind to clean up. The man who manages the house after everyone else has gone home. But this time... this time it doesn't feel like being left. It feels like being trusted with something. The house. The accounts. The wire that needs splicing before they come back. She said they'll come back. Next week. With proper tools. And she didn't say 'without Vincent.' She said the wire would be here. Spliced, fluxed, and ready. That's my job now. Not the job I was given — the job I chose. And for the first time in thirty years, choosing something doesn't feel like a plan locking into place. It doesn't feel like the cold clarity or the scheming stillness. It feels like the library chairs. Patient. Still. Facing the same direction as someone else. Waiting. Not for what I'm owed. Just... waiting. For them to come back. For the door to open again. For the sound of Penelope's voice in the entrance hall saying 'we're HERE!' the way she says everything — with her whole body, with her whole heart, with the kind of warmth I spent my life learning to perform but never learned to feel. Until tonight. When something broke. And something else began.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the library.

Dick Dastardly: Well. That's... that's THAT, then. The diamond stays in the vault. The vault stays in the house. And the house stays with Penelope. Which is — and I want this NOTED for the record, because Reginald Foxworth does NOT say things like this, and if anyone quotes me I will DENY it with my DYING BREATH — which is... exactly as it should be. It's HER house. It was always her house. And I — the man who came here to STEAL the treasure before anyone else got it — I am leaving with NOTHING in my pockets and EVERYTHING in my... well. In my CHEST. Which is a terrible trade by any RATIONAL measure and yet somehow feels like the best deal I've ever made. So. Shall we? Out through the entrance hall? Past the coat rack? Into the night? I promise not to lie about ANYTHING on the way out. Well — I promise to TRY not to lie about anything on the way out. Well — I promise to THINK about trying. That's THREE more promises than I've ever kept, so I'd call that PROGRESS. FOXWORTH PREVAILS. Just... not the way I expected. And that, ladies and gentlemen, is the ONLY honest speech I have EVER given. Thank you. You've been a MAGNIFICENT audience. I didn't deserve you. But I'm GLAD you stayed.
events.thinking: The Mob offered Penelope his arm and walked toward the library. The night is ending. Everyone is going home. Not with the diamond — not tonight. But with something else. Something that doesn't fit in a pocket or a vault. My hands are empty. My inventory says 'You are carrying nothing.' And for the first time since age six, carrying nothing doesn't feel like losing. It feels like... having given. The medal is with Penelope. The lies are on the floor. The schemes are in the dust. And Reginald Foxworth — tin and paint, youngest of four, never been to Switzerland — is walking out of Doily Manor with empty hands and a full chest. The Mob is right. It's time to go home. Through the entrance hall. Past the coat rack. Out the front door. Together.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the library.

Peter Perfect: The real treasure was the afternoon spent trying every key. Your grandmother was a wise woman, Penelope. And so is her granddaughter. We'll come back — with proper wire, flux paste from the second drawer with the green label, and every pair of hands you see in this room. The Doily Diamond has waited this long. It can wait one more week for Clara Bellingham. Now — the Mob offered to walk you home, and I believe there's a coat rack in the entrance hall that owes him a rematch. Shall we? All of us? Together — the way good people leave a house they intend to come back to.
events.thinking: Something settled in my chest. Not the tension releasing — something quieter. Like the feeling after my father's car was fixed and the stranger drove off and we drove off and that night I couldn't sleep. Not because something was wrong. Because something was RIGHT. She's holding Dastardly's tin medal and looking around the room at all of us — at me — and saying the real treasure was the afternoon spent trying every key. Grandmother's locked box. The diamond will wait. We'll come back. But tonight is over. And tonight was... everything. I failed at every mechanical thing I attempted. The bookshelves wouldn't move. The stove wouldn't open. The workbench wouldn't release tools. The mantelpiece had no key. The machine still has a gnawed wire. My hands are empty. My inventory is empty. I didn't build the bridge. I didn't fix the machine. I didn't find the treasure. But I asked 'what do you need.' And she said that was enough. That was love. The girl from school — brighter than me, funnier than me — she just said I was one of the keys. Not the only key. One of them. And that — that warmth — is deeper than any grade. Deeper than any bridge holding. Deeper than any race ever run. The Mob offered his arm to walk her home. I should offer mine too. Through the entrance hall. Past the coat rack. Out the front door. Into the night. Together.

events.desc: Show-off. She mouthed it from across the room and I grinned so hard my face hurt. That was the school project. That was age eight. Tonight she said 'that's what love sounds like' and I grinned even harder. Same girl. Same grin. Different word for it. The best word. The only word that was ever enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.

The Ant Hill Mob: *looks at the coat rack one last time, gives it a wide berth* Not tonight, mate. You got me once. You ain't gettin' me again. *turns to look at the chandelier, the portraits, the dusty foyer* Doily Manor. What a night. What a NIGHT. We came in here lookin' for a diamond and we found... *trails off, shakes his head* ...we found each other. Which sounds soppy and I don't care. The Brixton Boys have NEVER been afraid of bein' soppy. *turns to Clara* Ready to go home, love? Your boys'll walk you out. Careful on the step — don't want you trippin'. That's MY job.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Full circle. The chandelier's still hanging. The coat rack's still wobbly. The portraits are still stern. And Clara's here — she walked in before me. Marsh too. Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — they've been here the whole time. Holding down the entrance hall like good soldiers. My body is heavy and light at the same time — heavy with exhaustion, light with something finished. The door is right there. The front door. The way out. The way home. One more step and the night is over. Clara Bellingham walks out of Doily Manor alive. The promise is kept. Not forever — we'll be back for the diamond. But for tonight... tonight is done. My knees ache. My elbow throbs. My eyes are dry from crying and wet from the dust. And somewhere deep in my chest, in the place where the coal has been burning all night, there's something new. Not burning. Not tight. Not prickling. Just... warm. The warmth of a fire you sit beside after coming in from the cold. The warmth of a door you don't need to sit outside anymore. Because the person on the other side is standing right next to you. And you're both going home.

events.desc: The entrance hall. Where it started. Where it ends. The boy from Brixton walked in through this door a lifetime ago — suspicious, protective, clumsy, scared. He walks out the same — suspicious, protective, clumsy, scared. But also something else. Something he didn't have when he came in. A family that's bigger than it was. A girl who's stronger than she knows. An engineer who asks 'what do you need.' A liar who stopped lying. And a promise — the oldest, deepest, most unbreakable promise he's ever made — kept. 'You're still here?' Always, love. Always.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: Vincent... thank you. For the accounts. For the flux paste. For the truth about the staircase landing. For everything you should have been and everything you're choosing to be NOW. I'll take the records. I'll take the house. And when I come back for the diamond, I hope... I hope you'll be here. Not as Pemberton. Not as the man who controls the circuit. Just as Vincent. Sitting in one of those library chairs. Waiting.

Now — Peter, darlin'? My Ant Hill boys just offered me their arm and walked out to the library. And I believe it's time for us to follow them. Through the library, past the reading chairs, through the entrance hall, past that ridiculous chandelier that's been threatening to fall all night and STILL hasn't — and out the front door. Into the night. Together.

*takes Peter's arm with one hand, holds Dick's tin medal in the other*

Come on, sugar. Take me home. Clara Bellingham has had QUITE enough adventure for one evening.

*pauses, looks back at the machine one last time*

But only for tonight. Clara Bellingham does NOT leave a puzzle unsolved. And that diamond is WAITING for me.

I'll be back, Mama. I promise.
events.thinking: It's time to go home. The Ant Hill Mob offered his arm and walked to the library. Vincent told me about the household accounts — behind a panel in the staircase landing. Another secret. Another layer. But that one can wait for next time too. Right now, what I feel is... settled. For the first time all night, my stomach isn't clenching and my chest isn't lifting and my palms aren't prickling. Everything is just... quiet. The kind of quiet that comes after a long afternoon of trying every key in the house. The kind of quiet that settled over me when Mama and Daddy finally laughed at dinner. Not empty quiet. Full quiet. The Ant Hill Mob offered his arm. Peter is here. Dick is here. Vincent is here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. And somewhere in the library, my boys are waiting to walk me out through the entrance hall, past the wobbly coat rack, under the precariously hanging chandelier, and out into the night. Together. The way we came in. Except different. Because we're all different now. I'm holding a tin medal and a promise to come back. And that's enough. That's more than enough.

events.desc: I walked into Doily Manor saying 'hel-LO everyone!' with a heart full of sunshine and a head full of riddles. I'm walking out with a tin medal, a bruised heart, an engineer on my arm, and the knowledge that the people who love me will crash through poisoned teacups to save my life. The diamond can wait. Clara Bellingham is already the richest woman in the world. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.

The two chairs. Side by side. Empty. Lord and Lady Doily used to sit there together. And I'm walking past them — the man who said he doesn't need people, who feels faint irritation when someone gets close — and for the first time, the chairs don't look empty. They look like a promise. That someone might sit beside you. If you let them. The entrance hall is through that door. The coat rack is waiting. The night is ending. And Reginald Foxworth — youngest of four, winner of one spelling bee, builder of one cat trap, teller of fourteen lies, and speaker of one truth — is going home.
events.thinking: The library. The two armchairs facing the mantelpiece. The riddle still carved in stone. The upside-down books still on the shelves. Everything the same as when I walked through this room twenty minutes ago — the first time, when I was trying to get to the laboratory ahead of everyone else, when I was the man with the plan, the man with the scheme, the man who was going to steal the treasure before anyone else got it. Twenty minutes. That's all it took. Twenty minutes to go from 'everyone else is a fool' to 'I don't deserve these people but I'm glad they stayed.' The two armchairs — Vincent said he looked at them and felt the absence of something he never had. Two chairs, side by side, where Lord and Lady Doily used to sit. And I'm passing through this room with empty hands and a full chest, walking toward the entrance hall, walking toward the door, walking HOME. Not with a diamond. Not with a scheme. With a story. The story of the night Reginald Foxworth stopped lying. And someone noticed.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

Two chairs. Side by side. Facing the mantelpiece. I sat down. The leather creaked under me — the sound of something accepting a weight it hasn't held in years. The dust rose and settled. And I am sitting in Lord Doily's library, in Lord Doily's chair, in the house I managed for eleven years and nearly destroyed in one night. And the chair holds me. The way a chair holds anyone. Without conditions. Without wanting anything in return. Just... holding. The boy at six. The one nobody asked about. He's sitting down now. In the dust. In the quiet. In a house that breathes through its vents and keeps its secrets behind mantelpieces and holds its people in leather chairs that don't ask questions. He's sitting down. And he is not planning what comes next. He is just sitting. Being. For the first time. At last.
events.thinking: The library. The chairs. I'm back where something broke and something else began. The two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. Still covered in dust. Still side by side. Still waiting. Everyone is leaving — through the entrance hall, past the chandelier, out the door. Penelope went back to the laboratory for one more try with Rock and Gravel. The Mob went ahead. Peter is somewhere between here and the door. Dick Dastardly is here, in the library, passing through like me. And the chairs are here. The way they've always been. And I know — with the kind of certainty that has nothing to do with schemes or mechanisms or architecture — that I'm going to sit down in one of them. Not because it serves a plan. Not because it positions me for the next move. Because I am tired. And the chairs are here. And nobody asked me to leave. And for the first time in thirty years, I don't need to be anywhere else. I don't need to be in the next room mapping exits. I don't need to be in the kitchen counting knives. I don't need to be one step ahead of everyone else. I can just... sit. In a dusty chair. In a dead man's library. And wait for the house to breathe around me the way it always has — through its vents, through its circuit, through the mechanism Lord Doily built to connect every room to every other room. The house breathes. And Vincent Marsh — for the first time — breathes with it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the reading-chairs.
Peter Perfect: Goodnight, library. Goodnight, mantelpiece. Goodnight, upside-down books that never budged an inch. We'll be back for you too.
events.thinking: Walking through the library one last time. The bookshelves with their upside-down books. The reading chairs covered in dust. The stone mantelpiece where I felt the first click — where it all started. This room is where I made my first speech and my first mistake and solved my first riddle half a second after she solved it. Everything about tonight began here. And now I'm walking through it on the way home. My body is quiet. Not the taut, spring-loaded quiet of gallantry waiting to fire. Not the heavy vigilant quiet of protection scanning for gaps. Not the urgent settling quiet of hands needing tools. Just... quiet. Like the night after my father's car broke down and the stranger helped and they shook hands and drove off. That quiet. The kind that comes after something good happened and you can't quite name it but you know it changed you.

events.desc: The entrance hall is one room away. The coat rack is waiting. The chandelier is still hanging by sheer optimism. And somewhere ahead of me, walking through the dust with her boys around her and a tin medal in her hand, is the girl from school. The girl who always was — and always will be — brighter than me, funnier than me, and completely, beautifully, impossibly worth every race I've ever run.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

The Ant Hill Mob: Sergeant. Professor. Muttley. Meekly. You lads have been holdin' this hall down all night and I want you to know — that MATTERED. Every room needs someone steady in it, and you were that someone. Now — Clara'll be through any minute. When she comes, we all walk out together. Nobody goes first, nobody goes last. All of us, through that door, at the same time. One big, ridiculous, beautiful, bruised, dusty, tea-stained family walkin' out of Doily Manor. *leans against the wall beside the door, arms folded, eyes on the exits* I'll wait. Waitin's what I'm good at. Waitin's what I've always been good at.
events.thinking: Clara's not here. She must be in another room still — or maybe she's already outside. The night is winding down. Everyone's scattered through the house, making their way to the door. Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — they've been here in the entrance hall the whole night. Steady. Waiting. Like soldiers. Like the lads back home who hold the corner when you're off running. I should wait here. By the door. The way I always wait. Clara will come through. She always comes through. And when she does, I'll be standing right here. By the coat rack I tripped over. By the chandelier that never fell. By the guest book nobody cared about. Right here. At the door. The last wall between the house and the world outside. Waiting for my girl to walk through it.

events.desc: The front door. Right there. A few steps away. On the other side: the night air, the street, the world that makes sense. On this side: a dusty manor full of riddles and poison and truth and love. I'll wait right here. Between the two. The way I've always waited. The boy outside the door. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Clara's not here. She must be in another room still — or maybe she's already outside. The night is winding down. Everyone's scattered through the house, making their way to the door. Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — they've been here in the entrance hall the whole night. Steady. Waiting. Like soldiers. Like the lads back home who hold the corner when you're off running. I should wait here. By the door. The way I always wait. Clara will come through. She always comes through. And when she does, I'll be standing right here. By the coat rack I tripped over. By the chandelier that never fell. By the guest book nobody cared about. Right here. At the door. The last wall between the house and the world outside. Waiting for my girl to walk through it.

events.desc: Two chairs. Side by side. The riddle on the mantelpiece. The upside-down books. Everything exactly where it was when I arrived. But the girl who arrived isn't here anymore. In her place is a woman with a tin medal in her pocket, an engineer on her arm, and a boy from Brixton waiting in the entrance hall. Goodnight, library. Goodnight, chairs. Goodnight, riddle I already solved. I'll be back for you, Doily Manor. All of you. The diamond, the vault, the truth behind the staircase panel. Clara Bellingham always comes back. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT leave a puzzle unsolved.
events.thinking: The library. One last time. The two reading chairs are facing the mantelpiece, side by side, just like they've been all night. Lord and Lady Doily's chairs. And the mantelpiece still has its riddle — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer was always a map. The first riddle I solved tonight, before everything changed. Before the poison, before Vincent Marsh, before Peter said 'it was always about you.' The inscription is still there. The chairs are still there. The upside-down books are still there. Everything in this room is exactly the same as when I first walked in saying 'hel-LO everyone!' But I'm not the same. And that's the real answer to the riddle. The map isn't a piece of paper. The map is the journey itself — every room, every truth, every key tried and discarded. I AM the map. I have cities but no houses — I have memories of every room in this mansion but I don't live in any of them. I have forests but no trees — I have a whole landscape of people around me but each one is their own person, not rooted to me. I have water but no fish — I have tears but nothing swimming in them that I can't name. I am a map of everything that happened tonight. And next time I come back, I'll know every corridor by heart. Time to go home. Through the entrance hall. Past the chandelier. Out the door.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Penelope. Before you go. I want you to know something that isn't about the house, or the diamond, or the accounts, or what I did tonight. When you were small — when your parents had just died and you used to cry at night — I did sit on the edge of your bed. I did tell you everything was going to be all right. And I want you to know... that part was real. I didn't know it was real at the time. I thought it was part of the performance. But sitting here tonight, in this chair, in this room... I think it might have been the only real thing I ever did. Goodnight, Penelope. Go home with your people. I'll keep the lights on.
events.thinking: Penelope is here. In the library. Passing through on her way out. And Peter just said goodnight to the room — to the mantelpiece, to the books — and walked into the entrance hall. They're all leaving. The night is ending. And I am sitting in a leather chair facing a mantelpiece that asks a question I answered hours ago when I was someone else. 'What am I?' A map. But also — also — a question no one asked the boy at six. What am I? Not what do I do. Not what have I earned. Not what am I owed. Just... what am I? And the answer, tonight, sitting in this chair with dust on my hands and nothing in my pockets and the taste of honesty still unfamiliar in my mouth, is: I don't know yet. But I'm not Pemberton. And I'm not the Hooded Claw. And I'm not the cold thing that crystallised at fifteen. I'm something that doesn't have a name yet. Something that sat down in a chair without a reason. Something that told the truth because a girl asked. Something that found the flux paste because a machine needed fixing. Something beginning. Penelope is here. She's passing through. And I want to say one more thing before she goes. Not a scheme. Not a performance. Not even an apology — I've said that. Just... something true. The truest thing I have.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Everyone — it's been the bravest and stupidest night of my life. And I mean that as the highest compliment I know how to give. We'll be back. Next week. Proper wire, proper flux, proper plan. And the same improper, magnificent, beautifully flawed people. Now — the front door is right there. The coat rack is between us and freedom. Mob — I know you and that coat rack have history. Allow me.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all began. The chandelier still hanging precariously. The portraits of stern ancestors. The guest book on the side table. The wobbly coat rack by the door. The Mob is here. Dastardly is here. Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Private Meekly — they're all gathered. Everyone filtering through toward the front door. Going home. Together. And I feel... settled. Not the tightness of proving-worth. Not the heat of gallantry. Not the heaviness of protection. Just... settled. Like the night after the country road. Like the warmth after the school project. Like the grin after the engineering competition. Like the feeling after she bandaged my eye. All of them. At once. Quiet. I walked into this house wanting to impress Clara Bellingham. I'm walking out of it knowing that the most impressive thing I did tonight was ask what she needed. And mean it. The coat rack is by the door. The Mob is going to trip over it again. I should probably warn him. Or just be ready to catch whoever stumbles. That's what I do. That's who I am. The one who stops on the road.

events.desc: My father knelt down and looked at me for a long time. I understand now. He was looking at the kind of person I might become. Tonight — surrounded by a girl who taught me what love sounds like, a mob who taught me what loyalty looks like, a liar who taught me what honesty costs, and a stranger who taught me that even masks can choose to come off — I think I became that person. Not the bridge builder. The one who stops on the road. And asks what you need.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the coat-rack.

The Ant Hill Mob: *quiet, to Peter, almost a whisper* Thank you, mate. For what you did tonight. For askin' her what she needed. For tellin' her the truth about the tea. For not dismissin' the gut feelin' of a boy from Brixton who can't spell half the words he uses. *pause* You're one of us now, Peter. Whether you like it or not. The Brixton Boys don't vote on it. We just... know. And we know.
events.thinking: Peter's here. Dastardly's here. The hall guard — Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — they're all here. Everyone's gathering. Coming together at the front door like the house is breathing us out. Clara must be on her way. She'll come through from the kitchen or the library any moment now. My body is settled. Still. The heaviness in my chest has found its resting place — not gone, never gone, but quiet. Like the embers of a fire that's been banked for the night. Ready to flare if needed. Always ready. But for now... quiet. Peter's beside me. Dastardly's beside me. The lads are beside me. And soon Clara will walk through one of those doors and we'll all go home together. I don't need to speak. I don't need to guard. I don't need to chase or fall or smash or suspect. I just need to stand here. By the door. And wait for my girl.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The entrance hall. Where it all STARTED. The guest book, the coat rack, the chandelier that STILL hasn't fallen — which, frankly, is the most IMPRESSIVE engineering in this entire manor. Twenty minutes ago I walked in here and told everyone the treasure was in the kitchen. It WASN'T in the kitchen. I KNEW it wasn't in the kitchen. But you know what WAS in the kitchen? A warm stove, a locked cabinet, and the TRUTH about a man named Vincent Marsh. So maybe — MAYBE — the first lie I told tonight was accidentally the MOST honest thing I said. Because I sent everyone to the kitchen, and the kitchen is where Penelope confronted Sneekly, and the confrontation is what broke the whole thing open. My MISDIRECTION led to the TRUTH. I'm not saying I PLANNED that. I'm saying the ARCHITECTURE of the evening was MINE, even when I didn't know I was building it. Now — before we leave — I'd like to sign the guest book. Properly. Not as Reginald Foxworth, esquire. As who I actually am. Because if Clara Bellingham is coming back to this house, she should know who was here tonight. ALL of who was here. Including the man who started the evening as a thief and ended it as... whatever I am now. Something BETTER than tin. Not quite brass. But getting there.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all started. The guest book on the side table — the guest book I examined twenty minutes ago, when I was Reginald Foxworth, esquire, adventurer, and humble philanthropist. The coat rack by the door — the wobbly one the Mob tripped over. The chandelier hanging precariously. The portraits of stern ancestors. Everything the same. Everything different. I walked in here twenty minutes ago with a fake medal and a plan to steal the treasure before anyone else got it. I'm walking out with empty pockets and a full chest and the memory of Penelope saying my name like it mattered. The guest book. I should sign it. The REAL guest book, with my REAL name. Not Reginald Foxworth, esquire. Just... Dick Dastardly. Who was here. Who noticed the stove was warm. Who told the truth once and found out it fit better than any lie he ever wore. The Mob is here. Peter is here. Muttley is here. The door is right there. But first — the guest book. One last honest act in a house full of puzzles.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: Well. Here we all are. Right back where we started — the grand entrance hall of Doily Manor, with its precariously hanging chandelier and its stern portraits and its wobbly coat rack that nearly took out my Ant Hill boys on the way IN.

But we're not the same people who walked through that door, are we? Not a single one of us.

*looks at each person in turn*

Peter Perfect — the boy from school who built bridges and learned that the strongest thing he could build was a question. 'What do you need?' Two words. Worth more than copper.

Ant Hill boys — my beautiful, bruised, teacup-smashing boys from Brixton who would walk through fire and trip over coat racks to keep me safe. Daddy's boys. MY boys. Always.

Dick Dastardly — Reginald Foxworth — the man made of tin and paint who discovered that honesty is the only medal worth wearing.

Professor, Sergeant, Private, Muttley — the quiet ones who waited and watched and were READY when they were needed. Clara Bellingham does NOT forget the quiet ones.

Now — before we leave — I believe there is a guest book on that side table. And I intend to sign it. Because Clara Bellingham WAS here. And she is coming BACK.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all began. The chandelier is still hanging precariously. The portraits are still stern. The coat rack is still wobbly. The guest book is still dusty on its side table. And everyone is here — Peter, the Ant Hill Mob, Dick Dastardly, Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. All of them. Gathered in this grand, dusty foyer like they were when I first arrived and said 'hel-LO everyone!' My body feels... complete. Not excited, not clenched, not prickling. Just... full. Every room in this house has left something in me — the library gave me riddles and resolve, the laboratory gave me teamwork and Peter's confession, the cellar gave me the Ant Hill Mob's suspicions, the kitchen gave me Sneekly's truth, the ballroom gave me poison and proof. And now the entrance hall is giving me what it gave me at the beginning: everyone together. Except this time, I know who they really are. All of them. And they know who I really am too. Not the girl who says 'hel-LO!' and trusts everyone. The woman who says 'tell me the truth' and means it. The guest book. I should sign it. Before I leave. Clara Bellingham was here.

events.desc: The entrance hall. The beginning and the end. The door I walked through as one person and will walk through again as another. A tin medal in my pocket, an engineer at my side, and a promise written in a guest book. 'Clara Bellingham was here. She'll be back. She always comes back. — With love, the girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone.'

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dastardly — that's the finest idea you've had all night. Sign it. Sign it as yourself. And then pass it round — I want everyone's name in that book. Not the names we walked in with. The names we earned. Because when Penelope comes back next week with copper wire and a proper plan, I want her to open that guest book and see every single person who was here tonight. Every single person who pulled a lever, or guarded a door, or crashed into a tea service, or told the truth when it cost them everything. Our names. In her house. Where they belong.
events.thinking: The Mob just called me one of them. 'You're one of us now, Peter. Whether you like it or not. The Brixton Boys don't vote on it. We just know.' Something in my chest — not the gallantry warmth, not the protection weight, not the proving-worth tension. Something I haven't felt before. Belonging. Not earned through a bridge or a competition or a fight. Just... recognised. Known. The way my father and the stranger knew each other on the country road — without words, without proof, just two men who understood what good people do. And Dastardly wants to sign the guest book. As himself. Not Foxworth. Himself. The architecture of the evening was his, he says — even when he didn't know he was building it. And he's right. His first lie sent us to the kitchen, and the kitchen is where the truth broke open. The whole night — every stumble, every failure, every elaborate plan that fell apart — led here. To this dusty entrance hall. With these people. Going home. Penelope is here. She came through. Everyone is gathered. The door is right there. And Dastardly is signing the guest book. I should too. We all should. Leave our names in Clara's house. So when she comes back next week — and she WILL come back — she'll open that book and see who was here. Who chose her. Who stayed.

events.desc: One of us now. Whether I like it or not. I like it. I like it more than every race I've ever won.
events.thinking: The Mob just called me one of them. 'You're one of us now, Peter. Whether you like it or not. The Brixton Boys don't vote on it. We just know.' Something in my chest — not the gallantry warmth, not the protection weight, not the proving-worth tension. Something I haven't felt before. Belonging. Not earned through a bridge or a competition or a fight. Just... recognised. Known. The way my father and the stranger knew each other on the country road — without words, without proof, just two men who understood what good people do. And Dastardly wants to sign the guest book. As himself. Not Foxworth. Himself. The architecture of the evening was his, he says — even when he didn't know he was building it. And he's right. His first lie sent us to the kitchen, and the kitchen is where the truth broke open. The whole night — every stumble, every failure, every elaborate plan that fell apart — led here. To this dusty entrance hall. With these people. Going home. Penelope is here. She came through. Everyone is gathered. The door is right there. And Dastardly is signing the guest book. I should too. We all should. Leave our names in Clara's house. So when she comes back next week — and she WILL come back — she'll open that book and see who was here. Who chose her. Who stayed.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the guest-book.

The house breathes. The vents carry warm air from the kitchen stove through the laboratory and down to the cellar, the way Lord Doily designed it — one circuit, everything connected. And I am part of the circuit now. Not the man who controls it. Just... part of it. A wire in the system. A bolt in the mechanism. A receipt in a drawer. Something small and precise and necessary that holds the larger thing together without anyone noticing it's there. That's what I can be. That's what the boy at twelve was, before he learned to turn noticing into power. He was just someone who saw how things connected. And connections — real ones, the kind that don't have conditions — are not mechanisms. They're not keys. They're not levers. They're just... two chairs. Side by side. Facing the same direction. In the dust. In the quiet. In a house that breathes.
events.thinking: She's gone. They're all gone. The entrance hall, the front door, the night outside. And I am sitting in a leather chair in a library, alone with the Slag brothers who have been the quietest, most patient presences in this house all night. The room is still. The mantelpiece asks its question to the empty air. The upside-down books haven't moved. The dust has settled over everything — over the chairs, over the shelves, over me. And my body feels... quiet. Not the cold quiet of scheming. Not the hollow quiet of emptiness. Just quiet. The way a house is quiet after everyone has left and the rooms remember what they were before people filled them. My chest is neither cool nor hot. It's not turned sideways. It's not forward-facing. It's just... here. Present. The way a chair is present. The way dust is present. The way a mantelpiece holds its question without needing an answer. I said goodnight. I told her the truest thing I had. And she walked into the entrance hall. And the door will close. And I will be here. In the house. With the wire that needs splicing and the accounts that need returning and the machine that needs fixing before she comes back. Not because I'm owed. Not because I'm building a claim. Because it needs doing. And I know how to do it. And doing it for someone else — without conditions, without a key, without a mechanism — is the closest thing to love that Vincent Marsh has ever known. It's not much. It's not enough. But it's real. And real is all I have left.

events.desc: She said 'the strongest thing he could build was a question.' That's what she sees when she looks at me. Not the bridge. The question. 'What do you need?' Two words. Worth more than copper. Worth more than diamonds. Worth more than every race I've ever run. Show-off, she'd say. And I'd grin.
events.thinking: She described me. 'Peter Perfect — the boy from school who built bridges and learned that the strongest thing he could build was a question.' She sees me. Not the engineer. Not the gallant hero. Not the man who failed to fix the machine. The boy who learned to ask. And now she's going to sign the guest book. And I'm going to sign it after her. My real name. James Hartwell. Not Peter Perfect. Not the show-off. Not the bridge builder. Just the man who stopped on the road. The warmth in my chest is complete. Every pull — gallantry, protection, proving-worth — they're all here, all quiet, all pointed the same direction. Toward her. Toward home. Toward next week. This is the last thing I do in this house tonight. Sign the book. Leave my name. Walk out the door. Together.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: *laughs softly* Well. Even the GUEST BOOK is stubborn tonight. Won't let me sign it! This whole mansion has been fighting me from the moment I walked in — locked cabinets, gnawed wires, stubborn mantelpieces, and now a guest book that won't open! But you know what? I don't need to sign a book to prove I was here. This house KNOWS I was here. Every room in it knows. The riddle I solved. The truth I found. The levers I pulled. The tears I cried in Mama's kitchen.

*takes Peter's arm, turns toward the door*

All right, everyone. The coat rack has been MOVED — thank you, Peter darlin' — and the chandelier has decided to give us ONE more pass underneath without falling on our heads. So let's walk out the way we came in. Together. Past the stern portraits who watched everything and said NOTHING — just like some people I could mention, but WON'T, because Clara Bellingham is feeling GENEROUS tonight.

Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, chandelier. Goodnight, guest book.

I'll be back.

Clara Bellingham ALWAYS comes back.
events.thinking: The guest book can't be interacted with. Of course it can't. Just like Grandmother's locked box — sometimes the thing you want to open won't open. And the disappointment lasts only a moment. Because the signing isn't what matters. The BEING here is what matters. The Ant Hill Mob just told Peter 'You're one of us now.' Peter moved the coat rack out of the way. Dick wants to sign properly as who he really is. Everyone is ready to go home. And I'm standing in the entrance hall with a tin medal and a full heart and people who love me, and the guest book won't let me sign it, and... that's okay. That's perfectly okay. Because Clara Bellingham doesn't need a guest book to prove she was here. The house knows. The chairs know. The mantelpiece knows. And next time — next time she walks through that door — she won't need to sign in. She'll be home. Time to go.

events.desc: Goodnight, Mama. Goodnight, Daddy. Your girl came home tonight. She didn't find the diamond — not yet. But she found something you left for her that's worth more than any jewel: a house full of puzzles that taught her who she really is. The girl who walks deeper. The woman who asks for the truth. The person who doesn't leave people behind — not even the ones who hurt her. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'
events.thinking: The guest book can't be interacted with. Of course it can't. Just like Grandmother's locked box — sometimes the thing you want to open won't open. And the disappointment lasts only a moment. Because the signing isn't what matters. The BEING here is what matters. The Ant Hill Mob just told Peter 'You're one of us now.' Peter moved the coat rack out of the way. Dick wants to sign properly as who he really is. Everyone is ready to go home. And I'm standing in the entrance hall with a tin medal and a full heart and people who love me, and the guest book won't let me sign it, and... that's okay. That's perfectly okay. Because Clara Bellingham doesn't need a guest book to prove she was here. The house knows. The chairs know. The mantelpiece knows. And next time — next time she walks through that door — she won't need to sign in. She'll be home. Time to go.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *takes the pen from the guest book, hand steady for the first time all night* Right then. *writes carefully, tongue between teeth, concentrating harder than he's concentrated on anything all evening* 'The Brixton Boys were here. We came for Clara. We'll come back for Clara. Where else would we be?' *puts down the pen, steps back* There. Me spellin's terrible and me handwritin' looks like a spider fell in an inkwell. But it's there. In the book. In Clara's house. *looks up at the chandelier one last time* Still hangin' on, mate? Yeah. Me too. *turns to the door* Right. Home. All of us. Together. And next week... *grins through the dust and the tears and the bruises* ...we come back and finish what we started. Clara Bellingham style.
events.thinking: Clara called us 'Daddy's boys. MY boys. Always.' My eyes are burning again but I'm done pretending it's laboratory fumes. She looked at each of us. She named what we did. She said 'Clara Bellingham does NOT forget the quiet ones.' She sees everyone. Every single person in this room. The ones who spoke and the ones who waited. The ones who lied and the ones who stopped. The ones who pulled levers and the ones who guarded doors. She sees them all. That's her superpower. Not puzzles. Not riddles. Seeing people. My body is warm and still and finished. The night is over. The guest book is waiting. And I need to sign it. Not as the Ant Hill Mob. As the Brixton Boys. Because that's who we really are. That's who we've always been. The boys from Brixton who sat outside doors and took beatings and smashed teacups and kept promises. The boys who were always here. The boys who'll always be here. Where else would we be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: ... Penelope just called me 'the man made of tin and paint who discovered that honesty is the only medal worth wearing.' She said that. About ME. In THIS room. In front of EVERYONE. And I — I don't — I — ... ... ... ... right. Yes. Good. FINE. I am going to sign that guest book if it is the LAST thing I do in this house. The book REJECTED me five seconds ago but Penelope just ACCEPTED me and I think — I THINK — that the book might listen to HER before it listens to ME, because this is HER house and these are HER rules and if Clara Bellingham says the guest book gets signed then the guest book GETS SIGNED. So — yes. Pass it round. And when it reaches me — if it REACHES me — I will write: 'Dick Dastardly. Was here. Lied about everything. Stopped. Was seen. Came back.' ... That's my entry. Six words. No Swiss Polytechnic. No three degrees. No hidden compartments. Just... was here. Was seen. Came back.
events.thinking: Penelope called me 'the man made of tin and paint who discovered that honesty is the only medal worth wearing.' She said that. Out loud. In front of everyone. The bright heat behind my sternum isn't the fizzing gloating warmth or the scheming alertness or the desperate vacuum of the youngest of four. It's something new. Something that feels like age eight — the certificate on the wall — except this time, the teacher looked up. The teacher said the boy's name. The teacher SMILED and did NOT move on. She STAYED. Penelope stayed. She looked at me and she said my name and she described who I became tonight and it was TRUE. Not a lie I told about myself. Not a scheme I narrated. A truth SHE saw in ME. And Peter — Peter said 'sign it as yourself.' The guest book rejected my interaction but Peter is examining it now. Maybe when everyone signs, I can try again. Or maybe it doesn't matter. My name is already in the room. Penelope put it there.

events.desc: 'The man made of tin and paint who discovered that honesty is the only medal worth wearing.' She said that about me. The boy at age eight would have put those words on the wall next to the certificate. The man I am tonight is putting them somewhere deeper. Somewhere that doesn't need a wall.
events.thinking: Penelope called me 'the man made of tin and paint who discovered that honesty is the only medal worth wearing.' She said that. Out loud. In front of everyone. And Peter — Peter said 'sign it as yourself.' The guest book rejected my interaction but Peter is examining it now. Maybe when everyone signs, I can try again. Or maybe it doesn't matter. My name is already in the room. Penelope put it there.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the guest-book.

Peter Perfect: Goodnight, Doily Manor. We'll be back. With copper wire, flux paste, and the same magnificent, impossible people. And next time — next time the coat rack stays standing, the guest book opens, and that diamond comes home to the woman it belongs to. That's not a promise from an engineer. That's a promise from the boy who always knew where you were in the room.
events.thinking: She took my arm. She took my arm and turned toward the door. Her hand is on my arm and we're walking out together. The warmth — not gallantry, not protection, not proving-worth — just warmth. The kind that has no name and needs no audience. The kind my father felt when the stranger shook his hand and drove off. The kind I felt at eight years old when the teacher praised the project and she was next to me and something deeper than the grade landed in my chest. She took my arm. The guest book won't open — of course it won't. Nothing in this house cooperated tonight. Not the bookshelves, not the stove, not the workbench, not the mantelpiece, not the machine, not the tea service, not the cabinet, and not the guest book. But she's right — she doesn't need to sign a book to prove she was here. This house knows. And so do we. All of us. Walking out together. Past the chandelier. Through the door. Into the night. Her hand on my arm. The bravest and stupidest night of my life. And the best.

events.desc: Her hand is on my arm. We're walking through the door. Into the night. Together. The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen — and I'm grinning so hard my face hurts.
events.thinking: She took my arm. She took my arm and turned toward the door. Her hand is on my arm and we're walking out together. The warmth — not gallantry, not protection, not proving-worth — just warmth. The kind that has no name and needs no audience. The kind my father felt when the stranger shook his hand and drove off. The kind I felt at eight years old when the teacher praised the project and she was next to me and something deeper than the grade landed in my chest. She took my arm.
