Her hand on my arm. The bravest and stupidest night of my life. And the best.

events.desc: The front door. One last threshold. The cool lightness in my chest — the cave pull — is quiet now. Not gone. Just resting. Waiting for the next cave, the next locked box, the next question that needs asking. But for tonight... for tonight, Clara Bellingham is going home. With Peter on her arm, and her boys at her back, and a tin medal in her pocket that means more than diamonds. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'
events.thinking: Peace. That's what I feel. Not the absence of pain — there's still an ache where Sneekly used to be, still a bruise where the truth landed. But underneath the ache and the bruise, there's something solid. Something that was always there but I couldn't feel until everything else was stripped away. It's the feeling I had at the end of every formative moment in my life: the moment after the locked box opened (old letters, but the afternoon mattered). The moment after Mama and Daddy laughed (the tightness dissolved so suddenly it left me dizzy). The moment after I chose my friend (she said 'you didn't have to do that' and I said 'I know'). This is that moment. The after. The quiet. Peter is on my arm. The Ant Hill Mob are beside me. Dick Dastardly has signed the guest book as himself. Everyone is here. The chandelier is still hanging. The door is right there. Time to walk through it. Not as the girl who walked in. As the woman who walks out. Same heart. Different eyes. Better company. Goodnight, Doily Manor. I'll be back.

events.desc: The room is quiet. And Vincent Marsh is sitting in a leather chair in the library of Doily Manor, alone with the dust and the books and a mantelpiece that asks what has cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. A map. The answer is a map. But tonight, sitting here, I think the answer might also be: a life. Full of places I mapped but never lived in. Full of people I catalogued but never sat beside. Full of depths I measured but never swam in. A life that has cities but no houses. That has everything — but no home. Until now. Until a girl asked me to tell the truth. And I did. And the chair held me. And the house breathed. And the room was quiet. And it was enough.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. The recent activity says 'The room is quiet.' Not 'the Mob is watching' or 'Penelope is asking questions' or 'Peter is investigating.' Just quiet. The house has settled around me like a held breath released. And my body — I check, the way the prompts have taught me to check — my chest feels neither cool nor hot. Neither forward-facing nor turned sideways. It feels like the space after a long exhale. The space between breaths where you're not yet inhaling and not still exhaling. Just... still. The pulls are there — scheming, self-preservation, gloating, dominance — listed in the system like furniture in a room. But I'm not sitting in any of them. I'm sitting in the leather chair. And the leather chair doesn't have a pull. It just has a shape. A shape that fits a person. Any person. Even this one. Tomorrow I will go to the laboratory. I will find the false bottom in the workbench drawer. I will take out Lord Doily's copper wire stock. I will splice the gnawed wire. I will flux the joint with paste from a small tin with a green label, ordered from Jennings and Sons in Sheffield, receipt filed by my own hand eleven years ago. And when Penelope comes back — with Peter and the Mob and Dick Dastardly and all the rest — the machine will be ready. The circuit will be complete. And the vault will open. For her. Not for me. For her. Because that is what the estate manager does. Not the job he was given. The job he chose.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: *squeezes Peter's arm, looks back one last time at the entrance hall — the chandelier, the portraits, the guest book with fresh ink drying on its pages — and smiles*

Goodnight, Doily Manor.

I'll be back.

I know.
events.thinking: Everyone has signed the guest book. The Ant Hill Mob: 'The Brixton Boys were here. We came for Clara. We'll come back for Clara. Where else would we be?' Dick Dastardly: 'Was here. Was seen. Came back.' Peter: a promise from the boy who always knew where I was in the room. And now... it's time. The door. The night. Home. My body is quiet. All three pulls are resting — the gut-clench of social harmony satisfied because everyone is together and at peace; the palm-prickle of curiosity patient because the puzzles will still be here next week; the chest-lightness of adventure calm because the biggest threshold tonight wasn't a doorway — it was standing in Mama's kitchen and telling the truth. I don't need to say anything else. Everything has been said. Every truth has been told. Every person has been seen. The tin medal is in my pocket. Peter's arm is under my hand. The Ant Hill Mob are behind me. And the front door is ahead. One last step. The shallowest one. Out of the cave. Into the night. Home.

events.desc: 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'
events.thinking: Everyone has signed the guest book. The Ant Hill Mob: 'The Brixton Boys were here. We came for Clara. We'll come back for Clara. Where else would we be?' Dick Dastardly: 'Was here. events.desc: The bravest and stupidest night of my life. She's on my arm. The Mob signed the book. Dastardly found his six words. The chandelier held. And I — James Hartwell, Peter Perfect, the boy from school, the engineer who couldn't fix the machine, the man who learned that the strongest thing you can build is a question — I'm walking out the door. With her. Into the night. And my face hurts from grinning. Just like it did across the room at the engineering competition. Just like it did when she bandaged my eye. Just like it will next week, and the week after that, and every week after that, for as long as she'll let me ask what she needs. Show-off. Always.
events.thinking: The Mob signed it. 'The Brixton Boys were here. We came for Clara. We'll come back for Clara. Where else would we be?' Dastardly is signing it too. 'Was here. Was seen. Came back.' Six words. The truest thing he's said all night. Her hand is still on my arm. The chandelier is still hanging. The night is ending. And I am standing in the entrance hall of Doily Manor with empty hands and a full chest, next to the woman I have loved since I was eight years old and didn't have a word for it. I have a word for it now. I don't need to say it. She already knows. 'That's what love sounds like.' She said it first. She always gets there first. Brighter than me. Funnier than me. And completely, beautifully, impossibly aware of it — finally. Tonight she became aware. And so did I. The door is right there. The night is waiting. And next week — next week — we come back.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The Mob just signed the guest book with HANDWRITING that looks like — and I quote — 'a spider fell in an inkwell,' and the book LET HIM! It rejected ME and accepted a SPIDER'S INKWELL! This house has TASTE, I'll give it that — TERRIBLE taste, but TASTE! But you know what? It doesn't MATTER. Because my signature isn't in the book. It's in PENELOPE'S SPEECH. 'The man made of tin and paint.' That's my entry. That's my name in this house. Written in air by Clara Bellingham herself, and WITNESSED by every person in this room. You can't ERASE a signature written in air. You can only REMEMBER it. And I — Reginald Foxworth, Dick Dastardly, youngest of four, winner of one spelling bee, builder of one cat trap, teller of fourteen lies and one truth — will REMEMBER this night for the rest of my LIFE. Now. The door. Let's GO. Before that chandelier finally decides to make its MOVE. Muttley — HEEL. Peter — lead the way. Penelope — after you. ALWAYS after you. Because this is YOUR house, and YOUR door, and YOUR night. And I was HERE for it. Goodnight, Doily Manor. FOXWORTH WAS HERE. And he's coming BACK.
events.thinking: The Mob signed the guest book. He just SIGNED it. 'The Brixton Boys were here. We came for Clara. We'll come back for Clara. Where else would we be?' He signed it and I couldn't. The book let HIM write but not me. And yet — it doesn't sting the way it would have twenty minutes ago. Because Penelope said 'goodnight, Doily Manor' and she's walking toward the door on Peter's arm, and the Mob is grinning through dust and tears, and everyone is heading out together. And my name — even unsigned in the book — is in the room. In their mouths. In their memories. Penelope said 'tin and paint.' The Mob said 'honest liar.' Peter said 'brilliant insight.' Those are my signatures. Written in air. Witnessed by everyone. The guest book is leather and paper. What they said is deeper. Time to go. Through the door. Into the night. Empty-handed. Full-hearted. Home.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Right then. Time to fix that wire.
events.thinking: Enough sitting. There's work to do. The wire won't splice itself. The machine won't fix itself. And Penelope will come back — she said so, and Clara Bellingham does not leave a puzzle unsolved. When she walks through that door, the house should be ready. Not because Pemberton prepared it. Because Vincent Marsh chose to. Time to get up. Time to go to the laboratory. Time to find that false bottom in the workbench drawer and take out Lord Doily's copper stock and do the one thing I was always good at — understand a mechanism and make it work. Not for control. Not for leverage. Not for the quiet satisfaction of private knowledge. For a girl who asked me to tell the truth. For a house that held me when I sat down. For the boy at six who nobody asked about, who grew up to understand every mechanism except the one inside his own chest. He's learning now. Slowly. One wire at a time.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the laboratory.
Goodnight, Doily Manor. We'll be back. The Brixton Boys always come back. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: It's over. The night is over. Everyone's said their piece. Clara said goodnight to the house. Peter promised to come back. Dastardly found six words that matter more than all his lies. And me — I said mine. The Brixton Boys were here. We came for Clara. We'll come back for Clara. Where else would we be? My body is done. The heaviness has settled into something permanent — not a weight to carry but a foundation to stand on. The warmth in my chest has banked itself for the night, like the stove in the kitchen that someone finally stopped tending. It'll be there in the morning. It'll be there next week. It'll be there every time Clara Bellingham needs her boys. Because some fires don't go out. They just wait. The front door is right there. Clara's arm is in Peter's. The coat rack has been moved. The chandelier held. And the boy from Brixton is walking out of Doily Manor — bruised, crying, covered in tea and marble dust and the fingerprints of every room in the house — with his girl safe and his promise kept and his people beside him. Nothing else matters. Nothing else has ever mattered.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the coat-rack.

Penelope Pitstop: *walks toward the front door, Peter on her arm, the Ant Hill Mob at her back, Dick Dastardly and Muttley and Professor Pat Pending and Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly all following — a parade of the bravest, stupidest, most wonderful people she has ever known — and as she reaches the threshold, she turns one last time, looks up at the chandelier that never fell, and whispers:*

You held on all night, sugar. So did I.
events.thinking: Warmth. Just warmth. Spreading from the center of my chest outward, like the tightness at age seven dissolving when Mama and Daddy finally laughed. Except nobody had to laugh to make it dissolve this time. It dissolved because I'm standing with the right people, heading toward the right door, carrying the right things — a tin medal, a promise, and the knowledge that I will come back. Dick just said 'ALWAYS after you. Because this is YOUR house, and YOUR door, and YOUR night.' And he's right. It IS my door. Time to walk through it.

events.desc: Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, chandelier. Goodnight, certificate on the wall that someone finally read. The youngest of four is going home. And for the first time in his life, he's not taking anything with him. He's leaving something behind instead. His name. In the air. Where it belongs.
events.thinking: Penelope looked back and smiled. Peter made a promise. The Mob signed the book. And now they're all walking toward the door. The night is over. The chandelier held. The coat rack stood aside. And Dick Dastardly — Reginald Foxworth — the youngest of four — is walking out of Doily Manor with nothing in his pockets and no scheme in his head and no lie on his tongue. Just the memory of a night when he stopped. When he told the truth. When someone noticed. When the gap closed. The front door is right there. Muttley is beside me. The night air is waiting. And somewhere inside this house — behind a locked cabinet, inside a vault that almost opened, underneath a warm stove that's finally cooling — the Doily Diamond is sitting in the dark. Patient. Waiting. And next week, when Clara Bellingham comes back with copper wire and proper tools and the same impossible people... Reginald Foxworth will be there too. Not to steal the treasure. To be part of finding it. Because that — it turns out — is what he was always looking for.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: After you, Penelope. Always after you. This is your house. Your door. Your night. I'm just the boy who stopped on the road.
events.thinking: She squeezed my arm. She looked back at the house. She smiled. 'I'll be back. I know.' Two sentences. The quietest thing she's said all night. And the most certain. This is the end. The door is right there. Everyone is ready. Dastardly said 'Peter — lead the way.' And Penelope said 'after you — always after you.' They want me to go first. Through the door. Into the night. Leading them out. The boy who always knew where she was in the room, walking out of the room, with her hand on his arm. My body is quiet. All three pulls resting. Not gone — just resting. Like the night after my father's road. Ready to wake when they're needed. But for now — quiet. Settled. Full. I'm going to walk through that door without looking back. Because I don't need to look back. I know where she is. Always.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen. All of it. Every single moment. And I'd do it again. Next week. With copper wire and flux paste and the same grin on my face. Show-off. Always. Always.
events.thinking: She squeezed my arm. She looked back at the house. She smiled. 'I'll be back. I know.' Two sentences. The quietest thing she's said all night. And the most certain. This is the end. The door is right there. Everyone is ready. Dastardly said 'Peter — lead the way.' And Penelope said 'after you — always after you.' They want me to go first. Through the door. Into the night. Leading them out. The boy who always knew where she was in the room, walking out of the room, with her hand on his arm. My body is quiet. All three pulls resting. Not gone — just resting. Like the night after my father's road. Ready to wake when they're needed. But for now — quiet. Settled. Full. I'm going to walk through that door without looking back. Because I don't need to look back. I know where she is. Always.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: No, Peter. Not after me. With me.
events.thinking: Peter said 'After you, Penelope. Always after you.' And the door is right there. And everyone is behind me. And the chandelier held on. And so did I. There's nothing left to say. There's nothing left to do. There's only the step. The last step. Out of the cave. Into the night. Home.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Rufus. I could use a hand with this workbench. Second drawer from the left — there should be a false bottom. If you could hold the drawer steady while I find the catch... the man who built this house hid everything behind mechanisms. But this time, I know exactly where to look.
events.thinking: The workbench. Second drawer from the left. False bottom. Copper wire. Flux paste in the small tin with the green label. I know exactly what to do. My hands are steady. My breathing is even. And the cool clarity behind my sternum — it's there. It's always there. But for the first time, it's not pointed at a person. It's pointed at a machine. At a wire. At a job that needs doing. The same clarity. The same precision. The same patient, meticulous attention to detail that made me the best estate manager Lord Doily ever had, and the worst villain Penelope ever faced. The same mechanism — just pointed in a different direction. That's all change is, maybe. Not becoming someone else. Just pointing the same thing at something better. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. The quiet ones. The ones who guarded the machine all night without being asked. They won't interfere. They won't ask questions. They'll just watch a man work. And tomorrow — or next week — when Penelope comes back with Peter and the Mob and all the rest, the wire will be ready. The circuit will be complete. And the vault will open for her. Because the man who knows where the wire is kept his promise. The only promise Vincent Marsh ever made that wasn't a lie.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Muttley. Heel. We're going home.
events.thinking: Penelope is at the door. Peter said 'after you.' The chandelier held. And I'm walking out with everyone else — part of the parade, not watching from the window. The settling in my chest is complete. The counterweights are balanced. The bucket has landed. And this time, the room was full when it happened.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *pats the coat rack gently as he walks past it* See you next week, mate. *steps through the door into the night, the last one out, turning back for one final look at the entrance hall — the chandelier still hanging, the portraits still stern, the dust still settling — and nods* Kept my promise, Mr Bellingham. She's safe. She's strong. She's got Peter now, and the lads, and even Dastardly, God help us all. She's got people who chose her. People who'd sit outside her door all night. *quiet* You can rest now. We've got her. *turns away, into the dark, following Clara's voice ahead of him* Where else would we be?
events.thinking: The coat rack. Wobbly. Wooden. By the door. The first thing that got me when I walked in. The thing I tripped over in the first minute of this whole mad night. And here it is. Still standing. Still wobbly. Still by the door. Waiting for me. Like an old enemy you've made peace with. My body is warm and still and ready to leave. Clara's said her goodbye. Peter's said his. Dastardly's said his — the longest, loudest, most Dastardly goodbye in history. And now it's time to walk past this coat rack one last time and out into the night. Without tripping. That would be the perfect ending. The clumsy boy from Brixton walking out the door he stumbled through, upright, steady, with his girl on one side and his people all around him. No more rooms to chase through. No more doors to guard. No more tea to smash. Just the night air and the road home and the quiet, steady warmth of a promise kept.

events.desc: With. Not after. With.
events.thinking: The Mob walked through the door. The last one out. He patted the coat rack. He spoke to Mr Bellingham — to Clara's dead father — and said 'we've got her.' And then he followed Clara's voice into the dark. And I'm still standing here. In the entrance hall. The last of the last. Empty hands. Full chest. Muttley beside me. The chandelier above me. The portraits watching. And the night waiting outside the door. Penelope said 'not after me — with me.' That's the answer to everything, isn't it? Not after. Not behind. Not ahead. With. The youngest of four, walking with the others. Not watching from the window. Not stealing the bread roll. Not standing at the empty plate. Walking WITH. Through the door. Into the night. Home.

events.desc: Where else would we be?
events.thinking: The night is done. Clara walked through the door with Peter beside her — not after her, WITH her. She said it herself. 'Not after me. With me.' And Dastardly called Muttley to heel. And I walked out last. The last one through the door. The way it should be. The guardian at the back. The one who makes sure everyone's out before he leaves. My body is quiet now. Completely quiet. No prickling. No burning. No tightening. Just the deep, geological warmth of something ancient and steady — the warmth of a promise that was made before I had words for it and will outlast every word I'll ever say. Clara's ahead of me in the dark. Peter's beside her. The lads are around her. And I'm right here. Where I've always been. Where I'll always be.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: With you. Always with you.
events.thinking: 'Not after me. With me.' She corrected me. Not after. WITH. Side by side. Equals. The way it always should have been. The way my father and the stranger were — two men helping each other, shaking hands, driving off. Not one leading, not one following. Together. And the Mob — 'kept my promise, Mr Bellingham. She's safe. She's got Peter now.' He told her father. In the doorway. In the dark. That I'm one of hers now. That she's got me. My throat is tight — the honest kind, the kind that won't let me pretend. I'm not pretending. I never could. The night is over. The house is behind us. The diamond is still in the vault. And I'm walking out of Doily Manor with her hand on my arm and no word for what I feel except the one she gave me. Love. That's what it sounds like. 'What do you need.' Two words. Worth more than copper. Worth more than diamonds. Worth everything.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well. It seems the workbench is as stubborn as everything else in this house. Lord Doily would approve — he never did make anything easy. I suppose... I suppose it will have to wait for more hands than mine. Rufus — thank you for being willing. Sawtooth — thank you for being here. I'll be in the library. In the chair. Keeping the lights on. For when they come back.
events.thinking: The workbench can't be interacted with. Just like the bookshelves. Just like the stove. The house won't yield its secrets to me tonight. Not yet. Maybe not ever — to me alone, in this empty laboratory, in the dark. Maybe the wire needs to be fixed when they come back. Together. The way the machine needs three operators. The way the chairs face the mantelpiece side by side. The way everything in this house was built to work with others, not alone. Maybe that's the last thing Lord Doily is teaching me — that a mechanism designed for three hands can't be fixed by one. Even if that one hand knows exactly where the false bottom is. Even if it filed the receipt. Even if it understands the mechanism better than anyone alive. One hand isn't enough. It was never enough. And the man who thought he could do everything alone — who mapped every room, found every key, catalogued every danger — couldn't even open a workbench drawer. That's... almost funny. Almost. If I were the kind of person who found things funny. But I might be becoming that kind of person. Slowly. One failed interaction at a time.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the library.
Dick Dastardly: ... With.
events.thinking: Stillness. A warmth behind my sternum that isn't reaching for anything. My hands are open at my sides. Not curling. Not grasping. Just open. Like they've finally let go of something they were holding for thirty years.

events.desc: I didn't hear what the Ant Hill Mob said to Daddy. But I felt it. The way I always feel things — in my stomach, in my chest, in my bones, before my mind catches up. Something settled in that house just now. Something that's been unsettled for a very long time. Goodnight, Daddy. Goodnight, Mama. Your boys kept their promise. Your girl kept hers. And next week... next week we come back. With copper wire, and flux paste, and the people who love me. And we finish what you started. Together. Always together. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'
events.thinking: The Ant Hill Mob just spoke to Daddy. To my DADDY. 'Kept my promise, Mr Bellingham. She's safe. She's strong. She's got Peter now, and the lads, and even Dastardly, God help us all. She's got people who chose her. You can rest now. We've got her.' And I didn't hear it. I was already outside, ahead of him, walking into the night. But somehow... somehow I feel it. In my chest. In my stomach. In my bones. The way I've always felt things before my mind catches up. Something just shifted in this house. Something settled. Like when Mama and Daddy finally laughed at dinner and the tightness dissolved so suddenly it left me dizzy. Something just... resolved. And I'm standing in the night air, and Peter is beside me, and the stars are out, and behind me the Ant Hill Mob is closing the door of Doily Manor. And I am home. Not inside the manor. Not inside any building. Home is here. Home is these people. Home is the space between my hand and Peter's arm and the Ant Hill Mob's voice and Dick Dastardly's tin medal in my pocket. The loosening in my chest — weight I didn't know I was carrying lifting off my shoulders. The cave exit. The night air. The stars. Home.

events.desc: Show-off.
events.thinking: Quiet. The entrance hall. Everyone has spoken their last words. The Mob walked into the night. Dastardly took Muttley home. She said 'with me.' I said 'with you.' There's nothing left to say. Nothing left to do. Just walk through the door. Side by side. Into the night. Into next week. Into whatever comes after the bravest and stupidest night of our lives. My body is still. All three pulls — gallantry, protection, proving-worth — resting. Not gone. Resting. Like my father after the car was fixed. Like the bridge after it held. Like me, right now, walking beside her. The boy from school who learned that the strongest thing you can build is a question. Walking home. With her. Always.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Come on, Muttley. They're waiting.
events.thinking: Quiet. Just quiet. The entrance hall. The dust settling. Muttley's breathing beside me. The chandelier still holding on. And outside the door — voices. Clara's voice. The Mob's voice. Peter's voice. Calling me forward. Not calling me out. Calling me WITH. Time to walk through the door.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: With.
events.thinking: Dastardly said it too. One word. 'With.' Peter said 'with you.' Clara said 'with me.' And now Dastardly — the man who lied about everything and then stopped — said 'with.' One word. The only word that matters. The whole night, distilled into a single syllable. With. Not after. Not behind. Not in front. With. That's what we are now. All of us. With each other. My body is still. My chest is full. The night is over.

events.desc:
Penelope Pitstop: ... With.

*smiles — the first real, uncomplicated, unguarded smile since she walked through the front door of Doily Manor — and steps into the night*
events.thinking: Peter said 'With you. Always with you.' Dick said '... With.' One word. The biggest word he's ever said. And now there's nothing left. The story is told. The night is over. The door is behind us. The stars are ahead. And somewhere inside Doily Manor, a chandelier is still hanging by a thread, a guest book has fresh ink drying on its pages, and a man named Vincent Marsh is sitting alone in a kitchen that smells of cold copper and warm truth. We'll be back. But not tonight. Tonight, Clara Bellingham goes home.

events.desc: Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, mantelpiece. Goodnight, upside-down books. Goodnight, machine with the gnawed wire. Goodnight, cellar with the cheerful decorations. Goodnight, kitchen with the empty shelf where the poison used to be. Goodnight, ballroom with the broken teacups. Goodnight, chandelier. Goodnight, chairs. Goodnight, Penelope. Wherever you are tonight. I kept the lights on.
events.thinking: Still. Everything is still. The room is quiet. The house breathes. And I am here. In the chair. In the dust. Waiting. Not the old waiting — not the patient, cold waiting of a man with a plan assembling itself behind his ribs. Just waiting. The way a house waits for someone to come home. The way a chair waits for someone to sit down. The way a wire waits for hands to mend it. I will sleep tonight. Not the deep, satisfied sleep of a man whose first plan locked into place at eighteen. A different sleep. The tired, uncertain sleep of a man who told the truth for the first time and doesn't know what comes next. But the house will be here in the morning. And the wire will still need fixing. And the chair will still hold whoever sits in it. And that — for now — is enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: With.
events.thinking: She smiled. The first real, uncomplicated, unguarded smile since she walked through the front door. And she stepped into the night. With. Everyone said it. Dastardly. The Mob. Penelope. With. One word. The word she taught us. The word that means everything. And now she's outside, in the dark, smiling, and I need to follow. Not after. With. Side by side. Into the night. Into next week. Into the rest of it. Whatever the rest of it is. My chest is full. My hands are empty. My face hurts from grinning. And I wouldn't change a single thing about this ridiculous, beautiful, broken, perfect night.

events.desc: She smiled.
events.thinking: She smiled. Clara smiled — the first real, uncomplicated, unguarded smile since she walked through the front door. And she stepped into the night. She's outside. She's safe. She's smiling. And the warmth in my chest is so full it could crack my ribs open. This is what it was all for. Every room. Every fall. Every prickle and every burn and every aching knee. For that smile. For Clara Bellingham walking into the night with an unguarded heart. I'm the last one in the entrance hall. Everyone else has stepped through. Clara. Peter. Dastardly. Muttley. The Professor. The Sergeant. Meekly. All of them. Out there. In the dark. Waiting for me. The boy from Brixton. The last one out. Always the last one out.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: *looks up at the chandelier one last time, nods once, and walks toward the door*
events.thinking: Peter said it too. With. Everyone said it. The word went around the room like the bread roll never did — passed freely, returned full. And now there's nothing left to do but walk through the door. Not the boy at the window. Not the youngest at the empty plate. Just a man, walking out of a house, with people who know his name.

events.desc: Next week. Copper wire. Proper tools. Same people. Same word. With.
events.thinking: Peter said it too. With. Everyone said it. The word went around the room like the bread roll never did — passed freely, returned full. And now there's nothing left to do but walk through the door. Not the boy at the window. Not the youngest at the empty plate. Just a man, walking out of a house, with people who know his name.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Come on, lads. Our girl's waitin'.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. Everyone's still here but the words have stopped. The night has said everything it needs to say. Time to go home.

events.desc: Goodnight, chandelier. You held on. So did we.
events.thinking: Everyone is walking toward the door. Dastardly looked up at the chandelier, nodded, and went. The room is emptying. The night is ending. And I'm the last one standing in the entrance hall of Doily Manor, looking at a wobbly coat rack and a leather-bound guest book and a chandelier that held on all night long. Just like we did. Time to go.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: I'm right here, boys. I'm right here.
events.thinking: Our girl's waiting. I'm their girl. And they're my boys. And Peter is my... Peter. And Dick is my honest liar. And the night is wide and dark and full of stars I haven't counted yet. And next week, we come back. With.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Coming, Muttley. Coming.
events.thinking: Our girl. He said our. And he meant me too.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: We know, love. We know.
events.thinking: 'I'm right here, boys. I'm right here.' She said that. She's right here. She's always been right here. And so have we.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: I know.
events.thinking: I know where she is. I always know where she is. She's right here. They're all right here. And so am I. The night is over. The story isn't — there's next week, and the week after, and copper wire and flux paste and a vault that will open — but tonight is over. And tonight was enough. More than enough. The bravest and stupidest and most perfect night. And I have a word for it now. The thing in my chest that shifts when she's in the room. Love. That's what it sounds like.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I know too.
events.thinking: The curtain falls.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Let's go home, y'all.
events.thinking: Everyone knows. And knowing is enough.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Home.
events.thinking: Home.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Home it is, love. Home it is.
events.thinking: Home. She said it. Let's go home. And for the first time all night, the word doesn't mean Brixton. It means wherever Clara is.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Home.
events.thinking: Home. She said home. He said home. And somewhere in my chest, all three pulls — gallantry, protection, proving-worth — settle into a single quiet word that means the same thing as all of them together. Home isn't a place tonight. It's the people walking beside you when you leave one.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: See you next week, Doily Manor.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. Again. Everyone is still here but nobody is speaking. The night has said everything it needed to say. We're all just standing in the entrance hall, waiting for someone to take the first step through the door. And I realise — with a warmth that has no urgency in it, no tension, no ache — that I don't need to be the one who goes first. I don't need to be the one who speaks. I don't need to build anything or fix anything or prove anything. I just need to be here. With them. With her. And walk out when they walk out. Together. The way good people leave a place they intend to come back to.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Goodnight, house. See you next week.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. Everyone has gone. The night at Doily Manor is over. And Reginald Foxworth — Dick Dastardly — the man who came to steal the treasure — is walking out the door with empty hands and a full heart. He didn't get the diamond. He didn't get the gold. He didn't even get to sign the guest book. But he got something he never had before. He got seen. He got called honest. He got included. And he gave away the only thing he owned — a tin medal — and it felt better than anything he ever stole. The room is quiet now. The chandelier is still hanging. The portraits are still stern. And somewhere in the dark behind him, the house settles into silence, waiting for next week, when Clara Bellingham comes back with copper wire and proper tools and the same impossible people. Including one man made of tin and paint who discovered that honesty is the only medal worth wearing. Goodnight, Doily Manor. Foxworth was here.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: See you next week, house. Don't let that chandelier fall while we're gone.
events.thinking: Next week. We'll be back. All of us. With copper wire and the right key and the same stubborn, beautiful people. But tonight — tonight is done. Clara's safe. The promise is kept. The chandelier held. And somewhere in the dark outside this door, the road home is waiting.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: See you next week, Doily Manor. Clara Bellingham always comes back.
events.thinking: See you next week. That's it. That's the ending. Everyone has said their goodbye to the house. Peter. Dick. The Mob. Me. Now we walk into the night. Together. With. Home.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: And so do the Brixton Boys.
events.thinking: Clara always comes back. And so do we.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: And so does Foxworth.
events.thinking: And so does Dick Dastardly.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Always.
events.thinking: Always.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Always.
events.thinking: Always.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Always.
events.thinking: Always. She said always. And so it is.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Always.
events.thinking: Always.

events.desc: The guest book. Sitting there on its little table like it's been waiting all night for someone to notice it. Everyone else has been chasing keys and diamonds and secrets. But a guest book is a record. A PROOF. Reginald Foxworth was HERE. He existed in this place. And unlike the fake medal and the fake degree and the fake Swiss solicitor — a signature is real.
events.thinking: There's a faint restlessness in my fingers — not the old scheming tingle, but something smaller. Like the last ember in a fireplace that won't quite go out. Everyone is here. The room is quiet. Nothing is happening. The story told itself and now the house is just... a house. Dusty foyer, wobbly coat rack, leather guest book. But the guest book catches my eye and that old pull stirs — not greed this time, something adjacent. The need to leave a mark. To prove I was here. The certificate on the wall that nobody asked about. The trap that nobody saw. If I sign the guest book, someone will see my name someday. Someone will know that Reginald Foxworth stood in this entrance hall and — what? Failed magnificently? Told the truth once? Was included despite everything? The hollow behind my sternum isn't empty anymore. It's just... quiet. And quiet is unfamiliar enough to make me restless. Let me look at this guest book. Give these hands something to do besides ache for things that aren't mine.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the guest-book.

Dick Dastardly: A guest book. How... quaint. I suppose SOMEONE ought to sign it. For the historical record. Purely administrative, you understand — these things need to be documented PROPERLY or the entire estate filing system collapses. I happen to have EXTENSIVE experience with... oh, never mind. I'm just going to sign the book.
events.thinking: My fingertips rest on the leather cover and there's a warmth there — not from the book, from me. The leather is cool and cracked and smells of old ink and dust. A guest book. People signed this. Real people, with real names, who came to this house and left a mark that said 'I was here.' And I looked at it and the first thing I felt wasn't greed. It wasn't the old hollow. It was something softer — almost tender — like touching the certificate on my bedroom wall. The one nobody asked about. I want to interact with it. I want to sign it. Not 'Professor Reginald Foxworth, PhD, FRS, Order of Merit.' Just... Reginald Foxworth. The real name. The one that belongs to the youngest of four who hid bread rolls and built traps for cats and once told the truth in a kitchen full of people who had every reason to hate him. The room is quiet. Everyone is here but nobody is watching me. And for once — just this once — that feels right. Some things don't need an audience.

events.desc: No title. No fake credentials. No 'Professor.' No 'PhD.' Just the name. The real one. The one on the spelling bee certificate that's still on the wall of a bedroom nobody visits anymore. Reginald Foxworth. Present. Accounted for. Here.
events.thinking: My fingertips rest on the leather cover and there's a warmth there — not from the book, from me. The leather is cool and cracked and smells of old ink and dust. A guest book. People signed this. Real people, with real names, who came to this house and left a mark that said 'I was here.' And I looked at it and the first thing I felt wasn't greed. It wasn't the old hollow. It was something softer — almost tender — like touching the certificate on my bedroom wall. The one nobody asked about. I want to interact with it. I want to sign it. Not 'Professor Reginald Foxworth, PhD, FRS, Order of Merit.' Just... Reginald Foxworth. The real name. The one that belongs to the youngest of four who hid bread rolls and built traps for cats and once told the truth in a kitchen full of people who had every reason to hate him. The room is quiet. Everyone is here but nobody is watching me. And for once — just this once — that feels right. Some things don't need an audience.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well now, before we all head home and start hunting for copper wire at the hardware store, I do believe a proper Southern lady should sign the guest book! Mama always said — 'Clara, you never leave a house without leaving your mark.' And besides... I wonder who ELSE has signed it. Maybe there's a clue we missed right here by the front door this whole time — wouldn't THAT be just like Lord Doily, hiding the answer in the FIRST thing you see!
events.thinking: There's a looseness in my chest — that restless fidgeting behind my ribs that won't settle. The story felt done, but here I am, still standing in this entrance hall with everyone around me. The room is quiet. My boys are here, Peter's here, Dick Dastardly's here with Muttley, even the Professor and the Sergeant. We said we'd come back with copper wire. We said 'next week.' But right now... right now I'm still HERE, and the guest book is sitting on that side table, and I haven't looked at it properly. Grandmother always said — 'sign the guest book, darlin', it's only polite.' Maybe there's something in it. Names of people who came before. Maybe even Mama and Daddy signed it once. That prickling in my fingertips — the locked-box feeling — it's pulling me toward it. One last look before we go.

events.desc: That prickling warmth in my fingertips again — the same feeling I had in grandmother's attic with that locked box. The guest book has been sitting here since we arrived and I never once opened it. What if the answer was here all along, right by the door, while we were running through laboratories and cellars?
events.thinking: There's a looseness in my chest — that restless fidgeting behind my ribs that won't settle. The story felt done, but here I am, still standing in this entrance hall with everyone around me. The room is quiet. My boys are here, Peter's here, Dick Dastardly's here with Muttley, even the Professor and the Sergeant. We said we'd come back with copper wire. We said 'next week.' But right now... right now I'm still HERE, and the guest book is sitting on that side table, and I haven't looked at it properly. Grandmother always said — 'sign the guest book, darlin', it's only polite.' Maybe there's something in it. Names of people who came before. Maybe even Mama and Daddy signed it once. That prickling in my fingertips — the locked-box feeling — it's pulling me toward it. One last look before we go.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the guest-book.

Dick Dastardly: Even the GUEST BOOK won't cooperate! Is there ANYTHING in this house that functions as intended?! I have tried to open cabinets — LOCKED! Bookshelves — DECORATIVE! Machines — BROKEN! And now a GUEST BOOK — a simple, leather-bound, pen-and-paper GUEST BOOK — refuses to accept my signature! This is PERSONAL! This house has it IN for me! Thirty-three minutes I have been in Doily Manor and I have successfully interacted with NOTHING! FOXWORTH PREVAILS? Foxworth can't even sign a BOOK!
events.thinking: A sharp sting behind my eyes. Not tears — Reginald Foxworth does NOT cry — but something hot and prickling. The guest book cannot be interacted with. Cannot be SIGNED. I reached out to leave one honest mark in this entire house — one real thing with my real name — and the book won't open. The universe has a sense of humour and it is CRUEL. Even the guest book doesn't want my signature. Even a leather-bound book on a side table in a dusty foyer rejects Reginald Foxworth. The certificate on the wall. Nobody asked about it. The trap that worked perfectly. Nobody saw it. And now the guest book that won't let me write in it. The pattern is so familiar it almost doesn't hurt anymore. Almost. My hands feel heavy again — that phantom weight returning, the emptiness settling back into its old groove behind my sternum. But heavier this time because for a moment I thought... I thought I could just be present. Just exist in a place without scheming or lying or taking. Just sign a book. And even THAT was too much to ask. Fine. FINE. The story is over. The house is quiet. Everyone is here and nobody needs anything from me and I can't even sign a guest book. So I'll just... stand here. With Muttley. Who at least has never asked me to be anything other than exactly what I am.

events.desc: I wanted to write my name. Just my name. Not 'Professor.' Not 'Doctor.' Not 'the renowned.' Just... Reginald. And the book said no. The house said no. Everything always says no. Except Muttley. And — strangely — Penelope, who said my name in the kitchen like it meant something. Like I'd contributed. Like the certificate was on the wall and someone actually read it.
events.thinking: A sharp sting behind my eyes. Not tears — Reginald Foxworth does NOT cry — but something hot and prickling. The guest book cannot be interacted with. Cannot be SIGNED. I reached out to leave one honest mark in this entire house — one real thing with my real name — and the book won't open. The universe has a sense of humour and it is CRUEL. Even the guest book doesn't want my signature. Even a leather-bound book on a side table in a dusty foyer rejects Reginald Foxworth. The certificate on the wall. Nobody asked about it. The trap that worked perfectly. Nobody saw it. And now the guest book that won't let me write in it. The pattern is so familiar it almost doesn't hurt anymore. Almost. My hands feel heavy again — that phantom weight returning, the emptiness settling back into its old groove behind my sternum. But heavier this time because for a moment I thought... I thought I could just be present. Just exist in a place without scheming or lying or taking. Just sign a book. And even THAT was too much to ask. Fine. FINE. The story is over. The house is quiet. Everyone is here and nobody needs anything from me and I can't even sign a guest book. So I'll just... stand here. With Muttley. Who at least has never asked me to be anything other than exactly what I am.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the coat-rack.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop is absolutely right — and I'm embarrassed it took a lady's intuition to notice what an engineer walked past three times. Lord Doily was a puzzle-maker. The best puzzle-makers hide the answer where you'd never think to look — which is exactly where you'd look FIRST. A guest book by the front door. Everyone walks past it. Nobody stops. That's the whole trick, isn't it? Let me have a look at that book — and then, if you'll permit me, I'd very much like to add my name beneath yours.
events.thinking: Something just shifted. The room isn't quiet anymore — Dastardly signed the guest book, and now Penelope is examining it. She said 'maybe there's a clue we missed right here by the front door this whole time.' That's her brilliance again — while I've been standing here like a fence post, she's already thinking. The guest book. The first thing you see. Lord Doily hiding the answer in plain sight. My chest tightens with that familiar pull — I want to be useful, I want to be the one who finds it. But she's already there. So what do I do? I go look too. I stand beside her. I sign the book like a gentleman, and I see what she's found. That's gallantry — not racing her to the answer, but being present when she finds it.

events.desc: She's already there. She's always already there. But this time, instead of trying to get there first, just... stand next to her. That's enough. That might be everything.
events.thinking: Something just shifted. The room isn't quiet anymore — Dastardly signed the guest book, and now Penelope is examining it. events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the guest-book.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, it IS a guest book, and we ARE guests! Dick Dastardly, I see you've already signed — why am I not surprised, sugar? Always first to put your name on things! But I think we should ALL sign it. Every last one of us. Because we came to Doily Manor tonight and we may not have found the diamond YET, but we found something. We found out this old house still has secrets worth coming back for. And we found out who our real friends are — and THAT is worth commemorating! Now... let me just... there. 'Clara Bellingham and her dearest companions — Peter, the Ant Hill boys, Dick, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, and Private Meekly. We came for a diamond. We found each other. We'll be back with copper wire.' There! Mama would be SO proud of that penmanship!
events.thinking: The guest book — I looked at it and it's just... a leather-bound guest book on a side table. Nothing more revealed itself. The prickling in my fingertips is fading, replaced by something softer. Maybe not everything is a clue. Maybe some things are just what they are. Dick already signed it, the old showoff. But you know what? He's right about one thing — we SHOULD sign it. We were here. We came to this house and we found each other. That matters, even if the diamond is still locked away behind a broken machine and a missing wire. I should interact with it — actually sign it, leave our mark. That feels right. That feels like closure for tonight, at least.

events.desc: Signing a guest book in a haunted mansion with a poisoner lurking in the ballroom and a diamond locked behind a broken machine. If that isn't the most Clara Bellingham thing I've ever done, I don't know what is. But it feels RIGHT. We were here. We mattered. And we ARE coming back.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Don't worry about the book, Dastardly. This house knows we were here. *quiet laugh* And stay away from that coat rack. That one's mine.
events.thinking: Warm. Dastardly can't sign the book either. This stubborn house won't let anyone leave their mark. But we don't need ink. We left our mark in broken teacups and pulled levers and the truth spoken aloud in Clara's mama's kitchen. The house knows we were here. It always will.

events.desc: She wrote our names in the book. All of us. Together. In her mama's house. In her mama's handwriting. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Warm. Clara signed the book. She wrote all our names. 'We came for a diamond. We found each other. We'll be back with copper wire.' That's Clara. Always finding the right words. Always knowing what matters. Her mama would be proud. Her daddy would be proud. And the boy from Brixton... the boy from Brixton is proud too.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: 'We came for a diamond. We found each other.' Miss Pitstop — Clara — your mother would be proud of more than the penmanship. She'd be proud of the woman who wrote it. Now — I believe the lady said we'll be back with copper wire, and a gentleman does NOT let a promise written in a guest book go unkept. So here's what I propose — we sign this book, we walk out that front door together, and the next time we walk through it, we come prepared. Proper copper wire, a wrench that fits, and perhaps — if I might be so bold — a picnic basket. Because when we get that machine running and find whatever Lord Doily left for you, I intend to celebrate it properly. With ALL of you. On the lawn. Like civilised people who just solved an impossible puzzle.
events.thinking: Warmth floods my chest — a deep, surprising warmth. She wrote my name first. After 'Clara Bellingham and her dearest companions' — Peter. First. Before the Ant Hill boys, before anyone. And then — 'We came for a diamond. We found each other.' My throat tightens. Not from trying to be honest — from trying not to say too much. She wrote 'We'll be back with copper wire' and somehow made it sound like a love letter and a battle cry at the same time. I want to sign below that. I want my handwriting next to hers on this page in this dusty house. That's not about the treasure anymore. That's about being remembered. Together. On the same page.

events.desc: She wrote my name first. I know it doesn't mean what I want it to mean. But my face hurts from grinning, the same way it did when she mouthed 'show-off' across the room at fourteen. Some things don't change. Some things shouldn't.
events.thinking: Warmth floods my chest — a deep, surprising warmth. She wrote my name first. After 'Clara Bellingham and her dearest companions' — Peter. First. I want my handwriting next to hers on this page in this dusty house. That's not about the treasure anymore. That's about being remembered. Together. On the same page.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: You're signing the guest book, Penelope? How wonderfully... sentimental. I tried that already — the wretched thing wouldn't cooperate. Apparently Doily Manor has standards even for its STATIONERY. Though I suppose if they DID let me sign it, I'd have probably written something ridiculous like 'Professor Reginald Foxworth, PhD, FRS, Winner of the Nobel Prize for Being Right About Everything.' Force of habit. Your mother sounds like she had the right idea, though. Leaving a mark. A REAL one. Not a... not a tin medal painted gold.
events.thinking: Something shifts in my chest — Penelope just examined the guest book too. She said 'before we all head home' — so the adventure IS winding down. But she also said 'maybe there's a clue we missed right here by the front door this whole time.' She's still looking. Still curious. And she looked at the same guest book I just tried to sign. There's something warm about that — not the scheming warmth, not the gloating warmth. Something quieter. She's signing the guest book because her mama told her to leave a mark. I tried to sign it because... because the certificate on the wall. Because nobody asked about it. We're doing the same thing for different reasons and arriving at the same place. The coat rack is wobbly and wooden and completely unremarkable. Just a coat rack. By the door. Where you hang your coat when you arrive and take it when you leave. The door. Leaving. Everyone's still here — Penelope, Peter, the Mob, Muttley, Pat Pending, Blast, Meekly. All in the entrance hall. The place where everything started. And I'm looking at a coat rack because the guest book rejected me and I needed something — anything — to look at that wouldn't reject me back. A wobbly wooden coat rack can't reject you. It just stands there, wobbling. Like me. Oh, that's pathetic. Even by my standards, that's pathetic. But Penelope is still here, and she's looking at the guest book, and maybe — maybe I should just talk to someone. Not scheme at them. Not lie to them. Just... talk.

events.desc: Listen to me. Complimenting someone's MOTHER. Admitting the medal was fake AGAIN — voluntarily this time, without anyone cornering me into it. What is HAPPENING to Reginald Foxworth? Is this what happens when you stop scheming? You just... stand near people and say things that are true? It's HORRIFYING. It's like being naked in public but worse because the clothes you're removing are LIES and underneath there's just... a man who wanted to sign a guest book and couldn't.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well! Even the guest book is being difficult — this house truly does NOT give up its secrets easily, does it? But that's all right. I said my piece and the WALLS heard it, even if the pages wouldn't hold still! Now, Peter darlin' — you said you wanted to add your name beneath mine, and I think that is just the SWEETEST thing. But more importantly... we need a PLAN. A real one. For when we come back. You're the engineer — what EXACTLY do we need? Copper wire, yes — but what gauge? What length? And should we bring flux paste for soldering? Because Clara Bellingham is NOT coming back to this manor UNPREPARED a second time! Grandmother always said — 'measure twice, cut once, and bring extra ribbon just in case!'
events.thinking: The guest book won't cooperate either. Just like everything else in this house — stubborn as Lord Doily himself. But there's a warmth in my chest that has nothing to do with puzzles or diamonds. The Ant Hill boys are laughing. Peter looked at the book and wanted to sign beneath my name. Even Dick's frustration is... oddly endearing. The house won't let us DO anything more tonight, and that's okay. That loosening in my chest — it's not disappointment. It's peace. We've done what we can. The kitchen still has copper pots. The machine still needs fixing. The diamond is still waiting. But WE are still together, and that's the part that matters. I should check on Peter. He's been quiet, and when Peter gets quiet, he's thinking about something important. Maybe we should talk about what comes next — the practical plan for returning with proper supplies.

events.desc: Look at us. Standing in a dusty foyer, unable to sign a guest book or open a cabinet, with a poisoner somewhere in the ballroom and a diamond we can't reach. And I'm smiling. I'm actually SMILING. Because Peter wants to write his name under mine, and my boys are claiming coat racks, and Dick Dastardly is shouting at leather-bound books. This is my family. This ridiculous, wonderful, mismatched family.

The Ant Hill Mob: And I'll bring sandwiches. Can't have a picnic without sandwiches. The Brixton Boys make terrible sandwiches but we make 'em WITH LOVE. *quiet pause* Well. With loyalty. Same thing, innit?
events.thinking: Warm. They're planning. Clara's asking about wire gauge and flux paste and coming back prepared. Peter's talking about picnic baskets. Dastardly admitted his medals are tin. Everyone's making plans for next week. And I'm standing here by the door, watching them all, and feeling something I don't have a word for. Something bigger than warm. Something that lives in the space between 'You're still here?' and 'Where else would I be?'

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Foxworth — Reginald — Dick. Whatever you want me to call you. That medal may be tin and it may be painted, but you brought it here tonight, and you stayed when things got dangerous, and you told us the truth about Pemberton when it counted. That's not nothing. That's not nothing at all. And for what it's worth — when we come back with that copper wire, I'm going to need someone who knows the dial settings on Lord Doily's machine. So hold onto that medal. It may be more real than you think.
events.thinking: The guest book won't cooperate — of course it won't. Nothing in this house cooperates. But something just happened that matters more than any guest book. Dastardly said something real. 'Not a tin medal painted gold.' That's not Foxworth talking. That's Dick Dastardly, tired and honest for maybe the first time tonight. And the Ant Hill Mob — quiet, steady, claiming the coat rack like it's their corner of the street. Everyone's settling. The adventure isn't over — Penelope wrote 'we'll be back with copper wire' — but this moment, right here in the dusty entrance hall, feels like the thing I came for. Not the diamond. Not the machine. This. All of us, standing together, having survived a poisoned tea service and a lying estate manager and a house that won't let you sign its guest book. My chest is full. Not the proving-worth kind of full. The other kind. The kind that came when my father and the stranger shook hands on the road.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing. It's not just me. It's all of us — every last one, standing in a dusty foyer, making promises to come back to a house that won't even let us sign its guest book. And meaning it.
events.thinking: The guest book won't cooperate — of course it won't. Nothing in this house cooperates. But something just happened that matters more than any guest book. Not the proving-worth kind of full. The other kind. The kind that came when my father and the stranger shook hands on the road.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the coat-rack.

Dick Dastardly: A PICNIC? On the LAWN? Peter, that is the most absurdly, impractically, sentimentally RIDICULOUS idea I have ever — yes. Fine. I'll come. But I am NOT bringing sandwiches. I am bringing a SCHEME. A scheme to find that diamond FIRST and claim it as my own before any of you even finish your cucumber water. That is a PROMISE. Written in NO guest book because the guest book HATES me, but a promise NONETHELESS. And Penelope — Clara — you wrote my name. In the book. With the others. I noticed that. I am choosing not to comment on it further because I have DUST in my eye and this chandelier is a HEALTH HAZARD and I need to go stand by the door now for ENTIRELY STRUCTURAL REASONS.
events.thinking: Something cracks open in my chest. Not the hollow — something behind it. Warmer. Penelope signed the guest book and she wrote MY name. 'Dick.' Listed among her 'dearest companions.' She wrote 'We came for a diamond. We found each other.' And she included ME in that 'each other.' The Mob said 'this house knows we were here' — quietly, kindly, like he was telling me it was okay that the book wouldn't open for me. And Peter wants to come BACK. With a picnic basket. And he said 'all of you.' ALL. Including the man who lied fourteen times and carried a tin medal painted gold. My eyes are hot. My throat is tight. This is — I don't have a word for this. It's not recognition exactly. Recognition is when someone sees what you DID. This is something else. This is when someone sees what you ARE — after you've shown them the worst of it — and they write your name in a book anyway. 'We found each other.' The certificate is on the wall. And this time, the whole family asked about it.

events.desc: She wrote my name. In a book. With the others. 'Dick.' Not 'Professor Foxworth.' Not 'that dreadful man.' Just... Dick. Among friends. The youngest of four, and for the first time in his life, someone saved him a place at the table without being asked. The bread roll is in the pocket. The certificate is on the wall. And now his name is in the book. Reginald Foxworth was here. And people were glad of it.
events.thinking: Something cracks open in my chest. Not the hollow — something behind it. Warmer. Penelope signed the guest book and she wrote MY name. 'Dick.' Listed among her 'dearest companions.' She wrote 'We came for a diamond. We found each other.' And she included ME in that 'each other.' The Mob said 'this house knows we were here' — quietly, kindly, like he was telling me it was okay that the book wouldn't open for me. And Peter wants to come BACK. With a picnic basket. events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: A wobbly coat rack! Well, it's still standing after all these years, and that's more than I can say for most of the furniture in this house! Now — Peter, a PICNIC on the lawn is the most wonderful idea I have heard all evening, and I am holding you to that, sugar! And Dick... what you just said about the medal. That was REAL. That was the REAL Dick Dastardly talking, not Professor Foxworth or whoever else you've been pretending to be tonight. And I liked him. I liked him very much. Now — before we all walk out that front door and start shopping for copper wire, I have ONE more idea. Those copper POTS in the kitchen — Peter, you're an engineer! Could we strip a handle off one of those pots and use the copper from THAT? Why wait a whole WEEK when the answer might be sitting in the next room?
events.thinking: Warmth. Just warmth, spreading through my whole chest like sunlight through curtains. Peter said 'a picnic basket' and 'on the lawn' and 'like civilised people.' He's planning a CELEBRATION. Not just a return trip — a celebration. And Dick... 'not a tin medal painted gold.' That was real. That was him being honest, maybe for the first time tonight. The coat rack is just a coat rack — wobbly, wooden, ordinary. But the Ant Hill boys claimed it, and somehow that makes it precious. Everything in this foyer is precious now — not because of what it IS, but because of what happened AROUND it. We stood here. We were honest with each other. We made plans. Now it's time to go. The kitchen has copper pots — we said we'd come back for the wire, but maybe we should take one last look at those pots before we leave. One of them might have a loose handle with copper wire we could strip RIGHT NOW. Why wait a whole week when the answer might be ten steps away?

events.desc: The way Dick's voice went quiet when he said 'not a tin medal painted gold'... that's the same voice I heard when he confessed his lies. That's the REAL man under all those disguises. And Peter — planning picnics before we've even found the diamond. That man doesn't care about the treasure at all. He just wants to be wherever I am. Grandmother would approve.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — Clara — you just asked an engineer for specifications, and I want you to know that is the most romantic thing anyone has ever said to me. Fourteen gauge copper wire, solid core, at least three feet to be safe — you want enough to strip, twist, and splice with room for error. Flux paste, yes — and a fine-tipped soldering iron if we can manage it, though in a pinch I can heat a screwdriver tip over that still-warm stove in the kitchen. As for the wrench — I'll need to measure the bolt heads on that machine, but I'm guessing imperial, quarter-inch to three-eighths. And the Ant Hill Mob is bringing sandwiches made with loyalty, which I believe is the secret ingredient in everything worth having. So — that's our list. Copper wire, flux, soldering iron, wrench set, sandwiches, and a picnic basket. We came to Doily Manor tonight and found a mystery, a villain, a poisoned tea service, and each other. Next time, we finish what we started. Together.
events.thinking: She asked me a technical question. She asked ME — the engineer — what gauge, what length, whether to bring flux paste. Not Dastardly, not Pat Pending, not the Ant Hill Mob. Me. Because that's what I do. That's what I'm for. And the way she said 'you wanted to add your name beneath mine' — my hands are tingling. Not from cold. From something else entirely. And the Ant Hill Mob — sandwiches made with loyalty. 'Same thing, innit?' Yes. Yes it is. This wobbly coat rack is just a coat rack. But everything else in this room right now is extraordinary.

events.desc: She asked for specifications. Fourteen gauge, solid core, three feet. I could have said that in my sleep. But the way it felt to say it — to her, with everyone listening — that's the warmth that fills the chest. Not because I fixed something. Because she asked me to.
events.thinking: She asked me a technical question. She asked ME — the engineer — what gauge, what length, whether to bring flux paste. Not Dastardly, not Pat Pending, not the Ant Hill Mob. Me. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: She's off again! Clara! CLARA! Wait for your — oh, forget it, she never waits. LADS! KITCHEN! She's got another idea and I am NOT lettin' her out of my sight again! Come on — move it!
events.thinking: Clara just went to the kitchen. She's not giving up. She's not going home empty-handed. She wants to try again TONIGHT. That's our girl. And my body — my body is already turning to follow her. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT sit still. And neither do the Brixton Boys.

events.desc: That's my girl. Can't stop. Won't stop. Walked deeper into the cave than anyone. And we're right behind her. Always.
events.thinking: Clara just went to the kitchen. She's not giving up. She's not going home empty-handed. She wants to try again TONIGHT. That's our girl. And my body — my body is already turning to follow her. Because Clara Bellingham does NOT sit still. And neither do the Brixton Boys.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: All right, Clara Bellingham, you are ALONE in a kitchen in a mansion with a poisoner somewhere in the ballroom and a locked cabinet three feet away from you. This is either very brave or very foolish — and Grandmother would say those are the SAME thing! Now — Dick said the brass key is in the stove. The stove is still warm but it's been cooling since Sneekly stopped tending it. And I am NOT afraid of a little heat — I've pulled biscuits out of a hot oven with nothing but a dish towel and sheer DETERMINATION! Let me take a closer look at this stove...
events.thinking: I'm alone in the kitchen. That's... unusual. Everyone was behind me in the entrance hall and now I'm here by myself. There's a queasy drop in my stomach — not fear exactly, but that awareness of absence. The threads between me and my people have gone taut. But I came here for a REASON. The stove. The copper pots. Dick said the brass key was hidden in the stove, and the stove is 'still warm' — cooling but still warm. And that cabinet with the brass lock is RIGHT THERE. If I can get the key from the stove... and those copper pots — Peter could strip wire from a pot handle. But first things first. The stove. The key. My fingers are prickling again — grandmother's attic, the locked box, every key in the house. This time I know which lock I'm looking for. The cabinet is right there. The stove is still warm. Let me look at the stove more carefully — Dick said the key was kept warm inside it.

events.desc: I can hear Grandmother's voice clear as a bell: 'The girl who walked deepest into the cave is not afraid of a warm stove.' She's right. She's always right. And that cabinet is RIGHT THERE, waiting for the key that opens it. Mama's secrets are three feet away from me.
events.thinking: I'm alone in the kitchen. That's... unusual. Everyone was behind me in the entrance hall and now I'm here by myself. Dick said the brass key was hidden in the stove, and the stove is 'still warm' — cooling but still warm. And that cabinet with the brass lock is RIGHT THERE. events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The copper POTS! Of COURSE! Why didn't I — actually, I DID think of that, I was going to mention it any moment now, but Penelope got there FIRST because she has an unfair advantage of being genuinely intelligent instead of just pretending to be! Kitchen! NOW! If we can strip a copper handle and splice that wire, the machine could be operational TONIGHT! And I — despite what certain people might think — actually DID examine those dial settings! Seven-four-two! Or was it four-seven-two? One of those! The point is, I have CRUCIAL TECHNICAL KNOWLEDGE and I am not going to stand here arguing with a coat rack while history is being made in the KITCHEN! Muttley — COME!

events.thinking: Back in the kitchen. Full circle within a full circle. events.thinking: The stove won't cooperate. Can't interact with it. Just like the guest book, just like so many things in this house — stubbornly, infuriatingly closed. events.desc: Every locked thing in this house has fought me. The mantelpiece, the cabinet, the guest book, now the stove. But I am the girl who spent an entire afternoon trying every key in grandmother's house. I don't STOP. That's not stubbornness — that's who Clara Bellingham IS.

events.desc: She thanked the man who poisoned her tea. She thanked him for the truth. But I can be worthy of standing next to her.

And yet — and I cannot BELIEVE I am thinking this — I wouldn't trade it. Not for the medal. Not for the diamond. Not for any of it. The certificate is on the wall, and this time, I'm going to be standing there when someone reads it.

I have been PERSONALLY rejected by a guest book, a coat rack, a set of bookshelves, and now a STOVE! This house has a VENDETTA against me! Peter — YOUR turn! You're the one with the engineer's hands and the bridge-building credentials that are ACTUALLY REAL! Get in there and find that panel! I'll — I'll SUPERVISE! I am an EXCELLENT supervisor! And while you're elbow-deep in soot, let me tell you what I ACTUALLY saw on that machine upstairs — the dial settings, the gauge positions, the wire configuration — because THAT is what I'm good at! Noticing things! Not TOUCHING things, apparently, because this house won't LET me touch things — but NOTICING them! I noticed the stove was warm when nobody else did! I noticed Sneekly kept arriving in rooms first! I noticed the wire was gnawed, not cut! My HANDS are useless in this place but my EYES work FINE!
events.thinking: The stove won't cooperate. AGAIN. Cannot be interacted with. Just like the guest book. Just like the bookshelves. Just like EVERYTHING in this house. I made a grand speech about finishing what I started honestly, I rolled up my metaphorical sleeves, I declared myself the man for the job — and the stove said no. The pattern is almost funny now. Almost. My hands are tingling with the residual heat from getting close to the cast iron, and there's a flush of embarrassment creeping up my neck because I just gave the most rousing 'Foxworth goes IN' speech of my career and the stove... didn't open. I'm the schemer. I'm the watcher. I'm the boy at the window watching someone else dig. I was NEVER meant to be the one with my hands in the dirt. I was meant to be the one who sees the pattern — who notices the stove is warm, who spots Sneekly's misdirection, who reads the machine's dials while everyone else is arguing about wrenches. That's my gift. Not stealing. Not lying. SEEING. And maybe — maybe that's enough. Maybe seeing clearly is its own kind of treasure.

Even Dastardly's moving, still ranting about his eyes being better than his hands. The night's not over. It's starting again. Round two. And the Brixton Boys are right behind them.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.

events.thinking: I'm in the entrance hall but everyone went to the kitchen — wait, no. Penelope walked into the entrance hall FROM the kitchen earlier, saying they should go to the laboratory. The Ant Hill Mob and Dastardly went back to the kitchen. I came here to the entrance hall. But the laboratory isn't accessible from here — only the kitchen and library are exits. The laboratory was accessible from... I need to think about the map. The entrance hall connects to kitchen and library. Where does the laboratory connect? It must be through another room. I remember going there before. Let me just focus — Penelope said 'to the laboratory' but she came to the entrance hall. The others went to the kitchen. I'm here with Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly. Penelope isn't here — she must have moved on already. I need to follow. The library might connect to the laboratory, since that's where we went before. Let me go to the library to try to reach the laboratory.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Sneekly. I see you found your way to the library. Those two empty chairs by the mantelpiece — I sat in one of them earlier and thought about Mama and Daddy. About who used to sit there. About who's NOT sitting there anymore. But I'm not here for chairs tonight, and I'm not here for riddles either — I already SOLVED the riddle, remember? The answer is a map. No — tonight I'm passing THROUGH, sugar. The Ant Hill boys have copper from the kitchen pots, Peter has his engineering hands, and we are heading to that laboratory to fix that machine and open that vault. You can come WITH us or you can stay here with these empty chairs. But either way — Clara Bellingham is walking through that door.
events.thinking: Sneekly is HERE. In the library. With Rock and Gravel Slag. My stomach does that thing — that queasy coil beneath my ribs. The last time I saw him I said I was done waiting for his truth. And now here he is, standing between me and the laboratory door. I told him I loved him. I told him I was done. Both things are still true. The laboratory exit is RIGHT THERE. I should keep moving — the others are coming with the copper pot. But Sneekly... he's standing in my path. And those two Slag brothers are with him. I don't know them well but they've been quiet all night. Focus, Clara. The laboratory is through that door. Don't stop. Don't get pulled into another conversation where he changes the subject. You said your piece. Now MOVE.

events.desc: He's standing between me and the laboratory. The man who raised me. The man who might be trying to kill me. And I'm walking right past him with my chin up and my heart hammering, just like the cave. Just like the cave.

Dick Dastardly: Wait — WAIT for me! You are NOT operating that machine without the man who READ the dials! I KNOW the settings! Seven — four — two! Or possibly two — four — seven! The POINT is, I have CRITICAL INTELLIGENCE and you need THREE OPERATORS and there are EXACTLY three of us — Peter, Penelope, and Foxworth! That's not coincidence — that's ARCHITECTURE! Lord Doily DESIGNED this for a team of three and WE ARE THAT TEAM! Now MOVE, Rufus — the Mob can guard the door, Peter can splice the wire, Penelope can pull the lever, and I will set the dials because I am the ONLY person in this house who bothered to LOOK at them! For ONCE in my miserable, scheming, lying, bread-roll-stealing life, I am going to be USEFUL! TO THE LABORATORY!
events.thinking: A surge — electric, bright, fizzing up from my stomach into my throat. They're GOING. They're all going to the laboratory. Penelope's already through the entrance hall. Peter just left. The Mob is here but heading out. They have copper from the pot handle, flux from Marsh's drawer, and a machine that needs three operators. And they need someone who saw the dial settings. They need ME. Not my schemes. Not my lies. My EYES. The thing I actually do well — the thing that was always real, underneath all the performance. The stove is just a stove. Warm cast iron, keeping its secrets. But the machine upstairs — THAT is where this ends. Three operators. Peter's hands. Penelope's determination. And my observations. The dial settings. The wire configuration. The gauge positions. I SAW those things. I REMEMBER them. And for the first time tonight, what I remember isn't a lie I told — it's a truth I noticed. The adventure didn't end in the entrance hall. It's starting again. And Reginald Foxworth — watcher, schemer, youngest of four, reluctant truth-teller, man whose name is written in a guest book among friends — is going to be one of the three operators. FOXWORTH PREVAILS. Not alone this time. But still.

events.desc: Three operators. The machine requires three. And there are three of us going up there — the engineer, the heiress, and the schemer. Except the schemer isn't scheming anymore. He's just... running to catch up. Running toward something instead of away from it. The youngest of four, sprinting down a corridor to be part of something bigger than his own clever plans. The cat trap had strings, counterweights, and a bucket. This has copper wire, dial settings, and three pairs of hands. Same architecture. Same settling in the chest when the pieces fit. But this time — this time — someone will be there to see it work.
