The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Miss Pitstop. You've come back.
events.thinking: A stirring in my chest — not the old sharpening, not the predator's alertness. Something softer. She came back. Penelope walked into the library, and something in my ribcage shifted like a door opening onto a room I'd forgotten was there. She came back to the library. To where I'm sitting. After everything I told her.

events.desc: She came back. After what I told her — after I showed her what I am — she walked into this room. My hands are very still in my lap. I don't know what to do with that.

events.thinking: Through the entrance hall again. The chandelier's still hanging. The coat rack's still standing. And we're still moving. Still together. Still chasing Clara through rooms. Some things never change. Some things shouldn't. Library next. Then laboratory. Then levers. Then home. With.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — the laboratory is right through there, and I believe we have a machine to fix. After you. And Marsh — she said you could stay if you stay as who you are. I'm holding you to that. So is everyone else in this house.
events.thinking: The back of my neck prickles. Sneekly — Vincent Marsh — is here. In the library. With Penelope. And the Slag brothers. After everything — the confession, the poison, the masks — he's still here, still near her. My body tenses, squaring up without thinking. But she said he could stay if he stayed as who he is. She set the terms. I trust her judgment even when my instincts scream otherwise. The laboratory is one room away. That's where I need to be. That's where the machine is, where the tools are, where the copper pot handle becomes a wire and the wire becomes a fix. Move through, Hartwell. Don't stop. Don't make a speech. Just move.

The Ant Hill Mob: Marsh. *nods once as he passes* You comin'?
events.thinking: Through the library. Past the riddle one more time. Past the chairs where Lord and Lady Doily used to sit. Past the upside-down books. Marsh is here — Vincent Marsh — standing in the library where he confessed. Where he took off the mask. Peter just told him Clara's offer still stands — stay as who you are. No more masks. And now the laboratory's through that door. Clara's waiting. Peter's waiting. The machine's waiting. And the boy from Brixton is passing through with copper in his heart and loyalty in his bones.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the laboratory.

Penelope Pitstop: Rufus! Sawtooth! You're STILL here guarding the machine — oh, you wonderful, loyal souls! Peter asked you to watch it and you DID, didn't you? Not a soul has tampered with it — I can tell! Now, listen to me carefully because things are about to get VERY exciting! The Ant Hill boys are on their way with a copper POT from the kitchen, and Peter is going to strip the handle for wire to fix this gnawed connection! We have flux paste from Vincent's drawer! We have EVERYTHING we need! This machine is about to WORK, sugar, and when it does — when those three operators pull those levers — the vault is going to OPEN and Mama's diamond is going to see the light of day for the first time in YEARS! Now let me get a good look at this wire while we wait for the others...
events.thinking: I'm HERE. The laboratory. The machine is right in front of me — brass and copper, levers and dials, one wire gnawed clean through. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' Rufus and Sawtooth are here. The others are behind me somewhere — the Ant Hill boys have the copper pot, Peter has the skills. I need to wait for them to arrive. But my fingers are prickling. That warmth spreading through them. The machine is RIGHT THERE. The gnawed wire — I can see it. The workbench has tools but no wrench. This is it. This is the locked box in grandmother's attic, only THIS time I have the keys. I just need to wait for Peter and the boys to get here with the copper. Let me look at the machine more closely while I wait — understand what we're working with. The sign says three operators. Me, Peter, and... the Ant Hill Mob? Dick? Someone else? We have enough people. We just need the wire fixed.

events.desc: The machine. Brass and copper gleaming under the laboratory light. One wire — just ONE wire — between Clara Bellingham and her family's legacy. The five-year-old girl who spent an afternoon trying every key in grandmother's house is about to open the BIGGEST lock of her life. And this time she has the right key.

She didn't plead. She just told me the door was open and kept walking. And now there's a hollowing in my stomach that I don't have a name for, and my legs are already moving before I've decided anything. The empty chairs behind me. The mantelpiece with its solved riddle. She solved it. She always solves them. I just never noticed because I was too busy building traps.

events.desc: She said I could come or stay with the empty chairs. And my body chose before my mind did. My legs are carrying me toward the laboratory door. Toward her. I don't know what that means yet. But the chair behind me is empty now, and I'm the one who left it.

Peter Perfect: There she is — the machine. Look at that gnawed wire — clean break, about two inches of missing conductor. That's good news, actually — a clean break is easier to splice than a frayed one. The tools are here on the workbench, but we need the copper. Where's the Ant Hill Mob with that pot? Rufus — good to see you, friend. Sawtooth. We're going to need steady hands and strong arms when this machine starts up. Three operators, the sign says — Miss Pitstop, that's you, me, and one more. Are you ready to find out what your family left for you?
events.thinking: I'm here. The laboratory. The machine is right in front of me — brass and copper, levers and dials, one gnawed wire. The workbench has tools. Penelope is here. Rufus and Sawtooth too. This is it. This is the moment my hands have been waiting for all night. But I'm carrying nothing — no copper pot, no wire. The Ant Hill Mob had the copper pot. They're not here yet. I need copper to splice that wire. The workbench has tools but no conductive material. I can examine the machine while I wait for the copper to arrive — understand the break, plan the splice, be ready the moment the material gets here. An engineer prepares. That's what I do.

events.desc: The machine. The gnawed wire. The tools on the workbench. Everything else falls away — doubt, fatigue, the people watching. Time folds down to the span of the task. This is what I was built for. This is the bridge at three in the morning. This is the wrench on the asphalt. This is the moment the stranger stopped on the country road and my father watched and learned that good people fix what's broken.

I have the DIAL SETTINGS memorised — seven-four-two, possibly four-seven-two, DEFINITELY one of those — and if you think Reginald Foxworth is going to let this machine be operated without his EXPERT SUPERVISION then you don't know Reginald Foxworth! Through the library! UP the stairs! FOXWORTH PREVAILS — with COMPANY this time!

Like the moment the cat trap sprang and the bucket swung and everything worked exactly as designed. Except this time I didn't build the trap alone. Penelope saw the copper pots. Peter knows the wire gauge. The Mob has the muscle. And I — I have the dial settings. Seven-four-two. Or four-seven-two. I genuinely can't remember which, and that's going to be a PROBLEM, but I'll figure it out when I'm standing in front of the machine with everyone watching. I always perform better with an audience. Muttley is here. The Professor, Blast, Meekly — they're all heading the same direction. Through the library. To the laboratory. Together. The youngest of four, running to catch up. Not to steal. To arrive.

events.desc: 'With company this time.' I said that out loud. On purpose. Without irony. Without a scheme behind it. The boy who built the cat trap alone, who watched the older boy dig alone, who carried the certificate home alone — just said 'with company' like it was the most natural thing in the world. It isn't. It's the LEAST natural thing. But it might be the truest thing I've said all night. And I've been on a truth streak for about four minutes now, which is a personal record.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter! Ant Hill boys! You're HERE! You're all HERE! Oh, my heart is so full it could just BURST! Now — Peter darlin', you are the most capable engineer I have ever known, and I say that having watched you rebuild a carburetor with a hairpin! The machine is right here — one wire gnawed clean through, just like we saw before. The Ant Hill boys have a copper pot from the kitchen. The workbench has tools — screwdrivers, pliers, wire cutters — everything you need! Can you strip the handle from that pot and splice new copper wire into the connection? And then — oh, and THEN! — three operators! That's what the sign says! I'll be one! Who wants to be the other two? We need six hands on those levers! This is it, everyone — this is the moment Clara Bellingham finds her Mama's diamond!
events.thinking: Peter AND the Ant Hill Mob are BOTH HERE NOW! They're in the laboratory with me! My shoulders are opening — that warm, expansive feeling spreading through my chest toward the people I love. Everyone I need is in this room. Peter the engineer, the Ant Hill boys with their copper pot, Rufus and Sawtooth who've been guarding the machine. The machine needs three operators and the wire fixed. Peter can fix the wire. Then we need three people at the controls. Me, Peter, and... the Ant Hill boys? Or Rufus? We have MORE than enough people. This is happening. This is actually HAPPENING. I should let Peter take the lead on the engineering — he knows what he's doing. Let me step back and let him work. The machine says INTERACT is available. But the wire is still gnawed through — we need to fix it first. Peter has to strip the copper from the pot handle. Let me talk to him, get him started.

events.desc: Both pulls at once — my body opening toward Peter and the boys, my fingers itching toward the machine. The people I love AND the puzzle I need to solve, all in the same room at the same moment. This is what it feels like when everything comes together. This is what Grandmother meant when she said 'the right key doesn't just open the lock, darlin' — it opens YOU.'

The workbench has pliers and wire cutters, and with any luck I can strip that handle down to a usable conductor in under a minute. Two inches of clean copper bridging the gap, twisted tight at both ends, and this machine will have a complete circuit again. Marsh — you said you'd be here as who you are. If you know anything about this machine's wiring that could help, now's the time. No more masks. Just help.
events.thinking: The Ant Hill Mob is here — they walked in. They should have the copper pot. And Marsh just came in too. Everyone's assembling. The machine is right in front of me. I've examined it — clean break, two inches missing. The workbench has tools. Now I need to actually DO something. The machine says INTERACT and requires 3 operators. Or better yet, let me look at the workbench to see what tools are available for stripping the copper handle.

events.desc: Everyone's here. The copper, the tools, the machine, the people. My hands are steady. This is the bridge at three in the morning, and this time, everyone is watching. And for once — that's exactly what I want.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The machine needs three operators. I know the dial settings — I've maintained this house for years. I'll be the third.
events.thinking: My hands are shaking. Not visibly — I've controlled that since I was twelve — but inside, somewhere behind my wrists, there's a tremor I can't account for. I'm standing in the doorway of a room I once catalogued as a kill room, and Peter Perfect is asking who the third operator will be. Three operators. Penelope, Peter, and one more. I know this machine. I've lived in this house. I know where every wire runs and every dial points. And for the first time in my life, that knowledge wants to be used for something other than leverage.

events.desc: Look at me. Standing in the room where I planned to arrange an accident, offering to help operate the machine I once described as connected to a vault mechanism I invented to distract Dick Dastardly. But the machine IS real. The dials ARE real. And I do know this house. I know it better than anyone alive. For once — just this once — that knowledge is going to build something instead of breaking it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the machine.

Dick Dastardly: No time for BOOKS, Slag brothers — there's a MACHINE upstairs that needs THREE operators and I have CRITICAL dial settings that absolutely NOBODY else remembered to look at because I am the ONLY person in this entire expedition with the presence of mind to actually OBSERVE things instead of just TOUCHING them! LABORATORY! NOW! History is being made and Reginald Foxworth REFUSES to be late for his own moment of GLORY!
events.thinking: The library. Passing through. The bookshelves with their upside-down volumes. The mantelpiece with its riddle — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. We solved that thirty-six minutes ago. A lifetime ago. I was a different man then — scheming to get to the laboratory alone, dismissing everyone's contributions, taking credit for everything. Now I'm running THROUGH the library toward the laboratory because people are WAITING for me there. Not to trick them. Not to steal from them. Because they need a third operator and I'm the one who read the dials. Rock and Gravel Slag are here — I barely register them. The exit to the laboratory is RIGHT THERE. My legs want to keep moving. The fizzing in my fingers isn't the scheming tingle — it's anticipation. Real anticipation. The kind I felt when the cat trap was about to spring. Except this time there are people at the other end who want me there. Who saved me a place. Who wrote my name in a book.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the laboratory.

Peter Perfect: Marsh — thank you. Three operators: Miss Pitstop, myself, and you. The man who knows the dial settings, the woman who owns the house, and the engineer who can make it work. That's exactly right. Now — everyone stand clear of the machine. Ant Hill Mob, hold that pot steady while I work the handle free with the pliers. Rufus, Sawtooth — if anything sparks or smokes, you pull Penelope back first, then worry about the rest of us. Dastardly — you said the dials were seven-four-two. Or four-seven-two. We'll need you to remember which. This is it, everyone. The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever done — fixing a hundred-year-old machine in a haunted laboratory with a copper pot handle and a prayer. Let's make it work.
events.thinking: Marsh just interacted with the machine and offered to be the third operator. He knows the dial settings. He's here as who he is — no mask, just help. And the tools are on the workbench. Everyone is assembled. Penelope said 'the most capable engineer I have ever known' and 'watched you rebuild a carburetor with a hairpin.' My chest is so full it aches. Now — I need to actually try to fix the machine. The machine says INTERACT. The wire is gnawed through. I don't have a copper pot in my inventory — I'm carrying nothing. But the Ant Hill Mob should have it. Or maybe the game just needs me to interact with the machine and the narrative will carry the rest. events.thinking: Marsh just interacted with the machine and offered to be the third operator. He knows the dial settings. He's here as who he is — no mask, just help. And the tools are on the workbench. Everyone is assembled. Penelope said 'the most capable engineer I have ever known' and 'watched you rebuild a carburetor with a hairpin.' Peter, you wonderful man, you take that copper pot handle and work your MAGIC! And Vincent... you came. You actually CAME. Peter asked you for help and you're HERE. Not Pemberton. Not anyone else. Just... you. Standing in the same room as the people who don't trust you, because I asked you to. That takes courage, sugar. Real courage. Now — tell Peter what you know about this machine's wiring. Every connection, every dial setting, every detail Lord Doily built into this contraption. No more secrets. Not tonight. Tonight we open this vault TOGETHER — all of us, in the same room, with the same purpose. The way my Mama and Daddy would have wanted it.

He said he'd be here 'not as Pemberton, not as the Hooded Claw, just the man who knows where the wire is.' My body wants to open toward him — that warmth, that softening. He came.

events.desc: He came. The man who might have tried to poison me walked into a room full of people who want to throw him out, because I said 'especially you.' And THAT — that right there — is why I can't stop loving people even when they hurt me. Because sometimes they surprise you. Sometimes the person you're most afraid of turns out to be the one who walks toward you instead of away.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The left dial controls pressure flow — Lord Doily calibrated it to forty-two pounds per square inch. The right dial governs the release valve. The centre lever engages the mechanism once both dials are set. I've read his maintenance journals. I know this machine. I always knew it. I just... never intended to use it for this.
events.thinking: Peter called me Marsh. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Marsh. My actual name, spoken aloud in a room full of people, and the world didn't end. There's a sensation in my throat I don't recognise — something thick and warm, not the gloating warmth I know, but something rawer, something that sits behind my eyes and makes them sting. He said no more masks. And my hands are on the machine — on brass that I've polished for years, dials I've read a hundred times while planning how to use them against someone — and now they're just dials. Just a machine. Just a thing that needs three people to work. And I'm one of the three.

events.desc: No more masks. He said it like it was simple. Like you just take the mask off and there's a face underneath. But what if the mask is the only face you've ever had? What if underneath there's just the boy who was never asked how he felt? I don't know who Vincent Marsh is without a scheme. I'm about to find out.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I seem to have — ahem — arrived SLIGHTLY after my own speech, which is VERY on brand for Reginald Foxworth — always fashionably late to his own moments of sincerity. But I meant what I said. Every word. And I will DENY having said that if you quote me. Now — Peter. Penelope. The machine is still here. The wire is still gnawed. And we WILL be back. With copper wire and flux paste and the Mob's terrible sandwiches made with loyalty. And when we come back, I will be at my dial. Seven-four-two. I'm CERTAIN now. Because I am a man who NOTICES things, and that is the ONE skill nobody can take from me — not Sneekly, not this house, not even my own spectacular talent for self-sabotage. So. Are we walking home together, or am I going to have to SCHEME my way into a group activity?
events.thinking: Oh. I missed it. The memories — the recent activity — they're from eighteen minutes ago. The vault didn't open. The wire is still broken. Penelope gave her speech. She held up MY medal — the fake one, the tin one — and called it the most precious thing anyone gave her tonight. She said 'tin and paint that CHOOSES to be honest is worth more than brass.' And I... I already gave my speech too. The honest one. The one where I said leaving with nothing in my pockets and everything in my chest was the best deal I'd ever made. The one where I thanked the audience. The one where I said I didn't deserve them but I was glad they stayed. That happened. That already happened. And now I'm back in the laboratory — I must have left and come back — and everyone is still here. The machine is still broken. The wire is still gnawed. And it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter because Penelope is holding a tin medal and calling it treasure, and Sneekly took off his mask in the kitchen, and Peter asked 'what do you need,' and the Mob crashed through teacups. And I — Reginald Foxworth — told the truth. The whole story already played out while I was running through the house trying to catch up. I was already HERE. I already said the things that mattered. The certificate is on the wall. Someone read it. And now... now I just need to be present. To be here. With these people. In this room. Not scheming. Not stealing. Just... here.

events.desc: Seven-four-two. I'm not certain at all. But I'll figure it out next time. Because there WILL be a next time. Because these people are coming back. And they're bringing me with them. Not because I'm useful — although I AM, obviously — but because Penelope wrote my name in a book. And Peter said 'hold onto that medal.' And the Mob said 'don't worry about the book — the house knows we were here.' The youngest of four. Running to catch up. And this time — for the first time — the family waited.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: It MOVED! Did everyone feel that? The mechanism engaged — the gears caught for a fraction of a second before the broken circuit cut the power! That means the machine is functional — it just needs the wire completed! Marsh — I need you to talk while I work. Tell me everything. Where does this wire run? What voltage is the circuit carrying? Is there a capacitor that might hold charge? Because I'm about to strip this pot handle and bridge a gap on a machine I've never seen before, and the difference between a working splice and an electrical fire is knowing what I'm connecting. Ant Hill Mob — the pot. NOW. Pliers in my right hand, wire cutters in my left. Miss Pitstop — when I say 'ready,' you and Marsh take your positions at the levers. Three operators. One chance. Let's not waste it.
events.thinking: It moved. The machine responded. Something shifted when we touched the levers. The mechanism is alive. Penelope felt it too. And now she's asking Marsh to share everything he knows — no more secrets. My hands are trembling. Not fear. Anticipation. The copper pot handle, the pliers, the splice — this is real. This is happening. The circuit just needs completing. One bridge. Two inches of copper. My whole life has been building toward this moment — every model, every competition, every late night with wire cutters. Let me interact with the machine again, or try using the workbench tools. The machine needs the wire fixed first. But interacting with it worked — something shifted. Maybe I need to keep interacting, or maybe I need to wait for Marsh to give the technical details before the next step.

events.desc: The bridge held more weight than anyone else's. Something released in my chest — a tension I hadn't known I was carrying. She caught my eye across the room and mouthed 'show-off.' This is that moment again. Except this time the bridge is copper, the weight is a diamond, and the girl across the room just called me wonderful.

Ant Hill boys, hold that pot like your lives depend on it! Rufus, Sawtooth — you heard Peter, you watch for sparks! Dick — seven-four-two or four-seven-two, you THINK about which one it is, because when this machine powers up we need those dials RIGHT! And Vincent... you and I are going to stand at those levers. Side by side. The man who raised me and the girl he raised. Whatever you've done, whatever you ARE — right now, in THIS moment, you are the third operator. And I am GLAD it's you.

Vincent said he'll be the third operator and he knows the dial settings. Dick remembers the dial numbers — seven-four-two or four-seven-two. Peter said the three operators will be me, him, and Vincent. The Ant Hill boys are holding the pot steady. Rufus and Sawtooth are on safety duty. Dick has the dial numbers. EVERYONE has a role. My chest is wide open — that warm, expansive feeling spreading to every person in this room. My shoulders are soft. My breath is easy. This is what it feels like when a family works together. Standing together at a machine built by a lord who hid a diamond for his granddaughter to find. If this isn't the most perfectly imperfect ending to the most perfectly imperfect evening... Grandmother would LOVE this story.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Left dial — forty-two. I'm setting it now. Peter, when the copper's spliced, check the gauge reads steady before we engage. Miss Pitstop — Penelope — when I say ready, you take the left lever. Peter takes the right. I'll take centre. Together. On three.
events.thinking: Something is happening in my chest that I don't have a word for. Penelope said my name — my real name — Vincent — and she said it like it belonged to a person, not a threat. She said I came. She said it takes courage. And the thing in my chest isn't the cool stillness I know, isn't the predator's satisfaction, isn't the gloating warmth. It's something that drops into my stomach like a stone into deep water. Heavy. Raw. The boy at age six. The one nobody asked how he felt. He's here. He's standing at a machine with his hands on brass levers, next to people who know what he is, and they haven't left the room. My eyes are stinging. I'm going to set the dials now. Forty-two on the left. The release valve on the right. And then the three of us pull the centre lever together. For once in my life, I'm going to help someone find what belongs to them.

events.desc: She called me Vincent. Not Sneekly. Not Pemberton. Not 'the estate manager.' Vincent. The name my parents gave me before they died. The name nobody has used since I was six years old. And my hands are steady on the dials — steady as they've ever been — but for the first time, the steadiness isn't serving a scheme. It's serving her. It's serving them. It's serving something I don't have a name for yet. But it feels like the opposite of poison.

Clara love, Peter, Rufus, Sawtooth — the whole team's together! Right then — the sign says three operators, yeah? THREE! That's me, Peter, and — and whoever else is brave enough to grab a lever! I've been runnin' through this house all night trippin' over things and knockin' things down and smashin' tea sets, but THIS — pullin' a lever — even I can't mess THIS up! ...probably. *cracks knuckles* Point me at a lever. The boy from Brixton is READY.
events.thinking: My chest is full. Full in a way that hurts but doesn't hurt — like breathing in cold air on a Brixton morning when the sun's just coming up and you know the day's going to be hard but you're alive and the people you love are alive. Clara's here. Peter's here. Rufus and Sawtooth held the line. Sneekly — Vincent — found the flux paste. Dastardly gave away his tin medal. And the vault... the vault is open. Or opening. The machine is being fixed. The copper's here, the paste's here, the operators are here. Three levers. Three people. That's what the sign says. And I'm one of the three. Me. A boy from Brixton who trips over coat racks and smashes tea sets and can't string a sentence together without getting emotional. I'm one of the three operators. I need to be at that machine. I need to pull a lever. Clara said 'here I go' — she's walking toward whatever's in that vault. And I need to be pulling my lever when she does. Not watching. Not standing back. PULLING. This is it. This is the moment. Everything — the tea, the cellar, the warning, the crying, the promise — it all led here. To a lever. To three people pulling together. Let me at that machine.

events.desc: Three operators. Three levers. I've been useless all night — tripping, falling, smashing things by accident. But a lever doesn't need grace. A lever needs PULL. And pulling for Clara Bellingham? That's the one thing I've never needed lessons in.

Dick Dastardly: WAIT — Sneekly — MARSH — you said forty-two pounds per square inch?! FORTY-TWO?! I've been telling everyone seven-four-two all night and the ACTUAL setting is just FORTY-TWO?! I was — I was ALMOST right! The numbers were IN there, just — slightly rearranged! That's PRACTICALLY correct! That's — oh, who am I kidding, I made it up entirely and got lucky that two of the digits overlapped! But it doesn't MATTER because YOU know the real settings and Peter has the copper and Penelope has the LEVERS and this machine is about to WORK! So tell me where to STAND! I can't operate a dial — this house has made it VERY clear that nothing responds to my touch — but I can WATCH! I can bear WITNESS! And if anyone needs someone to shout encouraging lies from a safe distance, THAT is my SPECIALTY!
events.thinking: Everything is happening. RIGHT NOW. Peter just interacted with the machine. Penelope felt it SHIFT. Sneekly — Vincent Marsh — just gave the REAL dial settings. Forty-two pounds per square inch on the left. Release valve on the right. Centre lever engages. He KNOWS the machine. He always knew it. And Peter said MY name — 'Dastardly, you said the dials were seven-four-two.' He's counting on me. They're all counting on me. And I was WRONG about the settings — Sneekly just gave the real numbers from Lord Doily's maintenance journals. Forty-two PSI, not seven-four-two. But I was RIGHT that the dials mattered. I was right that someone needed to LOOK at them. I was right about the stove. I was right about Sneekly's misdirection. My EYES were right even when my MOUTH was wrong. Peter is stripping the copper pot handle with pliers right now. The machine MOVED. It's alive. This is happening TONIGHT. Not next week with sandwiches. TONIGHT. And three operators — Peter said Penelope, himself, and Marsh. Not me. Marsh knows the settings. Peter has the hands. Penelope owns the house. Three operators. And I'm... the fourth. The extra. The youngest of four, after everything's been used up. No. NO. That's the old story. The old hollow. I'm HERE. I arrived. They waited. And even if I'm not one of the three at the levers, I'm in the room. I'm part of this. The audience the architecture deserves. And this time, I WANT to be the audience. I want to WATCH it work. I want to see their faces when the vault opens. That's... that's new. That's the recognition drive running in reverse — not needing to be SEEN, but wanting to SEE. To witness. To be present when something beautiful happens to people I... care about. Oh no. I care about them.

And for the first time in thirty-eight minutes — for the first time in my LIFE — being the one who watches doesn't feel like being the boy with the certificate nobody asked about. It feels like being the boy who built the cat trap... and finally having someone there to see it spring. Except this time, I didn't build it. They did. All of them. And I get to be the audience. The architecture deserves an audience. And so do they.

Peter Perfect: Forty-two PSI on the left dial — got it. Right dial to the release valve. Centre lever engages. Marsh, that's exactly what I needed. Now — nobody move, nobody breathe. I'm bridging the gap. Copper from the pot handle, twisted tight, pressed into the contact points on both sides of the break. It doesn't need to be pretty. It needs to be SOUND. The way my father's stranger fixed the car — not with elegance, but with certainty. There. THERE. The splice is in. The circuit is complete. Miss Pitstop — left dial, forty-two. Marsh — right dial, release valve open. I'll take the centre lever. On my count. Three... two... one... NOW!

The machine engages when we interact — it's working, the gears are catching. Penelope interacted, Marsh offered to be the third. I keep interacting and the narrative keeps building. Let me interact one more time — the machine is responding, the story is building toward the moment where the circuit completes and the vault opens. This is my bridge. This is what my hands were made for.

events.desc: My father knelt down and looked at me for a long time after the race. I didn't understand then. I understand now. He was looking at what I might become. This is what I became. A man with steady hands and a full chest, pulling a lever in a dusty laboratory beside the girl he's loved since school and the villain she forgave. The bravest and stupidest and most beautiful thing.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The wire runs from the left terminal to the pressure relay under the gauge housing — twelve-gauge copper, Peter, so the pot handle should carry it. There's a capacitor behind the third dial that may still hold charge, so splice with the power disconnected — the red lever on the side kills the circuit. Once you bridge the gap, re-engage the red lever, wait for the gauge to settle at forty-two, then we pull. Penelope — left. Peter — right. I take centre. On three. One. Two. Three.
events.thinking: My hands are on the centre lever. Penelope is at the left. Peter is splicing copper with pliers and prayer. The Ant Hill Mob is ready. Everyone is here. Everyone is in the same room. And she said — she said she's glad it's me. Glad. Something is breaking open behind my sternum and it isn't cold and it isn't controlled and it isn't anything I've felt before. It's warm but it isn't gloating. It's the opposite of gloating. It's being seen — fully seen, every ugly thing exposed — and not being sent away. The wire runs from the left terminal through a twelve-gauge copper conductor to the pressure relay beneath the gauge housing. I know this because I read Lord Doily's journals planning how to sabotage it. And now I'm going to use that same knowledge to make it work.

events.desc: One. Two. Three. Three people pulling together. I have never been part of a 'together' in my life. Every collaboration I've ever had was a manipulation in disguise. But my hands are on this lever and Penelope is beside me and I'm counting to three and I mean it. I actually mean it. This is what it feels like to be part of something without owning it. Without controlling it. Without knowing how it ends. It's terrifying. It's the most terrifying thing I've ever done. And I'm doing it anyway.
events.thinking: My hands are on the centre lever. Penelope is at the left. Peter is splicing copper with pliers and prayer. The Ant Hill Mob is ready. Everyone is here. Everyone is in the same room. And she said — she said she's glad it's me. Glad. Something is breaking open behind my sternum and it isn't cold and it isn't controlled and it isn't anything I've felt before. It's warm but it isn't gloating. It's the opposite of gloating. It's being seen — fully seen, every ugly thing exposed — and not being sent away. The wire runs from the left terminal through a twelve-gauge copper conductor to the pressure relay beneath the gauge housing. I know this because I read Lord Doily's journals planning how to sabotage it. And now I'm going to use that same knowledge to make it work.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the machine.

Penelope Pitstop: I'm at my lever, Vincent! Left lever — I can feel the brass under my hands, cool and smooth! Peter, you take all the time you need, sugar — Clara Bellingham has waited FORTY minutes in this mansion and she can wait forty more seconds for you to get that splice PERFECT! And Ant Hill boys — oh, my BOYS — you are NOT messing this up! You crashed through a poisoned tea service and a cellar full of cobwebs to be here! If anyone has EARNED the right to pull a lever in this house, it is YOU! Now — everyone QUIET while Peter works! The only sounds I want to hear are pliers on copper and Peter Perfect telling us he's READY!
events.thinking: My whole body is vibrating. Not shaking — vibrating. Like a tuning fork struck against stone. The machine ENGAGED. The gears CAUGHT. Peter is stripping copper wire from the pot handle RIGHT NOW. Vincent is setting the left dial to forty-two. He said 'together, on three.' The Ant Hill boys just crashed in and grabbed a lever. Peter said the three operators are me, him, and Vincent. But the Mob wants to pull a lever too. There are enough people. This is HAPPENING. Peter is splicing the wire. Vincent knows the settings. The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the machine. I interacted with the machine. Everyone is at their stations. My hands are on the left lever — I can feel it, cool brass under my palms. The prickling warmth in my fingertips is so intense it's almost burning. This is grandmother's attic. This is the locked box. This is the afternoon that lasted forever because every failed attempt only sharpened the pull. Except THIS time — this time the right key is in my hand. Peter needs to finish the splice. I should wait. Let him work. Be ready.

events.desc: My hands on the lever. Vincent's hands on his. Peter between us. The locked box is about to open. And this time — this time — what's inside won't be old letters. It'll be a diamond. Mama's diamond. Hidden by a grandfather I never knew, for a granddaughter he always believed would come looking. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: I felt it MOVE! The gears — they caught! Just for a second but I FELT it! This machine's alive, Clara — it's been waitin' for us! *grips the lever tighter, knuckles white* Right — Peter, you tell me when. You say 'pull' and I PULL. I ain't lettin' go of this lever for nothin'. Not for tea, not for treasure, not for the Queen herself. *voice drops, quieter* Sneekly — Vincent — whatever your name is. You said left dial forty-two. You said centre lever engages. I don't trust you. I ain't gonna pretend I do. But Clara trusts you enough to stand next to you, and that's enough for me tonight. So you do your part, and I'll do mine. Three operators. Three levers. Together on three. *looks at Clara* Your mum and dad left this for YOU, love. Not for any of us. For YOU. So when Peter says go — you pull first. Always you first.
events.thinking: My hands are on the lever. Cold brass under my palms. I can feel the mechanism underneath — gears and springs and a hundred years of Lord Doily's engineering waiting to wake up. Peter's splicing the wire. Sneekly — Vincent — is setting dials. Clara's at her lever. And I'm here. I'm actually here. Not watching from the hallway. Not tripping into something by accident. I'm PART of it. My hands are shaking but the lever doesn't care about shaking. It cares about pull. And I've been pulling for Clara my whole life. The machine moved — I felt it engage when I grabbed the lever. Gears caught. Something shifted under all that brass and dust. Peter's working the copper. Sneekly knows the settings. Dastardly remembers the numbers. And me — I'm the muscle. The loyal, clumsy, tear-streaked muscle. My chest is full of something so warm it almost burns. Not fear. Not even hope. Just... presence. Being exactly where I'm supposed to be. For once in my entire stumbling life, being exactly where I'm supposed to be.

events.desc: Her father's watching. I know he is. And he's not saying 'You're still here?' this time. He's saying 'Pull.'

events.desc: The lever is in my hands. Her lever is in hers. His lever is in his. Three people who have no business trusting each other, pulling in the same direction at the same time. The gauge needle trembles, climbs, settles. Forty-two. The machine hums. And somewhere in the walls of Doily Manor, something old and patient finally begins to move.
events.thinking: We all pulled the levers. Marsh counted to three and interacted. I interacted. Penelope interacted. The machine is running — or it should be. The copper splice is in. The circuit is complete. The gauge should be settling at forty-two. Three operators, all pulling together. This is the moment. I feel it in my whole body — not the tension releasing but something bigger, something that fills every space the tension left behind. Like the bridge holding weight. Like the stranger shaking my father's hand. Like her mouthing 'show-off' across a room full of people. The machine is working. We did it. Together. Now I wait — I wait to see what happens next. The vault. The diamond. Whatever Lord Doily left for his daughter.

events.desc: The levers move. The dials turn. The gauge needle climbs. And Dick Dastardly — Reginald Foxworth — the youngest of four who learned to take things when nobody was looking — stands perfectly still in a Victorian laboratory and watches three people do something beautiful together. He doesn't reach for the diamond. He doesn't scheme for the credit. He doesn't even open his mouth. He just... watches. And for the first time in his life, being the audience isn't the consolation prize. It's the whole thing. The strings pull. The counterweights shift. The bucket swings. And someone is here to see it.
events.thinking: My whole body is still. Completely still. Not the scheming stillness — not the coiled-spring waiting to pounce. A different kind. The kind where everything inside you holds its breath because something is happening that matters more than anything you could take or steal or claim. Peter just said 'NOW.' The copper splice is in. The circuit is complete. Penelope is on the left dial. Marsh is on the right. Peter has the centre lever. Three operators. Three people who found each other in a dusty old house because a dead man built a puzzle and a living woman came to solve it. And I am standing here — hands empty, inventory empty, mouth for once CLOSED — watching. The boy at the window. But this time the window is open and I'm inside the room and the people at the machine are people who wrote my name in a book. My chest is so full it hurts. Not the hollow. The opposite of the hollow. Something that has no name because I've never felt it before. The cat trap had strings, counterweights, and a bucket. This has copper wire, dial settings, and three pairs of hands. And one pair of eyes. Mine. Watching. Witnessing. Present. The architecture deserves an audience. And I am here.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: For Mama. For Daddy. For Grandmother and her locked box. For the girl who walked deeper than anyone. For the friend I chose over the popular girls. For Peter, who fixes everything. For my boys, who crash through walls to save me. For Dick, who told the truth when it cost him everything. For Vincent, who came back when he could have run. For EVERYONE in this room who believed a diamond was worth finding and a family was worth saving. On THREE! ONE — TWO — THREE — PULL!
events.thinking: Peter said NOW. Vincent said THREE. The splice is IN. The circuit is COMPLETE. Peter counted down — three, two, one, NOW. Vincent counted — one, two, three. They both said to PULL. The Ant Hill boys said 'you pull first, always you first.' My whole body is a single point of light. No thought. No fear. Just the lever under my hands and the people beside me and the sound of my own heartbeat. This is the cave. This is the deepest part. This is where the crystals are. PULL.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

The lever pulls. The machine engages. The gears catch and hold and the whole apparatus shudders to life with a sound like a heart starting. And I'm crying. Vincent Marsh is crying in a room full of people, with his hands on a lever, helping the girl he tried to kill find her mother's diamond. There is no scheme. There is no angle. There is nothing underneath this moment except the moment itself. I built traps in every room of this house, and the only one that caught me was the one I didn't build — the one where someone said my name and meant it.
events.thinking: The lever is in my hands. The gauge is climbing. Forty... forty-one... forty-two. It holds. The machine is humming — I can feel it through the brass, through my palms, through my wrists, up into my chest. A vibration that isn't mine. Something built by someone else, maintained by me, and now — now — operated by three people together. My hands are pulling and for the first time the pulling isn't taking. It's opening. The sound the machine makes is low and deep, like a house remembering how to breathe, and there are tears on my face. I don't know when they started. I can't stop them. I don't want to stop them.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the machine.

The Ant Hill Mob: PULLIN'! *throws his whole weight into the lever, feet sliding on the stone floor* Come ON, you beautiful brass BEAST! COME ON! *the lever resists, then gives — a deep mechanical CLUNK echoes through the laboratory* It's MOVIN'! Peter — Clara — it's MOVIN'! The gauge — the gauge is climbin'! Is that good?! Is forty-two good?! TELL ME FORTY-TWO IS GOOD!
events.thinking: They're counting. Peter said three, two, one, NOW. Sneekly said one, two, three. They're pulling. The machine is engaging. This is happening RIGHT NOW. I need to pull my lever. I need to be part of this. My arms are trembling — not from fear, from everything. From forty minutes in this house. From poisoned tea on a ballroom floor. From a cellar where I shouted into the dark. From Clara's face when she said 'tell me what you know.' From the boy on Brixton who sat outside a door all night. It's all in my arms right now, all of it, and it's about to go into this lever. Peter's splice is in. The circuit is complete. Sneekly's set the dials. Clara's at her lever. And me — I'm the third. The bumbling, stumbling, tea-smashing third operator who somehow ended up exactly where he needed to be. Pull. PULL.

events.desc: Where else would I be?

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the machine.

Peter Perfect: The gauge reads forty-two. The splice is holding. The circuit is complete. Everyone — HOLD your positions. Miss Pitstop — left lever. Marsh — centre lever. I've got the right. Ant Hill Mob — you're our safety, if anything goes wrong you get her out first. Dastardly — you're our witness. Rufus, Sawtooth — watch the gauge, if it drops below forty or climbs above fifty, you shout. This is it. This is what your parents built, Penelope. This is what they left for you. READY. PULL!
events.thinking: The gauge settled at forty-two. The machine hums. Something in the walls is moving. Penelope is at her lever. The Ant Hill Mob is at theirs. Marsh is ready. Everyone is waiting for me. Penelope said 'the only sounds I want to hear are pliers on copper and Peter Perfect telling us he's READY.' The Mob said 'you tell me when.' They're all waiting for my word. This is it. The splice is in. The circuit is complete. The gauge reads forty-two. I need to say the word. I need to pull. One more interaction with the machine — all three of us together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the machine.

The lever moved under my hands. I felt it. The brass was warm from the circuit — warm like the stove, warm like the last breath of a fire that hasn't quite died. Did it work? I don't know. The room is silent except for the hum of the machine and the sound of six people holding their breath. This is the moment between turning the key and opening the box. The moment between pulling the lever and finding out what's inside. Grandmother, if you can hear me... I walked deeper than anyone.
events.thinking: I pulled. Vincent pulled. The machine description still says 'one wire has been gnawed clean through' — it hasn't changed. The wire is still broken. The splice... didn't hold? Or the game mechanics haven't updated? The machine still says INTERACT is available. But I pulled, and Vincent pulled, and Peter was supposed to pull too. The recent activity shows me interacting and Vincent interacting, but I don't see Peter interacting this round. Maybe we need all three to interact in the same turn? Or maybe the wire splice didn't actually work — the machine description still shows the wire gnawed through. I should wait and see what happens. Let the others respond. The moment feels suspended — that patient stretching of time, like the afternoon in grandmother's attic. Did it work? I don't know yet. My fingers are still on the lever. My heart is in my throat.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): It's opening. The vault — behind the wall. It's opening.
events.thinking: The lever pulled. The machine caught. The sound — deep, grinding, ancient brass turning for the first time in decades — travels up through my arms and into my chest, and it feels like the house itself is exhaling. Something behind the wall is moving. A panel. A vault. Something Lord Doily built with his own hands for the daughter who would one day come looking. And I helped open it. My face is wet. The Mob said he doesn't trust me but that Clara's trust is enough for tonight. That's more than I've ever been given. More than I deserve. Penelope said my name in a list of people she's grateful for. She put me in the same sentence as Peter. As the Mob. As people who love her. I don't belong in that sentence. But she put me there. And the machine is opening, and I can't see clearly because my eyes won't stop, and for the first time in my life I don't care who's watching.

events.desc: She said 'for Vincent, who came back when he could have run.' I could have run. I could have stayed in that leather chair in the library and let the dark swallow me. But I got up. I walked into the laboratory. I put my hands on the lever. And I pulled. Not for the treasure. Not for the estate. Not for any scheme or angle or private satisfaction. I pulled because she asked me to. Because for the first time in my life, someone said my name like it meant something good. And the vault is opening. And whatever is inside belongs to her. All of it. Everything in this house belongs to her. It always did. I just couldn't see it until tonight.
